Contract and transfer talks and the board's job-security judgment have no matching mechanics in the taxonomy (proposed as negotiation and board-confidence). The series began as Championship Manager in 1992 and was relaunched under this name with FM 2005 in 2004.

mechanics.note: Fixtures are simulated event by event from each player's attributes, condition, and morale and the manager's tactics and touchline instructions, shown in 2D or 3D.
Players' attributes are shown only as well as the club's scouts know them; scout knowledge accumulates per region and is shown as a percentage from FM 2018.
Players and staff are signed through transfers, loans, and contracts with wages, bonuses, and agents.
Player attributes develop through training schedules, match experience, and coaching quality up to individual potential.
Players peak and decline with age, retire, and are replaced by yearly youth intakes.
Generated youth players enter the database each season alongside the real ones.
Personality and hidden attributes such as professionalism affect development and reactions.
Squad hierarchy, cohesion, and player opinions of the manager are tracked from FM 2018.
Team talks and private conversations with players praise, criticize, or promise, changing morale.
Press conferences pose questions with answer options that change morale and media relations.
Club and manager reputation set who will sign; board and fan confidence decide whether the manager is sacked.
Club finances cover wage and transfer budgets, with taxes added in FM 2013.
Data analysts and statistics screens report player and team performance.
Transfer fees are negotiated with selling clubs and contracts with players and their agents over wages, length, bonuses, and clauses, and talks can break down.
The board sets season expectations and, with fan confidence, judges results against them; falling confidence brings warnings and then sacking.

games.name: Football Manager
games.summary: A football club management series in which the player sets tactics, training, transfers, and finances while a match engine simulates games from the attributes of players drawn from a researched database of real footballers.

games.core_loop: paint residential, road, patrol, and forestry zones -> villagers build homes inside them -> assign workers and production chains -> trade with neighbors and pay taxes -> advance Labor, Clergy, or Kingdom estates -> assemble monuments from parts
games.design_notes: Foundation separates intent from layout: the player paints areas for homes, roads, patrols, and forestry, and housing appears inside them without a grid. Major buildings are not fixed footprints but assemblies of parts, so a monument's function and capacity follow from the modules chosen. Progress runs along three estates, which can be specialized or combined.

mechanics.note: A painting tool marks areas for homes, roads, patrol routes, and forest extraction; homes fill residential zones organically.
Buildings and monuments are assembled from individual parts whose choice sets function and appearance.
Buildings are placed and rotated without a grid.
Trade with neighboring villages.
Progress unlocks through tiers guided by a book, along Labor, Clergy, or Kingdom estates.

games.name: Foundation
games.summary: A gridless medieval city builder in which painted zones grow homes organically, monuments are assembled from modular parts, and the village advances along Labor, Clergy, or Kingdom estates.

games.core_loop: carry sand, water, and lava with the Breath -> reshape terrain to open paths -> send villagers to totems to found villages -> vegetation spreads across soil -> divert tsunamis, floods, fires, and eruptions -> unlock powers and reach the portal
games.design_notes: Designed by Eric Chahi and presented as a spiritual successor to Populous, it replaces discrete land raising with a continuous material simulation: water flows and erodes, lava cools into solid rock, and soil lets vegetation spread once a village is founded, fast enough that islands can be reshaped within minutes. The cursor, called the Breath, carries matter and changes appearance to match it, replacing a conventional HUD. Disasters are announced shortly before they hit, so each map alternates between building and short preparation windows.

mechanics.note: The Breath picks up and deposits sand, water, and lava in real time to build land bridges, dams, and barriers.
Water flows over the terrain, erodes it, and floods low ground and villages; tsunamis sweep across islands.
Lava cools into solid rock, water erodes soil, fire burns vegetation, and powers can jellify or remove water.
Powers such as jellifying water are granted by completing objectives; magical stones protect against water and fire.
Tsunamis and eruptions, announced shortly before by shamans.
Wildfires spread through vegetation and can be extinguished.
Villagers are sent to totems to found villages.
Each map is cleared by settling every totem to open a portal.

games.name: From Dust
games.summary: A god game in which the player carries sand, water, and lava across islands whose material simulation erodes, floods, and hardens terrain, protecting a tribe as it founds villages at totems.

games.core_loop: keep the coal generator fueled -> heat districts and insulate buildings as temperatures fall -> assign workers to gather coal, wood, steel, and food -> sign laws that trade welfare for productivity -> balance hope and discontent -> survive the storm
games.design_notes: The city is radial around one generator that heats a circular area, so layout is a function of heat range and fuel, and a coal shortage or overload can end the run. The Book of Laws sequences laws so that early compromises such as child labor or extended shifts open harsher later options, and Order or Faith paths lead toward totalitarian rule, turning policy into moral pressure tracked by hope and discontent. Building heat versus falling outside temperature has no exact taxonomy mechanic (see run proposal); 11 bit studios cites This War of Mine as the origin of its aim for meaningful entertainment, now applied to a whole society.

mechanics.note: The Book of Laws offers adaptation laws such as child labor, extended shifts, and prosthetics, plus Order or Faith paths whose later laws are harsher.
Hope and Discontent meters respond to laws, events, and conditions; hope too low or discontent too high for too long ends the game in revolt.
Temperature falls on a schedule toward the Great Storm, which the main scenario must be survived through.
The generator heats a circular area whose range and level the player raises; buildings outside heat need insulation or heaters.
Coal, wood, steel, and food come from thumpers, sawmills, mines, and hunters.
Workers, engineers, and children fill different job types.
Citizens work daylight shifts; emergency shifts extend hours at a cost.
Scouts explore the frozen wasteland map for survivors and resources, the only way to grow the workforce.
Individual decisions, such as how to handle an injured child, offer choices that shift hope and discontent.
Workshops research heat, extraction, and automaton technologies.

games.name: Frostpunk
games.summary: A survival city builder in which the leader of the last city around a coal generator must keep falling temperatures at bay while signing laws that trade citizens' welfare against productivity under hope and discontent meters.

games.core_loop: build food, housing, extraction, and industry districts -> heat districts from the generator -> factions propose ideas and laws -> negotiate council votes -> faction tension rises or falls -> survive whiteouts and found colonies
games.design_notes: Frostpunk 2 moves from single buildings to districts and from one leader's decree to a council: 100 delegates, each tied to a faction, vote on every proposed law, with 51 votes for most laws and two thirds for laws that expand the Steward's power. Negotiated promises that are not kept anger factions, and tension between factions can escalate into murder and civil war, so the developer describes social survival as more important than environmental threats. Population is handled as district-level aggregates rather than individual workers.

mechanics.note: Districts for food, housing, extraction, and industry are placed on frost; buildings inside add functions.
A council of 100 faction delegates votes on each proposed law; 51 votes pass most laws, two thirds pass laws that grant the Steward more power.
Factions with conflicting ideals react to adopted ideas and laws; radicals grow within factions.
Laws are proposed, negotiated with promises, and enacted when the council approves.
Faction tension can escalate into murder and civil war.
An Idea Tree of faction-proposed ideas to solve problems.
Whiteouts are severe storms prepared for with fuel reserves.
Food, coal, oil, and steam come from frostland deposits and districts.
Utopia Builder mode sets an objective and optional challenges that fail the run if missed.

games.name: Frostpunk 2
games.summary: The sequel to Frostpunk, in which the Steward builds whole districts on the frost and must pass laws through a council of 100 faction delegates while faction tension can escalate into civil war.

games.core_loop: jump to a beacon -> resolve an event or fight -> allocate reactor power and direct crew under fire -> repair breaches, fires, and systems -> spend scrap on upgrades -> stay ahead of the rebel fleet to the flagship
games.design_notes: FTL models a ship as rooms with oxygen levels, doors, systems, and crew positions; hits create breaches, fires, and system damage that crew must walk to and repair, so a combat is a spatial triage problem as well as a damage race. The reactor's power bars are the central budget shared by shields, engines, weapons, oxygen, and medbay, and the player shifts them during paused combat. Manual reactor power allocation and per-system damage that removes capacity until repaired have no dedicated taxonomy ids (power-grid is the closest fit); both are recorded as new-mechanic proposals.

mechanics.note: Each room has an oxygen level that equalizes through open doors, drains through hull breaches and opened airlocks, and is refilled by the oxygen system; crew suffocate in empty rooms.
Hits and events start fires that spread between rooms, damage systems and crew, and burn oxygen; crew extinguish them or the player vents the room.
Each jump advances the rebel fleet across the sector map; overtaken beacons yield hard fights and no reward, forcing a trade between exploration and speed.
Losing the ship or all crew ends the run and deletes the save; dead crew members are gone.
Crew gain skill in piloting, engines, shields, weapons, repair, and combat through use, improving station bonuses.
Eight species have fixed traits such as faster repair, fire immunity, or extra combat damage.
The player moves crew between rooms to man stations, repair systems and breaches, fight boarders, and put out fires; crew act on their own only within the room they occupy.
Each sector is a generated map of about twenty beacons with stores, hazards, and events.
Beacon events offer text choices, with extra options unlocked by specific crew, systems, or equipment, and some quests chain across beacons.
Beacon contents are unknown until visited unless revealed by upgrades such as long-range scanners.
Pause is the main tactical tool for issuing orders mid-combat.

Reactor power bars are assigned among shields, engines, weapons, oxygen, medbay, and other systems, usually while paused in combat; each system caps how many bars it accepts, and damage removes usable bars until crew repair it.
Each weapon shot rolls against the target's evasion, shield layers absorb hits, and hits damage the room and the system inside it.

Hits damage the system in the struck room (shields, weapons, engines, oxygen, piloting), removing its usable power bars until crew repair it, and the player targets enemy rooms to disable specific systems.

games.name: FTL: Faster Than Light
games.summary: A roguelite starship sim where the player allocates reactor power and directs crew through room-level oxygen, fire, breach, and system-damage simulation while fleeing a rebel fleet across eight sectors.

games.core_loop: choose topic, genre, platform, and audience -> allocate focus across three development stages -> design and technology points accumulate with bugs -> reviews score the game -> sales and fans -> research, engines, and hires
games.design_notes: Game Dev Tycoon reduces game making to a configuration problem scored by a hidden market model: each topic and genre pair, each genre and audience pair, and each platform carry fit weights, and each genre favors a particular split of effort across the development stages. Review scores compare the new game against the player's previous best, so the bar rises as the studio improves. A fictional timeline of parody consoles enters and leaves the market from the 1980s onward, which forces platform bets (date-driven availability is proposed as dated-tech-timeline). Greenheart released its own cracked copy in which piracy bankrupts the in-game studio.

mechanics.note: Each game is a topic, genre, platform, and audience pick plus focus sliders across three development stages; reviews score its fit and quality against the studio's best.
After moving out of the garage, the player hires designers and programmers with design, technology, and speed stats and assigns them to development tasks.
Research points unlock new topics, genres, and engine features; custom engines bundle researched features and raise technology output.
Staff gain experience and can be sent to training to raise stats or specialize.
Salaries, office upkeep, and development costs drain cash between releases; running out ends the game.
Bigger offices, R&D and hardware labs, and larger projects unlock as money and fans grow.
A fan count from past releases scales sales of future games.
Industry news, console launches, and studio events fire on a fixed historical timeline.
Mods are written in JavaScript through the gdt-modAPI and shared on the Steam Workshop.
Marketing campaigns bought during development raise a game's hype, which boosts its launch sales.
Fictional consoles launch and retire on a fixed in-game calendar from the 1980s onward, so platform choice is a bet on a console's remaining market life.

games.name: Game Dev Tycoon
games.summary: A game-studio business sim where the player picks topic, genre, and platform for each game, splits development effort across design and technology focus areas, and lives or dies by review scores across the history of the industry.

games.core_loop: place live cells on the grid -> apply birth on 3 and survival on 2 or 3 neighbors to every cell at once -> pattern stabilizes, oscillates, dies, or emits gliders -> observe -> edit the seed and rerun
games.design_notes: Conway's rule is the minimal case of emergence from local update: each cell's next state depends only on how many of its eight neighbors are alive, all cells update simultaneously, and the only input is the initial pattern. The rule is Turing complete, so whether an arbitrary pattern stops changing is undecidable, and decades of discovery (Gosper's period-30 glider gun of November 1970, the R-pentomino's 1,103-generation run) came from players searching seeds. Simulators such as Golly add Hashlife for large time jumps and scripting for rule variants. A general cellular-automaton rule is not yet a mechanic in the taxonomy (proposal cellular-automaton-rule); adjacency-scoring is the nearest existing id.

mechanics.note: A dead cell with exactly 3 live neighbors is born, a live cell with 2 or 3 survives, and all others die; the neighbor count is the whole update rule.
The player's only act is toggling cells on the grid to set the seed before running generations.
Implementations store patterns as files and libraries that can be stamped into a grid and shared.
Simulators step one generation at a time or run fast, and Hashlife in Golly jumps far ahead in time.

games.name: Conway's Game of Life
games.summary: A zero-player cellular automaton on an infinite square grid in which each cell lives or dies by the B3/S23 neighbor-count rule, producing gliders, oscillators, and universal computation from a seeded pattern.

games.core_loop: spawn props, ragdolls, and NPCs -> move and freeze them with the physics gun -> weld, rope, and motor them with the tool gun -> test the contraption or scene -> share it, or play a community game mode built on the same tools
games.design_notes: Garry's Mod exposes the Source engine's rigid-body physics directly: the physics gun grabs, rotates, and freezes any prop, and the tool gun adds welds, ropes, axles, motors, thrusters, and other constraints, so contraptions are built from rigid bodies and joints. Its larger contribution is that the whole game is scriptable in Lua and servers download addons on join, so most play happens inside player-made game modes such as Trouble in Terrorist Town, Prop Hunt, and DarkRP, and the add-on Wiremod adds sensors and logic gates. Garry's Mod began as a free Half-Life 2 mod in 2004 and became a paid Steam product in 2006.

mechanics.note: Every spawned prop and ragdoll is a physics object; the physics gun lifts, rotates, and freezes them, and collisions, gravity, and buoyancy follow the Source physics engine.
The tool gun joins props with welds, ropes, axles, sliders, winches, motors, wheels, and thrusters, turning loose props into vehicles and machines.
A Lua API covers entities, weapons, HUD, and game rules; servers send addons to clients on join, and community game modes (TTT, Prop Hunt, DarkRP) became the main way people play.
The player is a first-person character who walks, flies with noclip, and wields the physics and tool guns.
Steam Workshop distributes saves, dupes, maps, and addons.
The Wiremod addon adds wires, sensors, gates, and programmable chips to contraptions.
The duplicator tool and Advanced Duplicator addon copy and paste multi-prop contraptions.

games.name: Garry's Mod
games.summary: A Source engine physics sandbox in which players spawn props, ragdolls, and NPCs, join them with welds and constraints, and script whole new multiplayer game modes in Lua.

aliases: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior

claims.text: In the two-day end-to-end run, relationship network density rose from 0.167 to 0.74 and five agents attended the Valentine's Day party.

games.core_loop: agents perceive nearby events and objects -> observations enter the memory stream -> retrieve memories by recency, importance, and relevance -> plan the day and react -> converse and act -> reflections summarize memories -> plans and relationships change
games.design_notes: Park and colleagues replace authored behavior trees with a loop of language-model calls on gpt-3.5-turbo. Every observation is stored as text with timestamps; retrieval scores memories by recency (decay 0.995 per game hour), importance (rated 1-10 by the model when stored), and embedding relevance, each normalized and weighted equally. When the summed importance of recent events passes 150 (two or three times a day) the agent writes reflections, and plans are decomposed from a day outline into hour and 5-15 minute chunks. Seeding one agent with the intent to host a Valentine's Day party led to 13 of 25 agents hearing about it and five attending over two game days, at a cost of thousands of dollars in API credits. The open-source release steps the town 10 game seconds per step.

mechanics.note: Each agent's memory stream stores observations, plans, and reflections as text; retrieval ranks them by recency (0.995 decay per game hour), model-rated importance (1-10), and embedding relevance, and reflections fire when summed importance exceeds 150.
Each morning the model drafts a day plan of about five to eight broad chunks, decomposed into hour-long and then 5-15 minute actions that agents revise when they react to events.

Information spreads only through agent conversations; over two game days awareness of a mayoral candidacy rose from 1 to 8 agents and of a party from 1 to 13, with 6 of 453 awareness answers hallucinated.
Plans, dialogue, importance ratings, and reflections are all generated by gpt-3.5-turbo calls at runtime.
Users address agents in natural language as a persona or as the agent's inner voice, and can rewrite the status of objects in natural language.
Researchers interview agents and read their memory streams to evaluate believability.
Agents form acquaintances through conversation; network density rose from 0.167 to 0.74 over two game days.

games.name: Generative Agents (Smallville)
games.summary: A research sandbox in which 25 language-model agents in a Sims-like town keep natural-language memory streams, reflect, and plan their days, producing unscripted information spread and social coordination.

games.core_loop: dig into and build up voxel terrain -> assign settlers to roles and jobs -> settlers meet needs and mood shifts -> seasons change food supply -> raiders and beasts attack the walls -> research, build higher, and take in newcomers
games.design_notes: It follows the RimWorld pattern of named settlers with traits, perks, skills, needs, and moods, and is widely compared to RimWorld and Dwarf Fortress. Its distinctive layer is a fully three-dimensional voxel map: the player can dig cellars and caverns, raise multi-storey stone and timber forts, and reshape earth and water, so defensive geometry and storage depth are design problems in three dimensions. Early access ran from June 2021 to the 1.0 release in March 2026.

mechanics.note: A 3D terrain toolset digs out or fills voxel earth and water on a randomly generated multi-level map, so cellars, moats, and caverns are carved from the ground.
Settlements stack multi-storey buildings above ground and cellars and caverns below, connected by stairs and ladders.
Settlers track needs such as hunger, sleep, clothing preferences, and religion, and meeting them keeps settlers content.
Repeated bandit raids and animal attacks are met with walls, traps, and settlers equipped and commanded in battle.
Settlers in poor conditions become dissatisfied and may leave the settlement.
Backgrounds, traits, and perks set at settler creation.
Skills such as Animal Handling improve through use, including hunting and combat.
Settlers are assigned to roles that fit their skills.
Built structures need support, and unsupported sections collapse.
Workshops, chapels, libraries, and bedrooms are furnished and decorated rooms.
Seasonal changes govern food production and storage.
Food keeps longer in cool storage such as cellars.
Research unlocks medieval technology.

games.name: Going Medieval
games.summary: A colony sim set after a plague in which settlers with traits, needs, and moods dig into and build up a multi-level voxel terrain to survive seasons and raids.

games.core_loop: pass license tests -> enter championships -> win credits and prize cars -> buy cars and performance parts -> tune the car -> enter higher-class events
games.design_notes: Simulation mode made car ownership and driving skill the progression: driver's licenses earned through timed tests gate events, and credits from championships buy cars, parts, and tuning. Reviewers singled out the handling model and the tuning freedom, and criticized license tests that could be harder than the races they unlocked. It was the first game designed for the DualShock's analog control and rumble, and IGN called it the grandfather of modern console racing sims.

mechanics.note: Each of 140 cars has its own handling that responds to parts and tuning; reviewers rated it above any earlier racing game.
Simulation mode requires earning driver's licenses through timed tests before entering higher events.
Credits and prize cars build a garage drawn from 140 production cars.
The first game designed for DualShock analog control and rumble; license tests and races grade precise braking and cornering.
Credits buy performance parts and tuning that tailor a car to the player's driving style.
Championships award trophies, credits, and prize cars.

games.name: Gran Turismo
games.summary: A PlayStation racing game that paired a tuned handling model and 140 production cars with license tests, prize credits, and parts tuning in a Simulation mode career.

claims.text: GT Sophy 2.0 was added to Gran Turismo 7 as a rival in Quick Race across nine tracks and 340 cars in November 2023.
In 2025 GT Sophy 2.1 extended to Custom Race with tuning, tire, and fuel options.

games.core_loop: buy or tune a car -> race against AI or players -> earn credits -> expand the collection -> harder events
games.design_notes: Included because it is the clearest shipped case of a learned opponent in a simulation game. GT Sophy, trained with model-free deep reinforcement learning on parallel simulator instances, became selectable as a permanent rival in 2023 and was extended to custom races in 2025, one content update at a time.

mechanics.note: Tire, suspension, aerodynamics, and drivetrain models per car; tuning parts and settings change handling.
Racing lines, braking points, and throttle control on wheel or pad decide results; GT Sophy is trained to the same physics.

games.name: Gran Turismo 7
games.summary: A console racing simulator that combines a detailed vehicle dynamics model and car collection with GT Sophy, a deep reinforcement learning opponent added as a permanent rival in 2023.

claims.text: Hamurabi derives from The Sumerian Game (1964) by Mabel Addis and William McKay; Dyment wrote the FOCAL version after learning of it, and David Ahl expanded it in BASIC.

games.core_loop: read the steward's yearly report -> trade grain for land at a random price -> allocate grain to food and seed -> harvest, rats, arrivals, and plague resolve -> next year
games.design_notes: Three stocks (people, acres, bushels of grain) and three yearly allocations make the whole game one stock-and-flow puzzle: grain is food, seed, and the currency for land at once, so every bushel has competing uses. Randomness enters only through harvest yield, rat losses, a land price of 17 to 26 bushels per acre, arrivals, and a plague that halves the population, so the player manages expected value under variance. Dyment wrote it in FOCAL for the PDP-8 from a description of The Sumerian Game (1964); David Ahl's BASIC version spread it as a type-in listing and seeded Kingdom, Dukedom, and Santa Paravia en Fiumaccio.

mechanics.note: Ten rounds, each one year: a status report, then three typed decisions (acres to buy or sell, bushels to feed, acres to plant) before the year resolves.
People must be fed grain each year; if at least 45 percent starve in one round the game ends early.
Planted acres consume seed grain and return a random yield per acre at year end; each person can farm only a set amount of land, so labor caps planting.
Each year carries a chance of plague that halves the population.
Rats eat a random amount of stored grain each year, a loss on holding stock.
Each round opens with a steward's report of births, deaths, harvest, rat losses, and land price.

games.name: Hamurabi
games.summary: A ten-turn text game in which the player, as the Babylonian king Hammurabi, splits a grain stock between feeding people, planting acres, and buying land while harvests, rats, and plague vary at random.

games.core_loop: start a shift -> scan the ship -> vent pressure and make power, fuel, coolant, and reactor systems safe -> cut parts free -> grapple them to the correct receptacle -> salvage value pays down debt -> buy tool upgrades
games.design_notes: Each ship is a physics assembly of joined parts and typed hazards rather than an authored level: cutting into a pressurized room causes explosive decompression, cutting live electrical wires or coolant pipes can explode, and a reactor removed from its casing must be delivered before it melts down. The order of disassembly is the puzzle, and the taxonomy lacks a mechanic for it (proposed as salvage-deconstruction). Oxygen and thruster fuel act as survival stocks, and shifts are timed except in Open Shift mode.

mechanics.note: Ships are assemblies of separable parts; freed parts keep mass and momentum in zero gravity and are pulled or flung with the tether grapple toward the right receptacle.
The laser cutter severs structure at cut points and joints; cutting live electrical wires or coolant pipes can cause an explosion, so where and in what order to cut is the core decision.

Systems must be made safe in order: pressurized rooms vented, electrical and coolant lines avoided, and reactors delivered before they melt down; mistakes produce the physical result rather than an error.
Rooms hold atmosphere, and an uncontrolled decompression flushes the player and loose objects out of the ship.
Oxygen and thruster fuel deplete during a shift and must be replenished.
Shifts are timed; Open Shift mode removes the limit.
The character owes $1.2 billion to Lynx Corporation, and salvage earnings pay it down.

games.name: Hardspace: Shipbreaker
games.summary: A zero-gravity salvage sim in which the player cuts derelict ships apart with a laser cutter and grapple, manages decompression and volatile systems, and sorts salvage to pay down a large debt.

games.core_loop: clear land and plant seasonal crops -> water daily and tend livestock -> ship produce for money -> buy animals, seeds, and upgrades -> build relationships and attend festivals -> marry and raise a child before the father's evaluation
games.design_notes: Director Yasuhiro Wada started the project with three principles (no fighting, uniqueness, and tactile real-time action), and a team of 8 to 10 people at Pack-In-Soft scaled it back to fit SNES limits. The farm rules are forgiving but daily: unwatered crops stop growing instead of dying, chickens need only feed but can die if left outside, and cows must be fed, talked to, brushed, and milked or they sicken. Play is bounded by a two-and-a-half-year term that ends with the father's evaluation of the farm and family, which makes marriage and a child goals alongside crops and livestock.

mechanics.note: Crops need water every day; a missed day halts growth rather than killing the plant, and each crop belongs to a season.
Chickens must be fed and kept indoors or they can die; cows need daily feed, talking, brushing, and milking, and fall sick or die if neglected.
A four-season calendar sets which crops can grow and when festivals occur.
A stamina pool limits work each day; power berries found around the map raise it.
Five eligible women can be courted; marriage and a child count toward the final evaluation.
Villagers' and candidates' affection rises with talking and gifts.
After two and a half years the father evaluates the farm, family, and relationships.
After dark only the bar stays open, so shopping and visits must fit daylight.

games.name: Harvest Moon
games.summary: An early farming sim for the Super Famicom in which the player has two and a half years to restore an inherited farm through daily crop watering, livestock care, and courting one of five eligible women.

games.core_loop: pick national focuses and spend political power -> assign civilian factories to construction and military factories to equipment -> design and train divisions -> draw fronts and battle plans -> divisions fight on supply, terrain, and weather -> capitulate rivals or hold
games.design_notes: HOI4 separates the industrial war from the field war: civilian factories build capacity and military factories turn resources into equipment, so divisions fight only as well as stockpiles and supply allow. Battle plans let the player act at army-group scale and leave division movement to the AI. National focus trees are the authored branching layer that steers countries toward historical or alternate paths, while battles resolve from unit statistics (proposal stat-combat-resolution).

mechanics.note: Division templates combine battalions (infantry, tanks, cavalry, motorized, mechanized) and support companies, and the mix sets combat statistics and equipment needs; tank, ship, and plane designers added by DLC apply the same idea to equipment.

Supply hubs connect to the capital by railway, with hub capacity set by railway level and limited by the weakest link; supply falls off per province from the hub, and divisions at 35% supply or less suffer attrition and combat penalties.
The player draws front lines and offensive arrows for armies under generals, and the AI moves divisions to carry out the battle plan; divisions can also be ordered directly.

Research runs in parallel slots, and each country has a national focus tree in which one focus at a time is completed for bonuses such as extra factories or events; at launch only Germany, the UK, the USSR, and the US had unique trees.
Military factories turn strategic resources into equipment on production lines, dockyards build ships, and civilian factories build infrastructure and handle trade.
Countries join factions and guarantee others; world tension from 0 to 100 gates what democracies can do.
Mobilization, conscription, and trade laws and ministers are bought with political power.
Ideology popularity among democratic, communist, fascist, and non-aligned groups shifts the government and can end in civil war.
Sea and air regions have weather that affects operations.
Political power accrues over time and is spent on laws such as mobilization, conscription, and trade, on ministers, and on decisions.
States are core or non-core, armies occupy enemy states during war, and peace conferences transfer ownership.
When a country capitulates, winners take turns spending peace conference points on annexation, puppets, and other demands.
Divisions fight in hourly combat rounds comparing attacks against defense or breakthrough, draining organization and strength under terrain, weather, and supply modifiers.

games.name: Hearts of Iron IV
games.summary: A World War II grand strategy game starting in 1936 or 1939 in which the player builds factories, turns resources into equipment, designs divisions, follows a national focus tree, and directs fronts and battle plans across land, sea, and air.

games.core_loop: take email jobs for cash -> buy a rundown house -> clean, demolish, paint, tile, furnish -> buyers evaluate fit and bid -> sell at a profit -> buy bigger properties
games.design_notes: Each property is judged by a small set of buyer profiles with requirements such as cleanliness or a family room, and their auction bids reward matching a profile rather than maximizing generic quality. Labor is performed with coverage tools (paint roller, mop, window cleaner, plaster tool) that show visible progress, and tool use earns experience spent on faster tools. Email jobs paid by size and quality supply the capital for the first purchase.

mechanics.note: Paint roller, mop, window cleaner, and plaster tool apply coverage to walls, floors, and windows with visible progress; tiling and demolition use the same direct tool loop.
Neighbors send email jobs (cleaning, painting, installing heaters, showers, or air conditioners, furnishing) whose pay depends on job size and quality.
Each property has potential buyers with different needs, such as cleanliness or a family room, who bid according to how well the renovated house suits them.
Sales are resolved by buyers bidding at auction.
Furniture, doors, windows, and wallpaper from a catalog are placed freely.
Using tools earns experience that is spent on tool upgrades that speed up work.

games.name: House Flipper
games.summary: A first-person renovation sim in which the player cleans, paints, demolishes, and furnishes rundown houses, then sells them to buyers whose bids depend on how well the house fits their needs.

games.core_loop: start with water, fire, wind, and earth -> drag two elements together -> look up the pair in the shared database -> if new, a language model names the result and picks an emoji -> result is cached for everyone -> combine the new element further
games.design_notes: At runtime the model is consulted only on a cache miss: the game checks a global database for the unordered pair, and if no result exists, Llama 2 (later Llama 3.1) generates a short element name, capped at twenty tokens, plus an emoji; the result is stored so the same pair returns the same element to every player. The recipe graph is therefore written collectively and lazily by players and the model, and a First Discovery label marks players who triggered a generation. Pairwise combination discovery is not yet a mechanic in the taxonomy (proposal combination-discovery). It is a boundary case: there is no simulated system beyond the generated recipe graph.

mechanics.note: On a cache miss, a Llama model generates the combined element's name (up to twenty tokens) and emoji; the result is written to a shared database so later requests are deterministic.
Players accumulate discovered elements and First Discoveries, which mark elements no player had made before.
Every action combines two owned elements; on a cache miss a Llama model names the result, the result is stored so every player gets the same answer, and new results earn a First Discovery label.

games.name: Infinite Craft
games.summary: A browser crafting game in which combining any two elements yields a new element whose name and emoji a language model generates on first request and a shared database then fixes for all players.

games.core_loop: create Zois and build homes -> Zois act on needs and personality -> player directs actions or prompts thoughts -> jobs, relationships, rumors, and illness move through the city -> edit the city and generate new items -> share on Canvas
games.design_notes: inZOI casts the player as an intern at AR Company who manages a city of virtual people and its karma system. It pairs a Sims-style needs model (hunger, hygiene, bathroom, fun, social, energy, sleep, recognition) with city-scale free will that the developers say produces rumors, trends, and disease, plus optional direct control of a Zoi or vehicle. Generative models sit mainly in the creation layer: text prompts generate patterns and images for clothing and furniture, 2D images convert to 3D props, and an on-device small language model lets typed prompts steer a Zoi's thoughts and actions. City-wide progression of unplayed Zois is the offscreen-life-progression mechanic; karma has no mechanic id.

mechanics.note: Eight needs (hunger, hygiene, bathroom, fun, social, energy, sleep, recognition) decay and drive Zois' free-will choices.
Text prompts generate patterns and images for outfits, props, and furniture; 2D images become 3D in-game objects; uploaded video becomes character motion.
An on-device small language model lets the player type prompts that influence a Zoi's thoughts and actions.
Autonomous interactions generate rumors that spread among Zois.
The developers list disease, alongside rumors and trends, among the outcomes that spread through Zois' autonomous interactions.
Personality and life experience shape each Zoi's actions and relationships.
Careers include active jobs played on site.
Zois age and die.
Build mode places walls, roofs, stairs, fences, and gates; city edit changes streets, properties, and weather.
Canvas is the in-game platform for sharing characters, homes, and stories.
Players can switch from point-and-click orders to direct control of a Zoi or a vehicle.

City-wide free will keeps Zois across the city living autonomously while the player directs one household, producing rumors, trends, and disease; the fidelity of the update for distant Zois is not documented.

games.name: inZOI
games.summary: A Krafton life sim in early access since March 2025 in which the player oversees autonomous Zois with eight needs in dense cities, with optional on-device language model prompts and generative tools for patterns and objects.

games.core_loop: join a scheduled official race -> qualify and race on laser-scanned tracks -> incidents and results update Safety Rating and iRating -> license promotion opens higher series -> buy cars and tracks for the next season
games.design_notes: iRacing grew from Papyrus's NASCAR Racing 2003 Season code with a new tire model and LIDAR-scanned cars and tracks. Its distinctive layer is the competitive structure: a no-fault Safety Rating from incident points per corner gates license classes (Rookie, D, C, B, A, with Pro reserved for esports), an Elo-style iRating sorts drivers into sessions and divisions, and 13-week seasons rotate tracks weekly. Skill rating and matchmaking have no mechanic in the taxonomy (proposed as skill-rating-matchmaking).

mechanics.note: A new tire model replaced the one in the NASCAR Racing 2003 Season code iRacing was built from, and cars and tracks are LIDAR-scanned.
Races are against human drivers on the publisher's servers, so results depend on the driver's braking, throttle, and line precision.
Licenses progress Rookie, D, C, B, A, with Pro for esports qualifiers; promotion depends on a per-discipline Safety Rating computed from incident points and corners per incident.
Cars take damage and tires wear over a race, which pit stops address.

games.name: iRacing
games.summary: A subscription online racing sim with laser-scanned cars and tracks in which drivers race scheduled official series and advance through license classes gated by a no-fault Safety Rating, while an Elo-style iRating sorts fields.

games.core_loop: choose a building from the inventory -> preview its point value from neighbors and terrain -> place it permanently -> score thresholds restock and offer a choice of two packs -> fill the gauge to move to a new island
games.design_notes: Islanders reduces the city builder to its placement rule: no resources, traffic, citizens, or research, only point values from proximity to compatible structures and natural features and penalties for incompatible ones. Placements are permanent, so each choice consumes space, and the run ends when buildings or space run out before the next threshold. It is included as a boundary case for adjacency scoring, since nothing in the world evolves without the player.

mechanics.note: Each building scores points from nearby compatible buildings and natural features and loses points for incompatible ones; the preview shows the total before placing.
Buildings are placed freely on the island and cannot be removed or built over.
Reaching a point threshold restocks the inventory and offers a choice of two building packs; filling the gauge unlocks a new island.
Each island is procedurally generated.

games.name: Islanders
games.summary: A minimalist placement puzzle in which every building scores points from compatible and incompatible neighbors on a procedural island, and score thresholds unlock new building packs and new islands.

games.core_loop: job bot gives a task -> grab and manipulate objects with tracked hands -> appliances and props react physically -> task completes -> next task until the job ends
games.design_notes: Included as a boundary case for its interaction model: nearly every object within reach is a physics object that can be picked up, thrown, or combined, and fixed appliances expose buttons, levers, and dials. Tasks are authored and loose, so variety comes from physical improvisation such as choosing pizza toppings or tire styles rather than from a modeled occupation. After all four jobs, modifiers alter the physics.

mechanics.note: Most objects within reach can be picked up and manipulated with tracked controllers, fixed appliances expose buttons, levers, and dials, and post-game modifiers change the physics.
The player's tracked head and hands are the avatar at a room-scale workstation; a smaller human mode adjusts reach.
Four jobs (Office Worker, Gourmet Chef, Store Clerk, Auto Mechanic) each run a sequence of task requests from job bots.

games.name: Job Simulator
games.summary: A room-scale VR comedy set in a museum run by robots, where the player performs parodied office, kitchen, store, and garage tasks by grabbing and manipulating physics objects.

games.core_loop: send expeditions for fossils -> sequence DNA and modify genomes -> incubate dinosaurs -> meet feeding and social needs in enclosures -> guests spend while divisions offer contracts -> contain storms and breakouts -> raise the star rating to unlock islands
games.design_notes: Jurassic World Evolution turns a park sim into a containment problem. Each species has feeding, social, and territory needs; unmet needs lower comfort, and low-comfort dinosaurs fight, break fences, and escape to attack guests. Three divisions (Science, Security, Entertainment) offer contracts and track reputation, and letting one fall triggers sabotage such as a power shutdown or disease outbreak, which turns faction standing into a source of hazards. Genome modification changes a species' stats, aggression, and appearance, and the player can drive ranger and ACU vehicles to sedate, medicate, transport, and repair. Dinosaurs do not breed in this game; adding modern-species DNA to a genome trades stats against aggression, a rule the taxonomy lacks (proposed as genome-modification).

mechanics.note: Dinosaurs have feeding and social needs plus grassland, forest, and population limits; unmet needs lower comfort, and carnivores hunt herbivores and attack fences and guests.
Science, Security, and Entertainment divisions track reputation; low standing in one triggers sabotage such as power cuts or disease outbreaks.
Each division offers contracts with requirements and rewards that unlock research and story missions.
Storms damage fences and power and set dinosaurs loose; breakouts must be contained before guests are hurt.
Facilities need power from plants through substations; outages open electric fences.
Guests want viewing of varied species plus shopping, food, and amenities, and flee or die during breakouts.
Fossil DNA completion unlocks species, and the research center unlocks buildings, upgrades, and genome modifications.
The Expedition Center sends teams to global dig sites that yield fossils for DNA and for sale.
The player can drive ranger jeeps and ACU helicopters to resupply feeders, repair fences, and tranquilize dinosaurs.
Diseases spread among dinosaurs and must be treated by rangers or ACU.
Island star ratings unlock the next island in the Las Cinco Muertes archipelago.

games.name: Jurassic World Evolution
games.summary: A dinosaur park management game in which the player excavates fossils for DNA, breeds and modifies dinosaurs, and keeps them contained through storms, sabotage, and breakouts while balancing three division contracts.

games.core_loop: wander the world with a squad -> fight, trade, steal, or get captured -> injuries and hunger reduce stats while skills train from use -> recruit and found an outpost -> factions react and world states shift
games.design_notes: There is no main character: every recruit and NPC is a potential equal, with no hero units given stronger stats, and the world and shops do not scale to the player, so early characters are weaker than most people they meet. Progress comes from use-based skill gain, which makes losing fights a form of training. Deaths of notable faction leaders change world states, such as towns taken over by a new faction. Chris Hunt developed it alone until 2013, and it was one of the first games in Steam Early Access.

mechanics.note: Each limb has its own health; limbs can be damaged or severed and replaced with prosthetic or robotic limbs, and blood loss and injuries reduce stats and movement while squadmates carry the wounded.
Skills rise from the actions they describe, such as stealing for thievery and fighting for combat, with stats and appearance changing as characters grow.
The player commands any squad member directly in real time with pause; no character is privileged, and the squad acts together.
Many factions and species with relations to each other; the player can aid or oppose them, and deaths of notable figures shift world states.
Player standing with each faction changes access and hostility.
Starvation reduces character stats.
Outposts are built and upgraded into fortified havens or businesses.
Squad members keep job lists for base work and production.
Zone soil types and terrain affect outpost farming.
Research unlocks equipment and technologies.
Outposts must be defended against attackers.
Some weather, such as acid rain, harms characters.
Fights resolve from character combat skills, weapon stats, and armor, with damage applied to individual limbs.

games.name: Kenshi
games.summary: A squad-based open-world RPG with no hero character, where any recruit can starve, lose limbs, train skills by doing, be enslaved, or found an outpost among reactive factions.

games.core_loop: assemble a craft from parts -> launch and stage through the atmosphere -> plan maneuver nodes and burn for orbit or transfer -> land, dock, or crash -> return science, funds, and reputation -> unlock parts and design a more ambitious craft
games.design_notes: Stock orbits use a patched-conic approximation: a vessel is attracted by one body at a time and switches at sphere-of-influence boundaries, so there are no Lagrange points, but coasting vessels can be propagated on rails during time warp. Vessels are trees of parts joined by joints of limited strength, so mass distribution, thrust placement, and staging order decide whether a design flies, wobbles, or tears apart. Failure (stranded or dead Kerbals, debris) is a source of player stories rather than a hard stop, and Career mode layers funds, reputation, and contracts on top of the physics sandbox.

mechanics.note: Patched conics: a vessel orbits one body at a time and switches at sphere-of-influence boundaries; maneuver nodes preview delta-v and the resulting trajectory; planets ride fixed rails rather than n-body motion.

Craft are built in the Vehicle Assembly Building or Spaceplane Hangar from pods, tanks, engines, decouplers, wings, and science parts; part order sets the staging sequence, and each stage's mass, thrust, and fuel set its delta-v.
Each part is a rigid body joined to its parent with a joint of limited strength; excess force breaks joints, so tall stacks wobble and hard impacts shed parts or kill Kerbals.
Drag, lift, and control surfaces govern ascent profiles, spaceplanes, and aerobraking.
Atmospheric entry heats parts; heat shields absorb it and overheated parts are destroyed.
Science from experiments unlocks part nodes in Science and Career modes.
Career contracts pay for objectives such as reaching an orbit or testing a part, with deadlines and penalties.
Career funds pay for parts, fuel, crew, and facility upgrades; contract payouts are the income.
Career reputation rises with completed contracts and falls with failures and Kerbal deaths.
Manual ascents, landings, and docking reward piloting skill; SAS assists attitude hold.
Kerbals die in crashes and EVA accidents; Career mode costs reputation for deaths, and a difficulty option sets whether lost crews respawn.
Drills mine ore on planets and asteroids that converters turn into fuel, a system adopted from mods.
On-rails time warp skips long coasts; physics warp speeds powered flight at reduced stability.
C# plugins and part configs extend the game; mods such as Real Solar System and Principia replace the planetary system and the orbital model.
Parts are destroyed individually by impact or overheating, removing their engines, tanks, or controls from the craft.

games.name: Kerbal Space Program
games.summary: A space flight sim where the player assembles rockets from parts and flies them under patched-conic orbital physics and atmospheric aerodynamics through a scaled-down planetary system.

games.core_loop: place a keep and houses on an island -> peasants farm, cut wood, and quarry -> store food for the annual winter -> tax peasants to pay workers and unlock buildings -> stack castle blocks into walls and towers -> repel vikings, dragons, and ogres
games.design_notes: Kingdoms and Castles pairs a light town economy with a block-built castle: walls and towers form from how blocks are stacked, and taller archer towers reach farther, so defense is shaped geometry rather than a building menu. Each villager and resource is individually simulated, and an annual winter that destroys crops sets a regular survival check. Raiders kidnap peasants and burn buildings, and a dragon targets granaries, linking defense to food security.

mechanics.note: Vikings kidnap peasants, steal resources, and burn the town; dragons torch granaries; ogres attack; soldiers and archer towers defend.
An annual winter destroys crops, so food must be stored in granaries to prevent starvation.
Castle blocks stack into walls and towers whose shape forms automatically; taller archer towers have longer range.
Peasant taxes pay workers and unlock buildings.
Happiness from layout, churches, taverns, and festivals.
Happiness and housing attract new residents.
Lightning starts fires.
Plagues spread and must be healed.
Foresters cut and replant trees.
Diplomats make trade agreements, alliances, and wars with AI kingdoms.

games.name: Kingdoms and Castles
games.summary: A medieval town builder in which peasants farm and stockpile for an annual winter while the player stacks castle blocks into walls and towers to defend against vikings, dragons, and ogres.

games.core_loop: read the weather report -> choose glasses to make, signs to buy, and price per glass -> demand resolves into sales -> profit or a storm loss -> reinvest the next day
games.design_notes: Lemonade Stand reduces a business to three daily inputs (glasses made, advertising signs, price per glass) and one exogenous variable, the weather (sunny, cloudy, or hot and dry), which shifts demand. Shocks are random: thunderstorms on cloudy days wipe out the day's investment, and street closures or wind that blows signs away also occur. Up to 30 players can each run an independent stand under the same weather. Signs are an early case of advertising spend used as a demand lever; the taxonomy has no mechanic for marketing spend, so the run proposes advertising-awareness.

mechanics.note: Aggregate customers buy more at lower prices and with more advertising signs; sales are capped by the glasses made that day.
Each day is sunny, cloudy, or hot and dry, and the weather sets the demand level the price and sign choices act on.
Twelve rounds of one day each: the player makes decisions, the day resolves, and an earnings report follows.
Cash on hand limits how many glasses and signs can be bought each day.
Thunderstorms void a day's profits; street closures and blown-away signs also occur.
The weather for the day is shown before the player commits to production.
Advertising signs bought each day raise that day's demand alongside price and weather, with no carryover between days.

games.name: Lemonade Stand
games.summary: A 1973 educational business sim in which the player runs a lemonade stand for 12 days, setting glasses made, advertising signs, and price against a daily weather report.

games.core_loop: watch the resident's routine -> hunger, thirst, and mood drift -> deliver food, water, gifts, or pats -> type polite requests -> mood decides whether he complies -> repeat across sessions
games.design_notes: Rich Gold conceived the game and David Crane built it at Activision; the documentation presents the little people as real beings living inside the computer, with the player as their caretaker. Each disk's serial number seeded the resident's name (from 256), shirt color, personality, and behavior, so every copy hosted a different person. There is no win condition: the resident cooks, reads, plays piano, phones, and types letters about his feelings on a day of about six real-time hours, and his mood gates whether typed requests are obeyed. The cassette C64 version dropped memory, letters, and card games, which shows which systems carried the sense of a persistent person.

mechanics.note: Keyboard commands deliver food (CTRL+F), add water to his tank (CTRL+W), deliver dog food, pat him, or give records and books; a resident left unfed turns green and sick until he eats.
Hunger and thirst build between deliveries; unmet needs lower his mood and eventually make him visibly sick.
The disk serial number seeds his name from a pool of 256, his shirt color, personality, and behavior parameters.
He runs a routine of cooking, watching television, reading the newspaper, playing records, and dancing on a compressed day of about six real-time hours.
Typed requests such as 'Please play piano' are matched against a keyword vocabulary; politeness helps, and a sad or sick resident may refuse.
Seeded personality and mood parameters change which activities he prefers, how often he invites the player to cards or writes letters, and how readily he obeys.

games.name: Little Computer People
games.summary: A 1985 home-computer life sim in which one procedurally seeded little person lives in a cross-section of a three-story house, follows a daily routine, and depends on the player for food, water, and attention.

games.core_loop: draw curved roads and burgage plots -> families move in and staff workplaces -> fields, backyard extensions, and production chains feed the market -> taxes, tithes, and trade fund a retinue -> defend against bandits and rival lords
games.design_notes: Manor Lords drops the zoning grid: the player draws plots against freely curved roads, the game divides them into burgage plots, and households extend them with backyard gardens, chickens, or goats, so housing is also production. Fields carry soil fertility per crop that rotation preserves, and hunting depends on animal populations that overexpansion drives away. Militia levies come from the town's own families, so each battle death is a lost worker; the game remained in early access as of August 2026.

mechanics.note: Residential plots drawn along roads are divided into burgage plots that families build on and extend with backyard production.
Fields depend on soil fertility per crop; rotation and fallow maintain yields, and overuse exhausts soil.
Roads curve freely and plots and buildings take their shape from them.
Spring rains and winter snow change work and needs.
Raw materials pass through workshops into goods, weapons, and armor.
Households need basic goods and luxuries; shortfalls lower satisfaction.
Approval responds to supply, taxes, and tithes.
Six tax types, a yearly King's tax, and tithes on villagers.
Hunting grounds depend on animal populations; overexpansion drives deer away and deforests land.
Real-time battles with fatigue, weather, and equipment; retinue, mercenaries, and militia drawn from townspeople.
Bandit raids threaten the town and loot stores.
Surpluses sold to traveling merchants; imports and exports balanced through trade.

games.name: Manor Lords
games.summary: An early-access medieval city builder in which families settle gridless burgage plots along curved roads, fields depend on soil fertility and crop rotation, and the lord fields retinue and militia in real-time battles.

games.core_loop: pick aircraft, airport, and time -> preflight and start up -> take off into live or set weather -> navigate and hand-fly or use autopilot -> approach and land -> pick the next flight
games.design_notes: The world is data rather than authored terrain: Bing Maps imagery refreshed every 28 days, Blackshark.ai photogrammetry, and Azure AI 3D generation streamed from more than two petabytes, with Meteoblue weather and real air traffic fed in live. The flight model simulates over 1,000 control surfaces and wind over terrain, and a legacy model is kept as an option. No mechanic in the taxonomy covers simulation state driven by real-world data feeds (proposed as real-world-data-feeds).

mechanics.note: The physics engine computes forces over more than 1,000 control surfaces and models wind flowing over terrain; a legacy flight model option remains.
Meteoblue live global weather sets clouds, wind, and precipitation in real time, and wind interacts with the terrain model.
An in-game marketplace and third-party aircraft and airports extend the sim.

The whole Earth is built from Bing Maps imagery updated every 28 days and AI-generated 3D content streamed from more than two petabytes in the cloud, while Meteoblue live weather and live air traffic feed the sim at runtime.

games.name: Microsoft Flight Simulator (2020)
games.summary: A flight sim that streams a photorealistic model of the whole Earth built from map and photogrammetry data and flies aircraft through live weather with a surface-level aerodynamic model.

games.core_loop: choose a career job -> walk around the aircraft for preflight -> start systems -> fly the mission profile (firefighting, rescue, cargo hook, airline) -> earn experience, reputation, and certifications -> unlock specializations
games.design_notes: Career mode turns the 2020 sandbox into a progression game: aerial firefighting, search and rescue, crop dusting, helicopter cargo hook, outsize cargo in the Airbus Beluga, arctic cargo in the A400M, and airline flights are gated by certifications and specializations earned through experience and reputation. Aircraft physics and systems (electrical, fuel, pneumatic, hydraulic) were revised, and stones, gravel, and grass are modeled in 3D and affect wheels. The launch showed the cost of a streamed world: an overwhelmed database cache caused long loads and missing content.

mechanics.note: Aircraft physics were revised, and ground contact models 3D stones, gravel, and grass that affect wheels during takeoff, landing, and taxi.
Career jobs include aerial firefighting, search and rescue, crop dusting, helicopter cargo hook, Beluga outsize cargo, A400M arctic cargo, and airline passenger flights.
Starting from an airport the player chooses, experience earns certifications and specializations that unlock job types.
Career reputation accumulates alongside experience.
A walk-around preflight handles covers, doors, and service items, and revised electrical, fuel, pneumatic, and hydraulic systems gate start-up.
The pilot walks around the aircraft on foot during preflight.
The streamed whole-Earth world of the 2020 game continues, and the launch showed the dependence when an overwhelmed database cache caused long loads and missing content.

games.name: Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024
games.summary: The successor to Microsoft Flight Simulator (2020) that adds a career mode of certified aviation jobs, walk-around preflight, revised aircraft systems, and modeled ground surfaces to the streamed whole-Earth flight sim.

claims.text: Mindustry was created for the April 2017 itch.io Metal Monstrosity game jam and came to Steam in 2019 (version 3, store date 2019-09-26).
Coverage compares Mindustry to Factorio, and its README describes it as an automation tower defense RTS; the influenced_by edge reflects that widely noted lineage rather than a developer statement.

games.core_loop: drill ore -> belt items to the core and factories -> build and supply turrets -> survive scheduled enemy waves -> research new blocks with core resources -> capture sectors and launch resources between them
games.design_notes: Mindustry began as a 2017 itch.io jam game and fuses Factorio-style belt logistics with tower defense: turrets consume belted ammunition, power, and coolant, so the factory's layout is the defense, and survival maps send progressively stronger waves at the core on a timer. Version 6 (2020) added RTS units built in factories and upgraded through reconstructors, and Mindustry Logic, an assembly-like language that runs on processor blocks, reads sensors and memory cells, and can bind and command units. The campaign spans Serpulo and Erekir with 35 hand-made maps and 250+ procedural sectors whose production continues while the player is elsewhere and is moved between sectors by launch pads. The game is GPL-3.0 and free from the author while also sold on Steam, so community servers, plugins, and mods are unrestricted.

mechanics.note: Conveyors, junctions, routers, sorters, overflow gates, and bridges move items from drills to the core, factories, and turret ammo inputs.
Smelters, presses, kilns, separators, and mixers turn copper, lead, sand, coal, titanium, and thorium into graphite, silicon, plastanium, and surge alloy.
Enemy waves spawn on a schedule and path toward the core; about 18 Serpulo and 10 Erekir turret types consume ammo items, liquids, or power, backed by walls, menders, and shield projectors.
Survival maps send progressively stronger waves with tougher unit types and bosses as wave numbers rise; the cited sources do not tie wave strength to the player's own wealth.
Mechanical, pneumatic, laser, and airblast drills mine ore tiles at speeds set by drill tier and ore hardness, with optional water boosting.

Micro, logic, and hyper processors run Mindustry Logic, an assembly-like language with one operation per instruction that reads sensors and memory cells, controls linked buildings and turrets, and binds units with ubind to command them.
A visible timer counts down to the next wave, and wave timing can be changed in custom game rules.
Over 250 technology blocks are researched by spending core resources along a tree that also gates campaign sectors.
Combustion, steam, solar, thorium, and impact generators feed node-linked grids with batteries; turrets, shields, and factories draw power.
Conduits carry water, slag, oil, and cryofluid; optional coolant and lubricant raise turret and factory rates.
Since version 7 units can be selected and commanded RTS-style, while others follow default AI or logic control.
Schematics save layouts as shareable text and are traded on Steam Workshop.
Campaign sectors set win conditions such as surviving a number of waves or destroying enemy cores on attack maps.
The GPL-3.0 source allows unrestricted mods, and community servers run plugins for custom maps and game modes.
Optional coolant and lubricant fed to turrets and factories raise their rates, and water boosts drill speed.

games.name: Mindustry
games.summary: An open-source automation tower defense game in which the player belts ore into factories that supply turrets, units, and the core against enemy waves while capturing campaign sectors on two planets, with an assembly-like logic language for controlling blocks and units.

games.core_loop: explore a generated world -> mine blocks and gather resources -> craft tools, armor, and workstations -> build shelter before night mobs spawn -> farm, breed, and trade -> dig deeper or travel to the Nether and End for rarer materials
games.design_notes: The world is an effectively infinite grid of one-meter blocks generated from a seed with biomes, caves, and ore distributions, and every block can be removed or placed, so terrain is both resource and building material. Survival pressure is light (hunger, health, light-level mob spawning on a 20-minute day cycle) and leaves room for self-set goals. Redstone gives the block world wires, power sources, repeaters, and pistons, which players use to build farms, logic gates, and working computers. The game began as a public alpha in May 2009 and reached 1.0 in November 2011.

mechanics.note: Worlds generate from a seed into biomes, caves, ravines, villages, and ore layers that vary by depth; terrain extends effectively without limit in horizontal directions.
A 2x2 inventory grid and a 3x3 crafting table turn blocks and items into tools, armor, and blocks from shaped recipes; furnaces, anvils, and enchanting tables extend the recipe set.
Blocks are mined by hand or with tools whose tier (wood, stone, iron, diamond, netherite) sets mining speed and which ores drop items.
Survival mode has health and hunger bars; food restores hunger, high hunger regenerates health, and starvation, falls, drowning, and mobs deal damage.
A 20-minute real-time day; hostile mobs spawn in low light, so night and caves are dangerous, and beds skip the night.
Any block can be placed on the voxel grid, so building has no fixed footprint.
Redstone dust carries power from levers, buttons, and sensors through repeaters and comparators to pistons, doors, and dispensers.
Crops grow in stages on farmland, faster with water nearby and light.
Passive mobs breed when fed their preferred food and yield food, wool, and leather.
Water and lava flow a limited number of blocks out from source blocks; where they meet they form cobblestone, stone, or obsidian.
Fire spreads to nearby flammable blocks such as wood and wool and burns them away.
Material tiers gate progression: iron tools mine diamonds, diamond tools mine obsidian, and Nether materials gate brewing and the End.
Java Edition mods (Forge, Fabric) and Bedrock add-ons, datapacks, and server plugins are widely used.
Public multiplayer servers and Realms host worlds that persist for many players.
On death in survival the player's inventory and some experience drop at the death site and despawn after a few minutes if not recovered.

games.name: Minecraft
games.summary: A procedurally generated voxel sandbox where players mine blocks, craft tools, survive hostile night mobs and hunger, farm and trade, and build circuits from redstone.

games.core_loop: new stations appear -> draw or reroute lines -> trains carry shape-matched passengers -> weekly grant of new assets -> demand outgrows capacity -> a station overcrowds and the run ends
games.design_notes: Mini Metro abstracts a metro network into station shapes, passengers drawn as the shape of the station type they want to reach, and a scarce inventory of lines, locomotives, tunnels, and bridges. New stations keep appearing while supply arrives only as a weekly grant, so the player keeps redrawing a network that is always under capacity. Failure is local and visible: a station over its limit (typically six passengers) for long enough ends the run. Modes vary the rules: Extreme fixes lines once placed, Endless removes overcrowding, and Creative is a sandbox.

mechanics.note: The player draws colored lines between stations and assigns trains that load and unload automatically; ridership is the score.
Passengers wait at stations with limited capacity, typically six; interchanges raise capacity and loading speed, and a station overcrowded too long ends the game.
Passengers ride to any station of their target shape, transferring between lines when needed.
Each in-game week grants extra rolling stock and a choice of assets such as tunnels, bridges, new lines, or interchanges.
Time can be paused to reroute lines or move trains.

games.name: Mini Metro
games.summary: A minimalist subway-design game where the player draws and redraws lines between shape-coded stations under a weekly ration of trains and tunnels until a station overcrowds.

games.core_loop: design and build car parts -> hire drivers, designers, and mechanics -> set race weekend strategy -> race simulates with tyre, fuel, and weather calls -> results earn money and standing -> develop next season's car
games.design_notes: Motorsport Manager splits the job into a between-races engineering game and a live race game. Between races the player commissions car parts and chooses which go into next season's car, trading performance against development time. During races the simulation runs in real time with pause, and the player decides tyre compounds, pit timing, and whether to gamble on a fast pit stop or stay on slicks as dynamic weather changes. Drivers have personality types that cause team drama and respond to tough love or support. A simpler mobile game of the same name was released on iOS in 2014; this entry covers the 2016 PC game.

mechanics.note: Races are simulated in real time from driver attributes, car part performance, tyres, fuel, and weather, with the player intervening on strategy.
Car parts are designed and built over time, rated on performance, and chosen for next season's car, which sets pace at pre-season testing.
Drivers, team managers, mechanics, and designers are hired; skilled mechanics shorten pit stops.
Dynamic weather during sessions forces calls such as switching to intermediates or staying on slicks.
Drivers have distinct personality types that cause team drama and respond differently to tough love or support.
Tyres wear over a stint and car parts lose condition, so strategy balances pace against wear.
Prize money and sponsor income fund salaries and part development.
Races run in real time with pause and speed controls.
Driver and staff contracts are negotiated over wages, length, and bonuses, and candidates can reject offers and end talks.
The chairman sets objectives each season, and missing them lowers the chairman's confidence until the player is fired.

games.name: Motorsport Manager
games.summary: A racing team management game in which the player designs car parts across seasons, hires drivers and staff, and makes live strategy calls on tyres, pit stops, and weather while races are simulated.

games.core_loop: claim a land grant -> buy and outfit M.U.L.E.s and walk them to plots -> production with shortages and random events -> real-time auctions set prices -> buy or sell -> next round
games.design_notes: M.U.L.E. couples its four resources: food sets how long a player's development turn lasts, energy shortages stop plots from producing, and smithore supply sets M.U.L.E. prices and whether the store can manufacture more. Prices are set in real-time auctions in which buyers and sellers move avatars toward a price, so withholding goods and private deals between players are legitimate tactics. Danielle Bunten built catch-up rules into the systems: tied bids go to the player in the losing position, favorable events rarely hit the leader and harmful ones never hit last place, and land auctions were replaced by free grants because they compounded the leader's advantage. The taxonomy has no mechanic for systematic catch-up rules (proposed as catch-up-balancing).

mechanics.note: Each round resources trade in a real-time auction: sellers and buyers walk avatars toward a price line, trades fire when they meet, and ties go to the trailing player.
Store prices respond to supply: refusing to sell raises a resource's price in later rounds, and smithore scarcity raises the price of new M.U.L.E.s.
A M.U.L.E. outfitted for food, energy, smithore, or crystite harvests its plot each round; output depends on terrain and the plot's development.
Rounds run in fixed phases: land grant, timed development, production, then auctions for each resource.
Plots grouped with others producing the same resource get a production bonus.
Each player needs food and energy each round; low food shortens the next development turn and low energy stops some plots.
The store turns smithore into new M.U.L.E.s; with no smithore it cannot build more.
Sunspots, pirate raids, meteorites, and runaway M.U.L.E.s, targeted away from the last-place player.
Computer opponents fill empty seats and compete for plots and auction trades.
Players walk a colonist through town to buy and outfit M.U.L.E.s and lead them to plots under a turn timer.

games.name: M.U.L.E.
games.summary: A four-player economic strategy game on a colony planet where players outfit M.U.L.E. robots to produce food, energy, smithore, and crystite and trade them in real-time auctions.

games.core_loop: care for the dog by touch -> teach tricks by voice -> walk the dog and find items -> enter disc, agility, and obedience trials -> earn prize money and trainer points -> buy supplies and unlock new breeds
games.design_notes: Nintendogs was built to show off DS hardware: the touchscreen handles petting, grooming, and washing, and the microphone handles the dog's name and trick commands. Care runs on the DS clock, so hunger, thirst, and coat condition worsen with elapsed time, but dogs cannot die, breed, or age, which makes neglect a recoverable setback rather than a fail state. Trials have five classes from Beginner to Championship, and placing third or better promotes a dog. Bark Mode lets nearby players' dogs meet and exchange presents.

mechanics.note: Touch petting, brushing, and washing plus food and water bowls maintain hunger, thirst, and coat condition; walks, balls, discs, and toys add play.
When the dog strikes a pose such as sit, the player records a spoken command; repeating the pairing teaches the trick, and the dog later responds to the voice cue.
The microphone recognizes the dog's name and trick words by matching the player's voice against recorded samples.
Hunger, thirst, and dirtiness worsen with real elapsed time.
Care state advances with the DS internal clock and calendar.
Trial prize money and trainer points unlock new breeds and supplies.
Bark Mode lets nearby DS owners meet each other's dogs and exchange presents.

games.name: Nintendogs
games.summary: A Nintendo DS puppy sim in which the player pets, washes, feeds, and walks up to three dogs, teaches them tricks with recorded voice commands, and enters disc, agility, and obedience trials.

games.core_loop: descend into a procedurally generated biome -> fight enemies with wands that also reshape the pixel world -> survive fire, liquids, and gases set off by fighting -> buy or find spells and rebuild wands at the Holy Mountain -> descend again or die and restart
games.design_notes: Noita's Falling Everything engine simulates each pixel as a material with state (solid, powder, liquid, gas) and reaction rules, and solid bodies are Box2D rigid bodies that break into pixels when damaged. Because spells, enemies, and the player all act on that layer, combat routinely sets off chain events such as burning oil, steam explosions, flooding, and collapsing ceilings, and these kill the player as often as enemies do. Wand building composes spells with modifiers into programs with cast order and mana limits, and runs are permadeath.

mechanics.note: Every pixel of terrain is a material that falls, flows, or rises by local rules, so digging, explosions, and spills reshape the level in real time.
Materials react by rule: lava and water form rock and steam, wood burns into smoke, acid eats terrain, and alchemical liquids such as polymorphine or teleportatium apply their effects on contact.
A death ends the run and the world is regenerated; only some unlocks, such as new spells in the pool, persist.
Wands have stats such as capacity, mana, recharge, and cast delay; spells and modifiers placed in a wand's slots execute in order, so arrangement changes what the wand does.
Box2D rigid bodies such as crates, bricks, and detached terrain chunks can be kicked, thrown, and shattered.
Fire spreads through wood, grass, oil, and gunpowder and burns the player and enemies alike.
Liquids pool and flow and gases rise and spread through caves at pixel level.
Each seed generates biome layouts from hand-made tile pieces within a fixed order of biomes.
The player controls one witch with levitation, kicking, and wand casting.
Lua-based mods are supported and distributed through Steam Workshop.
Each world seed defines two secret alchemy recipes (Lively Concoction and Alchemic Precursor), each made from three materials that players must find by experiment.

games.name: Noita
games.summary: A roguelite action game in which every pixel of the world is simulated as a falling-sand material that burns, melts, flows, and reacts, and the player builds wands from spells to dig through procedurally generated levels.
