games.core_loop: land an HQ -> claim tiles and build extractors -> refine resources into goods -> sell into a market whose prices move with each trade -> buy black market sabotage and stock -> buy out every rival
games.design_notes: Soren Johnson replaced combat with a shared market: 13 resources trade at prices that move with every purchase and sale, so selling a large stockpile drives the price down and one player's bulk purchases create openings for others. Black market items such as nukes, EMPs, and mutinies act through the economy, and each purchase raises the price of the next one. Victory comes from equity: players buy shares in rivals until they hold a majority of every company, and buying back one's own shares makes a takeover more expensive. Johnson names M.U.L.E. and Railroad Tycoon as inspirations.

mechanics.note: Each of 13 resources has a market price that falls when players sell and rises when they buy, with shortages and gluts driving rapid swings.
Players buy shares in rival companies and win by holding a majority of every company; debt lowers stock price, and buying back one's own stock raises buyout cost.
Extractors on claimed hex tiles mine water, aluminum, iron, silicon, and carbon at rates set by tile richness.
Steel mills, glass kilns, electronics factories, greenhouses, and hydrolysis reactors turn raw resources into higher-value goods and life support.
Up to eight companies, AI or human, compete in one market and attack each other through black market sabotage such as nukes, EMPs, and mutinies.
Some resource tiles and patents are sold by auction.
Each HQ consumes life support resources such as water, food, oxygen, and power, which must be produced or bought.
Companies can run into debt, which depresses their share price.
Patents and HQ upgrades unlock buildings and bonuses.
Each match generates a new Martian map, so resource layouts and claims differ.

games.name: Offworld Trading Company
games.summary: A real-time economic strategy game on Mars where companies claim resource tiles, refine goods for a shared market whose prices move with every trade, and win by buying out every rival's stock.

claims.text: Opus Magnum is a refined version of Zach Barth's 2008 Flash game The Codex of Alchemical Engineering, which is not in this dataset; the influenced_by edge to SpaceChem records Barth's shared instruction-grid and histogram design rather than a stated influence in the cited encyclopedia.
A Nintendo Switch version, Opus Magnum The Complete Edition, released on 2026-03-17.

games.core_loop: read the reagents and product -> place arms, tracks, and glyphs on the hex grid -> write instructions on the timeline -> run until the required products are made -> compare cost, cycles, and area histograms -> export a looping GIF or optimize
games.design_notes: Opus Magnum refines Zach Barth's 2008 Flash game The Codex of Alchemical Engineering into Zachtronics' most permissive puzzle design: there is no part limit, any machine that delivers the products counts, and the difficulty is choosing among three competing metrics. Arms grab, rotate, pivot, extend, and move on tracks under a per-arm instruction tape, and glyphs bond, unbond, calcify, and project metals one step toward gold. Solutions are ranked on cost in gold, cycles, and area, with no in-game reward for optimizing, so motivation comes from friends' scores and the histograms. Barth's experience with solution recording in Infinifactory led to built-in export of seamlessly looping GIFs, which made solutions shareable outside the game; a puzzle editor feeds Steam Workshop.

mechanics.note: Each arm has a row on a shared instruction timeline of grab, drop, rotate, pivot, extend, retract, and track moves; the machine loops the program until the required number of products is output.
Solutions are scored on cost in gold, cycles to complete, and area in hex tiles, with the community adding an unofficial sum metric.
Cost, cycles, and area are shown on histograms of all players' scores and against friends' scores; Zachtronics deliberately attaches no rewards to optimization.

A machine is assembled from arms, extendable arms, tracks, and glyphs of bonding, unbonding, calcification, and projection, plus devices such as Van Berlo's wheel, with no limit on parts beyond their cost.
Each puzzle fixes the input reagents and the required product molecule; chapters must be completed to advance.
A puzzle editor publishes solvable user puzzles to Steam Workshop, curated puzzles appear in the Journal of Alchemical Engineering, and solutions export as looping GIFs.

games.name: Opus Magnum
games.summary: A programming puzzle game in which the player builds alchemical machines from arms, tracks, and glyphs on a hex grid, programs them on an instruction timeline, and compares each looping solution's cost, cycles, and area against other players' histograms.

games.core_loop: buy supplies at the outset and at forts -> choose food consumption and pace each leg -> random events, weather, and illness hit the party -> hunt for food and cross rivers -> reach Oregon or die on the trail
games.design_notes: Three student teachers wrote it in two weeks for a Minneapolis classroom, where it debuted on 3 December 1971; MECC distributed it on its time-sharing network from 1975 and on the Apple II from 1980. The 1971 model is a few stocks (food, bullets, clothing, supplies, cash) spent over about twelve two-week rounds, with one or two random events and weather drawn each round and typed hunting that rewards speed. The 1985 graphical version added adjustable pace and rations, river crossings by fording, caulking, or ferry, a party of five, professions that set difficulty and score, and tombstones left by earlier players.
games.developer: Don Rawitsch, Bill Heinemann, and Paul Dillenberger; later MECC

mechanics.note: Food, clothing, and medical supplies are stocks drawn down each round at a player-chosen consumption rate; low food, cold without clothing, and untreated illness kill the traveler.
Each round closes with one or two random events and weather, such as storms, wagon breakdowns, snakebites, or attacks, that cost supplies or health.
The trip is a sequence of two-week rounds with fixed phases: stop at a fort or not, hunt or not, set consumption, then travel and resolve events.
Weather each round affects travel and illness.
Dead party members are gone; the 1985 version leaves a tombstone with an epitaph.

games.name: The Oregon Trail
games.summary: An educational turn-based travel sim in which the player buys supplies and sets rations for a wagon journey to Oregon while random events, weather, and illness threaten the party.

games.core_loop: scout and draft players -> set rosters, lineups, and depth charts -> simulate games pitch by pitch -> players develop or decline -> trade, sign, and manage finances -> build a franchise across seasons
games.design_notes: OOTP simulates baseball pitch by pitch from player ratings and reports it as scrolling play-by-play text with a minimal diamond, plus 3D ballparks and ball flight from OOTP 15. Its range of setups defines it: real current leagues under the MLB and Minor League Baseball licenses from OOTP 16, historical play that drops the player into any era with real rookies arriving each season, and fictional leagues. Ratings are filtered through scouting, so the GM sees estimates rather than true values. The league keeps a full statistical history with HTML reports, so long careers build an almanac.

mechanics.note: Games are simulated pitch by pitch from batter, pitcher, and fielder ratings and managerial settings, in real time, pitch-by-pitch control, or bulk simulation.
Player ratings are shown through a scout's evaluation, so accuracy depends on the scouting staff; the system was recoded in OOTP 14.
The GM signs free agents, drafts amateurs, and hires managers, coaches, and scouts within a budget.
Player ratings develop and decline over careers, including fielding development added in OOTP 14.
Players age, retire, and are replaced by drafts and historical debuts.
Fictional players are generated for fictional leagues and amateur drafts.
League histories, records, and player careers are stored and exported as HTML reports.
Franchise finances cover payroll, revenue, and budgets; the system was reworked in OOTP 16.
Extensive statistics and reports cover every player, team, and season.

Contract offers to free agents and extensions to rostered players are accepted or rejected against each player's demands, and trades are proposed to AI general managers who accept, reject, or counter.
Owners set expectations, and the general manager's job security falls when results and finances miss them, ending in dismissal.

games.name: Out of the Park Baseball
games.summary: A text-based baseball management sim in which the player runs a franchise's roster, scouting, draft, trades, and finances while a pitch-by-pitch engine simulates games for career, historical, or fictional leagues.

games.core_loop: dig into the asteroid -> lay out rooms, pipes, and wires -> duplicants perform prioritized errands -> oxygen, heat, germs, and waste redistribute tile by tile -> stress and shortfalls surface -> rebuild toward closed, sustainable loops
games.design_notes: Each cell holds one element with a mass and a temperature, and heat moves between cells every 0.2 s tick by conduction, so insulation, phase changes, and overheating machines follow from one rule rather than from per-building scripts. Most machines emit byproducts (a natural gas generator makes 800 W plus polluted water and carbon dioxide), so the long game is closing loops so waste becomes input. Mood uses a morale-versus-expectation gap: learning skills raises a duplicant's expectation, so better-trained colonists need better food, rooms, and decor. Wikipedia names Dwarf Fortress, Prison Architect, and The Sims as design influences.

mechanics.note: Every tile holds one gas, liquid, or solid with a mass; gases diffuse and equalize when a chamber is opened, and liquids drain under gravity, so breathable oxygen must be produced and carbon dioxide managed.

Cells exchange heat each 0.2 s tick with q = dT x dt x k x 1000, with multipliers for solid-gas and liquid-liquid contact; insulated tiles divide conductivity, and temperature thresholds melt, freeze, boil, or damage things.
Machines and duplicants emit polluted water, polluted oxygen, carbon dioxide, and heat; a natural gas generator consumes 90 g/s of gas for 800 W and outputs 67.5 g/s polluted water and 22.5 g/s CO2.
Gas and liquid pipes carry packets between buildings; a liquid pipe segment holds 10 kg and moves packets once per second, capping a line at 10 kg/s, and pipe contents exchange heat with their tiles.

Morale is the sum of timed buffs (Mess Hall +3, Private Bedroom +3, food up to +16, decor up to +12) compared to an expectation that rises with skills learned; each point under adds 2.5% stress per cycle up to 25%, full stress triggers a stress response, and 8 or more points over can trigger overjoyed responses.
Every errand carries a priority, and each duplicant has per-errand-type priorities on the Priorities screen; duplicants pick the highest available errand and favor tasks they are good at.
Dig, build, mop, and deconstruct orders placed on tiles.
Germs live on tiles, items, gases, and liquids; exposure past per-germ thresholds gives a contraction chance of 0.5 - 0.5 x tanh(resistance / 4).
Coal, hydrogen, natural gas, and manual generators on wires and batteries; overloaded circuits take damage.
Automation wires, sensors, and logic gates control doors, pumps, and generators; extended by the Automation Innovation update.
Skill points are spent on skills, which raise morale expectations.
Traits such as Germ Resistant or Allergies change resistances and stress reactions.
Enclosed rooms that meet requirements become Mess Halls, Bedrooms, and similar rooms that grant morale buffs.
Decor around a duplicant is compared to its recent average and feeds morale.
Plants need specific temperatures, atmospheres, and irrigation.
Critters are ranched for food and for their conversion of inputs into useful outputs.
Food rots unless refrigerated or kept in a sterile atmosphere.
Oxygen, temperature, power, plumbing, and germ overlays show hidden cell state.
Research unlocks buildings.
Asteroids are procedurally generated.

games.name: Oxygen Not Included
games.summary: A side-view colony sim in which a few duplicants survive inside an asteroid where every tile holds an element with mass and temperature, so air, liquids, heat, and germs flow through the base.

games.core_loop: read the day's rules -> inspect each entrant's papers -> interrogate, fingerprint, or scan discrepancies -> stamp approve, deny, or detain -> citations and bribes adjust pay -> pay rent, food, and heat -> next day adds rules
games.design_notes: The inspection rules are predicates that accumulate day by day as the fictional state's politics shift, so the same entrant generator yields harder cases over time. Pay is per correctly processed entrant within a fixed shift and citations arrive by fax after each error, which makes speed and accuracy a direct trade. The household ledger converts that trade into moral pressure, and bribes and rule-bending choices feed scripted branches that lead to twenty endings.

mechanics.note: Each day adds or changes entry requirements; the player cross-checks passports, permits, and other papers, can interrogate, compare fingerprints, or order body scans, and receives faxed citations after protocol violations.
Each shift is a fixed real-time working day and pay is per properly processed entrant, so processing speed trades against error risk.
The end-of-day ledger adds wages and bribes, subtracts citation penalties, and requires paying rent, food, heat, and other necessities; going into debt ends the game.
Family members' condition worsens on days when food, heat, or other necessities go unpaid.
Scripted entrants pose choices such as admitting a supposed spouse without complete papers, trading rule compliance against helping people.
EZIC contacts and other scripted encounters branch the story toward twenty endings, including escape to Obristan.
Randomly generated entrants are mixed with scripted ones; the unlockable endless mode uses only generated entrants.

games.name: Papers, Please
games.summary: A border inspection game in which the player checks entrants' documents against daily-changing rules on a timed shift and spends the wages on a family's rent, food, and heat.

games.core_loop: design Parafolks in the Paramaker -> build a grid-less home -> Parafolks pursue needs and wants -> socialize, work, and build skills around town -> relationships, children, and aging change the household -> share homes and Parafolks on the Workshop
games.design_notes: Paralives began as Alex Massé's solo project, was funded through Patreon (over 15,000 supporters by November 2023), and entered Steam early access on 2026-05-25 with about two years planned before 1.0. Its building tools are its most distinctive system: walls and furniture resize, recolor, and stack, walls can curve, floors can split level, and a road-style wall tool was inspired by Cities: Skylines. Conversation fills a together bar that unlocks together cards, multiselect lets several Parafolks act as a group, and procedural animation adapts to preceding animations.

mechanics.note: Grid-less building with curved walls, split-level floors, and resizable, recolorable, stackable furniture; walls are drawn with a road-style tool modeled on Cities: Skylines.
Parafolks carry needs, wants, and emotions that steer their autonomous behavior and set the player's care tasks.
Conversation fills a together bar between two Parafolks, and a full bar unlocks together cards.
Jobs with flexible career progression paths.
Steam Workshop distributes community houses, Parafolks, and mods.
An in-game modding interface lets players edit or add content.

games.name: Paralives
games.summary: An indie life sim, in early access since May 2026, in which players build grid-less homes and guide Parafolks with needs, emotions, traits, skills, and careers in an open-world town.

games.core_loop: accept an email job -> order parts with a shipping tier -> open the case and diagnose or assemble -> install software, remove viruses, or overclock -> benchmark -> get paid -> pay rent and electricity -> unlock better parts
games.design_notes: Parts are licensed real components with compatibility rules, and a machine's performance is measured with the real 3DMark benchmark, so a build's quality is an output of its parts rather than a designer-set score. Assembly has physical consequences: a CPU cooler mounted without thermal paste lets the processor overheat and fail. The career wraps this in a small business with monthly rent and electricity, accept-or-reject email jobs, and timed jobs that become more common later.
games.developer: Claudiu Kiss and The Irregular Corporation

mechanics.note: Email jobs ask for virus removal, upgrades, fixes, or overclocking on customer PCs; the player opens the case, identifies the faulty or missing part, and swaps it.
PCs are assembled from licensed cases, motherboards, CPUs, coolers, GPUs, memory, and storage; part choice and installation details such as thermal paste decide whether and how well the machine runs.
Customer requests, discount alerts, spam, and scams arrive in an inbox; accepted orders left unfulfilled are rejected, and timed jobs grow more common as the career advances.
3DMark benchmarking scores built or repaired machines.
Leveling up from job experience unlocks more advanced parts.
Monthly rent and electricity bills must be paid or the player incurs debt.

games.name: PC Building Simulator
games.summary: A workshop sim in which the player takes email jobs to build, upgrade, repair, and overclock PCs from licensed parts and verifies the results with benchmark software.

games.core_loop: lay out housing, roads, and floodplain farms -> the yearly Nile flood waters the farms -> walkers deliver services, food, and goods to houses -> houses evolve and pay taxes -> appease five gods and build monuments to meet mission goals
games.design_notes: Pharaoh reuses Caesar III's walker model and adds a calendar driven by the Nile: floodplain farms can only be worked between floods, irrigation ditches raise fertility, and the god Osiris can improve or worsen the flood. Monuments need worker facilities and delivered materials and take in-game years, a construction-logistics system with no exact taxonomy match (see run proposal). Five gods (Ra, Bast, Osiris, Ptah, Seth) grant gifts when appeased with shrines and temples and send disasters when angered.

mechanics.note: Fire marshals, constables, and other service walkers roam roads from their buildings and cover the houses they pass.
Housing improves in level when demands for goods, services, and surroundings are met.
A yearly Nile flood waters floodplain farms; irrigation ditches extend fertile land, and Osiris can raise or lower the flood quality.
Floodplain and meadow farms yield by fertility and season.
The flood season fixes when floodplain land can be farmed.
Houses need food and goods to advance.
Raw materials and goods trade with other cities for money.
Missions set population, rating, and monument goals.
Buildings and monument crews draw workers from housing.
Monuments such as pyramids need delivered materials and worker crews over in-game years, and many missions require completing them.

games.name: Pharaoh
games.summary: An Egyptian city builder on the Caesar III engine in which a yearly Nile flood waters floodplain farms, walkers carry services to housing, five gods must be appeased, and monuments take years of labor and materials.

claims.text: The CDC invited creator James Vaughan to speak in March 2013 about the game's infection model.

games.core_loop: infect patient zero -> infections spread within and between countries -> earn DNA points -> buy transmission, symptom, and ability evolutions -> severity raises awareness and cure funding -> race to kill everyone before the cure completes
games.design_notes: James Vaughan's game inverts the epidemic model: the player owns the pathogen's parameters, and humanity's response (awareness, closures, cure research) is the opponent. The tension is between infectivity and severity, because visible symptoms and deaths accelerate the cure, so successful plans spread quietly and then turn lethal. Countries differ by climate and conditions the pathogen must adapt to, and the CDC invited Vaughan to discuss its infection model in 2013, though Ndemic has said it is not on par with scientific models. Evolved adds 10 disease types, 23 scenarios, versus and co-op modes, and a scenario creator with Workshop sharing.

mechanics.note: Infection spreads within countries and between them along travel links, at rates set by the pathogen's transmission traits and each country's conditions, until countries are fully infected and then depopulated.
DNA points buy nodes in three trees (transmission, symptoms, abilities); symptoms raise severity and lethality, and abilities resist climate and drugs.
Once the disease is noticed, countries fund cure research shown as a global progress bar; finishing it ends the run, so the player races to kill before it fills.
Hot, cold, and other national conditions slow a pathogen that lacks the matching resistance evolutions.
Evolved ships 23 scenarios and 10 disease types, each with altered rules.
The Evolved scenario creator builds custom plagues, worlds, and events, with over 10,000 shared on Steam Workshop.

games.name: Plague Inc.
games.summary: A strategy game in which the player evolves a pathogen's transmission, symptoms, and abilities to infect and kill the world's population before humanity's cure research finishes.

games.core_loop: sculpt terrain and build modular scenery -> design coasters and test their ratings -> guests choose rides, shops, and paths -> manage staff, prices, and finances -> share parks and blueprints on the Workshop
games.design_notes: Planet Coaster keeps the RollerCoaster Tycoon structure of rated rides and guests with preferences and moves the emphasis to construction: a hybrid spline and piece coaster editor, a voxel terrain editor, and modular pieces that snap into custom buildings. The Workshop is part of play, since players import coasters, scenery blueprints, and whole parks made by others. Frontier calls it a spiritual successor to its own RollerCoaster Tycoon 3, and both run on Frontier's Cobra engine. Career, Challenge (limited funds and research), and Sandbox (unlimited funds) modes share one simulation.

mechanics.note: Coasters are built in a hybrid spline and piece-by-piece editor, and structures are assembled from modular wall, roof, and prop pieces.
Coasters are test-run and rated on excitement, fear, and nausea, which set guest demand and ride value.
Thousands of guests with individual needs, preferences, and budgets choose rides and shops and show thoughts about prices and park conditions.
Coasters, scenery blueprints, and parks are uploaded to and downloaded from the Steam Workshop or Frontier Workshop.
Any selection of pieces can be saved as a blueprint and placed again.
Janitors, mechanics, entertainers, vendors, and security guards are hired and assigned.
Ticket, ride, and shop prices are weighed against ride ratings and guest budgets.
Rides age and break down without mechanic inspections.
A voxel terrain editor sculpts and tunnels the ground.
Challenge and Career modes gate rides and items behind research.
Guests need food, drink, toilets, and rest during their visit.
Career scenarios set goals such as building coasters, reaching park ratings, and hiring staff; a scenario editor was added in 2017.
Scenery around rides and paths raises guest happiness and ride appeal.
Coasters are built in a hybrid spline and piece-by-piece editor, joining track elements end to end.

games.name: Planet Coaster
games.summary: A 3D theme park builder with a spline and piece coaster editor, modular scenery, and individually simulated guests and staff, built around sharing creations through the Steam Workshop.

games.core_loop: build a habitat for a species' needs -> animals respond to space, terrain, enrichment, and group size -> breed and manage genomes -> trade or release animals for conservation -> guests pay and learn -> expand the zoo
games.design_notes: Planet Zoo gives each animal species a requirements profile (habitat size, land and water, terrain and plant biome, temperature, group size and sex ratio, enrichment, privacy, and guest exposure) and reports the shortfalls as welfare, so habitat design is a constraint-satisfaction problem. Each animal carries a genome that affects lifespan, size, health, and fertility; offspring inherit it, and inbreeding harms the young, which turns breeding into a population-genetics task. Franchise mode connects zoos to an online market where players buy and trade animals with conservation credits. It reuses Planet Coaster's construction and Workshop tools.

mechanics.note: Each species needs habitat size, land and water area, biome terrain and plants, temperature, shelter, and enrichment; welfare drops when any requirement is unmet.
Animals carry genomes that set lifespan, size, health, and fertility; offspring inherit them, and inbreeding causes harmful effects.
Animals have food, water, social, enrichment, and privacy needs whose shortfalls lower welfare and can cause illness.
In Franchise mode an online animal market shared across players lists animals for sale and trade, priced in conservation credits.
A conservation rating rises with endangered species, releases to the wild, and education.
Guests choose exhibits, shops, and talks and react to animal welfare and park layout.
Keepers, vets, mechanics, security, and vendors are hired with work zones and facility needs.
Animals age from juveniles to adults and die of old age.
Barriers, buildings, and scenery use Planet Coaster's modular piece system.
Vets research species to unlock knowledge and enrichment items.
Habitat and building blueprints are shared on the Steam Workshop.

games.name: Planet Zoo
games.summary: A zoo management game where the player builds habitats to meet each species' welfare needs, manages genetics and breeding, and raises a conservation rating, using Planet Coaster's building tools.

games.core_loop: read anchors, vehicles, and budget -> place beams and roads from materials -> run the simulation -> watch stress and failures -> trim cost or reinforce -> submit to leaderboard
games.design_notes: Bridges are trusses of joints and members in a side-view plane; each material (road, wood, steel, rope, cable, hydraulics) has its own cost, strength, and mass, and crossing vehicles load the structure until members exceed their limit and snap. The puzzle is minimizing cost under a level budget while keeping stress below breaking, and hydraulic phases tied to vehicle checkpoints let bridges move in sync with traffic. Failed runs are free to repeat, so the loop is fast iteration against a stress readout.

mechanics.note: Every member carries tension or compression shown as a stress color; a member past its material limit breaks and the load redistributes, often cascading into collapse.
Bridges are built from road, wood, steel, rope, cable, and hydraulic members connected at joints; materials trade cost against strength and weight.
A level passes when its vehicles reach their flags; total material cost against the level budget is the measure of a good solution, and Steam leaderboards compare results.
Cars, trucks, and other vehicles are physics bodies whose mass and speed load the bridge.
Levels fix anchor points, allowed materials, budget, and vehicle routes.
A multi-phase hydraulics controller fires pistons when vehicles reach checkpoints.
Sandbox designs are published as Workshop levels, and test runs export as GIF replays.

games.name: Poly Bridge
games.summary: A bridge-building puzzle game where the player places beams and roads from materials with different costs and strengths under a budget, then runs a physics test as vehicles cross.

games.core_loop: raise and lower land to make flat ground -> followers settle and build houses -> houses breed followers and raise mana -> spend mana on knights, earthquakes, swamps, volcanoes, and floods -> overwhelm the rival deity's followers
games.design_notes: Populous established the god game by making terrain the player's main tool and population the player's currency: flat land lets followers build larger houses, houses produce followers, and followers produce mana for powers, so shaping the land is also running the economy. The landscape type of each world (desert, lava, snow and ice) changes how followers develop. Population growth from housing has no mechanic id yet (proposal filed). The game ships 500 worlds, each won by outgrowing and destroying the opposing population.

mechanics.note: Raising and lowering land is the basic power; its main use is creating flat ground on which followers can build larger settlements.
Mana from the follower population unlocks progressively stronger interventions: knights, earthquakes, swamps, volcanoes, and floods.
A papal magnet and behavior modes send followers to settle, gather, or fight.
Landscape type changes how followers develop.
500 worlds, each won by defeating the enemy's followers.

games.name: Populous
games.summary: The first god game, in which the player raises and lowers land so followers can build and multiply, then spends the mana they generate on disasters against a rival deity's people.

games.core_loop: accept a job -> pick nozzle and soap -> wash surfaces -> per-part progress reaches 100 percent -> job pays -> buy washer upgrades -> next job
games.design_notes: The simulation is a per-surface dirt state: each surface carries layers (dirt, grime, lichen, moss, rust) that the spray removes according to nozzle, soap, and range, and every object reports its percentage done. Four nozzles trade power against spray width, so play is matching the tool to the layer and distance. Progress bars per object and a highlight for remaining dirt make completion fully legible, and the career's story arrives as client text messages rather than through the simulation.

mechanics.note: Four nozzles with different power and spray width and surface-specific soaps remove dirt, grime, lichen, moss, and rust; progress bars track each object and the level, and a button highlights remaining dirt.
Career mode in the town of Muckingham offers 38 main jobs plus bonus jobs whose pay buys upgrades and cosmetics.
Ladders and scaffolding reach higher surfaces.
Challenge mode limits water or time and ranks the result.

games.name: PowerWash Simulator
games.summary: A first-person cleaning sim in which the player power-washes vehicles and buildings, choosing nozzles and soaps to strip dirt layers until every part reports clean.

games.core_loop: set three activity periods for the month -> training and jobs change attributes, money, and fatigue -> events and festivals test her attributes -> rest or vacation to prevent illness -> she ages a year -> at 18 her attributes select a career ending
games.design_notes: Takami Akai designed the sequel to answer complaints that the original was repetitive, adding more reactions and events around a schedule-and-attributes core. Each month splits into early, middle, and late periods, each assigned to training (academic, artistic, religious, military, or magical), a part-time job, adventure, or free time, under a small annual income. Jobs unlock with age and pay promotion and streak bonuses, rival girls age alongside the daughter as benchmarks, and October festivals hold contests in martial arts, dance, art, and cooking. At 18 her attributes and history select one of 74 career endings, a branching-outcome model captured by the care-dependent-development mechanic.

mechanics.note: Training courses and part-time jobs raise and lower her attributes; attributes gate jobs, decide October festival contests in martial arts, dance, art, and cooking against rival girls, and select the final career.
Each month has three activity slots (early, middle, late), so every period spent training, working, adventuring, or resting is a period not spent on the others.
The daughter ages from 10 to 18; jobs and events unlock with age, and the game ends at 18.
Repeating a part-time job leads to promotions, higher pay, and bonuses for unbroken success streaks.
Stress from work and training is relieved by free time, vacations, spa stays, or bed rest; poor rest management leads to illness and weaker performance.
A small annual income pays for lessons, clothing, food, treatment, and shopping; jobs supplement it.
The month is the turn, split into three phases that resolve after the player sets the schedule.
Events and reactions fire on age, attributes, and season, leading into 74 career endings with retrospective sequences.
Eight years of scheduled training, jobs, and rest shape the daughter's attributes, and at 18 her attributes and history select one of 74 career endings.

games.name: Princess Maker 2
games.summary: A raising sim in which the player, as a father figure, schedules a daughter's training, part-time jobs, rest, and adventures from age 10 to 18, and her accumulated attributes decide one of 74 endings.

games.core_loop: build cells, canteens, and yards -> set the hourly regime -> prisoners pursue needs within the schedule -> unmet needs raise misconduct, contraband, and riots -> hire staff, run programs, and claim grants -> expand capacity for more prisoners and income
games.design_notes: Control is indirect: the player cannot order prisoners, only shape the regime, the buildings that satisfy each need, and the staff who enforce rules. Each of about 21 needs is a charge from 1 to 10 satisfied by specific objects for set durations (a phone booth takes 25 minutes, a shower 20), and needs left at the top charge produce side effects. Information itself is a staffed system: features such as viewing finances unlock only after hiring the matching staff member, such as an accountant. Prisoners fall into five security levels with different temperaments, sentence lengths, and cashflow, and reform and labor programs reduce recidivism, which feeds the prison's grade.

mechanics.note: About 21 prisoner needs (bladder, food, sleep, hygiene, freedom, family, privacy, spirituality, and others) each charge from 1 to 10 and are reset by specific objects or activities; a need at 10 triggers its side effect, and reports color needs from green to red.

Hiring a Warden unlocks an hourly regime per risk category with Lockup, Sleep, Eat, Yard, Shower, Free Time, and Work blocks; each block confines prisoners to areas rather than forcing actions, so needs are met only where the current block lets prisoners go.
The prison is drawn tile by tile: foundations, walls, doors, and objects are placed, then workmen build them, and room types are assigned to enclosed areas that contain required objects.
Needs left unmet for long periods make prisoners irritated, then likely to fight, attack staff, attempt escape, or riot, and violence spreads to nearby prisoners until guards restore order.
Guards, dog handlers, armed guards, and snitches counter contraband, gangs, and escape attempts through patrols, searches, and lockdowns.
Income per prisoner per day against staff wages and construction.
Staff such as guards, cooks, janitors, doctors, psychologists, and lawyers are hired individually, and administrators unlock features.
A bureaucracy research tree unlocked through administrative staff.
Federal grants pay out for meeting stated construction or program objectives.
Five security levels with different temperaments, sentence lengths, and cashflow, plus death row.
Crowd flow through doors and corridors shapes congestion and fights.
Generators and cables power doors, lights, and kitchens.
Water pumps and pipes supply showers and toilets.
Fires spread through the prison and must be fought by firemen.
Player prisons are shared online, and Escape Mode lets players break out of shared prisons.

games.name: Prison Architect
games.summary: A prison management sim in which the player builds a facility, sets an hourly regime, and staffs it while hundreds of prisoners pursue needs whose neglect leads to fights, escapes, and riots.

games.core_loop: sign insurer contracts -> patients arrive with complaints -> doctors order examinations and lab tests -> revealed symptoms narrow the diagnosis -> treat, hospitalize, or operate -> insurers pay -> build departments and hire staff
games.design_notes: Oxymoron Games reduced medicine to symptom rules: each diagnosis has symptoms with tuned occurrence frequencies, examinations reveal them, and a diagnosis becomes clear once enough are found; frequencies were set so a case is rarely obvious after the first exam. Patients reach the hospital through insurance company contracts, and the developers say the resulting economy came to resemble the American system. The free Doctor Mode update lets the player make individual doctors' exam and treatment choices, turning the facility sim into a diagnosis game.

mechanics.note: Each patient has a hidden diagnosis; doctors order examinations, lab tests, and equipment procedures that each reveal symptoms, symptom frequencies are tuned so one exam rarely settles a case, and treatment, hospitalization, or surgery follows.
The player hires and specializes doctors, nurses, lab staff, and janitors and manages their job satisfaction; the Hospital Services DLC adds staff training.
The player lays foundations, walls, floor tiles, doors, and windows and places equipment for each department, or starts from prefabs.
Doctor Mode (2019) lets the player choose exams, diagnoses, and treatments for individual doctors and their patients.
A campaign and six challenge levels set goals; sandbox mode removes them.

games.name: Project Hospital
games.summary: A hospital management sim in which the player builds departments and hires staff while doctors diagnose patients by ordering examinations that reveal symptoms until one diagnosis remains.

claims.text: Experiments ranged from 10 to 500 agents in reported results; runs above 1,000 agents were attempted but exceeded the Minecraft server's capacity.

games.core_loop: seed agents with personas and community goals -> concurrent modules perceive, remember, talk, and act in Minecraft -> cognitive controller commits a coherent decision -> roles specialize and rules are paid, debated, and amended -> beliefs and memes spread between towns
games.design_notes: PIANO runs about ten modules concurrently at different speeds (memory, action awareness, goal generation, social awareness, talking, skill execution), with fast non-language reflex networks and a cognitive controller that acts as a bottleneck and broadcasts one decision so speech and action stay consistent; GPT-4o was the strongest base model. In 30-agent runs agents settled into persistent roles (farmer, miner, engineer, guard, explorer, blacksmith) that collapsed without the social module. In a 29-agent constitution experiment with a 20 percent tax paid into community chests every 120 seconds, pro- and anti-tax influencers shifted votes, amendments passed, and payments followed the new rate. In a 500-agent run, Pastafarianism seeded by 20 priests spread to other towns; 1,000-agent attempts exceeded the Minecraft server's capacity. The preprint states no public code release.

mechanics.note: Constituents give feedback on a constitution, amendments are generated, agents vote, and the amended constitution is distributed on a fixed schedule (feedback at 300 s, vote at 420 s, distribution at 600 s).

Agents deposit a share of inventory into community chests every 120 seconds at the constitutional rate, starting at 20 percent; when amendments cut it to 5-10 percent, payments fell to about 9 percent.
Memes and a religion (Pastafarianism, seeded by 20 priests in one town) spread through agent conversations and travel; conversion was tracked by keyword use and had not saturated after two hours.
A memory module stores conversations, actions, and observations across short and long timescales.
A social-awareness module infers other agents' sentiment, and the paper compares perceived with true likeability.
Agents gather and craft Minecraft items; a 49-agent group plateaued at about 320 unique items over four hours.
Goal generation, talking, and the cognitive controller run on language-model calls, with GPT-4o as the base model in the strongest configuration.

games.name: Project Sid
games.summary: An Altera research demonstration that runs 10 to 1,000-plus language-model agents with the concurrent PIANO architecture in Minecraft to study role specialization, collective rule-making, and cultural transmission.

games.core_loop: loot houses and stores -> avoid or fight zombies drawn by sight and noise -> manage hunger, fatigue, injuries, and moodles -> utilities fail and seasons turn -> barricade, farm, and level skills -> survive until death
games.design_notes: The framing question is how the character dies, not whether: zombie infection is always fatal in an unmodified game, so play is about extending a doomed run. Water and power shut off within the first month, after which erosion and overgrowth spread, giving the sandbox a scheduled decline. Zombies respond to sight and hearing and hordes migrate, so noise from actions shapes risk; there is no mechanic id for noise attraction yet (proposal filed). The game has been in early access since a paid tech demo in May 2011, with Steam early access from November 2013 and Build 42 in open beta from December 2024.

mechanics.note: Moodles for hunger, thirst, fatigue, endurance, panic, stress, boredom, unhappiness, temperature, wetness, pain, bleeding, and sickness each grow in severity and penalize combat, movement, carrying, or healing.
Wounds such as scratches, lacerations, bites, and fractures are tracked per body part with bleeding and bandaging; zombie infection is spread by saliva and blood and is always fatal.
Skills such as carpentry and cooking level from activities, and skill books and magazines speed or unlock progress.
Water and power shut off within about a month, forcing preparation.
Occupation and positive or negative traits are chosen at character creation; occupation also sets spawn location.
Weapons, tools, and barricades are crafted; Build 42 overhauled crafting.
Carpentry builds walls, barricades, and forts.
A climate system with seasons changes gear needs.
Food rots, and refrigeration ends when power fails.
Vehicles have physics and part condition.
A vision cone limits what the survivor sees.
Death ends the character; a new survivor can start in the same world.
Full Lua modding through the Steam Workshop.
Zombies respond to sight and hearing, so noise from actions such as gunfire or breaking windows draws them toward the survivor, and hordes migrate.

games.name: Project Zomboid
games.summary: An isometric zombie survival sandbox in which one survivor manages moodles, injuries, skills, and failing utilities across a large Kentucky map until an inevitable death.

games.core_loop: pick a level goal -> choose an initiator, a target, and a social exchange -> rules score volition and acceptance -> relationships, statuses, and history update -> new exchanges open -> the goal is met or the story turns another way
games.design_notes: Prom Week runs on Comme il Faut (CiF), which its UCSC authors describe as making social relationships playable: characters have traits, interests, statuses, and directed networks of liking, attraction, and respect, and more than 5,000 social considerations govern what each character wants and how others respond. The player never writes dialogue but chooses which social exchange a character initiates; CiF offers the exchanges a character is inclined toward, ranked by likelihood, and resolves acceptance from the social state of everyone involved, including what third parties think. Levels set story goals such as getting two characters to date, which turns the rule base into a puzzle with many solutions.
games.developer: UC Santa Cruz Expressive Intelligence Studio

mechanics.note: Exchanges such as winking, being friendly, or being mean have preconditions; CiF rules decide whether the target accepts and update networks and statuses.
Directed social networks track how much each character likes, is attracted to, and respects each other character; exchanges and third parties' opinions move the values.
A character's volition for each exchange is scored from matching rules, and only exchanges it is inclined toward are offered, ranked by likelihood.
Traits and interests weight which rules apply to a character.
Past exchanges are stored as social history that later rules reference.
Each level sets social goals, such as getting two named characters to date.

games.name: Prom Week
games.summary: A 2012 browser social sim in which the player picks social exchanges among 18 high school students in the week before prom, with the Comme il Faut rule system deciding who wants to do what and how targets respond.

games.core_loop: lay track and place stations -> buy trains and set consists and stops -> carry cargo to stations where it is demanded -> revenue and industry growth -> raise capital through bonds and stock -> defend against rival barons
games.design_notes: Railroad Tycoon joins a train-operations model to a corporate-finance model. Stations come in four sizes (signal tower, depot, station, terminal) with growing service areas, and an economy setting chooses between a simple economy where big cities buy almost anything and a complex one where they buy only certain goods. The company starts with $1 million split between equity and a loan, raises more through bonds, and trades in a small stock market where rival barons attempt buyouts and rate wars. Meier took the idea from the board game 1830 and also cited SimCity. Track construction has no matching mechanic in the taxonomy (proposed as track-laying), and dated vehicle availability is proposed as dated-tech-timeline.

mechanics.note: Each train gets ordered stops and a consist of mail, passenger, and freight cars for nine commodity types; consists can be changed at any stop.
Stations supply and demand goods and passengers; under the complex economy cities accept only certain products, so routing follows demand.
A small stock market lets the player trade its own and rival stock; rivals use stock dealings to try to take over the player's railroad.
AI railroad barons build competing lines and start rate wars over shared stations.
Track is laid on a square tile grid and up to 32 stations are placed; the first station gets the engine shop where trains are built.
Depots, stations, and terminals draw cargo from progressively larger surrounding areas.
Signal towers act as passing loops and control train movements on shared track.
Industries consume delivered freight and produce new cargo; players can build additional industries.
Starting capital is half a loan; bonds raise more at interest rates tied to the economy.
Accounts settle in two-year periods across a century of play.
Players can take direct control of individual train movements.
Delivery revenue depends on cargo type, distance, and travel time, so fast trains earn more for passengers and mail.
New locomotive types become available as the calendar advances through the eras, from early steam engines toward diesels.
Track is laid tile by tile across terrain whose slope and features add cost, linking up to 32 stations.

games.name: Railroad Tycoon
games.summary: A railroad business sim in which the player lays track, builds stations, schedules trains to meet regional supply and demand, and battles rival barons through the stock market.

games.core_loop: fund civilian initiatives in regions -> popular support rises -> spending raises corruption and inflation -> an insurgency emerges and contests regions -> deploy troops, counter corruption, or negotiate -> stabilize the country to win
games.design_notes: Rebel Inc. inverts Ndemic's earlier Plague Inc.: instead of spreading a disease, the player contains an insurgency by building popular support, and spending itself generates corruption and inflation. The tension is between civilian initiatives that win support slowly and military spending that holds ground without building support. Corruption as a side effect of spending is not yet a mechanic in the taxonomy (proposal corruption-leakage).

mechanics.note: A monthly budget funds infrastructure, jobs, education, roads, and military spending; the more initiatives the player funds, the more corruption and inflation rise, and the Economist governor receives the whole budget annually.
An insurgency emerges partway through and contests regions against coalition forces; later, peace can be negotiated with insurgent leaders.
Civilian initiatives raise popular support region by region, and stabilizing the country without letting insurgents take control is the goal.
A governance tab offers anti-corruption measures.
Random events interrupt plans and offer choices.
Each region has its own geography, and selectable governors such as the Economist and the Warlord change the rules.
Funding more civilian initiatives raises corruption and inflation, which erode what the monthly budget achieves; the governance tab offers anti-corruption measures.

games.name: Rebel Inc.
games.summary: A counterinsurgency strategy game in which the player, as a coalition governor, spends a monthly budget on civilian and military initiatives to build popular support and stabilize regions of a war-torn country while corruption, inflation, and an insurgency push back.

games.core_loop: draw an adviser's card -> swipe left or right -> church, people, army, and treasury meters shift -> a meter hits empty or full -> the king dies -> the next reign begins with unlocked cards
games.design_notes: Reigns reduces governance to four bounded meters in which both extremes are fatal, so every choice is a balancing act rather than a maximization. The swipe interface, modeled on Tinder, keeps each decision binary and fast. It is a boundary case included for the dilemma-card mechanic and its use of death as progress between reigns.

mechanics.note: Advisers present cards that the player swipes left or right; each choice moves one or more of four meters (church, people, army, treasury), and the reign ends when any meter becomes completely full or completely empty.
When a king's reign ends, play continues with a new king; unlocked cards and some effects carry across reigns, and the in-game years keep advancing.
Story cards chain across reigns, such as the Devil's visits in the years 666, 1332, and 1998.
Completing tasks unlocks new cards.

games.name: Reigns
games.summary: A swipe-based card game in which the player, as a succession of medieval monarchs, accepts or rejects advisers' requests that push church, people, army, and treasury meters, and each reign ends when any meter empties or fills.

games.core_loop: designate work -> colonists self-assign by priority -> needs and moods shift -> storyteller injects events -> colony adapts or collapses
games.design_notes: Tynan Sylvester describes RimWorld as a story generator. Its systems are chosen for how legible and story-relevant their outputs are rather than for realism: thoughts are itemized with sources and durations, injuries are named body parts, and raids scale with colony wealth to keep tension.

mechanics.note: Selectable storytellers (Cassandra, Phoebe, Randy) choose incidents using a threat budget derived from colony wealth and time since the last major event.
Colonists track food, rest, recreation, comfort, beauty, and other needs whose levels feed mood.
Mood below trait-adjusted break thresholds triggers minor, major, or extreme mental breaks; high mood can grant inspirations.
Every mood effect is an itemized thought with a source and expiry, visible in the needs tab.
A work tab matrix sets 1-4 priorities per colonist per job type; colonists self-assign.
Bodies are hierarchies of parts with hit points, bleeding, infection, scars, and prosthetics that change capacities like moving and manipulation.
Raid strength scales with colony wealth, number of colonists, and difficulty, so growth raises danger.
Drafting switches a colonist from self-assigned work to direct player control for combat or emergencies.

games.name: RimWorld
games.summary: A colony sim where a few named colonists with needs, traits, injuries, and relationships survive on a frontier planet while a storyteller AI paces events.

games.core_loop: build paths, rides, and shops -> design coasters and test their ratings -> guests choose rides by intensity preference and budget -> thoughts reveal problems -> adjust prices, staff, and layout -> meet the scenario goal
games.design_notes: RollerCoaster Tycoon makes ride design measurable: every built ride is test-run and rated on excitement, intensity, and nausea, and each guest has a preferred intensity and a nausea tolerance, so the ratings decide who will ride and who gets sick afterward. Guests are individual agents with money, needs, and a stream of readable thoughts, which makes park problems inspectable one guest at a time. Rides lose reliability with age and break down unless mechanics inspect them on a player-set interval. Scenario goals (guest counts and park rating by a deadline) chain 21 base parks. OpenRCT2, a reimplementation of RCT2, carries the systems forward, and Planet Coaster and Parkitect are described as spiritual successors.

mechanics.note: Each ride is test-run and rated on excitement, intensity, and nausea from its track geometry, speeds, and g-forces; ratings set demand and fair price.
Guests have money, a preferred ride intensity, a nausea tolerance, and needs, and they report thoughts such as a ride being too intense or a price too high.
Coasters are built track piece by piece on a tile grid, choosing direction, height, steepness, and elements such as loops and corkscrews.
Guests compare ride and shop prices with ride value and their remaining cash; overpriced items show up as complaints in guest thoughts.
Ride reliability decays with use and age; breakdown chance rises as reliability falls, and mechanics inspect and repair on a set interval.
Handymen sweep, empty bins, and mow; mechanics fix rides; security guards prevent vandalism; entertainers cheer guests.
Clicking a guest shows cash, needs, thoughts, and ride history.
Guests get hungry, thirsty, tired, and need toilets during a visit.
Guests wait in ride queues and leave long lines unhappy.
Land can be raised and lowered and water added to fit rides and add appeal.
Each of 21 base scenarios sets a goal such as a guest count with a minimum park rating by a deadline; completing one unlocks the next.
Paid research unlocks new rides and improvements over time.
Scenery and trees improve guest views and ride appeal.
Parks start with a loan, such as $50,000 in Mega Park.
Guests navigate the path network and can get lost in mazes of paths.

The marketing panel runs time-limited paid campaigns, such as park or ride advertising and free-entry or half-price vouchers, that raise guest arrivals or demand for a chosen ride or stall while they last.
Coaster track is built piece by piece on the tile grid by direction, height, steepness, and elements such as loops and corkscrews, and the result is rated by test run.

games.name: RollerCoaster Tycoon
games.summary: An amusement park management game in which the player builds rides and custom coasters piece by piece, rated for excitement, intensity, and nausea, to satisfy guests with individual preferences and meet scenario goals.

claims.text: Press coverage compares Satisfactory's building to Factorio, and the game is widely treated as a 3D first-person take on Factorio's factory loop; the cited source records the comparison rather than a developer statement of influence.

games.core_loop: scout resource nodes -> place miners -> belt ore through smelters, constructors, and assemblers -> deliver parts to the HUB and Space Elevator -> unlock the next tier -> expand power and logistics to distant nodes
games.design_notes: Satisfactory moves the Factorio-style ratio puzzle into a hand-built 3D world explored on foot, so verticality, foundations, and architecture become part of layout and many players build for appearance as well as throughput. Resource nodes never deplete and are graded impure, normal, or pure (0.5x, 1x, 2x), so expansion is driven by needing more node types and output rather than by exhaustion. The power grid fails as a whole: when demand exceeds supply and storage is empty the fuse trips and every connected building stops until the player resets it, unlike grids that slow machines proportionally. Clock speed (1% to 250%, with Power Shards and a power exponent of about 1.32) and 106 alternate recipes from crash-site hard drives give each factory a recipe-selection layer that the taxonomy folds into production-chain; this run proposed a machine-boosting mechanic for clock speed and similar systems, and a megaproject-sink mechanic for the Space Elevator. There are no base-raiding enemies; fauna threaten only the pioneer.

mechanics.note: Smelters, constructors, assemblers, manufacturers, refineries, and blenders run per-minute recipes; 106 alternate recipes chosen from hard-drive scans swap inputs, and clock speed from 1% to 250% rescales any machine.
Six belt tiers carry 60, 120, 270, 480, 780, and 1,200 items per minute, with splitters, mergers, lifts, and smart splitters routing flows in 3D.
Miners Mk.1 to Mk.3 sit on infinite ore nodes whose purity multiplies output by 0.5, 1, or 2; water extractors, oil extractors, and resource well pressurizers tap fluids.
Generators from 30 MW biomass burners to 2,500 MW nuclear plants feed one grid; if consumption exceeds production with storage empty, the fuse trips and all connected buildings stop until reset.
HUB milestones are unlocked by delivering crafted parts tier by tier, Space Elevator phases gate tiers 3 to 9, and the MAM researches alien items, power slugs, and hard drives.
The pioneer walks, jetpacks, ziplines, and drives across a hand-built map, building only within reach and gathering power slugs, hard drives, and samples on foot.
Foundations, walls, and ramps snap to a grid at any height, so factories are stacked floors connected by belt lifts and pipes.
Pipelines carry 300 or 600 m3 per minute; liquids need head lift supplied by pumps, while gases do not.
Trains follow station timetables, trucks and tractors replay recorded routes, and drones shuttle between a home port and one linked port on battery or packaged fuel.
Block and path signals divide track so several trains can share a network.
A Blueprint Designer (40 x 40 m at Mk.1, larger tiers in 1.0) saves layouts that appear as build-menu entries and draw materials from storage or inventory.
Storage containers, fluid buffers, and industrial tanks buffer production; the Dimensional Depot uploads items for remote building.
Refinery recipes emit heavy oil residue or polymer resin that must be routed or the line backs up, and nuclear plants emit waste that has to be stored or reprocessed.
Early parts are crafted at a craft bench by holding a button, and equipment is made at the equipment workshop.
The community-run Satisfactory Mod Loader adds new buildings, recipes, and logic on top of the Unreal Engine game.

The Space Elevator takes five Project Assembly phases of crafted parts, from 50 Smart Plating in phase 1 to Nuclear Pasta and Ballistic Warp Drives in phase 5, and its phases unlock tiers 3 to 9 and the ending.
Clock speed from 1% to 250% rescales any machine; each of up to three Power Shards raises the cap by 50 points, and power scales with exponent about 1.32, so 250% draws about 336% of base power.
Trucks and tractors replay a route the player records by driving it once, stopping at truck stations along the recorded path.

games.name: Satisfactory
games.summary: A first-person 3D factory automation game in which a pioneer taps infinite resource nodes on an alien planet and connects machines with belts, pipes, trains, and drones to deliver project parts to FICSIT's Space Elevator.

games.core_loop: grow or cook a base product -> mix in ingredients to add effects -> sell to customers who want those effects -> avoid police searches and curfews -> hire dealers and staff -> buy properties -> unlock new regions
games.design_notes: Schedule I runs a production business through a first-person avatar: the player waters plants, operates mixing and cooking stations, and walks or drives deals across Hyland Point before hiring dealers, botanists, cooks, and janitors to automate the chain. Mixing common ingredients such as soft drinks or paracetamol into a product adds effects that raise its sale value, and customers want particular effects, so recipe discovery is the product-development layer. Police pressure rises with growth through random searches, roadblocks, and curfews, and being seen breaking the law sets a wanted status, a player-heat rule the taxonomy lacks (proposed as heat-wanted-level). The game is in early access, with an exit planned for Q4 2027.

mechanics.note: Mixing ingredients such as soft drinks or paracetamol into a base product adds named effects that raise its value and match customer preferences.
Customers have preferred effects and price tolerances; matching them builds repeat orders and relationships that open further customers.
Plants are grown in pots with soil and water over a growth timer, then harvested as the base product.
The player personally grows, cooks, mixes, and delivers in first person until staff take over.
Dealers sell to their own customer lists for a cut, and botanists, cooks, and janitors run production at owned properties.
Police pressure grows with operations through patrols, random searches, roadblocks, and night curfews; being seen raises a wanted status that can end in arrest.
Higher products need multi-step chains such as cooking methamphetamine at chemistry stations.
Product quality varies with inputs such as soil and additives and affects price.
A daily clock with a night curfew shapes when deals can be made.
Grow tents, stations, and storage are placed inside bought properties.
Rank and story progress unlock new regions, customers, and equipment.

games.name: Schedule I
games.summary: A first-person crime business sim in which the player grows and cooks drugs, mixes ingredients to create products with effects customers want, sells them around a city under police pressure, and automates production with hired staff.

claims.text: In late 2014 Screeps was publicly playable in its browser Simulation mode during its Indiegogo campaign, and a December 2015 post dates the initial launch a year earlier; the persistent MMO opened to backers in May 2015, and the Steam full release followed on 2016-11-16. `year` records the 2014 public launch.

games.core_loop: write and commit JavaScript -> each tick the script reads room state and issues orders -> creeps harvest energy for spawns, extensions, and the controller -> controller levels unlock structures -> claim and defend rooms against other players' code -> profile and rewrite code within the CPU limit
games.design_notes: Screeps removes direct control entirely: the only input to the persistent world is the player's main module, which the server runs once per tick against a fixed snapshot, queuing commands that resolve together at tick end, so the colony keeps acting while the player is offline. Computation is the scarce resource: each tick has a CPU limit (20 without CPU Unlock, otherwise rising with Global Control Level to 300), with unused CPU banked in a 10,000-unit bucket that allows bursts of up to 500. Creeps are designed in code as bodies of up to 50 parts (WORK, CARRY, MOVE, ATTACK, RANGED_ATTACK, HEAL, CLAIM, TOUGH) that set cost, ability, and fatigue, and they die after 1,500 ticks, so a colony is a replacement pipeline. Room Controller Levels 1 to 8 unlock structures and decay if not fed energy, and every player's AI meets the others in shared 50x50 rooms, so strategy is emergent competition between programs. The server is open source and runnable privately.

mechanics.note: Players write JavaScript (or C, C++, Rust, Go, C#, and others via WebAssembly) whose main loop runs every tick under a per-tick CPU limit with a 10,000-unit bucket; globals reset between ticks and actions resolve together at tick end.
Official shards run continuously with ticks every 2 to 5 seconds, so colonies harvest, build, and fight while their owners are offline; rooms link through exits and shards through portals.

Code spawns creeps from up to 50 body parts of eight types; part counts set harvest, carry, attack, and heal rates, MOVE parts offset fatigue of 1, 2, or 10 per part on road, plain, or swamp, and each part has 100 hits.
WORK parts harvest energy from sources that refill every 300 ticks, and extractors at RCL 6 mine minerals for labs and the market.

Energy spent on a room controller raises its level from 1 to 8 at cumulative costs up to 10.9 million, unlocking spawns, extensions, towers, storage, links, labs, terminal, factory, observer, and nuker; unfed controllers downgrade and become neutral.
Towers, ramparts, and walls defend rooms against other players and NPC invaders, and a newly placed first spawn grants safe mode.
Terminals post public buy and sell orders priced in credits with a 5% order fee; the party executing a deal pays an energy cost that grows with distance, and NPC terminals sit at highway crossroads.
Movement costs are 1 on roads, 2 on plains, and 10 on swamps, and route searches consume the player's CPU, so caching paths is a core optimization.
Roads and other structures lose hits over time and must be repaired by creeps.
Every creep dies after 1,500 ticks, so code must schedule replacements before roles go unfilled.
The open-source private server supports mods and community servers that change rules and tick rates.

Each tick has a CPU limit (20 without CPU Unlock), unused CPU banks in a bucket of up to 10,000, a tick may burst to 500, and scripts are terminated at the limit, so pathfinding and caching strategies are shaped by CPU cost.

games.name: Screeps
games.summary: A persistent MMO strategy game in which players control colonies only by writing JavaScript that the server runs every tick, directing creeps assembled from body parts to harvest energy, upgrade room controllers, trade, and fight other players' code under a CPU budget.

games.core_loop: check the tank each real day -> adjust heat, clean water, and feed -> talk to Seaman through the microphone -> it learns words and asks about the player -> the life stage advances through breeding and die-off -> raise the Frogman generation and release it
games.design_notes: Yoot Saito built Seaman around speech: a microphone accessory lets the player answer questions and make small talk, early Gillmen repeat the player's words back as gibberish, and the creature's vocabulary grows while it keeps insulting the player. The care loop is sparse but strict, with roughly one check per real day needed to keep it alive, so the game paces itself to the player's calendar. Its life cycle is scripted and harsh: Gillmen fight until two remain, Podfish die after mating, Tadmen eat each other until two remain, and the final Frogmen are released into the wild. Leonard Nimoy narrates the English version as a guide who explains only part of the rules.

mechanics.note: The player sets tank heat, cleans dirty water, and supplies food, and later runs a sprinkler to keep Frogmen moist.
Microphone speech is matched against the creature's current vocabulary; it asks for the player's birthday and other details and answers in conversation.
Mushroomer, Gillman, Podfish, Tadman, and Frogman stages; Podfish parents die after mating and the aquarium becomes a terrarium.
Time follows the real calendar; going much longer than a day without a check can kill the creature.
Vocabulary grows through conversation, and the creature becomes tamer over time.
It remembers facts the player shares, such as a birthday, and later tells historical events from that date.
Tank temperature and water cleanliness must suit the current life stage.
A neglected creature dies permanently.

games.name: Seaman
games.summary: A Dreamcast virtual pet in which the player talks through a microphone to a sardonic human-faced fish, managing its tank's heat, water, and food while it matures through five life stages.

games.core_loop: customize an avatar -> buy or rent land in a region -> build objects from prims and mesh -> script behavior in LSL -> sell creations, land, or services for Linden Dollars -> exchange Linden Dollars on the LindeX
games.design_notes: Linden Lab describes Second Life as a platform rather than a game: it has no set objective, and almost all content is built and scripted by residents, who keep copyright to it. It is a boundary case included for its user-content pipeline, server-side object scripting, and a virtual currency with a real-money exchange that produced real income for some residents. Each region is simulated on its own CPU core with Havok physics, which caps how many avatars and objects a place can hold.

mechanics.note: The world is a grid of 256 by 256 meter regions, each simulated on a dedicated CPU core with Havok physics and capped at 40 avatars on the mainland or 100 on private islands.
Objects run Linden Scripting Language scripts on Linden Lab's servers, which is how built objects become interactive.
Residents trade land, goods, and services for Linden Dollars, which are bought and sold for real currency on the LindeX exchange; the Marketplace has listed about 2.1 million items.
Objects are built from linked primitives, up to 256 per linked set, or from imported mesh.
Creators keep copyright to their content and sell it to other residents.
Groups give residents shared chat and voice channels.

games.name: Second Life
games.summary: A persistent 3D virtual world in which residents build objects from prims and meshes, script them in the Linden Scripting Language, own land in server-simulated regions, and trade goods and land for Linden Dollars exchangeable for real currency.

claims.text: shapez 2 is the sequel to Shapez (2020, also known as shapez.io), which has no entry in this dataset, so the lineage is recorded here rather than as an influenced_by edge.
Early access began on 2024-08-15 and version 1.0 released on 2026-04-23.

games.core_loop: read the requested shape code -> extract raw shapes from asteroids -> cut, rotate, stack, and paint on belts across levels -> deliver to the Vortex -> earn platform units and research -> build bigger platforms and train networks
games.design_notes: shapez 2 removes enemies, money, and building costs (all buildings are free) and keeps only the throughput puzzle: the product is an abstract shape of up to four layers of four quadrants, each part with a type and one of nine colors, written as a shape code. Parts obey a support rule (no floating pieces) and crystals shatter when cut from or stacked onto other crystals, so processing order is part of the puzzle. Space is the scarce resource: machines sit on space platforms whose count is limited by Platform Units earned from goals, and platforms connect through edge notches, space belts, and colored train lines whose routing is set per color at splitters. After the fixed milestones, operator goal lines grow exponentially in cost per level (for example 15,000 shapes at 18% growth), turning the endgame into scaling a design rather than designing a new one.

mechanics.note: Cutters, rotators, stackers, swappers, painters, pin pushers, and crystal generators each transform shapes by fixed rules; a target shape code implies a processing sequence the player must lay out.
Belts, splitters, mergers, and lifts move shapes across three building levels per platform, and space belts carry them between platforms.

Delivering each milestone's required shapes to the Vortex unlocks the next buildings and mechanics, such as fluids, painting, crystals, and trains; afterwards, operator goal lines with exponentially rising shape costs reward platform units, blueprint points, and research points.
Space platforms in 20x20 chunks are the limited building surface, capped by Platform Units, with notches at chunk edges as the only connection points between platforms.
Copying and pasting factory sections costs Blueprint Points earned from goals, making repeated modules the intended way to scale.
Each platform has three stacked building levels, and shapes carry up to four or five vertical layers that must be supported from below.

Space trains load fixed-size packages at loader stations and unload at stops; each rail carries trains of several colors that take their own color's branch at splitters, and wagons hold one package per machine level.
Pipes and space pipes carry fluids such as paint from asteroid pumps to painters, and fluid launchers move them across notches.
Wire machines carry signals that read and control machines, and wireless senders and receivers pass signals across platform notches.
Asteroid miners and pumps on platforms extract raw shape fields and fluid deposits from a procedurally generated world.
Mods load natively through the ShapezShifter API and are distributed on Steam Workshop.
After the fixed milestones, operator goal lines at the Vortex demand shapes in quantities that grow exponentially per level (for example 15,000 shapes at 18% growth), absorbing late-game output.

games.name: shapez 2
games.summary: A combat-free factory automation game in which the player builds multi-level factories on space platforms that cut, rotate, stack, and paint layered geometric shapes and deliver them to a central Vortex to meet escalating milestone and operator goals.

games.core_loop: receive a patrol grid -> transit under time compression -> detect contacts -> identify the target and solve speed, angle on the bow, and gyro angle -> fire torpedoes -> evade escorts -> return to base and promote crew
games.design_notes: The campaign engine generates convoys, destroyer escorts, and task forces in each patrol area rather than scripting engagements, so a career starting between 1939 and 1943 is a sequence of unplanned encounters. Realism settings scale the procedure: at the hardest, the player identifies class and nationality and computes speed, angle on the bow, and gyro angle; with manual targeting off a Weapons Officer solves the problem while approach geometry still matters. Crew members persist between patrols with rank, experience, morale, and decorations.

mechanics.note: The campaign engine generates convoys, destroyer escorts, and task forces in assigned patrol grids, and the player chooses targets and approaches.
Manual targeting requires identifying a vessel's class and nationality and computing its speed, angle on the bow, and gyro angle before setting torpedo depth and spread.
Crew members carry rank, experience, morale, and decorations between patrols.
A career begins at the rank of Lieutenant, Jr., with a U-boat base assignment between 1939 and 1943.
With manual targeting off, a Weapons Officer computes the firing solution.
Torpedoes run at a set speed, depth, and gyro angle toward an intercept computed from target speed and angle on the bow, so a bad solution misses.

games.name: Silent Hunter III
games.summary: A World War II U-boat sim with a dynamic campaign that generates convoys and escorts, manual torpedo targeting, and a persistent crew that gains rank, experience, and morale across patrols.

games.core_loop: steer the yellow ant -> lay trails and recruit followers to food or the red nest -> colony grows under caste allocation -> fight the red colony and survive hazards -> send young queens and drones to found new nests -> take the yard and drive out the humans
games.design_notes: Will Wright drew on Hölldobler and Wilson's The Ants to show emergence: individual ants follow simple rules, and the player's main lever on the colony is the trail field that other ants follow, not orders. The player embodies one ant and can swap into any other, which pairs a direct-avatar view with colony-level allocation of workers, soldiers, and breeders. Rain washes away trails and floods nests, and lawnmowers, bug spray, spiders, and antlions kill ants, so the environment erodes the information the player lays down. Trail-following agents are not yet a mechanic in the taxonomy (proposal stigmergic-trails).

mechanics.note: The player is one yellow ant that digs, carries food and pebbles, receives food by trophallaxis, and fights; double-clicking another ant moves control to it.
The yellow ant lays trails to food or enemy nests that other black ants follow, and can recruit a group of nearby ants to follow it into fights against spiders, caterpillars, antlions, or red ants.
The colony divides into workers (forage, dig, tend brood), soldiers (fight, eat more, cannot tend brood), the queen, and winged breeders, and the player sets the balance.
The queen lays eggs that become larvae and adults; young queens and drones mate to found colonies in new map squares.
Rain washes away trails and can flood nests.
Human footsteps, lawnmowers, bug spray, and electrical outlets kill ants without warning.
Surface yard play is viewed from above while nests are shown in side view underground.

games.name: SimAnt
games.summary: A Maxis ant-colony simulation in which the player controls one yellow ant that lays trails and recruits nestmates while managing a black colony's castes against a rival red colony, predators, and the household.

games.core_loop: zone residential, commercial, and industrial land -> connect roads and power -> RCI demand and land value grow zones -> collect taxes each year -> fund police, fire, and roads -> respond to crime, pollution, traffic, and disasters
games.design_notes: Will Wright grew the game out of the map editor he built for Raid on Bungeling Bay and drew its model from Jay Forrester's Urban Dynamics. The simulation is a set of coarse grid maps (land value, crime, pollution, traffic density, police and fire effect) recomputed in passes, plus three RCI demand valves that integrate city-wide balance; a zone grows when its local score plus the valve passes a random test. The 2008 GPL release as Micropolis made these update rules, including crime = 128 - land value + density - police effect, inspectable.

mechanics.note: The player paints 3x3 residential, commercial, and industrial zones; simulated developers build, densify, or abandon them.
Three valves move by the ratio of projected to actual residents, commerce, and industry plus a tax offset, clamped to +/-2000 or +/-1500 (Micropolis source).
Each 2x2 block's value falls with distance from the population-weighted center, rises near trees and water, and drops with pollution and high crime, clamped to 1-250.
Zones must connect to coal or nuclear plants through power lines or adjacent zones; unpowered zones do not grow and lower the city score.
Tax revenue is collected periodically from population, land value, and tax rate; police, fire, and road funding fractions scale their effects, and underfunded roads decay.
