Water tanks and warehouses buffer droughts.
Water wheels and other generators power workshops and bots through a connected network.
Sensors, relays, and counters control dams and factories.

games.name: Timberborn
games.summary: A city builder for beaver colonies in which simulated water flows over terrain, recurring droughts and toxic badtides cut or poison it, and players dam, channel, and store water while building upward.

games.core_loop: draw walls, paths, and building outlines -> procedural rules assemble bricks, roofs, doors, and supports to fit -> reshape terrain and add water -> ivy grows and sheep wander the paths -> keep editing
games.design_notes: Tiny Glade takes the Townscaper approach to freehand strokes: a path drawn through a building produces a door, and raising a building adds columns and beams to support it, so local rules respond to how elements meet. The two-person studio built it on a custom fork of the Rust engine Bevy. It is a boundary case: the only autonomous elements are ambient life such as growing ivy and wandering sheep.

mechanics.note: Walls, paths, and building outlines are turned into detailed geometry; a path through a building creates a door and raising a building adds supporting columns and beams.
Strokes are drawn freely without a grid.
Terrain height can be changed and rivers and ponds added.

games.name: Tiny Glade
games.summary: A medieval building sandbox in which drawn walls, paths, and building outlines are assembled by procedural rules into detailed castles and cottages, with no goals, management, or failure states.

games.core_loop: add Miis to the apartment -> Miis develop friendships, crushes, and quarrels -> they raise problems such as food, clothes, or advice -> solve problems to fill happiness and earn money -> level-up gifts and new island venues unlock -> couples marry and have children
games.design_notes: The player is an omnipotent observer who cannot control Miis directly and instead answers their requests, so most of the comedy comes from autonomous pairings and quarrels among Miis whose looks, names, voices, and personalities the player designed. Key relationship changes pass through player consent: the player approves a confession before it happens and resolves fights indirectly. The apartment holds up to 100 Miis, and a filled happiness meter levels a Mii up and earns it a present, so care is paced by a stream of small templated problems rather than decaying meters.

mechanics.note: Miis form friendships and conflicts on their own; pairs can grow closer, fall into fights, or break up, and the player intervenes only indirectly.
Opposite-gender friends of similar age may develop crushes; the player approves the confession, couples can marry and have a child who later moves in or leaves via StreetPass.
Miis raise problems such as wanting a food or outfit, needing relationship advice, or asking for a minigame; solving them raises happiness and pays money.
Each Mii receives a personality at creation that shapes its behavior.
Adding Miis and completing objectives unlocks shops, an amusement park, a concert hall, a café, and other venues.
Miis can be imported from Mii Maker or by scanning QR codes.
StreetPass sends grown children to other players' islands.
Island time follows the 3DS clock; at night the player can listen to sleeping Miis' dreams.

games.name: Tomodachi Life
games.summary: A Nintendo 3DS life sim in which player-made Mii characters live in an island apartment building, form friendships, quarrels, and romances on their own, and ask the player to solve their problems.

games.core_loop: click to add or remove a colored block on the irregular grid -> the solver picks modules for that cell and its neighbors -> arches, stairs, roofs, and gardens appear -> keep editing
games.design_notes: The grid is a subdivided, jittered hex grid of irregular quads, and each edit triggers a real-time wave function collapse that narrows the valid corner modules for the changed cells and their neighbors before decoration is applied. The player expresses only occupancy and color; all architectural detail is derived, which makes the game a pure case of procedural build assist. It is a boundary case because nothing evolves without the player; its author calls it more of a toy than a game.

mechanics.note: Each block edit reruns a marching-cubes-style module lookup and a wave function collapse over affected cells, then adds windows, chimneys, and bushes; delay grows with structure size.
Colored blocks are added or removed anywhere on the grid, stacked vertically.
Enclosed areas are detected and filled with gardens rather than paving.

games.name: Townscaper
games.summary: A town-building toy in which clicking colored blocks onto an irregular grid lets a wave function collapse solver assemble houses, arches, stairways, bridges, and gardens, with no goals or resources.

games.core_loop: survey towns and industries -> build stations, track, roads, docks, and airports -> give vehicles order lists -> payment by cargo, distance, and delivery time -> station ratings and towns grow -> replace aging vehicles and expand
games.design_notes: Transport Tycoon extends Railroad Tycoon to four transport modes on one isometric map and makes cargo value decay with transit time, so mail suits short or fast routes while coal keeps its value over long hauls. Stations only collect from nearby towns and industries, and a station rating decides how much of an industry's output it receives, which rewards frequent, fast service. Vehicles lose reliability with age and new models arrive on a timeline from 1930 to 2030 (1950 to 2050 in Deluxe), so the fleet must be renewed; date-driven model availability is proposed as dated-tech-timeline. Town councils rate each company through the Local Authority system, which can block new stations. OpenTTD, a reverse-engineered reimplementation first released in 2004, continues the design.

mechanics.note: Trains, road vehicles, ships, aircraft, and helicopters run order lists between stations; revenue depends on cargo type, distance, quantity, and delivery time.
Stations accept and supply cargo only within a catchment around them, and station ratings set how much nearby industries hand over.
Vehicle reliability falls with age, breakdowns become more frequent, and vehicles must be serviced and eventually replaced; prototypes offer better specs with reliability risk.
Primary industries feed secondary ones and finished goods go to towns; poorly served industries can close.
Bi-directional signals in the original; Deluxe adds one-way signals.
Some resource sites run out and new ones appear.
Local Authority ratings per town fall with poor service and tree clearing and can block demolition and new stations.
Towns offer subsidies for serving specific routes.
Up to seven AI transport companies compete for the same towns and industries.
Deluxe adds trading company shares and buying out competitors.
The company starts with an interest-bearing loan.
Road vehicles use town roads and player-built roads from depots.
Revenue per delivery depends on cargo type, quantity, distance, and transit time; mail and passengers lose value quickly while coal tolerates long, slow hauls.
Road, rail, sea, and air models are introduced on a timeline from 1930 to 2030 (1950 to 2050 in Deluxe), new models carry reliability risk, and aging fleets must be renewed as better models arrive.
Rail track, including slopes, bridges, and tunnels, is laid piece by piece on the isometric tile map, with costs for terrain changes and demolition.

games.name: Transport Tycoon
games.summary: A transport business sim in which the player builds road, rail, sea, and air networks between towns and industries over a century, earning by delivery speed and distance while vehicles age and break down.

games.core_loop: build housing, jobs, and services across the islands -> each citizen's happiness and faction alignment shift with conditions -> issue edicts, trade, and raid to fund the treasury -> advance through four eras -> win elections or suppress rebels to stay in power
games.design_notes: Tropico couples a conventional production and services city builder to a political layer: each simulated citizen holds happiness and faction alignments, and those aggregate into election results and rebel recruitment. Edicts and policies trade one faction's approval against another's, so building decisions double as political ones. Tropico 6 moves play to an archipelago joined by bridges from the World Wars era onward and organizes progress into Colonial, World Wars, Cold War, and Modern eras.

mechanics.note: Political factions each approve or disapprove of El Presidente based on conditions and decisions that match their ideology.
Elections can be held or rigged; losing one removes El Presidente and ends the game.
Each citizen's happiness across categories such as food, housing, and liberty aggregates into approval.
Edicts with costs and effects on factions and citizens.
Low approval breeds rebels, protests, and coup attempts.
Buildings placed freely across the islands; bridges connect islands from the World Wars era.
Exports through docks fund the treasury.
Skilled jobs require citizens with high school or college education.
Relations with foreign powers affect trade and aid.

games.name: Tropico 6
games.summary: A political city builder in which El Presidente develops an island archipelago across four eras while individually simulated citizens' happiness and faction loyalties decide elections, protests, and revolts.

games.core_loop: build and decorate rooms -> hire staff with traits and train qualifications -> patients flow from GP to diagnosis to treatment -> cures earn money and reputation -> research and Kudosh unlock items -> earn stars to open the next hospital
games.design_notes: Two Point Hospital keeps Theme Hospital's room-blueprint and diagnosis-pipeline structure and adds a deeper staff layer: every hire has personality traits, a specialisation, and trainable qualifications, so the training room is a second production line beside the clinical one. Room prestige rises with room size and decoration and feeds staff happiness, which links interior design to staff retention. Progress spreads across many hospitals with one-to-three-star goals, and items unlock with Kudosh, a currency earned from challenges rather than money. Assistants can run marketing campaigns (proposed mechanic advertising-awareness).

mechanics.note: Patients start in a GP's Office and move through further diagnostic rooms until diagnosed, then to a treatment room; illnesses are comic, such as Light-Headedness and Mock Star.
Doctors, nurses, janitors, and assistants come with personality traits and specialisations that change performance; wages and morale must be managed.
Patients queue at rooms while their health falls; untreated patients die, and long waits lower satisfaction.
Rooms are drawn and furnished with required machines, plus corridors with toilets, cafes, vending machines, and staff rooms.
Staff earn qualifications in the training room that unlock or improve tasks.
Staff traits change efficiency and behavior.
Room prestige depends on size and decoration and affects staff happiness.
Patients and staff need toilets, food, drinks, and rest.
Later levels bring epidemics with a limited vaccine supply; immunizing every infected patient earns a reward.
Machines degrade and need janitor maintenance.
The Research room unlocks new rooms and machine upgrades.
Kudosh from challenges unlocks items; one star unlocks the next hospital.
Each hospital has star objectives; extra objectives raise the rating to two or three stars.
Steam Workshop support added in 2019.
Assistants in the marketing room run paid campaigns that draw more patients, optionally targeted at specific illnesses.

games.name: Two Point Hospital
games.summary: A hospital management game and spiritual successor to Theme Hospital in which the player builds rooms, trains staff with traits and qualifications, and cures comic illnesses across a chain of hospitals.

games.core_loop: practice skills by using them -> gather resources and craft goods -> trade with other players -> build and furnish a house -> fight monsters or other players -> recover from death and re-equip
games.design_notes: Ultima Online tried to simulate a world rather than a set of classes: skills grow with practice, goods come from player crafting, and houses persist on the map. Its planned artificial-life ecology, in which animal behavior responded to ecological events, was removed during beta because players killed creatures faster than they could spawn. Unrestricted player killing at launch led to the 2000 Trammel and Felucca split into consensual and open PvP facets, an early rule-zoned world (proposal pvp-security-zones); fans later reverse-engineered it to build server emulators.

mechanics.note: Progression is skill-based with no levels or classes; skills improve as the character uses them, so a character's abilities record what the player has practiced.
Shards keep persistent player houses and goods; unrestricted PvP at launch was split in 2000 into a consensual-PvP Trammel facet and an open-PvP Felucca facet.
The economy is craft-based: players gather materials and craft the weapons, armor, and goods other players buy.
Player guilds such as Shadowclan formed persistent communities.
Criminal acts against other players carry consequences whose rules changed over the game's life.
Players place houses on open land in the shared world.
A dead character leaves a corpse that other players can loot; item insurance, added in 2003, keeps chosen items for a fee.
The 2000 Renaissance expansion split the world into Trammel, where player-versus-player combat is consensual, and Felucca, where it is open.

games.name: Ultima Online
games.summary: A persistent fantasy MMO in which players progress through skills without classes or levels, craft goods for a player-driven economy, own persistent houses, and could attack each other anywhere until the 2000 split into Trammel and Felucca.

games.core_loop: load or build a system -> set masses, positions, and time step -> run gravity forward -> watch orbits, collisions, and climate respond -> tweak parameters or add bodies
games.design_notes: Every body attracts every other under Newtonian n-body gravity, so the player can test questions such as what happens if a star passes the Solar System and see the answer rather than read it. The current version (a rewrite released as Universe Sandbox 2 in 2014 and renamed in 2018, still in early access) adds composition from a small set of materials, collisions that leave molten craters, and a climate layer where sea ice tracks axial tilt and oceans boil near a star. The simulation is an instrument for parameter sweeps; there are no goals or agents.

mechanics.note: Newtonian n-body gravity acts between all bodies; the player edits mass, density, radius, and velocity and watches orbits, ejections, spin-apart breakup, and collisions follow.
Simulation speed runs from real time to years per second and can be paused; larger time steps trade against accuracy, so fast runs can diverge from slow ones.
Surface temperature, sea ice, and oceans respond to stellar distance and axial tilt; moving a planet can freeze or boil it.
Collisions and stellar irradiance heat bodies, shown as molten surfaces and temperature maps.
Planets are composed from materials such as water, rock, iron, and gases, and oceans and mountains can be shaped.
Orbit trails and surface temperature maps expose state that is otherwise invisible.
Player-made simulations are shared on Steam Workshop.

games.name: Universe Sandbox
games.summary: A space physics sandbox where the player builds and alters star systems and watches Newtonian n-body gravity, collisions, and simplified planetary climate play out at adjustable speed.

claims.disputes: Release year: 1982 per Wikipedia versus 1981 per Guinness World Records and the original skeleton. This entry uses 1982, the dated release.
claims.text: Wikipedia's infobox and lead date the Intellivision release to 1982-06-03 (Aquarius port 1983), while Guinness World Records names Utopia, released on the Intellivision in 1981, as the first city-building videogame.

games.core_loop: spend gold on houses, farms, factories, forts, and boats -> round timer runs while boats fish and clouds rain on farms -> end-of-round income and score from population welfare -> rebels, storms, and pirates strike -> next round
games.design_notes: Utopia runs as up to 50 real-time rounds of 30 to 120 seconds, so the turn boundary is a clock rather than a player action; income from factories arrives at round end while fishing and rain income depend on what happens during the round. Two players share one screen with no AI opponent, and each can fund rebels on the other's island or sink the other's fishing boat with a PT boat, so the welfare score is contested directly. It is commonly cited as the first city-building game, though its release year is disputed between 1981 and 1982.

mechanics.note: Each player places houses, schools, factories, hospitals, and forts on tiles of their own island, paid for with gold bars.
Rounds last 30 to 120 seconds for up to 50 rounds; factory output pays out and the score updates at each round's end.
Points depend on population and how well it is housed, fed, and kept happy; neglect lowers the score and invites rebellion.
Rebels reduce the score and can destroy buildings; a rival can pay gold to fund rebels on the other island.
Randomly generated rain clouds earn income when they pass over a player's farms; tropical storms and hurricanes also occur.
Fishing boats earn income only while positioned over a moving school of fish.
Players steer fishing boats and PT boats directly; PT boats sink the opponent's fishing boat.
Gold bars are the single currency for all construction.

games.name: Utopia
games.summary: A two-player Intellivision strategy game in which rival island rulers spend gold on buildings and boats in timed rounds, scoring points for how well their populations are housed, fed, and kept content.

games.core_loop: explore seeded biomes -> gather wood, stone, and ore -> build shelters that must be supported and roofed -> eat food for health and stamina -> craft better gear -> summon and defeat each biome's boss -> sail to harder biomes
games.design_notes: Food is a reward rather than a punishment: eating raises maximum health and stamina and speeds regeneration, and there is no starvation, so the survival layer pushes players toward better food rather than threatening death. This consumable-buff model does not fit survival-meters cleanly (proposal filed). Building uses a support model in which stability falls with distance from the ground, so architecture follows material limits, and uncovered wood decays to half durability in rain. Progression is gated by eight bosses, each summoned with an offering. Early access began in February 2021 and 1.0 shipped in September 2026.

mechanics.note: Stability runs from blue (grounded) to red; it falls with horizontal and vertical distance from ground, a piece cannot exceed its support's stability, and vertical limits are 16 m for wood and stone and 24 m for core wood.
Each world is generated from a seed and divided into biomes (Meadows, Black Forest, Swamp, Mountains, Plains, Ocean, Mistlands, Deep North, Ashlands), each with its own resources, enemies, and boss.
Workbenches, forges, and other stations craft tools, weapons, and building pieces; new materials unlock new recipes.
Food raises maximum health and stamina for a time instead of causing starvation; stamina drains when running or attacking.
Skills rise to level 100 through use and affect damage and stamina drain; dying reduces skill levels.
Comfort from nearby furnishings lengthens the Rested buff.
Each boss leaves a trophy that grants a power at a central altar and opens the next tier of materials.
Uncovered or submerged wood decays to 50% durability; tools lose durability.
Rain wets the player and rots exposed wood.
Random events send enemies against bases.
Some animals can be tamed and bred.
On death the player's equipment and inventory stay in a tombstone at the death site, and skill levels drop, so the player must travel back to recover gear.

games.name: Valheim
games.summary: A co-op Viking survival game in a seeded procedural world of biomes where players gather, build structurally supported shelters, eat for stat buffs, and defeat biome bosses to progress.

games.core_loop: choose a character and episode -> practices offer actions for the situation -> player acts or waits -> other agents simulate each option and take the best for their desires -> emotions, evaluations, and relationships update -> the episode reaches an outcome
games.design_notes: Richard Evans and Emily Short built Versu around social practices: recurring situations such as a meal or a conversation written as reactive joint plans that offer actions to participants without controlling them. Each agent tests a candidate action by applying it to the world state, scoring the result against its desires (over 300 in total), and undoing it, which the authors contrast with the estimated consequences used in The Sims. World state is a set of exclusion-logic sentences, and the Praxis language with a stress tester that runs hundreds of simulated instances supported over 1,000 parameterized actions. Linden Lab cancelled the project in early 2014; social practices have no mechanic id and are proposed as social-practices.

mechanics.note: Agents score each available action by executing it on the world state, evaluating the result against their desires, and undoing it; the best-scoring action is taken.
Social practices such as a dinner party or a conversation offer role-specific actions with preconditions, and most actions change how characters regard each other.
Agents hold evaluations of each other on roles such as attractiveness or breeding, which actions raise or lower.
Fine-grained emotions on Ekman's typology record their target and cause.
Character files assign each agent desires that weight its action scoring.
A drama manager agent can act to push an episode's authored plot.

games.name: Versu
games.summary: A 2013 iPad interactive story platform from Linden Lab in which the player controls one character among autonomous agents who choose actions by simulating their outcomes against hundreds of desires within authored social practices.

games.core_loop: queue construction of buildings -> buildings hire pops and run production methods -> goods trade at shifting market prices -> wages and needs set standard of living and interest-group support -> enact laws and pursue diplomatic plays -> expand industry
games.design_notes: Victoria 3 moves the player's main lever from units to the economy: the player queues construction and sets laws, and pops, prices, and wages respond, while armies are handled by generals assigned to fronts. Politics is an output of economics, since pops' economic status sets their interest-group affiliation and political strength. Diplomatic plays turn war declaration into a timed escalation of demands and counter-demands with a chance to back down (proposal crisis-escalation).

mechanics.note: Pops' political strength, from wealth and enfranchisement, flows into interest groups such as the Devout, Industrialists, and Rural Folk; clout is each group's share of the national total, approval comes from laws and government membership, and enacting a law runs phases whose advance or stall chances depend on group endorsement.
Buildings such as mines, farms, and factories convert input goods to outputs; switchable production methods change the input mix, output, and which professions are employed.

Each good has a base price, and the market price moves with the ratio of buy orders from consumption to sell orders from production, scaled by market access from infrastructure; prices feed back into building profitability, wages, and pops' cost of living.
The population is stored as pops by profession, culture, and religion in lower, middle, and upper strata, each with its own wages, needs, and political leanings.
Pops buy goods to meet needs, and the share met sets their standard of living.
Buildings hire pops by profession and qualification, so labor shortages throttle new industry.
Laws such as Free Trade and Laissez-Faire change economic and political rules.
Pops whose needs fall short become radicals, and radical interest groups can start a revolutionary movement with a revolution clock.
Diplomatic plays present a demand, allow counter-demands, run a countdown to mobilize and gather backers, and become war if unresolved.
Technologies such as the Atmospheric Engine unlock buildings and production methods.
Nested tooltips break values into contributing modifiers, extended to battle and market calculations.
Authority, influence, and bureaucracy are capacities with monthly supply and ongoing usage: decrees draw on authority and diplomatic pacts on influence.

Pops carry a culture and a religion; over time pops assimilate toward primary cultures and convert toward the state religion, and citizenship and church laws decide which identities face discrimination.
States change hands through diplomatic plays and wars, and newly acquired states are incorporated over time before they count fully.
Each side's war support falls with exhaustion until one capitulates or the sides settle on the demands from the diplomatic play.

games.name: Victoria 3
games.summary: An economic grand strategy game set from 1836 to 1936 in which the player industrializes a nation by building production chains, passing laws through interest-group politics, and pursuing diplomatic plays while population strata respond through wages, needs, and radicalism.

games.core_loop: dig, plant, and water the garden -> species outlines appear when appear requirements are met -> resident requirements turn visitors into residents -> residents meet romance requirements and lay eggs -> predators and sours disrupt -> sell or trade piñatas -> attract new species
games.design_notes: Viva Piñata turns habitat suitability into a readable checklist: each species has staged appear, visit, resident, and romance requirements, shown as a black-and-white outline that fills in when residency is met. Because piñatavores must eat other piñatas to become residents or breed, attracting one species can consume another, so the garden is a hand-built food web the player tunes by fencing, spacing, and timing. Sours and Professor Pester's ruffians supply authored pressure, and romance requirements can be bypassed with candy once a species has bred, trading early difficulty for collection speed.

mechanics.note: Each of the 60 species has staged requirements (garden contents, plants, water, terrain, or having eaten a specific item) that turn an outline into a visitor and then a resident.
Piñatavores must eat other piñatas to become residents or breed, and visiting predators eat residents to meet their own requirements.

Two residents of a species that meet romance requirements perform a romance dance and a maze minigame that yields an egg; piñatas are ungendered, and candy skips romance requirements after a species' first romance.
The journal of 60 species, each with requirements to discover, is the long-term goal structure.
Seeds sown with tools grow into flowers, vegetables, and trees that species eat or require; weeds spread and destroy vegetable rows if not removed.
The shovel and other tools plough soil, dig ponds, and sculpt terrain.
Eggs and piñatas could be sent to other players over Xbox Live.

games.name: Viva Piñata
games.summary: A garden sim in which the player shapes terrain, plants, and water to attract 60 piñata species, then meets each species' requirements to make them residents, breed them, and manage the predators among them.

claims.text: The Steam page discloses AI-driven NPC text and voice chat that responds to player input in real time; global PC release was 2025-11-14.

games.core_loop: explore the open world -> talk to NPCs in free text or voice -> take quests and fights -> build reputation and skills -> explore further
games.design_notes: Included as a boundary case for natural-language interaction at scale. The Steam AI disclosure describes NPC text and voice chat generated in real time from player input. The main questline and combat remain authored and rule-based, so the language model sits beside the simulation rather than inside its state.

mechanics.note: Players type or speak to NPCs and receive live generated replies, per the game's Steam AI disclosure.
Third-person martial-arts traversal and combat.

games.name: Where Winds Meet
games.summary: An open-world martial-arts RPG whose NPCs answer free-text and voice chat through a live language model, included as an early large-audience deployment of runtime LLM characters.

claims.text: Anuttacon, the developer, was formed in late 2023 by Cai Haoyu, and Whispers from the Star is its first game.

games.core_loop: Stella calls, texts, or sends voice messages about her situation -> player answers by voice or text -> model generates her spoken reply and choice -> her choices change whether she survives the situation -> story advances
games.design_notes: At runtime a model generates Stella's side of every exchange: the player's microphone or text input is answered with dialogue and a fully voiced performance that Anuttacon says was created in collaboration with an actor, with safety filters screening output. The store page says there is no script and that the player's words shape her choices and her survival, so advice acts as an indirect control on an agent the player cannot command. The surrounding structure is linear and story-driven per its store tags, which makes it a hybrid of authored situations and generated conversation. Anuttacon was formed in late 2023 by miHoYo co-founder Cai Haoyu, and this is its first game. It is a boundary case: the only simulated state is the conversation and Stella's choices.

mechanics.note: Open-ended conversation by voice (a microphone is required for the full experience) or text over Stella's communicator, through video calls, voice messages, and texts.
An AI model generates Stella's dialogue and voiced performance in real time, constrained by safety filters, and her in-story decisions follow from what the player says.
The store tags the game as linear and story-rich, so generated conversation plays out inside a sequence of survival situations.

games.name: Whispers from the Star
games.summary: A voice-driven sci-fi narrative game in which the player helps stranded astronaut Stella survive on the planet Gaia through open-ended spoken or typed conversation answered by an AI-generated, voiced performance.

games.core_loop: set up construction offices and deliver materials to sites -> extract and process over 30 commodities by truck, rail, conveyor, and pipe -> house citizens near jobs and transit -> supply food, clothing, heat, and services to keep health, happiness, and loyalty -> export at customs for rubles or dollars -> import what the republic lacks
games.design_notes: Workers & Resources treats construction itself as logistics: buildings and roads need delivered concrete, steel, and prefab panels plus workers from the player's construction offices, or imported foreign labor at a cost, a system the taxonomy lacks (see run proposal). Over 30 commodities move by mode suited to their form (pipes and tanks for liquids, conveyors and trucks for ores, covered vehicles for goods), so freight network design is the main puzzle. Trade runs through East and West customs houses, flooding one bloc's market lowers returns, and heating demand rising in winter ties utilities to the calendar.

mechanics.note: Over 30 commodities are extracted, processed, and stored in staffed plants.
Trucks, trains, ships, and aircraft are assigned to depots and routes that move goods and workers between buildings.
Exports and imports pass through customs houses at Eastern (rubles) and Western (dollars) borders.
Conveyors move ores and bulk goods between facilities.
Liquids, water, and heating travel through pipes and tanks.
Buses, trams, trains, subways, ships, and planes carry citizens.
Rail signals and interchanges govern shared track.
Flooding one market lowers returns there.
Citizens need food, clothing, and alcohol from shops.
Health and happiness decide whether citizens stay; low loyalty raises crime and lowers work efficiency.
Optional complex education gates skilled jobs.
Optional seasons raise heating demand in winter.

games.name: Workers & Resources: Soviet Republic
games.summary: A planned-economy city builder in which every building, commodity, and citizen moves through explicit logistics, from construction materials delivered by truck to exports at border customs for rubles or dollars.

games.core_loop: pick or design an aircraft -> set location and weather -> fly by hand or autopilot -> blade-element forces respond to geometry and air -> land -> revise the aircraft in Plane Maker
games.design_notes: X-Plane uses blade element theory: wings, control surfaces, and propellers are split into elements and aerodynamic forces are computed on each from geometry, rather than looked up from performance tables, so an aircraft drawn in the bundled Plane Maker flies according to its shape. That approach underpins its use in FAA-approved training systems when paired with suitable hardware. A plugin SDK exposes simulator data for instruments, cockpits, and external hardware.

mechanics.note: Blade element theory splits wings, control surfaces, and propellers into small elements and computes aerodynamic forces on each from geometry and physical parameters.
Plane Maker lets users define aircraft geometry and components and then fly the result in the simulator.
X-Plane 12 reworked clouds, turbulence, and atmospheric effects, and version 12.3 added a weather-radar system.
The plugin SDK lets developers read simulator data and add instruments, cockpit interfaces, and hardware support.

games.name: X-Plane
games.summary: A flight sim whose flight model computes forces on small elements of each wing, control surface, and propeller from aircraft geometry, used for entertainment and in FAA-approved training devices.

games.core_loop: spot a landmark -> climb, glide, or ride toward it under stamina limits -> solve shrines and fights with physics and elemental interactions -> gather and cook ingredients -> replace broken weapons -> push farther into the world
games.design_notes: The game is mostly authored content (map, shrines, story) and is included for its systemic layer. A modified Havok physics engine and a separate chemistry engine give objects material properties, so fire burns grass and creates updrafts, metal draws lightning and conducts electricity, wind carries flames and gliders, and cold or heat drains health unless countered by clothing or cooked food. Weapon durability and stamina force continual scavenging and route choice, and shrine puzzles accept any solution that satisfies the physical end condition.

mechanics.note: The chemistry engine gives objects properties such as flammable, metallic, or conductive; fire ignites wood and grass, metal attracts lightning in storms and conducts electricity, and ice melts near fire.

A modified Havok engine moves crates, boulders, and weapons; Magnesis lifts metal objects, Stasis freezes an object so stored hits launch it, and Cryonis raises ice pillars from water, giving shrines and fights unscripted solutions.
A stamina wheel limits sprinting, climbing, swimming, and gliding; hearts are health, and ambient cold and heat damage the player without matching clothing or elixirs.
Fire spreads across grass in the wind direction and produces updrafts that the paraglider can ride.
Rain makes surfaces too slippery to climb, and thunderstorms strike metal equipment with lightning.
Region temperature and fire sources set a temperature gauge that damages the player beyond tolerance.
Cooking combines up to five ingredients in a pot into meals or elixirs whose effects and duration depend on the ingredients.
Weapons, bows, and shields lose durability with use and shatter; the Master Sword recharges instead.
Time of day changes enemy and creature activity, and the Blood Moon respawns defeated enemies.
Link can climb almost any surface, glide, ride horses, and use runes.

games.name: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild
games.summary: An open-world action adventure whose physics and chemistry engines let fire, wind, electricity, temperature, and material properties combine, so puzzles and fights accept solutions the designers did not script.

games.core_loop: fence an exhibit -> match terrain, foliage, rocks, shelter, and toys to the species -> animals grow happy and breed -> guests visit, spend, and react -> awards and income -> research and adopt more animals
games.design_notes: Zoo Tycoon's core rule is exhibit suitability: each species reports how well its exhibit's terrain mix, foliage, rocks, shelters, toys, and keeper care match its needs, and that suitability drives animal happiness. Guest happiness depends on animal happiness, the species on show, buildings, and scenery, so the two satisfaction meters are chained. Failures are physical: incompatible species in one exhibit kill each other, fences decay, and escaped animals attack guests and staff. Too many complaints about unhappy animals block new adoptions until habitats are fixed.

mechanics.note: Each species has preferred terrain types, foliage, rocks, shelters, toys, and companions; suitability drives happiness, and incompatible species in one exhibit kill each other.
Guest happiness depends on the animals on show, their happiness, buildings such as restrooms and shops, and scenery.
Animals need food, water, cleaning, and keeper attention that keepers supply on rounds.
Fences, paths, buildings, foliage, and scenery are placed on a tile map.
Fences decay and must be repaired by maintenance workers to prevent escapes.
Zookeepers, maintenance workers, and tour guides are hired.
In freeform mode, money spent on research unlocks animals, buildings, and scenery.
Scenarios set targets such as a guest happiness level, exhibit suitability, animal count, or breeding a species.
Animals breed when content; babies grow into adults.
Scenery such as topiary, lamp posts, and benches gives a small guest happiness boost.

games.name: Zoo Tycoon
games.summary: A zoo management game in which the player builds exhibits whose terrain, foliage, shelters, and toys must suit each species, balancing animal happiness against guest happiness and income.

mechanics.definition: The game keeps a threat budget recomputed before each hostile event as a function of one or more proxies for player strength, multiplied by a difficulty scalar, and spends that budget on enemy count and composition. RimWorld computes raid points as (wealth points + pawn points) x threat scale x starting factor x adaptation factor, capped at 10,000: wealth points rise from 0 at 14,000 storyteller wealth to 4,200 at 1,000,000, each healthy colonist adds 15 to 200 points, a 0.7 starting factor applies through day 10, and an adaptation factor drops after colonist deaths or downings. Factorio's enemy evolution factor rises with elapsed time, pollution produced, and spawners destroyed, unlocking larger biters. Oblivion scaled enemy level to the player's level. Inputs: player state proxies and recent losses. Output: a scalar budget or tier consumed by the event or spawn system.
design_levers: which proxies define strength (wealth, population, time, kills, player level, recent damage taken)
the curve from proxy to budget, including dead zones, piecewise slopes, and the hard cap
difficulty multiplier presets and whether players can set them freely
adaptation or mercy terms that lower the budget after losses and raise it after easy wins
grace period length before scaling starts
how budget maps to enemy composition, such as tiers unlocked at thresholds versus more of the same unit
dynamics: Players optimize the ratio of combat value to counted value, producing lean, militarized bases.
Run length and difficulty converge across skill levels because the system rubber-bands toward a target challenge.
Coupled with permadeath, the adaptation term creates recovery arcs after a massacre instead of an immediate death spiral.
Coupled with pollution or expansion (Factorio), the threat becomes a cost of growth that players trade against output.
failure_modes: Scaling on wealth punishes building: RimWorld players practice wealth management, avoiding valuable furniture or art so raids stay small.
Scaling on player level makes progression feel null when every enemy keeps pace, a common criticism of The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion.
Proxies that ignore defensive investment let a cheap killbox beat budgets tuned for open combat, or let an undefended rich colony be overwhelmed.
Opaque formulas read as the game cheating when a large attack follows a burst of growth.
mechanics.name: Adaptive threat scaling
open_questions: Can a learned estimate of actual defensive capability, such as a fast simulated raid against the current base, replace wealth proxies and remove the incentive to stay poor?
What adaptation rate keeps tension stable without players perceiving rubber-banding?
mechanics.player_experience: Success is answered by stronger opposition, so the player never fully escapes danger. Players learn to read what the game counts as strength and manage it: converting wealth into combat power instead of decoration, or holding back expansion. After a disaster, mercy terms give a breathing window that feels like the world easing off.
mechanics.summary: Threat intensity is computed from a measure of the player's strength, such as wealth, population, time survived, or recent performance.

synergy.note: The director spends a threat budget that scales with wealth, keeping pressure proportional to success.
Raids grow with the colony, so defenses must scale.

tension.note: One rewards growth, the other punishes it; tuning both sets the game's attitude to expansion.

mechanics.definition: Each placeable type has a table of signed effects from neighbor types within a footprint, ring, or radius. When an object is placed (and in some games when a neighbor later changes), its value is recomputed as a base plus the sum of qualifying neighbor contributions, sometimes capped or with diminishing returns. The value feeds score, production yield, or desirability. Islanders (2019) previews the points a building will earn from nearby buildings before it is placed, and points unlock new building packs. Civilization VI (2016) gives districts adjacency yields from neighboring terrain and districts, such as science for a Campus next to mountains and gold for a Commercial Hub next to a river. Tile-laying builders such as Dorfromantik score matching edges between neighboring tiles. The state is the placement map plus the effect table; the update is a local sum.
design_levers: neighborhood shape: touching tiles, ring, or radius, and whether diagonals count
size and asymmetry of the effect table, including negative pairs that force separation
stacking rule for multiple neighbors: linear, capped, or diminishing
whether values freeze at placement or recompute when neighbors change later
how much of the calculation the preview shows before commitment
dynamics: Clusters of mutually reinforcing types form districts, and nuisance types get pushed to edges or buffers.
Scarce space turns adjacency into a packing problem in which early placements constrain later ones.
When adjacency feeds unlocks or income, early good clusters compound into a lead.
failure_modes: Once players find the best repeating cluster, every settlement uses the same stamp and the spatial puzzle ends.
Positive-only tables make maximum density always optimal, removing any reason to spread out.
Hidden or partly shown effect tables push players to wikis and calculators to plan placements.
Retroactive recomputation changes the value of old placements in ways players did not intend and cannot trace.
mechanics.name: Adjacency scoring
open_questions: Can a learned model of layout quality replace hand-written pairwise tables while staying predictable enough to plan against?
What table size and asymmetry keep a solved cluster template from appearing within a few hours of play?
mechanics.player_experience: Every placement is a small search problem with a visible answer. Players hover candidates to read preview numbers, reserve tiles for pieces they expect later, and feel clever when one placement lights up several neighbors. Penalties make them keep nuisances apart, so layouts acquire districts and buffers.
mechanics.summary: A placement's value is computed from a table of bonuses and penalties for the placements around it.

claims.text: Lemonade Stand's daily inputs are glasses made, advertising signs, and price per glass, set against a weather report.
In Two Point Hospital assistants run marketing.

mechanics.definition: Owns an awareness, brand, or hype stock per business, product, or venue and the rule that maps it onto customer traffic. Each period paid campaigns add to the stock with diminishing returns, and the stock decays toward a baseline when spending stops; its current level multiplies arrivals, the share of customers who consider the offering, or launch sales. Lemonade Stand (1973) reduces it to a daily input with no carryover: advertising signs bought before the day resolves raise sales alongside price and the weather. Two Point Hospital has assistants run marketing campaigns that bring in more patients. Capitalism and Game Dev Tycoon use advertising or marketing spend to build brand or pre-release hype. It differs from customer-value-choice, which owns how a customer who is already present chooses among offerings by price and value; this mechanic owns how many customers show up or consider the offering at all.
design_levers: cost per campaign unit and campaign duration
decay rate of awareness after spending stops
saturation curve, or diminishing returns per unit spent
targeting by customer segment, product, or condition
whether awareness raises arrivals, conversion, or willingness to pay
whether advertising can sell a poor product or only amplifies quality
dynamics: Advertising raises traffic and revenue that fund more advertising, a reinforcing loop limited by saturation.
Pre-release hype front-loads sales, so campaign timing and release timing couple.
Extra arrivals load service capacity, so a campaign can create queues that lower satisfaction.
failure_modes: Linear returns make maximum advertising always correct and remove the decision.
Effects too small to see in the statistics teach players to skip advertising entirely.
Without decay, one early campaign buys permanent demand.
Advertising that overrides quality lets poor products sell and undermines the product-quality systems.
mechanics.name: Advertising and awareness
open_questions: Could simulated customers with stated tastes respond to generated ad copy, making campaign content rather than only spend a lever?
Which decay and saturation curves keep advertising a recurring decision instead of a one-time setting?
mechanics.player_experience: Buying customers. The player decides how much to spend before the demand exists, watches arrivals rise and fall with each campaign, and learns that awareness fades: a store or game the market has forgotten needs fresh spending, while a strong brand lets prices rise.
mechanics.summary: Spending on advertising raises a demand or awareness stock that decays without upkeep and scales how many customers arrive or buy.

claims.text: The Super NES version of SimCity added Dr. Wright, an advisor character who appears to report problems in the city.

mechanics.definition: An advisor layer watches a set of indicators (budget balance, unemployment, crime, service coverage, happiness, military strength) and maps threshold crossings or rule matches to authored messages spoken by a named character, usually with a recommended action. It owns no simulation state: only trigger conditions, a priority per message, cooldowns, and an optional persona per department. Each evaluation interval it tests its conditions, ranks firing messages by severity, suppresses those still on cooldown, and presents the top one as a pop-up, voiced line, or entry in an advisor panel the player opens on demand. Inputs are aggregate state variables; outputs are text and, in some games, a one-click link to the relevant tool. Canonical forms: the department advisors of SimCity 2000 and SimCity 4, the Super NES SimCity advisor Dr. Wright who appears to report city problems, the advisor screens of the Civilization series, and Tropico's Penultimo.
design_levers: which indicators each advisor watches and the threshold or trend that triggers a message
diagnosis only versus a concrete recommendation or a one-click fix
one generalist advisor versus a council of department advisors with conflicting priorities
delivery mode: interrupting pop-up, voiced line, or passive panel opened on demand
cooldown and repetition rules per message
accuracy: whether advisors read true state, a lagged view, or a view biased toward their department
dynamics: Advisors act as an embedded tutorial whose value fades as the player's own causal model improves.
Department advisors arguing for opposite policies externalize tradeoffs such as tax revenue versus satisfaction.
When advice is trusted, player builds converge on what the advisor recommends, narrowing strategic variety.
failure_modes: A message keeps firing while the player cannot act on it, so players mute or ignore the advisor entirely.
Advice derived from a single indicator recommends the wrong fix when the cause is an interaction, such as more police when crime is driven by unemployment.
Advisors that are always right reduce the player to following instructions; advisors that are often wrong teach players to ignore all advice.
Lines written for early-game states become irrelevant or wrong at late-game scale.
mechanics.name: Advisors
open_questions: Can a language-model advisor grounded in live state queries answer arbitrary why-questions accurately enough to be trusted, and how should it express uncertainty?
Does advice deliberately biased by an advisor's department or personality produce better decisions than neutral advice?
mechanics.player_experience: The player gets a running diagnosis without reading every graph. Early on advisors teach which variables matter and what usually fixes them; later the player weighs advice against their own model, and conflicting advisors make tradeoffs explicit. Bad or repetitive advice is felt as nagging.
mechanics.summary: In-world advisor characters monitor simulation indicators, summarize problems, and recommend actions.

mechanics.definition: Selecting an individual agent opens a live panel that reads that agent's internal state: need levels, mood and its itemized contributors, current action and its target, queued actions, skills, traits, relationships, health by body part, inventory, and sometimes a log of recent thoughts or events. The mechanic owns only the selection and which fields are exposed; it reads state owned by other mechanics and refreshes each tick or on change. Its key design property is whether it shows reasons (why the agent is doing this) or only values. Canonical forms: The Sims need bars and visible action queue, RimWorld's needs, health, and social tabs with each mood thought listed with its source and expiry, Dwarf Fortress unit thoughts and preferences sheets, and RollerCoaster Tycoon guest windows listing a guest's thoughts, cash, hunger, and nausea.
design_levers: depth of exposure: raw meters, itemized reasons, or a full decision trace
whether each reason lists its source, magnitude, and remaining duration
live updating versus snapshot on open
which variables stay hidden (true personality, latent potential) to preserve uncertainty
whether every agent is inspectable or only a representative sample at large populations
supporting affordances such as follow camera, thought bubbles, and pinned favorites
dynamics: Players trace aggregate problems to individual causes, such as following one hauler to find a pathing bottleneck.
Named, inspectable agents raise the emotional cost of loss, which strengthens permadeath and injury systems.
Exposed reasons create pressure on designers to make the underlying model truthful, since players test it against what the panel says.
failure_modes: Panels with dozens of unranked numbers overwhelm players without telling them what matters.
The panel shows state but not the decision rule, so behavior still looks random even after inspection.

Inspection exposes shortcuts in the agent model; following citizens in SimCity (2013) revealed that agents took the nearest free home and job rather than keeping their own, undermining belief in individual citizens.
At city scale inspecting one agent is unrepresentative, so players cannot diagnose aggregate problems from it.
mechanics.name: Agent inspection
open_questions: For agents driven by language models, what inspection format (plans, memories, rationales) lets players predict behavior rather than just read it?
How much reason exposure maximizes attachment before it turns agents into transparent spreadsheets?
mechanics.player_experience: A crowd becomes individuals. When an agent misbehaves the player clicks it to find out why, reads the cause, and fixes the environment rather than the agent. Reading named thoughts and histories builds attachment and supplies the raw material for player stories.
mechanics.summary: Selecting an agent opens a panel that reveals its needs, mood contributors, current job, and the reasons behind its behavior.

synergy.note: Inspection panels expose the thought list, converting hidden state into narrative.

mechanics.definition: Owns a traversal representation (tile grid, navmesh, or waypoint graph) with per-cell or per-edge movement costs and permissions, plus each agent's current path or a shared direction field. On request a search returns a least-cost route from position to goal; A* (Hart, Nilsson, and Raphael, 1968) expands nodes by cost so far plus an admissible heuristic. Paths are invalidated and recomputed when the map changes or agents block each other. Scale variants trade exactness for speed: Factorio (2019) abstracts each 32x32 chunk into terrain components and runs a reverse resumable A* over them to supply the heuristic for tile-level A*; Supreme Commander 2 searches a portal graph between 10x10 m sectors and shares flow fields so many units read one direction field instead of each searching. Inputs: terrain and floor costs, doors and allowed areas, other agents. Outputs: routes, travel times, and occupancy along routes that feed hauling, traffic, and defense.
design_levers: movement cost per terrain, floor, road, or door type
search method and hierarchy (grid A*, navmesh, hierarchical abstraction, flow fields) and per-tick search budget
repath triggers and frequency when the map or obstacles change
local avoidance between agents (none, steering, reservation) versus passing through each other
agent map knowledge and permissions (full map, explored only, allowed areas, locked doors)
dynamics: Shortest-path choices concentrate trips on a few links, producing congestion that lowers throughput without any explicit traffic rule.
Defenders shape attacker routes with walls and gaps, so layout itself becomes the defense mechanic.
Travel time silently becomes the largest work cost, so compact bases and well-placed stockpiles dominate efficiency.
failure_modes: Agents take absurd detours or get stuck because the cost model or permissions disagree with what the player sees on screen.
Repathing storms after map edits become a late-game slowdown on large colony and factory maps.
Per-unit paths ignore other units and stall at chokepoints; Emerson describes Supreme Commander 2's earlier single-path system compounding collisions into stops.
Deterministic pathing invites exploits such as mazes and wall-hugging layouts that trivialize threats.
mechanics.name: Agent pathfinding
open_questions: Can learned crowd models or mean-field approximations replace per-agent search at city scale while preserving individual route choices?
How much should paths reflect imperfect knowledge and preferences such as scenery or safety rather than shortest cost?
mechanics.player_experience: The player notices pathfinding mostly through layout: where doors, stockpiles, and roads go decides how far agents walk. In defense play the player builds mazes that lengthen enemy routes; in colony sims the player winces as a colonist crosses the map for one item. Failures are visible and comic, so players learn the cost model by watching.
mechanics.summary: Agents compute routes through space using movement costs, and the routes they choose shape congestion, travel time, and access.

mechanics.definition: Each agent holds an experience stock and level per skill. Doing a task adds experience at a rate scaled by learning modifiers; crossing thresholds raises the level, and some games decay unused high levels. Level feeds work speed, success or botch chance, output quality, and minimum-level gates. RimWorld uses levels 0-20; experience to the next level rises from 1,000 at level 0 to 30,000 at level 19; passion sets learning to 35% (none), 100%, or 150%; skills above 9 decay by 30 to 3,600 XP per day; a daily cap of 4,000 XP per skill cuts further gains to 20%; construction speed is 50% plus 15% per level; some backstories make pawns incapable of a work type. The Sims raises skills through objects such as bookshelves and easels and gates promotions on them; Dwarf Fortress dwarves improve by repeating labors. Inputs: task time, learning modifiers. Outputs: speed, quality, eligibility for tasks.
design_levers: experience curve shape and level cap
learning-rate modifiers such as passions, traits, age, and teachers
decay of unused skills and daily learning caps
effect curves per level on speed, quality, and failure chance
hard gates (minimum level, incapable) versus soft penalties
dynamics: Specialization snowballs: the best agent at a job gets assigned it, which raises that skill further and widens gaps.
Losing a specialist opens a capability hole that forces retraining or recruitment; with permadeath this is a common crisis.
Coupled with quality tiers, item value depends on who made it, so assignment becomes an economic decision.
failure_modes: Uncapped or linear growth turns every long-lived agent into a master, flattening differences between characters.
Grinding: players set agents to repeat cheap tasks to farm experience, which RimWorld counters with a daily learning cap.
Steep effect curves make low-skill recruits useless, so new agents are dead weight rather than trainees.
Decay without clear feedback reads as random loss of competence.
mechanics.name: Agent skills
open_questions: Can skills be represented as learned competence (policies that actually improve) rather than numeric multipliers, and does that change player attachment?
Which decay and cap settings keep specialization meaningful without rewarding grinding?
mechanics.player_experience: Agents become individuals with track records. The player assigns specialists, trains newcomers on low-stakes work, and feels the loss when a master crafter dies. Skill growth gives each character a slow progression arc that runs alongside the base's growth.
mechanics.summary: Agents gain skill through practice or training, and skill sets work speed, quality, and access to tasks.

synergy.note: Hiring trades wage cost against skill, and skills grow with time on the roster.
Priorities route skilled agents to the jobs they do best.
Skilled workers produce higher-quality goods.

mechanics.definition: The feed subscribes to simulation events (raid arrived, agent died, contract completed) and to condition predicates over state (food below a threshold, building unpowered, storage full, entity damaged). It owns a list of active alerts, each with type, severity, timestamp, a deduplication key, a location or entity link, and a lifetime. Each tick it adds an alert on the rising edge of a predicate or on an event, merges alerts with the same key, removes condition alerts when the condition clears, and expires event alerts after a timeout or dismissal. Optional rules pause the game or drop speed on chosen types. Canonical forms: RimWorld's severity-colored event letters plus a persistent condition list (low food, colonist needs rescue), Factorio alerts for entities under attack or destroyed, trains out of fuel, and ghosts lacking construction materials, problem icons over buildings and the Chirper feed in Cities: Skylines, Dwarf Fortress announcements, and the Football Manager inbox.
design_levers: event alerts versus persistent condition alerts that clear themselves
severity tiers, color, and sound per alert type
auto-pause or speed-drop rules per alert type
aggregation: one alert for many identical problems versus one per entity
persistence until dismissed versus until the condition clears
click-through to location and player-side filtering
in-fiction framing (social posts, letters) versus neutral system text
dynamics: The alert set encodes what the designer considers a problem, so players optimize to keep icons off rather than toward their own goals.
With auto-pause, alert density sets the effective pacing of a real-time game.
Paired with an event director, alerts announcing incident arrival create a recognizable beat structure of calm, alarm, and response.
failure_modes: Alert fatigue: frequent low-value alerts bury the one that matters, and players miss a fatal problem.
In-fiction feeds read as noise; many Cities: Skylines players hid the Chirper feed with mods.
Predicates near a threshold, such as power just at capacity, flicker and spam add and remove cycles.
Alerts that report symptoms (no goods) rather than causes send players to fix the wrong thing.
mechanics.name: Alerts feed
open_questions: Can a learned salience model rank and merge alerts by predicted consequence so the feed stays useful at megabase or metropolis scale?
Do natural-language digests of many alerts help players more than icons, or do they slow reaction time?
mechanics.player_experience: In a system too large to watch, the feed decides where the player looks. The player triages, jumps the camera to the alert, and learns to dread specific alert types. Auto-pause on alerts turns real-time play into a series of decision points.
mechanics.summary: A notification layer surfaces discrete events and threshold crossings with severity and a link to their location.

mechanics.definition: Owns a herd of individual animals or a count per species, each with growth stage, food state, often affection or mood, and sometimes pregnancy and genes. Each day animals eat from grazing or stored fodder, grow toward maturity, and roll for products such as milk, eggs, or wool and for births; care actions raise affection or mood, which scales yield and quality. Stardew Valley tracks friendship from 0 to 1000 and mood from 0 to 255: unfed animals stop producing but do not die, mood under 70 can skip production, quality products need mood 150, and a nightly birth check governs pregnancies. RimWorld and Dwarf Fortress breed animals that must be fed, sheltered, trained, or slaughtered; Farming Simulator ties livestock productivity to feed. Inputs are feed, housing, and care; outputs are products, meat, and offspring.
design_levers: feed requirement per animal and the balance between grazing and stored fodder
time to maturity and product cycle per species
how care, mood, and affection scale yield and quality
breeding rate and population caps from housing size
losses: disease, predators, exposure, slaughter decisions
dynamics: Feed demand links husbandry to crop fields and storage, especially before winter.
Herds become targets for predators and raids, requiring fences and defense.
Breeding for traits ties husbandry to inheritance and long-term planning.
failure_modes: Unchecked breeding produces runaway herds that eat all fodder and then starve, a recurring colony-sim problem.
Daily care actions with no decisions become chores players automate away or abandon.
Animals that can never die or fall ill turn husbandry into passive income.
mechanics.name: Animal husbandry
open_questions: Can learned animal behavior and animation make individually simulated livestock expressive enough to deepen attachment without bespoke animation per species?
mechanics.player_experience: Routine care with compounding returns. The player builds pens and barns, keeps feed stocked through winter, and turns daily tending into reliable income. Animals can become personal: named, petted, and missed when lost to a predator or a hard winter.
mechanics.summary: Domestic animals are housed, fed, tended, and bred, and they yield products whose quantity and quality depend on their care.

claims.text: The Sims 2 gives each Sim an aspiration with wants and fears, and an elder's remaining lifespan depends on the aspiration meter; The Sims 3 replaced wants and fears with wishes that pay Lifetime Happiness.
The Sims 4 adults take a bonus trait from their chosen aspiration.

mechanics.definition: Owns, per agent, a long-term aspiration (a goal type such as family, knowledge, or fortune), a few open want slots, sometimes paired with fear slots, and a reward stock. A generator refills empty slots by sampling wants from a pool weighted by aspiration, traits, life stage, needs, and recent events; each want is a predicate over simulation state (make a friend, gain a skill level, get promoted) with a point value. When a predicate becomes true the want pays its points and leaves its slot, and a realized fear subtracts. Points feed a meter that shifts mood or behavior and usually a currency for rewards. The Sims 2 set the form: the aspiration biases which wants and fears appear, fulfilled wants fill the aspiration meter, and an elder's remaining lifespan depends on that meter. The Sims 3 replaced it with wishes that pay Lifetime Happiness, and The Sims 4 ties a bonus trait and a goal track to the chosen aspiration. Wants do not decay like needs; unlike a career ladder they are generated from state rather than authored as a fixed sequence, and unlike villager requests they are the agent's own goals.
design_levers: number of open slots and whether fears exist alongside wants
reroll, lock, and dismiss rules for slots
generator weights by aspiration, traits, life stage, and recent events
point value per want and what points buy (meter effects, reward objects, traits)
difficulty and time horizon of individual wants relative to play pace
whether unmet wants cost anything or simply expire
dynamics: Players chase wants that line up across household members, so generated goals couple separate characters' days.
Wants seeded by recent events (a promotion, a new baby) create follow-on arcs, an informal story chain driven by state.
Points buy rewards that make later wants easier to meet, a reinforcing loop toward a comfortable late game.
failure_modes: Wants that need unavailable or off-lot actions clutter the slots and teach players to ignore the panel.
Cheap repeatable wants let players farm points, so the reward store empties early and the meter stops mattering.
Generators that ignore context produce incoherent wants, such as wanting a first date the day after a spouse dies, which breaks the illusion of a mind.
Too many slots turn the panel into a checklist with no choice in it.
mechanics.name: Aspirations and wants
open_questions: Can a language model write wants from an agent's memories and relationships while keeping each want checkable as a predicate over game state?
Do fears add enough drama to justify goals the player cannot fully prevent from failing?
mechanics.player_experience: A stream of small, personal goals. The player reads what each character wants right now, plans the day around one or two of them, and collects a payout when they land, so an open sandbox gains a to-do list that comes from the character rather than the designer. Fears add dread: the player steers away from events the character would hate.
mechanics.summary: An agent's long-term aspiration and current state generate short-horizon wants, and sometimes fears, whose fulfillment pays into a reward meter or currency.

mechanics.definition: Each player runs a local simulation that publishes a small exported state to a server, such as surplus resources, service capacity, pollution, or a snapshot of a town, and periodically imports neighbors' exported state as boundary conditions. Exchanges resolve with delay, so play does not require both players online at once. In SimCity (2013), cities in a region connect by highways, rail, and waterways, trade resources, share services such as garbage collection or health care, see traffic and pollution cross borders, and pool wealth into Great Works such as an arcology; the connection was asynchronous, with brief disruptions tolerated. Animal Crossing island visits and Death Stranding's shared structures are related forms. Inputs: local surpluses and needs. Outputs: imported flows and shared projects.
design_levers: which variables are exported and imported (goods, services, pollution, visitors)
synchronization interval and conflict resolution
region size and how neighbors are matched (friends, public, random)
shared projects that require pooled contributions
fallback behavior when the server or a neighbor is offline
dynamics: Specialization emerges: one city goes industrial or hosts the hospital and the others import those services.
Externalities such as pollution and traffic cross borders, creating friction between players who never speak.
Shared projects create focal points that coordinate otherwise independent players.
failure_modes: Server dependence makes single-player play fragile; SimCity (2013) launched with outages and save problems, and an offline mode came later.
Abandoned neighbor cities leave dependent players short of the services they relied on.
Small play areas forced by the region design made specialization a necessity rather than a choice, which players criticized.
mechanics.name: Asynchronous shared regions
open_questions: Can AI-controlled stand-in neighbors, trained on real player cities, keep regions alive when players leave?
What exchange latency preserves the feeling of a shared region while keeping each player's simulation independent?
mechanics.player_experience: The player is part of a neighborhood without coordinating schedules. They specialize, relying on neighbors for what they lack, and notice others' choices arrive as traffic, pollution, or help. Cooperation feels light because commitments are small and delayed.
mechanics.summary: Separate players' simulations affect each other asynchronously through shared regions, visits, or exchanges of goods and services.

mechanics.definition: Owns the state of a contest in progress (score, clock, possession or positions, fatigue, morale) and each participant's attribute vector and tactical instructions. Each step the engine selects the next event (pass, shot, pitch, overtake) and resolves it by sampling probabilities computed from the involved participants' attributes, the tactics in force, fatigue, and context, then updates state and emits commentary or animation. Football Manager, which continues the Championship Manager series begun in 1992, renders its engine as text, as a 2D pitch from Football Manager 2005, and in 3D from Football Manager 2009; Out of the Park Baseball reports simulated games as text play-by-play; Motorsport Manager resolves races from driver and car ratings with player pit and pace calls. Inputs: lineups, attributes, tactics, in-match interventions. Outputs: results, per-participant statistics, injuries, and form that feed rosters, morale, and finances.
design_levers: event granularity (per possession, per pitch, per lap) and how many events are rendered to the player
mapping from attributes to event probabilities and the weight of randomness relative to ratings
tactical instruction set and how strongly each instruction shifts event probabilities
fatigue, morale, and home-advantage modifiers
in-match interventions such as substitutions, touchline shouts, and pit calls
dynamics: Results feed morale, form, finances, and transfers, so streaks compound into dynasties or collapses.
Communities reverse-engineer engine weights into a tactical meta, which yearly engine revisions then disrupt.
Simulated statistics become scouting data, coupling the engine to player valuation and transfer markets.
failure_modes: One tactic or formation dominates because the engine overweights a parameter, and the player community converges on it.
Low-variance engines make results feel predetermined by ratings; high-variance engines make tactics feel irrelevant.
Rendered visuals that disagree with the underlying event logic undermine trust in the simulation.
Players cannot tell bad luck from bad decisions because the attribute-to-outcome mapping is opaque.
mechanics.name: Attribute-driven match engine
open_questions: Can event models trained on real tracking or event data replace hand-tuned probabilities while keeping tactics legible to players?
Can generated commentary explain why an event happened in terms of attributes and tactics, so players can separate luck from decisions?
mechanics.player_experience: The player is the coach in the stands: setting lineups and tactics, watching a sampled stream of events, and reading results as evidence about whether decisions worked. Upsets feel earned or cruel; across a season noisy results become stories about form, slumps, and tactical identity.
mechanics.summary: Contest outcomes are simulated play by play from participant attributes, tactics, and randomness instead of being played directly.

synergy.note: Hidden attributes make scouting valuable because they drive simulated outcomes (Football Manager).

mechanics.definition: Owns a lot (item, quantity, optional reserve price), the standing bids, and a clock. Bidders submit or raise bids under a format: ascending open outcry, sealed bid, descending price, or a timed listing with a buyout price. When the clock ends or no bidder will go higher, the rule assigns the lot to the winner, transfers money, and settles fees. AI bidders bid up to a valuation computed from their needs and cash. M.U.L.E. (1983) runs real-time auctions for each resource, breaks ties in favor of the trailing player, and lets players who withhold supply raise prices on later turns; its designers replaced land auctions with one free plot per turn because auctioning land fed a runaway loop. MMO auction houses such as World of Warcraft's use timed listings with a minimum bid and an optional buyout price.
design_levers: auction format (ascending, sealed-bid first or second price, descending, timed listing with buyout)
tie-breaking and catch-up rules, such as awarding ties to the trailing player
reserve prices, minimum increments, and listing fees or deposits that act as money sinks
auction duration and whether bidding happens in real time or between turns
AI bidder valuation function and how much cash it holds back
which goods are auctioned versus sold at fixed prices or granted for free
dynamics: Withholding supply from an auction raises clearing prices on later rounds, enabling deliberate shortage play.
Bidding wars between two rivals let a third party buy cheaply elsewhere.
Reserve prices and fees act as money sinks that slow inflation in persistent economies.
failure_modes: Auctioning productive assets such as land lets the richest player buy more production, the snowball M.U.L.E.'s designers removed by granting free plots.
AI bidders with simple valuation rules can be baited into overpaying or never compete, so auctions become trivial.
Long timed auctions in MMOs reward bots and last-second sniping over judgment.
Collusion between human bidders suppresses prices when the rules cannot detect it.
mechanics.name: Auctions
open_questions: Can LLM bidders with private valuations and bluffing make single-player auctions as tense as multiplayer ones?
Which catch-up rules (tie-breaks, budget caps) prevent auction snowballs without feeling arbitrary?
mechanics.player_experience: Reading rivals. The player estimates what a lot is worth to each competitor, decides how far to push the price, and feels the sting of overpaying or the relief of a bargain. In real-time formats such as M.U.L.E. bidding is a test of nerve and timing; in timed listings it becomes patient sniping and undercutting.
mechanics.summary: Goods, land, or rights are allocated by bidding procedures in which players or agents compete on price under rules for timing, ties, and reserves.

mechanics.definition: Owns a global, per-agent, or per-category autonomy setting that gates which actions an agent may select for itself. Each decision cycle the setting filters or reweights the candidate set before action selection: at full autonomy the agent chooses among all actions; at reduced levels only urgent self-care or specific categories remain; at zero the agent idles until ordered. Player orders always take precedence while queued. The Sims (2000) exposes free will as an option, and even with it on, Sims need orders to pay bills, find jobs, exercise, or conceive. RimWorld's drafting switches a colonist from self-assigned work to direct control for combat or emergencies. Inputs: the setting, the order queue, urgency of needs. Outputs: the share of agent time under player versus agent control.
design_levers: number of levels and whether the setting is global, per agent, or per action category
which actions stay autonomous at each level (survival needs, social, self-care)
override rules when player orders conflict with urgent needs
quality of autonomous choices (competent versus deliberately flawed agents)
dynamics: Players run mixed teams of puppets and free agents, adjusting per character and per crisis.
Low-autonomy play exposes needs systems as chores, while high-autonomy play exposes utility-scoring quirks as personality.
With permadeath, the choice to delegate during danger (drafting colonists for a raid) becomes a risk decision.
failure_modes: Autonomous choices are worse than the player's, so players turn autonomy off and drown in micromanagement.
Autonomy that is too competent removes the player's role and turns the game into a screensaver.
Agents override intent at bad moments, such as wandering off mid-task, which reads as disobedience rather than personality.
Unclear boundaries between autonomous and ordered actions make failures hard to attribute.
mechanics.name: Autonomy levels
open_questions: Can language-model agents accept intent-level delegation (keep the house running during the party) as a richer replacement for discrete autonomy levels?
Do players attach more strongly to agents they control or to agents they watch, and which autonomy setting maximizes attachment?
mechanics.player_experience: Lets the player choose how much to micromanage. High autonomy turns play into arranging and watching; low autonomy turns it into puppetry with responsibility for every need. Players switch per situation: autonomy for routine life, manual control for crises and set pieces.
