mechanics.summary: The degree to which agents act on their own is adjustable, from full free will to explicit commands only.

tension.note: Agents with strong free will resist direct commands; designers must decide who is in charge.

claims.text: Factorio's blueprint library keeps a player's blueprints across saves, shares them with other players in multiplayer, and separately holds save-specific game blueprints.

mechanics.definition: A blueprint is a saved snapshot of a region's entities with relative positions, rotations, and configuration (recipes, filters, circuit settings, sometimes tiles). State owned: a library of blueprints plus placed ghosts awaiting construction. Capture copies selected entities into a blueprint; stamping projects its entities at a cursor with rotation or mirroring, checks placement validity, and creates ghost build orders that construction agents or the player fulfill. Export serializes a blueprint to a string or file that other players can import. Canonical form: Factorio blueprints, blueprint books, a personal library that persists across saves and is visible to other players in multiplayer, and exchange strings used by community sites. Others: Dyson Sphere Program and Satisfactory blueprints, Mindustry schematics shared as text, and Space Engineers ship blueprints rebuilt through projectors.
design_levers: unlock timing: available from the start or gated behind progression such as construction robots
what is captured: entities only or also configuration, tiles, and logic
parameterized blueprints that substitute items or values at placement
sharing scope: within a save, across saves, or exported strings and workshop integration
who fulfills placed ghosts: the player by hand or automated builders
validity rules when stamping over obstacles or partial resources
dynamics: Modular, tileable designs become dominant because they stamp cleanly, shaping the visual language of player bases.
Shared blueprint strings create a design culture of named, versioned community layouts.
Stamping lowers the marginal cost of expansion, so growth becomes limited by resources and logistics rather than player time.
failure_modes: Imported meta designs replace the core puzzle, and players report feeling they are executing other people's solutions.
Late unlock makes the repetitive early game tedious and drives players to mods.
Blueprints that break when stamped into slightly different terrain or orientation cost more time than rebuilding by hand.
mechanics.name: Blueprints
open_questions: Can generative models produce valid blueprints from a goal such as a 45 per second green circuit block, and does that remove or relocate the design puzzle?
How should parameterized blueprints be represented so designs adapt to terrain and recipes without becoming full programming?
mechanics.player_experience: Solving a layout once is enough. The player designs a module carefully, then scales it by stamping, which moves attention from placing pieces to designing systems. Imported community designs let newcomers skip solved problems; some players feel that copying removes the puzzle.
mechanics.summary: Player-made layouts can be saved, stamped as build orders, copied, and shared as text or files.

synergy.note: Stamping solved belt layouts lets players scale proven designs instead of re-solving them.
Shareable blueprint strings created whole communities of design exchange.

claims.text: In Football Manager the board judges the manager's performance.

mechanics.definition: Owns a set of expectations (league finish, cup progress, budget balance, profit, playing style, youth development) imposed or agreed at the start of a season or term, and a confidence stock held by an evaluator such as a board, owner, chairman, or fan base. After each match, report, or period the stock moves by the gap between results and expectations, weighted by importance and recency; crossing warning levels triggers meetings, ultimatums, or budget cuts, and falling below the floor ends the job. Expectations are re-set from the organization's reputation and resources, so success raises the bar. Football Manager has the board judge the manager's performance and, with fan confidence, decide whether the manager is sacked; other sports management games set owner or chairman goals for each season. It differs from elections, where an electorate decides tenure at fixed dates, and from scenario-objectives, which test a fixed goal at a deadline; here a continuously updated stock can end the job at any time.
design_levers: how expectations are set: imposed from reputation or negotiated with the player
weight per result and how fast older results fade
warning thresholds and the events they trigger (meetings, ultimatums, budget cuts)
firing threshold and whether the player continues in a new job
separate evaluators (board, owner, fans) and how they combine
grace period after hiring
dynamics: Players manage expectations as well as results, for example by accepting modest targets to buy safety.
High-variance match engines produce sudden sackings that become career stories.
Being fired and hired by another club turns failure into a career path instead of a game over.
failure_modes: Expectations re-set too aggressively after success make long tenures impossible, punishing good play.
Sackings driven by short streaks feel arbitrary when simulated results have high variance.
Confidence that forgives too easily makes the threat vanish after one good season.
Hidden weights leave players unsure which goal actually matters.
mechanics.name: Board confidence
open_questions: Can language-model board members with distinct priorities negotiate expectations with the player in conversation and remember broken promises?
What weighting of recent results makes sackings feel deserved under a high-variance match simulation?
mechanics.player_experience: A clock on the player's job. Every result moves a meter the player does not fully control, so a run of bad form becomes existential and a promised top-four finish hangs over every match. Success raises expectations, so security never fully arrives.
mechanics.summary: An evaluator such as a board, owner, or chairman sets expectations, updates a confidence stock from results against them, and fires the player below a threshold.

mechanics.definition: Owns one money stock and a ledger of flow categories. Each accounting period income (taxes, fees, sales, trade) is added and expenses (upkeep, wages, service funding, interest) are subtracted. Players often set a funding fraction per department, and service effectiveness scales with it. In Micropolis, the open-source SimCity engine, the collection every 48 city-time steps computes revenue = population x average land value / 120 x tax rate x a difficulty factor, sets required police and fire funds at 100 per station and road funds per road and rail tile, and converts the fraction actually paid into RoadEffect (0-32) and PoliceEffect and FireEffect (0-1000), so underfunded roads decay and coverage shrinks. A negative balance leads to loans, bonds, bankruptcy, or game over; SimCity 2000 ends the game after extreme deficit spending.
design_levers: accounting period length and whether flows post continuously or at fixed ticks
which expense categories are player-adjustable and how effectiveness scales with the funding fraction
upkeep per building relative to the revenue it enables
consequence of a negative balance (borrowing, forced cuts, bankruptcy, or game over)
how much ledger detail and forecasting the interface shows
dynamics: Surpluses fund expansion that raises both revenue and upkeep, so cash pressure returns at each growth stage.
Underfunding one service degrades a dependent system (roads, crime, fires), which later lowers the revenue base.
Periodic settlement creates sawtooth cash curves and end-of-period scrambles.
failure_modes: Upkeep that scales slower than revenue makes money irrelevant by mid-game, a common complaint about Cities: Skylines.
Funding sliders whose effects are delayed or hidden teach players to cut services without visible cost until a collapse.
Fixed upkeep with no link to growth produces an early cash trap with no recovery path.
mechanics.name: Treasury and budget
open_questions: Can an LLM advisor explain a deficit as a causal chain through the ledger well enough to replace spreadsheet-style budget panels?
What upkeep-to-revenue curve keeps money a meaningful constraint into the late game?
mechanics.player_experience: Periodic reckoning. The player watches a running balance and a monthly or yearly ledger, trims service budgets to stay solvent, and decides when a surplus should become new construction. Shortfalls show up as visible decay: crumbling roads, slower fire response, unpaid staff.
mechanics.summary: A money stock with income and expense flows such as taxes, upkeep, wages, and service funding; a negative balance leads to debt or failure.

synergy.note: Debt extends the treasury in time, trading future flexibility for present growth.

mechanics.definition: A recipe or activity emits one or more secondary outputs alongside its primary product, at a fixed ratio per cycle or per capita. The byproduct accumulates in a local output buffer or tile stock; when that stock hits a cap, the producer stalls, degrades, or releases it into the environment. The player must route it to a consumer, a sink (incinerator, landfill, vent), or a converter. In Oxygen Not Included a Natural Gas Generator burning 90 g/s of natural gas yields 800 W plus 67.5 g/s of polluted water and 22.5 g/s of carbon dioxide that must be piped away or vented into the base. In Factorio oil processing yields heavy oil, light oil, and petroleum gas together, so an unconsumed output backs up and halts the refinery. In Cities: Skylines buildings generate garbage that trucks must collect or it accumulates and flags the building as a problem. Inputs: production cycles or population. Outputs: a waste stock and an impairment signal (stall, pollution, illness, abandonment).
design_levers: byproduct ratio per cycle and whether it scales with efficiency upgrades
buffer size before the producer stalls or starts releasing waste into the environment
whether the byproduct is pure waste, a sellable good, or an input to another chain
available sinks and their costs, such as incinerators, landfills, vents, or voiding
the impairment when unhandled: production stall, pollution, disease, morale loss, or abandonment
dynamics: Waste outputs become inputs elsewhere, so industrial clusters form around reuse loops (polluted water to a water sieve in Oxygen Not Included, heavy oil cracked to light oil in Factorio).
Disposal capacity becomes a hidden ceiling on growth, separate from input supply.
Coupled with pollution spread, unhandled byproducts shift cost onto neighbors and land value.
Players overbuild storage for byproducts as a buffer, trading space for time before the next fix.
failure_modes: A cheap sink that destroys anything removes the problem and turns the mechanic into a one-time build tax.
Byproducts with no use and no penalty become clutter that players ignore.
Fixed-ratio multi-output recipes deadlock silently when one output has no consumer, and the stall appears far from its cause.
Waste that only matters late, such as a full landfill or spent nuclear fuel, surprises players who built for hours without a disposal plan.
mechanics.name: Byproducts and waste
open_questions: Can a generative chemistry model produce byproduct sets for new recipes that stay balanced without hand tuning?
What ratio of waste to useful output keeps disposal a design problem rather than a chore?
mechanics.player_experience: Every new building arrives with a cleanup problem attached. The player learns to ask where the waste goes before placing a producer, and designs sinks, reuse loops, or disposal districts. A full output buffer stopping a whole line teaches that the unwanted product sets the pace of the wanted one.
mechanics.summary: Production emits secondary outputs such as sludge, garbage, heat, or spent fuel that must be handled or they impair the system.

synergy.note: Waste outputs are the sources that pollution diffusion spreads.

claims.text: Tamagotchi (1996) has Hunger, Happy, and Training meters, life stages, and an adult form that depends on care.
Princess Maker 2 covers the daughter's life from age 10 to 18 and has 74 endings.

mechanics.definition: Owns, per raised creature or character, a running history of care and attributes (tallies of neglect and discipline, stat values, behavior counts) and a developmental table that maps ranges of that history to next-stage forms or final outcomes. Between stages the history accumulates from care actions and scheduled activities; at each stage boundary the table is evaluated, by first matching branch or best score, and the chosen form replaces the old one, setting appearance, stats, behavior, lifespan, or an ending. Tamagotchi (1996) chooses its adult character from the quality of care it received, so neglect yields a different creature rather than only a sick one. Princess Maker 2 (1993) develops the daughter's attributes from age 10 to 18 and then selects one of 74 career endings from her attributes and history. It differs from creature-care, which owns need meters and care actions; from lifecycle-aging, whose stages advance without branching; and from trait-inheritance, where form comes from the parents' genes rather than the individual's own history.
design_levers: which history variables are tracked and how they are weighted
number of stage boundaries and branches per boundary
threshold placement and whether ties resolve by priority or chance
visibility of the table (hidden, hinted, or shown)
whether later care can redeem an early bad branch
how different branches are mechanically, from cosmetic to changes in stats, lifespan, or ending
dynamics: Players compare outcomes socially (which character did yours become), turning private care into shared stories.
Replays to collect branches convert one raising loop into a collection game.
Players reverse-engineer the tables, and community guides become part of the game's culture.
failure_modes: Hidden tables push optimization to wikis and walkthroughs, after which players follow a recipe instead of raising.
Branches that differ only cosmetically make care history feel irrelevant.
Early branches that cannot be recovered punish new players for mistakes they could not understand.
A single best branch turns the table into a target and removes variety.
mechanics.name: Care-dependent development
open_questions: Can generative models produce a distinct form or ending for every care history, and do players value that over a small set of collectible authored branches?
How much of the table should be visible so that care feels intentional without becoming a recipe?
mechanics.player_experience: Raising with consequences. Every feeding, scolding, lesson, or missed call writes into a history the player cannot fully see, and the reveal at the next stage passes judgment on it. Players replay to see other branches, compare results with friends, and look up the tables to aim for a particular form or ending.
mechanics.summary: A creature's or character's accumulated care or attribute history selects which form or outcome it develops into at each stage boundary, from a fixed branching table.

claims.text: In The Sims 2 adult careers have ten levels and teen careers three; promotion requires advancing three skills, enough household friends, and high mood, and missing work two days in a row causes firing.

mechanics.definition: A career is an ordered list of levels, each with a title, pay, schedule, and promotion requirements. State owned: per character, current career and level, and a job performance meter. Update rule: each work period, performance changes based on attendance and inputs such as mood, skills, or task completion; when performance and the next level's requirements are met, the character is promoted; very low performance or missed shifts cause demotion or firing. Inputs come from other mechanics (skills, relationships, needs); outputs are income, schedule, and status. Canonical form: The Sims 2, where adult careers have ten levels, teen careers three, promotion requires advances in three skills, a number of household friends, and high mood, and missing work two days in a row gets a Sim fired; The Sims 4 adds daily career tasks and branching tracks.
design_levers: number of levels and spacing of requirements
requirement types: skills, relationships, mood, or task completion
performance meter rate and decay
branching tracks at upper levels
random work events with choices, such as The Sims chance cards
pay and schedule curve across levels
dynamics: Career requirements route characters' free time into skill and friend grinding, coupling work to social and needs systems.
Schedule conflicts between household members' careers create household logistics problems.
Promotions raise income and enable home upgrades, a reinforcing loop toward comfort.
failure_modes: Requirements become a checklist that drains spontaneity from life simulation.
Rabbit-hole careers where the Sim leaves the lot make the career invisible to play.
Pay grows faster than costs, so money stops mattering by mid-career.
mechanics.name: Career ladder
open_questions: Can generated workplaces with colleagues, tasks, and politics replace authored rabbit-hole careers without large writing costs?
Does requirement opacity, like a real workplace, make careers more engaging than explicit checklists?
mechanics.player_experience: A long-term arc for one character. The player schedules skill-building and socializing around work, watches the performance bar before a promotion, and feels the status jump of a new title and pay. It gives sandbox life a direction.
mechanics.summary: Characters advance through ranked job levels by meeting skill, relationship, and performance requirements.

claims.text: Victoria 3 uses a nested tooltip system in which highlighted terms inside a tooltip open further tooltips, a system introduced by Crusader Kings III.
Victoria 3 UX work repositioned tooltips so players can move into a nested tooltip without opening another, and added military tooltips that break down battle calculations.

mechanics.definition: Any displayed derived value (mood, stability, price, income, work speed, battle strength) can be hovered to list its contributing terms, each with a label, source, sign, and magnitude, usually as base plus additive modifiers times multiplicative modifiers. Terms that are themselves derived or that name a game concept can be hovered again, opening a nested tooltip. The mechanic owns no simulation state but requires the simulation to compute values as explicit lists of labeled modifiers rather than opaque formulas. Update rule: on hover, read the modifier list for the value, sort and render it, and attach hover targets to sub-terms. Canonical forms: Paradox grand strategy (Europa Universalis IV, Stellaris), Crusader Kings III, which introduced nested tooltips on highlighted terms that Victoria 3 adopted, Victoria 3 tooltips breaking down battle calculations, RimWorld info-card stat breakdowns (skill and capacity factors behind work speed), and Civilization yield breakdowns.
design_levers: recursion depth: one level of breakdown versus nested tooltips on every term
whether tooltips can be pinned or locked so the player can move into them
which modifiers are hidden from the breakdown, if any
presentation of additive versus multiplicative terms, ordering, and rounding
whether each modifier shows its remaining duration
glossary links from terms to concept explanations
dynamics: Full transparency speeds up optimization and exploit discovery, pushing play toward spreadsheet min-maxing.
Because each new effect appears in breakdowns automatically, modifier architectures are easy for modders to extend legibly.
Players learn the simulation's causal graph by walking tooltips, which lowers the need for external wikis.
failure_modes: Late-game modifier stacks grow into walls of numbers that no longer explain anything.
Rounded or partial terms that do not sum to the displayed value erode trust in the whole interface.
Values with clamps, caps, or nonlinear interactions are presented as simple sums and mislead.
Hover-dependent design moves essential information off the main screen and works poorly with controllers and touch.
mechanics.name: Causal breakdown tooltips
open_questions: When values come from a learned simulator instead of modifier lists, can attribution methods produce breakdowns players trust?
Do counterfactual tooltips (what single change would flip this outcome) teach faster than additive breakdowns?
mechanics.player_experience: The player can interrogate any number until the lever appears. Opaque systems become debuggable: why is stability falling, which modifier expires next, what would fix it. Players who enjoy optimization dig through several levels; others glance at the top line.
mechanics.summary: Hovering a derived value shows the named modifiers that produce it, and terms inside the tooltip can be hovered in turn.

synergy.note: Itemized modifiers are only legible when tooltips decompose them (Paradox titles).

mechanics.definition: Owns one aggregate score (or one per district or class) computed each evaluation period from service levels, problems, and events, usually smoothed toward its previous value. Downstream systems read it: growth and migration, productivity, tax tolerance, election odds, and unrest. In Micropolis, the SimCity engine, a yearly evaluation sums seven problem values (crime, pollution, housing cost as 0.7 x average land value, taxes as rate x 10, traffic, unemployment, fires), maps the sum to a 0-1000 score, multiplies it by penalties for missing stadium, airport, or seaport (0.85 each), underfunded roads, police, and fire, and the share of unpowered zones, adjusts for population growth, and averages it with last year's score; an approval poll then gives 100 citizens a yes with probability score / 1000. Frostpunk (2018) splits the score into Hope and Discontent, and the game ends in revolt if hope stays too low or discontent too high for too long.
design_levers: which inputs enter the score and their weights
smoothing or averaging period, which sets how quickly fixes show up
thresholds where satisfaction triggers growth, emigration, strikes, or game over
single score versus separate scores per class, district, or faction
how causes are explained (complaint lists, thoughts, polls, advisors)
dynamics: Low satisfaction drives emigration, which lowers demand for services and can partly restore satisfaction for those who stay.
Satisfaction tied to productivity creates spirals where unhappy workers produce less and services decline further.
Scores averaged over time let a short crisis pass without punishment but punish sustained neglect.
failure_modes: A single number hides which problem matters, so players chase the wrong fix without a breakdown view.
Easy maximization by stacking one cheap amenity makes satisfaction irrelevant.
Long smoothing makes improvements feel unrewarded and pushes players to over-correct.
mechanics.name: Citizen satisfaction
open_questions: Can LLM-voiced citizens explain their dissatisfaction in specific, accurate terms that point to real causes in the simulation?
Is one aggregate score better or worse for play than many per-group scores when citizens can explain themselves?
mechanics.player_experience: A report card on the whole system. The player watches one number rise and fall, digs into the complaint list or overlays to find the cause, and fixes the top problem. In crisis games like Frostpunk it becomes the meter the player is always defending.
mechanics.summary: An aggregate satisfaction score computed from services, conditions, and events modulates growth, productivity, and unrest.

synergy.note: Low satisfaction accumulates into unrest; unrest further lowers satisfaction.
Satisfaction becomes votes, tying tenure to welfare (Tropico).
Satisfied populations attract migrants; dissatisfied ones leave.

claims.text: Stardew Valley's Community Center has six rooms and thirty bundles; completing rooms repairs the quarry bridge, greenhouse, minecarts, and bus, and a Joja membership replaces bundles with payments.

mechanics.definition: The game defines named sets of collectibles (items, fish, insects, fossils, species, recipes) and tracks which members the player has obtained, donated, or observed. State owned: per set, a membership checklist and completion state. Update rule: when the player acquires or submits a qualifying item, mark it; when a set is complete, grant a reward or unlock. Collection drives engagement with other systems because members are spread across seasons, locations, and rarities. Canonical forms: Stardew Valley's Community Center, with six rooms and thirty bundles whose rewards repair the quarry bridge, greenhouse, minecarts, and bus, Animal Crossing: New Horizons' museum and Critterpedia, and Viva Pinata's species journal with per-species visit, resident, and romance requirements.
design_levers: set size and rarity distribution of members
seasonal, weather, or location gating of members
reward type: functional unlocks, cosmetics, or none
fixed versus randomized set contents, such as Stardew Valley remixed bundles
whether items are consumed by submission
visibility of missing members as silhouettes or hints
dynamics: Collection targets route player attention through seasons, weather, and locations they would otherwise skip.
Players share calendars and spreadsheets of where and when members appear.
Alternative completion routes, such as the Joja membership in Stardew Valley, frame collection as a moral choice.
failure_modes: The last few rare members take far longer than the rest, turning completion into a grind.
Members missable for a season or year punish players who fall behind.
Functional rewards locked behind collection force players who dislike collecting through it.
mechanics.name: Collection goals
open_questions: Can generated collectible sets tied to world state, such as species that evolved in this run, keep collection goals meaningful in procedural worlds?
What rarity curve keeps the final members exciting rather than grinding?
mechanics.player_experience: A gentle, open checklist. The player plans around a missing fish that appears only in rain in autumn, feels a click when a set completes, and has a reason to explore every corner of the simulation.
mechanics.summary: Catalogs of items, species, or bundles give the player sets to complete for rewards or recognition.

claims.text: Infinite Craft starts from water, fire, wind, and earth; a new pair is generated by Llama 2 or Llama 3.1 with an emoji under a twenty-token cap and stored so all players get the same result, and new results earn a First Discovery label.

mechanics.definition: Owns a recipe graph that maps combinations of elements, usually unordered pairs, to results, the set of elements the player has found, and per-recipe discovery records. A combine action looks up the chosen inputs: if a recipe exists the result joins the player's set, first-time results are announced, and the new element becomes an input for further combinations; if none exists nothing happens or a small cost is paid. The graph is hidden, so the loop is experimentation, and progress is counted in elements found rather than items used. Infinite Craft (2024) starts from water, fire, wind, and earth and has no fixed graph: on a cache miss a language model (Llama 2, later Llama 3.1) names the result, capped at twenty tokens, with an emoji; the result is stored so every player gets the same answer, and the player who triggered it earns a First Discovery label. Little Alchemy and Doodle God use authored graphs. It differs from hand-crafting, where known recipes turn carried components into useful items at workstations, and from generative-content, which owns the model call rather than the discovery loop.
design_levers: graph size and depth, authored or generated
number of inputs per combination and whether order matters
cost of a failed combination
hint systems and whether the count of remaining recipes is shown
shared first-discovery records and leaderboards
whether elements have any use beyond further combination
dynamics: Each discovery enlarges the input set, so the number of untried pairs grows roughly with the square of elements found.
A shared cache turns discovery into a race for First Discoveries and produces community lists of paths to rare results.
Players form folk theories about how the graph or the model reasons and test them systematically.
failure_modes: Without hints, players brute-force every pair or consult a list, which ends the discovery loop.
Authored results that do not follow from their inputs feel arbitrary.
Generated graphs drift into nonsense or offensive results and need moderation.
Elements with no use beyond combining make the collection feel hollow once novelty fades.
mechanics.name: Combination discovery
open_questions: Can generated combination results carry mechanical properties that make them useful inside a simulation, rather than only names?
What hint density keeps experimentation fun without turning it into lookup?
mechanics.player_experience: Curiosity as the whole loop. The player tries pairs on a hunch, laughs at or argues with the result, and chases rare elements by reasoning about what the designer or the model would think. Each find opens new combinations, so the field of untried ideas keeps growing.
mechanics.summary: The player combines owned elements to discover the products of a hidden recipe graph, and finding recipes is itself the goal.

claims.text: Zach Barth designed SpaceChem's global histograms so players could check their solutions without feeling overwhelmed by the top players a leaderboard would list.
Opus Magnum ranks solutions on cycles, cost, and area, and players combine them in an unofficial sum statistic.
Zachtronics deliberately offers no in-game rewards for optimization in Opus Magnum, so players who optimize do so for intrinsic reasons.

mechanics.definition: After a solution passes validation, the game computes several independent metrics that trade off against each other and shows the player's value on each as a marker on a histogram of all players' (or friends') values for that puzzle. State owned: per-puzzle score distributions aggregated on a server, plus the player's best per metric. Update rule: on completion, simulate the solution, compute metrics, upload them, and fetch the current distributions. The metrics come from a design-evaluation mechanic; this mechanic owns only the population comparison. Canonical forms are Zachtronics games: SpaceChem ranks instructions, cycles, and reactors, and Zach Barth designed its global histograms so players could check a solution without being overwhelmed by the top players a leaderboard lists; Opus Magnum compares cost, cycles, and area; TIS-100, Shenzhen I/O, Infinifactory, and Exapunks use the same pattern.
design_levers: number of metrics and how strongly they trade off against each other
global distribution versus friends-only comparison
bin width and handling of outliers or exploit scores
per-metric personal bests versus recognition of Pareto-optimal combinations
whether any reward is attached to good scores (Zachtronics deliberately attaches none)
dynamics: Players replay solved puzzles to move their marker, extending content life without new content.
Communities build external record trackers for Pareto frontiers that the in-game histograms do not show.
Friend comparison produces asynchronous rivalry without direct competition.
failure_modes: Metrics that do not trade off collapse into one dominant solution, and the histograms show a single spike.
Exploit or bugged solutions create impossible scores that distort the left tail.
Late puzzles are attempted only by skilled survivors, so average players appear below median on every metric.
Independent per-metric bars ignore balanced solutions; Opus Magnum players invented an unofficial sum metric to score them.
mechanics.name: Comparative histograms
open_questions: Can distributions seeded by automated solvers before launch give useful comparison targets without discouraging human players?
Does showing a Pareto frontier instead of per-metric histograms change which tradeoffs players explore?
mechanics.player_experience: Instead of a rank, the player sees where they sit in a crowd on each axis. A solution that is slow but cheap still feels good, and a visible tail of better scores invites returning to a solved puzzle to shave cycles. Comparison is social but low in intimidation.
mechanics.summary: A player's solution is plotted against distributions of other players' scores on several metrics.

synergy.note: Multi-metric ratings become social when plotted against everyone else's solutions (Opus Magnum).
Open-ended programming puzzles gain replay value from optimization histograms.

tension.note: Directed randomness makes scores incomparable across players.

mechanics.definition: Each host (agent, building, settlement, or country) carries a disease state from a small compartment set, usually susceptible, infected, recovered or immune, and dead. Each tick infected hosts transmit to susceptible contacts with a probability per contact (agent-based) or at a rate proportional to infected times susceptible (aggregate), and leave infection at a recovery or death rate. Inputs are contact structure (adjacency, shared rooms, trade and travel links), host resistance, and interventions such as quarantine, vaccination, or medicine; outputs are cases, deaths, and lost labor. Kermack and McKendrick showed that an epidemic occurs only above a threshold set by infectivity and recovery rates. Plague Inc. spreads a player-evolved pathogen between countries until a cure completes; Theme Hospital has contagious patients who infect others inside the hospital; World of Warcraft's 2005 Corrupted Blood debuff spread by proximity and escaped its raid through suspended pets and fast travel to cities.
design_levers: transmission probability per contact or aggregate rate, and which contacts count (adjacency, shared rooms, trade routes, flights)
infectious period, incubation length, and whether carriers can be asymptomatic
recovery, death, and immunity rules, including whether recovery confers lasting immunity
intervention set and costs: quarantine, closing borders or ports, vaccination, treatment
spatial resolution: per agent, per building, per settlement, or per country
how much disease state is shown: case counts, overlays, or only visible symptoms
dynamics: Hubs such as cities, hospitals, and transport nodes become superspreaders, so network topology matters more than total population.
Sick workers leave jobs, cutting production of the food, medicine, or care that would end the outbreak.
Agents or players bypass quarantine for convenience, so enforcement becomes its own problem, as in the Corrupted Blood outbreak.
Depletion of susceptible hosts ends waves on its own, producing boom-and-bust waves that can look like successful policy.
failure_modes: A reproduction number far above any real pathogen makes spread unstoppable and interventions pointless; Lofgren and Fefferman noted Corrupted Blood's exceeded any observed real disease.
Contact channels the designer did not model, such as Corrupted Blood's suspended pets and fast travel, carry infection past intended boundaries.
Hidden infection with no leading indicator reads as a random wipeout rather than a failed response.
Aggregate compartments with no spatial structure give every outbreak the same curve, so the player learns one fixed response.
mechanics.name: Contagion
open_questions: Can LLM-driven agents produce plausible behavioral responses to outbreaks (compliance, panic, rumor) that change the effective contact rate in play?
What is the minimum contact structure that still makes intervention placement a meaningful spatial decision?
mechanics.player_experience: Watching an invisible quantity become visible too late. Early cases look harmless, then counts climb faster than responses can be built, so the player learns to act on leading indicators: isolating carriers, closing links, stockpiling medicine, or, in Plague Inc., keeping symptoms mild so the disease spreads widely before lethality alerts the world. Most responses trade economic activity against spread.
mechanics.summary: Disease spreads between agents or regions via contact rates and moves hosts through compartments such as susceptible, infected, and recovered.

synergy.note: Health coverage determines whether outbreaks are contained.

mechanics.definition: A creation is serialized to a compact format, uploaded to a shared catalog with metadata, and ranked by downloads, ratings, or curation; other players browse and import it, or the game pulls catalog items into their worlds automatically. Spore uploaded every creature, vehicle, and building to the Sporepedia, ranked items by downloads, and redistributed them to populate other players' galaxies, with only a few kilobytes per item because the game rebuilds each creation procedurally from its template; it passed 100 million creations by May 2009, and players could filter or ban user content. Steam Workshop for Cities: Skylines, Planet Coaster blueprints, and Factorio blueprint strings are other forms. Inputs: serialized creations. Outputs: imported content and creator reputation.
design_levers: serialization format and size, such as procedural templates versus full assets
ranking and discovery signals (downloads, ratings, curation, subscriptions)
automatic versus opt-in import into other players' worlds
moderation tools and content filters
attribution and feedback to creators
dynamics: A small share of creators produce most of the popular content.
Shared blueprints spread optimal designs quickly, which compresses the discovery phase for later players.
Communities form around creator challenges and showcases.
failure_modes: Offensive or infringing uploads spread fast without moderation; Spore needed filters and in-game bans.
Popularity rankings concentrate attention on a few creators and bury new work.
Imported content that breaks balance or performance degrades the importer's game.
mechanics.name: Content sharing
open_questions: Can models classify and moderate uploaded creations at scale with fewer false positives than keyword or report systems?
How should catalogs recommend shared content without concentrating attention on a few top creators?
mechanics.player_experience: Creators build for an audience and check how their work spreads; browsers get far more variety than the developer shipped. Seeing another player's creature walk through your world, or importing a polished city block, makes the game feel populated.
mechanics.summary: Player creations such as buildings, creatures, or blueprints are uploaded, browsed, rated, and imported into other players' games.

synergy.note: Shared first discoveries give generated content social value (Infinite Craft).
Mods need distribution; sharing platforms need mods.

mechanics.definition: Owns a pool of offers, each with a requirement (cargo type and quantity, a service, or an object meeting a spec), an origin and destination or a client, a deadline, a payout, and often a penalty and a reputation gate. Offers are generated from templates and current simulation state, sit on a board until they expire, and are accepted by the player. On completion the rule checks the requirement, pays out (often scaled by distance, cargo value, or speed), and updates reputation; lateness or abandonment forfeits pay or charges a penalty. Euro Truck Simulator 2's freight market, Elite Dangerous mission boards, Farming Simulator contracts, Car Mechanic Simulator repair orders, and Transport Tycoon's time-limited subsidies are common forms.
design_levers: payout formula (distance, cargo value, urgency, risk) relative to running costs
deadline tightness and the penalty for lateness or abandonment
offer generation: random templates versus real shortages in the simulation
reputation or rank gates that unlock higher-paying work
number of simultaneous contracts allowed and board refresh rate
dynamics: Players chain contracts into loops that minimize empty legs, producing self-discovered trade circuits.
Reputation gating creates a ladder where risky early work buys access to lucrative later work.
When contracts are generated from real shortages, completing them dampens the shortage that created them.
failure_modes: Templated contracts detached from simulation state feel like grind, since taking the best payout per minute is the only decision.
Abandon-and-refresh exploits let players cherry-pick outliers when boards regenerate too freely.
Payouts that outscale costs make every contract profitable and remove route planning.
mechanics.name: Contracts and orders
open_questions: Do contracts generated by a language model from live simulation state (a town short of grain, a rival's broken supply line) feel less like grind than templated ones?
Can open-ended commissions be judged by learned evaluators, such as a model scoring whether a built structure meets a client's brief?
mechanics.player_experience: A steady menu of concrete goals. The player scans offers, weighs payout against distance, risk, and time, chains jobs so trips are never empty, and races deadlines. Contracts turn an open sandbox into a sequence of short, legible tasks.
mechanics.summary: Discrete jobs with requirements, deadlines, and payouts, such as deliveries or commissions, drive income and planning.

synergy.note: Contracts give routes a purpose and a deadline.

mechanics.definition: Belts form directed chains of tiles; each tile holds a fixed number of item slots per lane and moves items forward at a tier-dependent speed. Items enter from inserters, machines, or side-loading and exit at the end, onto another belt, or into a machine. Splitters divide and merge flows, often with priority and filter settings; undergrounds and bridges cross other belts. Factorio holds 4 items per lane per tile and carries 15, 30, 45, or 60 items per second across both lanes for transport, fast, express, and turbo belts. Internally it groups adjacent belts into transport lines and stores the gaps between items, so a free-flowing line updates only its end gaps each tick. Satisfactory, Dyson Sphere Program, and Mindustry use similar belt tiers, and Shapez raises belt speed through upgrades. Inputs: items placed on belts. Outputs: items delivered at a throughput capped by the slowest segment.
design_levers: throughput per tier and number of lanes
splitter, merger, and priority or filter options
crossing options such as undergrounds, bridges, or vertical lifts
item density and whether mixed items share a lane
belt cost and unlock schedule
dynamics: Main-bus and ratio-block conventions emerge from throughput caps, and players share them as blueprints.
Belt saturation sets factory module sizes, so each tier upgrade reshapes layouts.
Mixed-item belts create sushi designs and clogging failure modes.
failure_modes: Spaghetti layouts become unreadable and players stop understanding their own factory.
Lane imbalance and side-loading rules are opaque without wikis.
Belt counts at large scale cost simulation time; Factorio's transport-line rewrite was made to cut this cost.
mechanics.name: Conveyor transport
open_questions: Could layout assistants that propose belt routing under player constraints keep the puzzle while removing tedium?
What is the smallest set of belt primitives that still supports deep layout optimization?
mechanics.player_experience: Layout as the main puzzle. Players route belts around each other, balance lanes, and design compact buses, and they can see throughput problems as gaps or backed-up lines. A compressed belt feeding a full row of machines is a visible proof of a correct design.
mechanics.summary: Items move continuously on belts or lanes with throughput limits, splitters, merges, and priorities.

synergy.note: Belts make recipe chains spatial, turning ratios into a layout puzzle (Factorio, Satisfactory).

claims.text: In Rebel Inc. the more initiatives the player funds from the monthly budget, the more corruption and inflation rise, and a governance tab offers anti-corruption measures.

mechanics.definition: Owns a corruption level per polity, region, or city and the rule that turns it into losses. Each period the level rises with drivers such as the volume of spending or programs, distance from the seat of government, the number of administered territories, or weak institutions, and falls with countermeasures such as anti-corruption policies, courthouses, audits, or dedicated spending; some games accumulate it as a stock with slow decay, others recompute it each turn from current conditions. A share that grows with the level is then removed from tax revenue, trade, production, or program effectiveness, or added to costs. Rebel Inc. (2018) makes corruption a side effect of governing: the more civilian initiatives the player funds, the more corruption and inflation rise, and a governance tab offers anti-corruption measures. Civilization (1991) and Europa Universalis IV use other forms. It differs from taxation, which sets the rate of collection, and from stability-unrest, which owns grievance; corruption owns the leak between what the state raises and what it gets to use.
design_levers: drivers of corruption (spending volume, distance, territory count, institution quality)
what leaks and how much: revenue, output, program effectiveness, or costs
countermeasures and their price (policies, buildings, dedicated spending)
accumulated stock with decay versus a level recomputed each period
visibility, from a shown meter to losses visible only in the ledger
dynamics: Corruption caps efficient size, since each additional city, territory, or program returns less, a balancing loop on expansion.
Spending to win support raises corruption that erodes the budget for further spending, as in Rebel Inc.
Players invest in countermeasures first in regions far from the center, which shapes expansion order.
failure_modes: One cheap countermeasure, a single building or policy, zeroes corruption and removes the mechanic from play.
A flat percentage loss with no driver the player can influence feels like an arbitrary tax rather than a decision.
Distance-based corruption punishes spread-out realms so hard that one empire shape dominates.
Leaks without a breakdown make budgets feel randomly short.
mechanics.name: Corruption leakage
open_questions: Can corruption be modeled as agents (officials, contractors) who skim and can be investigated, rather than as a percentage, while staying readable?
Which drivers make corruption a strategic constraint rather than a flat tax?
mechanics.player_experience: Growth carries a hidden tax. The player watches part of every budget vanish, weighs how much to spend fighting it, and learns that expanding programs or territory faster than institutions can follow makes each new unit of spending worth less.
mechanics.summary: A corruption level driven by spending, administrative reach, or size removes a share of revenue or output until countermeasures bring it down.

mechanics.definition: Owns one or a few creatures, each with need meters (hunger, happiness, hygiene, health, discipline), a life stage, and often an affection or obedience value. Meters decay in game or real time, and the player restores them with direct care actions: feeding, cleaning, playing, giving medicine, or scolding. Neglect accumulates into sickness, a worse adult form, running away, or death. Tamagotchi (1996) shows hunger and happy meters and a discipline meter, leaves droppings that cause sickness if not cleaned, cures illness with medicine, and ages the pet through life stages in real time; Nintendogs adds stylus petting and voice-recognized commands; Seaman responds to the player's speech. Inputs are care actions and elapsed time; outputs are the creature's condition, form, and behavior.
design_levers: number of needs and their decay rates in game or real time
severity of neglect consequences: mood, sickness, altered growth, death, leaving
care actions available and whether they are menu choices or direct manipulation
whether care quality shapes the adult form or personality
pause or vacation options that suspend decay
dynamics: Check-in frequency becomes the main loop, coupling the game to the player's daily schedule.
Care quality branching into different adult forms motivates replays and comparison between players.
Shared or shown-off pets turn care quality into social status.
failure_modes: Real-time decay with no pause punishes absence; the first Tamagotchi units could stop time only through the clock-setting mode.
Once the optimal care routine is known, interactions become a checklist and attachment fades.
Creatures with too few reactions repeat the same animations, breaking the illusion of a living pet.
mechanics.name: Creature care
open_questions: Can language models give pets memory and open-ended conversational responses while keeping their needs legible?
Does generated animation or behavior reduce the repetition that ends attachment?
mechanics.player_experience: Responsibility and attachment. The player checks in often, notices small changes, and feels guilt when the creature gets sick from being forgotten. Care is direct and tactile rather than managerial, and the creature's growth or decline mirrors the player's attention.
mechanics.summary: The player directly feeds, cleans, and plays with a creature whose needs decay; neglect causes sickness, stunted growth, or death.

synergy.note: Wall-clock decay makes care a daily ritual and absence meaningful (Tamagotchi).

mechanics.definition: Owns a creature's learned decision parameters: weights linking perceived situations or objects to actions. After the creature acts, a reward or punishment signal (a player stroke or slap, or a change in an internal drive) adjusts the weights for that situation-action pair, so its future selection probability rises or falls and generalizes to similar situations. Creatures (1996) uses about 1,000 neurons in 9 lobes; a 16-cell decision layer picks the strongest-firing action; drive reduction releases a reward chemical and drive increase a punishment chemical, which reinforce excitatory or inhibitory synapses, so norns learn to eat when hungry but not when full. In Black & White (2001) the creature follows a belief-desire-intention model with desires as simplified perceptrons and opinions as decision trees; the player strokes or slaps it after actions and uses leashes to direct its attention. Inputs: player feedback, drives, perceived objects. Outputs: changed action probabilities.
design_levers: learning rate and how quickly old associations fade
credit assignment window that decides which recent action receives the feedback
granularity of the situation representation (object types, desires, contexts), which decides what generalizes
feedback channels such as stroke and slap, food, demonstration, and attention leashes
innate drives and biases the learning starts from
dynamics: Creatures from the same start diverge into distinct personalities, which drives players to share and compare them.
Learned behavior acts on the world, so training choices reshape villages, alignment, and appearance in Black & White.
Learning from internal drives without player input produces self-taught habits and odd local optima.
failure_modes: Credit assignment errors attach feedback to the wrong action or object, and players cannot tell why the creature learned something.
Learning too slowly makes training feel ignored; too quickly lets one slap erase hours of shaping.
Generalization surprises, such as a creature learning to eat villagers, read as bugs rather than lessons.
Emergent learned behavior varies by player, which makes testing and balancing expensive; Black & White was later called overrated for underusing its creature.
mechanics.name: Creature learning
open_questions: Can modern reinforcement learning or language-conditioned policies give creatures learning that generalizes the way players intend, with explainable credit assignment?
Does exposing a creature's learned associations improve attachment or destroy the illusion of a mind?
mechanics.player_experience: The player becomes a parent or trainer. Each reward is a bet about what the creature will generalize, and personality emerges from the history of training. Success feels like understanding; failure feels like a stubborn pet, and players blame themselves for bad habits.
mechanics.summary: A creature's behavior is learned from player reward and punishment or from neural adaptation over its life.

synergy.note: The creature learns from how the god acts, making the player's own behavior a training signal (Black & White).

mechanics.definition: Each map cell, district, or agent holds a crime level derived from a propensity function over conditions, minus a suppression term from policing. In the open-sourced SimCity engine (Micropolis), crimeScan sets each cell to 128 - land value + population density (capped at 300), subtracts a police-influence map smoothed three times from station positions and funding, and clamps to 0-250; the city average drives a high-crime warning above 100 and crime feeds back into land value. Agent-based variants such as Cities: Skylines 2 spawn criminals and crime events that police units respond to, with arrests flowing into jails and prisons of limited capacity. Tropico and SimCity 2000 use similar aggregate fields, and Prison Architect models the justice end, where reform and labour programmes lower recidivism and the prison is graded on recidivism, happiness, and violence. Inputs: land value, density, education, employment, happiness, police coverage and funding. Outputs: crime map, satisfaction and value penalties, incidents, and incarcerated population.
design_levers: inputs and weights of the crime propensity function (land value, density, unemployment, education, happiness)
police coverage radius, capacity, and the funding-to-effect curve
justice pipeline capacity: jail and prison slots and what happens when they fill
strength of crime's feedback into land value, migration, and satisfaction
aggregate field versus discrete crime events with agents
dynamics: Coverage creates safe islands around stations and crime pockets in gaps, so station placement becomes a covering problem.
Coupling with land value and zoning makes crime track inequality across the map.
Budget cuts to policing show up with a lag, producing oscillation when players react late.
failure_modes: When suppression is just coverage, the optimal play is blanketing the map with stations, and the social causes the model encodes stop mattering.
Crime lowers land value, which raises crime, so poor districts can lock into a spiral the player cannot read as a loop.
Hidden justice capacity limits make crime rise for no visible reason once jails fill.
mechanics.name: Crime and policing
open_questions: Can agent-level motives (need, opportunity, social ties) produce crime patterns that reward social policy over coverage, without becoming illegible?
Would generated investigations or court cases make the justice side of the loop a playable system rather than a capacity number?
mechanics.player_experience: The player reads a crime overlay, spots hot districts, and decides between adding stations, raising police funding, or fixing root causes such as low land value or unemployment. Crime is a visible symptom of neglected neighborhoods and a running cost of growth.
mechanics.summary: Crime levels arise from local conditions such as land value, density, or unemployment, and police coverage, prisons, and justice reduce them.

mechanics.definition: Owns a countdown to a scheduled crisis (in days, turns, or progress percent), the crisis's nature, and sometimes its expected severity. Each tick the counter falls; at zero the crisis applies a large state change such as extreme cold, an attack, a flood, or a scenario loss, which the player's preparation mitigates. The timer may be fixed, randomized within a known window, or driven by a rival process the player can slow. Frostpunk's main scenario builds toward the Great Storm, and its Last Autumn scenario races to finish an outpost before a storm; Plague Inc. runs a cure-research percentage that ends the game when it completes; Don't Starve's winter arrives on a fixed schedule; The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask frames play around a three-day falling moon. Inputs are elapsed time and actions that shift the clock; outputs are the crisis and its severity.
design_levers: warning lead time and whether the exact date is known
crisis severity and whether it is shown in advance
whether player actions can delay, accelerate, or weaken the crisis
single climactic crisis versus recurring crises of rising strength
failure handling: scenario loss, heavy damage, or partial survival
dynamics: Players shift from expansion to stockpiling as the counter runs down, creating distinct phases within a run.
Countdowns reward forecasting tools that project resource runways to the deadline.
Recurring crises such as winters or droughts escalate into a cycle of preparation and recovery.
failure_modes: A crisis with a fixed required preparation becomes a build order that players replay rather than a plan.
Too much lead time removes tension; too little makes the crisis an unavoidable random event.
A single climactic crisis gives a scenario a hard end and little reason to replay.
mechanics.name: Crisis countdown
open_questions: Can a director model choose crises that target the player's actual weak points while keeping the warning fair?
mechanics.player_experience: Dread and focus. Knowing what is coming and when, the player turns the remaining days into a plan: stockpile coal, insulate homes, finish the walls. The final days narrow choices to triage, and surviving feels earned because the preparation was the player's own.
mechanics.summary: A known future crisis such as a storm, winter, cure, or deadline is announced in advance, and the remaining time structures preparation.

synergy.note: A known winter or storm turns the season calendar into a preparation deadline.
Forecasts let the player plan against the countdown rather than be ambushed by it (Frostpunk).

mechanics.definition: Each planted cell or field holds a crop type, a growth progress value, and condition flags such as watered, fertilized, or diseased. Each tick or day, progress advances at a base rate multiplied by modifiers for soil fertility, water, light, temperature, and season; outside allowed conditions growth stops or the plant dies. At maturity the crop is harvested for a yield, sometimes scaled by care or skill, and the cell resets, regrows, or loses fertility. Harvest Moon and Stardew Valley require daily watering and tie crops to seasons of a fixed calendar; RimWorld scales growth by soil fertility and light and halts it outside a temperature band; Farming Simulator turns field preparation, sowing, fertilizing, and harvesting into vehicle operations; Manor Lords and Farthest Frontier track soil fertility per field and reward crop rotation. Inputs: seeds, labor or player actions, environmental conditions. Outputs: harvested goods and an updated field state.
design_levers: growth duration per crop and number of visible stages
which conditions gate growth (water, light, temperature, season, fertility) and whether violating them pauses or kills the crop
single-harvest versus regrowing crops
yield and quality modifiers from fertilizer, skill, or care
soil fertility depletion and recovery rules, including rotation or fallow
labor or action cost of planting, tending, and harvesting
dynamics: Harvests arrive in pulses, creating labor peaks that compete with construction and hauling.
Seasonal growth windows couple farming to storage and spoilage, turning winter into a stockpiling test.
Soil depletion pushes expansion onto new land or forces rotation schedules.
Weather events and blights can wipe out a season and cascade into famine.
failure_modes: Daily manual tending scales poorly, so large farms become rote clicking until automation such as sprinklers arrives.
One crop with the best value per day dominates and planting choice disappears.
Season-change crop deaths feel arbitrary when the calendar is not prominent.
Growth too fast relative to consumption makes food trivial; growth too slow with harsh winters makes early runs unwinnable.
mechanics.name: Crop cultivation
open_questions: Can learned plant growth models give crops plausible responses to microclimate that players can still reason about?
How much automation can farming absorb before cultivation stops being a decision?
mechanics.player_experience: Planning around a delayed payoff. The player commits land and time now for a harvest days or a season later, then guards the field against weather, pests, and neglect. In avatar farming games the daily watering round becomes a ritual; in colony sims the growing season becomes a deadline that sets how much must be stored for winter.
mechanics.summary: Planted crops progress through growth stages over days or seasons depending on water, soil, and season, then are harvested.

synergy.note: Watering and harvesting consume the daily energy budget, forcing farm sizing tradeoffs.
Season-locked crops create a calendar of planting decisions.

mechanics.definition: Owns a large population of visitor agents, each with preference parameters sampled at spawn (intensity range, nausea tolerance, tastes), a cash budget, and mood stocks such as happiness, energy, hunger, thirst, and toilet. When choosing what to do, a visitor filters attractions by preference and budget, picks among the acceptable ones, and on rejection or experience emits a named thought that changes happiness. In RollerCoaster Tycoon, per the OpenRCT2 reimplementation, a guest rejects a ride whose intensity rating is below its minimum or above its maximum preferred intensity (both widened by happiness), whose nausea rating exceeds its tolerance (300, 600, 800, or 1000 plus happiness), or whose price exceeds twice the ride's value (value quartered when the park charges entry); rejections lower happiness and create thoughts such as bad value, and guests with nothing left to ride head home. Outputs: attendance, spending, park rating, crowding.
design_levers: preference distributions sampled at spawn (intensity, nausea, tastes, budget)
acceptance rule (hard thresholds versus scored choice) and the price-to-value tolerance multiplier
thought vocabulary and how thoughts aggregate into a park or facility rating
mood decay rates and leave-the-park thresholds
crowd size and spawn rate tied to rating, marketing, or price of entry
dynamics: Preferences spread over intensity create demand for a portfolio of gentle and intense attractions rather than one best ride.
Rating raises attendance, and the larger crowd congests queues and paths until mood falls, a balancing loop on growth.
Players learn the value threshold and price every attraction just below it, a stable arbitrage the rule invites.
failure_modes: Price-value rules that ignore context let players overcharge a few attractions with no penalty, or punish small price changes too harshly.
Thought spam: hundreds of identical thoughts bury the actionable signal.
Narrow preference sampling makes the crowd behave like one average agent, removing segmentation decisions.
Large crowds cost pathfinding and update time, capping park size.
mechanics.name: Crowd preferences
open_questions: Can visitor preference models fitted to real attendance or survey data make tycoon crowds more segmentable without losing legibility?
How should thousands of thoughts be summarized so the player sees causes rather than noise?
mechanics.player_experience: The player reads the crowd as a distribution: thought feeds and aggregate complaints reveal what is missing, and the fix is a layout or pricing change rather than an order. Individual guests are funny and disposable; the crowd's mood is the scoreboard, and pricing becomes a dial between revenue and goodwill.
mechanics.summary: Large visitor populations with individual preferences, budgets, and tolerances choose attractions and react with visible thoughts.

synergy.note: Individual tastes and budgets make pricing and attraction mix matter.
Visible queues and complaints let crowds express capacity problems.

claims.text: Victoria 3 pops share profession, culture, religion, state, and workplace.
Crusader Kings III applies faith hostility opinion modifiers from 0 to -30 between characters.

mechanics.definition: Owns categorical identity attributes (culture, faith, and in some games ideology or ethics) per province, county, or population group, plus conversion progress or a per-period conversion share. Each period progress accrues from sources such as assigned missionaries or court officials, state religion and laws, assimilation into the majority culture, buildings, and the ruler's or government's alignment, against resistance from population size, development, or fervor; when progress completes the attribute flips, or in population-group models a fraction of each group switches. Other systems read the identities: a mismatch with the ruler or state adds unrest and opinion penalties, a match or accepted status grants bonuses, and shared or hostile identities shape alliances and wars. Victoria 3 stores its population as pops that share profession, culture, religion, and state. Crusader Kings III applies opinion penalties between faiths by hostility and lets rulers convert counties' faith and culture. Europa Universalis IV converts province religion with missionaries. It differs from population-strata, which owns class tiers and promotion; identity is orthogonal to class.
design_levers: conversion speed and the resistance factors (population size, development, fervor)
which agents or policies can convert (missionaries, court officials, laws, buildings)
binary flip per province versus a share of each population group per period
penalties and bonuses attached to matching or mismatched identities
tolerance and acceptance rules that let mixed identities coexist
whether players can found, reform, or hybridize faiths and cultures
dynamics: Majority identities grow by assimilation, a reinforcing loop toward homogeneous heartlands with contested borderlands.
Identity mismatch feeds unrest and revolt, coupling conversion to stability and military occupation.
Shared faiths and cultures become alliance lines, so identity maps shape diplomacy.
failure_modes: Cheap, certain conversion homogenizes every realm and erases the identity layer by mid-game.
Severe unrest from mismatched identity turns conquering other cultures into a trap and narrows play to one strategy.
Faiths and cultures that differ only in numeric modifiers feel interchangeable.
Treating the conversion of real faiths and peoples as a pure optimization can read as endorsing forced conversion.
mechanics.name: Culture and religion conversion
open_questions: Can language models generate new faiths and cultures whose doctrines produce consistent mechanical effects and believable schisms?
Can conversion run as diffusion through social networks of individual agents rather than as a per-province progress bar?
mechanics.player_experience: The map has a second layer of identity beneath its borders. The player conquers land that will not accept them, then spends missionaries, officials, or decades of policy converting it, choosing between tolerating diversity and its unrest or homogenizing at a cost. Faiths and cultures spreading, splitting, and reforming become the long arcs of a campaign.
mechanics.summary: Provinces or population groups carry culture and faith identities that drift or are converted by missionaries, policies, and rulers, changing unrest, opinion, and bonuses.

mechanics.definition: Owns each customer's (or segment's) preference weights and budget, and each offering's price and value attributes. When a customer wants a good or service, the rule scores every reachable offering, typically utility = perceived value x preference match - price - distance or wait, then buys the best one, samples in proportion to scores, or buys nothing when every price exceeds willingness to pay. Lemonade Stand (1973) reduces it to three daily inputs (glasses made, advertising signs, price per glass) whose sales vary with the weather report. RollerCoaster Tycoon guests refuse rides and stalls they judge too expensive for what they offer and say so in their thoughts. Capitalism weighs price, quality, and brand by product category to split demand among competing stores.
design_levers: shape of the utility function and which attributes (quality, brand, novelty, distance, wait) enter it
price sensitivity per customer segment, income class, or trait
heterogeneity: one representative customer versus sampled individual preferences
deterministic best choice versus probabilistic (logit) choice
whether customers explain rejections through thoughts, reviews, or complaints
dynamics: Competing sellers undercut each other until quality or brand differentiation ends the price war.
Choices propagate congestion: the best-value stall attracts queues that lower its effective value.
Segmented preferences reward a portfolio of offerings over one best product.
failure_modes: A single representative customer yields one optimal price that players find once and never revisit.
Hidden value thresholds read as random rejection unless thoughts or reviews explain them.
Weak price sensitivity lets players charge extreme prices with little loss, so gouging dominates.
mechanics.name: Customer value choice
open_questions: Can LLM-driven customers with stated tastes and budgets haggle or complain in language while staying consistent with a calibrated demand curve?
How much preference heterogeneity is needed before players stop finding a single dominant price?
mechanics.player_experience: Finding the price people will bear. The player probes prices, watches thoughts or sales drop when they overreach, and invests in quality or marketing to justify charging more. Small numbers become visible crowds walking past or lining up.
mechanics.summary: Customers choose among offerings by comparing price to perceived value and personal preference.

mechanics.definition: Owns a budget that refills at the start of each in-game day (energy points, stamina, clock hours, or a fixed number of time slots) and a cost per action. Actions spend from the budget; at zero the player is penalized or the day ends, and sleep restores the budget, sometimes less after staying up late. Stardew Valley gives 270 base energy, raised by Stardrops, charges energy for tool use, exhausts the farmer at 0, and makes them pass out at -15 energy or at 2 a.m.; passing out away from home costs 10% of gold up to 1,000g, and going to bed after midnight restores less. Harvest Moon set the stamina-and-clock farm day that Stardew Valley follows; Persona allocates a fixed number of time slots per day to activities. Inputs are action costs and restoration items; outputs are the actions completed per day.
design_levers: budget size and whether it grows with progression
cost per action and which actions are free
penalties at or past zero and for staying up late
restoration sources within the day, such as food
time slots versus a continuous pool
dynamics: Players batch tasks spatially to save time, which shapes farm and base layout.
Budget-expanding items become top priorities, forming an upgrade path.
Automation such as sprinklers frees the budget from chores for new activities, marking progression.
failure_modes: A budget that is too tight early makes the opening a grind; one that grows too fast stops mattering by midgame.
When one activity has the best return per point, every day becomes the same routine.
Harsh pass-out penalties push players to reload rather than accept a bad day.
mechanics.name: Daily action budget
open_questions: Can generated daily events or requests keep each day's allocation decision fresh without hand-authored content?
mechanics.player_experience: Every morning is a planning puzzle. The player picks which crops to water, whom to visit, or which job to take, knowing the rest must wait. The end of each day gives a natural stopping point and a sense of steady progress, and upgrades that stretch the budget feel substantial.
mechanics.summary: A per-day pool of energy, stamina, or time slots limits how many actions the player can take, and the day's end resets it and forces prioritization.

mechanics.definition: Owns a timetable per agent or group mapping time-of-day blocks to activity categories (sleep, work, eat, leisure), set by the player, authored, or generated. Each tick the current block filters or biases which actions an agent may choose and which areas it may enter; block boundaries trigger mass movement. Prison Architect regimes are hourly schedules per risk category (Lockup, Sleep, Eat, Yard, Shower, Free Time, Work variants) that confine prisoners to areas rather than forcing actions, and cooks start four hours before an Eat block. RimWorld's schedule assigns each colonist's hours to sleep, recreation, work, or anything. Generative Agents (2023) has a language model draft a day plan of five to eight broad chunks, then decompose it into hour-long and 5-15 minute actions and replan on events. Inputs: clock, block assignments, disruptions. Outputs: synchronized demand peaks and occupancy by room and hour.
design_levers: block granularity (hourly, shift-based, or free-form plans)
who sets the schedule: player, authored routine, or agent-generated plan
strictness: hard confinement, soft bias, or ignorable when needs are urgent
per-group or per-agent schedules and shift staggering
response to disruption: skip the block, delay, or replan
dynamics: Shared blocks produce peaks on food, transit, and services, generating queues and congestion at predictable hours.
Staggered shifts emerge as a player strategy that trades coordination effort for throughput.
Coupled with day-night cycles and crime, schedules create time-dependent risk such as unattended night hours.
failure_modes: Synchronized blocks create rush hours that overwhelm shared facilities such as canteens, showers, and transit.
Agents follow the schedule into danger because blocks override situational awareness.
Authored routines repeat visibly, so the world reads as clockwork after a few days.
Schedules that conflict with needs create deadlocks in which agents go hungry or sleepless between blocks.
mechanics.name: Daily schedules
open_questions: Can language-model day plans stay coherent across weeks of game time while remaining cheap enough for hundreds of agents?
How much schedule variation is needed before a town stops reading as clockwork?
mechanics.player_experience: The player thinks in time: staggering shifts so the canteen is not mobbed, protecting sleep, and noticing when one block is starved. Schedules make agents look like they have lives and give the world a daily rhythm the player learns and exploits.
mechanics.summary: Agents follow time-blocked routines for work, sleep, and leisure that create rhythms of demand across the day.

synergy.note: Synchronized commutes produce rush-hour peaks that stress the network.
Schedules decide when needs can be met, creating crowding at meals and bedtime.

mechanics.definition: A map mode recolors the world by one per-cell, per-building, or per-segment field: land value, pollution concentration, crime, service coverage, traffic volume or speed, power and water connectivity, temperature, gas composition, germs, or political ownership. It owns no simulation state; it samples a field and maps it through a color ramp or categorical palette, sometimes adding glyphs such as flow arrows. Update rule: when active, sample the field each frame or on change and redraw; some games switch an overlay on automatically when the player places a related building. Canonical forms: the data maps of SimCity and SimCity 2000, Cities: Skylines info views, the oxygen, temperature, power, plumbing, decor, and germ overlays of Oxygen Not Included, Factorio's pollution cloud on the map view, and the map modes of Europa Universalis IV.
design_levers: which fields get an overlay, since exposing a field makes it an optimization target
continuous gradient versus thresholded bands
fixed absolute scale versus auto-normalized to the current map range
automatic display while placing a related building
instantaneous value versus time-averaged value
single overlay at a time versus composites, and colorblind-safe palettes
dynamics: An exposed field becomes a painting target: players lay out coverage grids until no red remains.
Visible spatial externalities push players toward land-use separation, such as industry far from housing.
In games with diffusing fields (heat, gas), overlays are how players discover emergent flows they did not intend.
failure_modes: Auto-normalized color ramps make a minor problem look red and a severe one look identical.
Overlays without legends or units show where something is high but not how high.
Overlays of fields with hidden formulas, such as land value, show where but not why.
Red-green ramps are unreadable for many colorblind players.
mechanics.name: Data overlays
open_questions: Can automated annotation of overlays (this plume originates from these three sources) close the gap between where and why?
Which fields should stay without an overlay to preserve discovery and uncertainty?
mechanics.player_experience: A hunch becomes a picture. The player sees the shape of a hidden field, such as a pollution plume or a coverage gap, and responds spatially by moving, adding, or separating buildings. Overlays are the main debugging tool for layout.
mechanics.summary: Map layers visualize hidden variables such as land value, pollution, coverage, or traffic.

synergy.note: Overlays make invisible diffusion fields legible.
Traffic overlays turn congestion from a vague complaint into a located problem.
Coverage overlays show gaps that would otherwise surface only as complaints.
Land value maps are the canonical city-builder overlay.

tension.note: Full-information overlays undercut hidden-information play; games must choose what to reveal.

mechanics.definition: Owns a catalog of models (vehicles, consoles, components, building types), each with an introduction date, a retirement or obsolescence date, and stats, plus the rule that checks the in-game calendar each period and adds models to or removes them from what the player can buy or target. Availability depends only on the date, not on player spending, so every company gains the same options at the same time. New models often arrive with lower launch reliability or a short exclusive preview, and retired models can no longer be bought while existing units keep aging. Transport Tycoon (1994) introduces road, rail, sea, and air models on a timeline across its calendar, so fleets are renewed as better vehicles arrive and old ones lose reliability; Railroad Tycoon releases locomotives by era; Game Dev Tycoon launches and retires fictional consoles on a fixed timeline that forces platform bets. It differs from tech-tree, where unlocks are bought with accumulated research in an order the player chooses; here time alone unlocks.
