design_levers: introduction and retirement dates per model, and whether they vary slightly between games
start year and calendar speed, which choose the eras a game covers
prototype or exclusive preview windows and launch reliability
whether old models are withdrawn or stay buyable
size of each generational jump
dynamics: Fleet renewal waves follow major introductions and cause cash crunches and service gaps.
Every company gains new models at once, so competition shifts to who adopts and finances renewal best.
Launch and retirement dates decide which platform bets pay off, as with console choice in Game Dev Tycoon.
failure_modes: Games that run past the last introduction date stall with nothing new to buy.
Retiring a model without a successor leaves a role with no buyable vehicle or platform.
Fixed dates become memorized, so experienced players plan purchases around known release years.
Generational jumps so large that switching is always immediate remove the renewal decision.
mechanics.name: Dated technology timeline
open_questions: Could introduction dates respond to simulated demand and rival research, making the timeline emergent rather than fixed?
Does a historical timeline reward knowledge of real history in ways that help or hurt replayability?
mechanics.player_experience: History arrives on schedule. The player watches the calendar for the next locomotive or console, plans when to switch, and lives with a fleet or catalog that ages out from under them. A new era is a forced renewal decision rather than a reward the player earned.
mechanics.summary: New vehicle models, platforms, or products enter and leave availability on a calendar tied to in-game dates rather than to research, forcing fleet or platform renewal.

mechanics.definition: Owns a time-of-day value that advances each tick and wraps at a fixed day length, usually split into phases such as day, dusk, and night. Each phase sets ambient light, sometimes temperature, and flags read by other systems: agent schedules, spawn tables, growth, sanity or fear, and shop hours. Don't Starve uses an 8-minute real-time day of sixteen 30-second segments whose day, dusk, and night split shifts with the season; in total darkness the monster Charlie attacks and sanity drains at 50 per minute. Minecraft has a 20-minute day and spawns hostile mobs in low light, and The Long Dark makes nights colder. Inputs are elapsed time and season; outputs are phase flags and light levels.
design_levers: day length in real time and the day, dusk, and night split, fixed or varying by season
how dark night gets and whether light sources are required to act
which systems read the phase: spawns, agent schedules, temperature, growth, prices
penalty for being caught in darkness, from reduced visibility to direct damage
whether the player can skip the night by sleeping
dynamics: Bases cluster around light sources, and trips shrink to what can be done before dusk.
Combined with daily schedules, synchronized agents create rush hours at dawn and dusk.
Night becomes a high-risk, high-reward window when rare resources or creatures appear only in darkness.
failure_modes: Night that is only darker visuals with no mechanical difference becomes an annoyance players remove by raising brightness.
Nights that are too punishing make every night identical: retreat and wait, wasting play time.
Long real-time days make planning trivial; very short ones make players feel unable to finish trips.
mechanics.name: Day-night cycle
open_questions: Can learned relighting or neural rendering make time-of-day visual variety nearly free, moving authoring effort to behavioral differences?
mechanics.player_experience: A rhythm of safety and threat. Day is for travel and work, dusk is a warning to head home, light fires, or finish tasks, and night is spent defending, sleeping, or risking the dark for better rewards. The player plans each day around the remaining light and learns to read the sky as a clock.
mechanics.summary: A diurnal cycle changes light, visibility, temperature, and which agents are active, so activity follows the hour of the day.

mechanics.definition: Each decorative object, floor, or surface has a beauty value, and dirt, corpses, and filth are negative. The game aggregates values over a radius or a room and samples the result for agents or attractions. In RimWorld a room's beauty is total beauty divided by a weighted size (the size if above 40 tiles, otherwise 20 plus half the size), graded from hideous (below -3.5) to unbelievably beautiful (100 or more), and combined with wealth, space, and cleanliness into impressiveness that sets mood thoughts; colonists also get mood from the beauty around them. In RollerCoaster Tycoon 2, as documented by OpenRCT2, scenery within 5 tiles of a ride's station adds 0.05 excitement per item up to 47 items. The Sims 4 rates rooms by an environment score from decor. Inputs are placed objects; outputs are mood, ratings, or prices.
design_levers: beauty value and cost of each object, and negative values for filth and industry
aggregation rule: per tile, per radius, per room, with or without size normalization
caps or diminishing returns on how much decoration counts
which systems consume beauty: mood, ratings, prices, or visitor choice
per-agent taste variation by trait or culture
dynamics: Traffic creates filth that lowers beauty, which creates cleaning jobs that compete for labor.
In RimWorld, decoration raises colony wealth, and wealth raises raid points, so beauty carries a security cost.
Prosperity funds decoration, and decoration raises mood or ratings and so prosperity, a slow upgrade treadmill.
failure_modes: One object with the best beauty per cost dominates, so players spam it regardless of how the space looks.
Proximity rules that count only a hot spot, such as scenery near a ride station in RollerCoaster Tycoon 2, reward decorating one spot and ignoring the rest of the ride.
Beauty values that disagree with the art (an ugly-looking object rated beautiful) break trust in the system.
If the score is hidden, decoration reads as optional and the mechanic goes unused.
mechanics.name: Decoration and beauty
open_questions: Can a vision model score the composition of a space instead of summing per-object beauty values, and would players accept its judgment?
Does generated decor reduce the asset cost enough to make beauty a deep system rather than a spam target?
mechanics.player_experience: Cosmetic choices get a mechanical payoff, so players dress up rooms and paths and watch moods or ride ratings rise. The tension is between beautiful and efficient: every statue costs resources and floor space that production could use.
mechanics.summary: Decorative objects and scenery carry beauty values that are aggregated over tiles, rooms, or radii and feed agent mood or ratings.

synergy.note: Room quality depends on furnishings and beauty, rewarding interior design.

claims.text: Stellaris launched with a limit on directly controlled core worlds, beyond which penalties applied, and sectors run by governors who develop planets under a player-set focus and taxation.

mechanics.definition: The player assigns a subsystem (a city, sector, colony, fleet, department, or set of planets) to an AI controller and sets objectives and constraints: a focus, a budget, permissions, and policies. Each decision interval the controller runs the same decision logic the game's opponent AI uses, restricted to that subsystem, and issues actions on the player's behalf. State owned: assignment, goal settings, and permissions per delegated unit; the rest is read from the subsystem. Inputs: subsystem state and player settings. Outputs: build, research, production, or movement actions. Canonical forms: Stellaris sectors, which a 2016 dev diary justified with a core-world limit and in which sector governors develop planets and build mining stations under a player-set focus, Hearts of Iron IV battle plans executed by AI-controlled generals, automated workers in the Civilization series, Football Manager staff responsibilities, and automated traders and miners in X4: Foundations.
design_levers: granularity of goals: single focus, weighted priorities, or explicit rules
permissions such as may build, may demolish, may spend reserves
transparency: whether the manager explains its choices
manager competence relative to a good player
incentives to delegate: hard limits on direct control versus voluntary convenience
ease of reclaiming control and per-item overrides
dynamics: Delegation allows simulations far larger than one player could micromanage, shifting play to allocation among managers.
Partial delegation creates principal-agent tension: players watch managers and intervene at thresholds.
Delegated units pursuing local goals can conflict with each other, such as two governors competing for one resource.
failure_modes: Managers that underperform a competent player turn delegation into a penalty that players avoid at all costs.
Opaque managers make unexplained choices that players cannot correct without micromanaging.
Managers that are too strong remove the game: the optimal play is to delegate everything.
Forced delegation through control caps is widely resented; Stellaris sectors were reworked in later updates.
mechanics.name: Delegation to AI managers
open_questions: Can language-model managers take natural-language mandates (keep morale high but never let the treasury go negative), explain their tradeoffs, and remain competent?
Does delegation to a learned policy trained against the game's simulation make managers better than humans, and what is left for the player if so?
mechanics.player_experience: The player moves up a level of abstraction and manages managers. Delegation trades control for attention and enables play at empire scale. When the AI does something dumb it feels like losing control; when it works it feels like governing.
mechanics.summary: Subsystems are handed to AI managers or governors that pursue player-set goals within bounds.

tension.note: Automating a subsystem removes the skill expression that made it the point.

claims.text: Transport Tycoon pays for deliveries by delivery time as well as distance and cargo.
OpenTTD orders include transfer with partial payment for feeder services.

mechanics.definition: Owns a payment table per cargo type (a base rate, a distance weight, and a value curve over time in transit) and computes revenue at delivery from quantity, base rate, and distance, multiplied by a time factor that falls as transit time grows; in common implementations the factor holds flat for a cargo-specific grace period before it declines. Fast-decaying cargo such as mail and passengers rewards short or fast routes, while bulk cargo such as coal keeps its value over long, slow hauls. Cargo moved in stages can be paid in parts at transfer points. Transport Tycoon (1994) pays by cargo type, distance, quantity, and delivery time, and OpenTTD keeps the model and adds transfer orders with partial payment for feeder services. It differs from vehicle-route-scheduling, which owns the order lists that move cargo, and from contracts-orders, which owns discrete jobs with fixed payouts and deadlines; here every delivery is priced continuously by how long it took.
design_levers: base rate per cargo type
shape of each cargo's value curve (grace period, slope, floor)
distance measure, straight-line between endpoints or route length
partial payment rules for transfers and feeder legs
inflation or era scaling of rates
dynamics: Cargo sorts by mode, with mail and passengers on fast services and bulk goods on slow ones.
Faster vehicles pay back through higher rates, coupling payment to fleet renewal.
Congestion and signal delays cost money directly, so network design is priced.
failure_modes: Paying by route length rather than endpoint distance rewards deliberate detours.
Near-identical curves make every cargo the same and remove route specialization.
Transfer credits shown at feeder stations can make feeder vehicles look profitable while the final leg shows a loss, confusing players about which vehicles earn money.
Decay so steep that slow modes earn nothing collapses mode choice to the fastest vehicle.
mechanics.name: Delivery-time payment
open_questions: Could time sensitivity come from simulated recipients' needs, such as a town short of food paying more for fast grain, rather than fixed per-cargo curves?
mechanics.player_experience: Speed has a price per cargo. The player matches cargo to mode, putting mail on fast trains or aircraft and coal on slow freight, and reads every delay at a junction as lost money. Upgrading to faster vehicles becomes an investment with a visible return.
mechanics.summary: Payment for a delivery depends on cargo type, quantity, distance, and transit time, with each cargo losing value at its own rate the longer it travels.

mechanics.definition: Each deposit holds a remaining quantity that every extraction cycle decrements. At zero the node disappears or the extractor stops; some games instead decay the extraction rate toward a floor. Factorio ore patches store an amount per tile that mining drills consume, while crude oil fields report a yield percentage in which 1% equals 300 pumpjack cycles and depletion stops at a 20% floor. Warcraft and Age of Empires gold mines and The Settlers II mountain mines run dry. Satisfactory is the counterexample: its nodes are infinite and differ only in purity. Inputs: extraction cycles. Outputs: remaining amount, current rate, and an exhaustion event that idles the extractors and any chain they feed.
design_levers: starting quantity per deposit and its distribution across the map
whether depletion ends output or decays the rate toward a floor
efficiency upgrades that change output per unit removed, such as Factorio mining productivity research
visibility of remaining amounts and warnings before exhaustion
whether deposits regenerate, can be rediscovered, or have substitutes
dynamics: Pushes expansion outward, which raises defense, logistics, and threat costs at new outposts.
Creates contested chokepoints in competitive maps as the last deposits run out.
Drives substitution toward recycling, alternate recipes, or trade once local supply ends.
Staggers rebuild cycles, giving long games a rhythm of boom at new sites and decline at old ones.
failure_modes: Depletion that is too fast makes relocation the whole game and punishes building anything permanent.
Depletion that is too slow is never felt within a session.
Hidden remaining amounts cause sudden collapses that read as bugs.
Infinite nodes or high rate floors remove expansion pressure, so the map stops mattering after the first claims.
mechanics.name: Deposit depletion
open_questions: Can procedural geology models generate deposits whose size players can estimate from surface signals, turning prospecting into inference?
What depletion time relative to session length keeps relocation interesting rather than tedious?
mechanics.player_experience: A visible timer the player cannot stop. Every mine is temporary, so the player keeps scouting, claiming, and rebuilding at new sites, and judges how much infrastructure a deposit deserves given how long it will last. Losing a key deposit mid-chain creates a scramble to relocate before stocks run out.
mechanics.summary: Extractable deposits hold finite quantities and run out, forcing expansion, relocation, or substitution.

mechanics.definition: The player builds a design (a coaster track, a bridge, a machine program), the game runs or analyzes it, and a metric vector is computed from what happened. Metrics gate success, set income, or rank the design. In RollerCoaster Tycoon 2, as documented by OpenRCT2, a test run yields excitement, intensity, and nausea from peak positive, negative, and lateral g, number of drops, highest drop, inversions, and nearby scenery; excitement stops rising after 9 drops and 6 inversions, is cut 25% when intensity exceeds 10 with further cuts at 11, 12, 13.2, and 14.5, and is halved when lateral g exceeds 3.1. Poly Bridge drives vehicles over a bridge and shows member stress under a budget. SpaceChem scores solutions on cycles, reactors, and instructions, and Opus Magnum on cost, cycles, and area. State: the design and its last metric vector; update: re-evaluate on test or edit.
design_levers: which metrics exist and how many are orthogonal
formula shape, caps, and penalties, such as excitement penalties for excessive intensity
hard pass or fail thresholds versus continuous scores
when evaluation runs: an explicit test run, continuous re-evaluation, or end of level
how much of each metric's derivation the game exposes
comparison against other players' results
dynamics: Designs converge on formula sweet spots, such as stopping at the drop and inversion caps that end excitement gains.
Multiple competing metrics produce distinct design schools, such as cheap versus fast solutions in Zachtronics games.
When ratings set prices or demand, design quality couples directly to the economy.
failure_modes: Players optimize the formula instead of the fantasy, producing designs that score well but look absurd.
A single scalar score collapses the design space onto one optimum.
Opaque formulas require community reverse engineering; RollerCoaster Tycoon 2's rating rules are documented in detail only through the OpenRCT2 project.
Scores that contradict intuition (a ride that looks thrilling rates low) make the simulation feel arbitrary.
mechanics.name: Design performance rating
open_questions: Can a learned critic rate open-ended designs on qualities like elegance or thrill that hand formulas miss, without becoming a new exploit target?
Does showing per-term contributions to a score widen or narrow the range of designs players explore?
mechanics.player_experience: Build, test, read the numbers, revise. Players learn the hidden physics through the scores, enjoy beating a threshold, and then chase better tradeoffs between metrics that pull against each other.
mechanics.summary: Player-built designs are run or analyzed and scored on simulated metrics such as ride excitement, bridge stress, or cost and cycles.

synergy.note: Rating the assembled design closes the build-test loop.
Stress and load ratings turn structural rules into a score (Poly Bridge).

mechanics.definition: The player paints a designation onto tiles or objects (mine, chop, harvest, build, haul, deconstruct, hunt) instead of commanding a specific agent. Each designation creates a job entry with location, type, required skill or tool, and priority. Agents that are free and allowed to do that work query the job pool, score candidate jobs by priority, distance, and reachability, reserve one, path to it, and execute it; the designation clears on completion. State owned: the set of designations and their job entries and reservations. Inputs: player marks; outputs: jobs consumed by agent action selection. Canonical forms: Dwarf Fortress dig, chop, and gather designations, RimWorld mine, cut, haul, and deconstruct designations, Oxygen Not Included errands with 1 to 9 priorities, Dungeon Keeper digging, and Going Medieval.
design_levers: per-designation priority levels
job claiming: nearest agent, best-skilled agent, or first free
reservation and timeout rules for unreachable or abandoned jobs
area painting tools versus per-object marking
whether designations wait on prerequisites (materials, tools) or fail immediately
interaction with per-agent work priorities and restrictions
dynamics: Throughput depends on agent count, travel, and hauling, so mass designation exposes logistics bottlenecks.
Accidental designations produce stories, such as mining into an aquifer or magma.
Order of designation becomes a planning skill, since agents take jobs in the order the claiming rule finds them.
failure_modes: Unreachable designations jam the queue and agents repeatedly attempt and abandon them.
Agents cross the whole map for a single low-value job because claiming ignores travel cost.
Large designations starve critical work such as feeding and hauling without clear priority overrides.
Players cannot see why a designation is not being worked: no one allowed, no path, or no materials.
mechanics.name: Designation orders
open_questions: Can players state work goals in language (dig a three-room hall near the stockpile) and have a model translate them into designations reliably?
Which claiming rule best balances efficiency with legible agent behavior?
mechanics.player_experience: The player states what should happen and watches agents figure out who and how. Painting a mine and seeing dwarves converge on it feels like management rather than puppetry, and the gap between intent and execution, such as a dwarf walking across the map for one job, becomes a source of frustration and stories.
mechanics.summary: The player marks tiles or objects for work such as dig, chop, or build, and autonomous agents claim and execute the jobs.

synergy.note: Designated work creates items that must be hauled, chaining jobs.

mechanics.definition: A machine is a tree of parts with a removal-order dependency graph, each part carrying a condition or fault state. A job arrives with symptoms; the player uses tests and tools to reveal hidden part states, removes covering parts in valid order, replaces or repairs faulty ones, reassembles, and verifies with a final test. In Car Mechanic Simulator 2018 and its 2021 sequel the player examines engine, suspension, and chassis, removes parts in a realistic order to reach a damaged component, buys a replacement or repairs it at higher levels, and uses a test track to find brake and suspension problems. PC Building Simulator applies the same loop to computers. Unlike diagnosis-treatment, the target is a machine whose state is fully deterministic once revealed. Inputs: fault state, symptoms, tools. Outputs: repaired machine, payment, and experience.
design_levers: how symptoms map to faults, and how many faults hide behind one symptom
tool set and what each test reveals
disassembly depth and how many parts block access
repair versus replace economics
job time limits and payment for partial fixes
dynamics: Players build mental models of real machine structure and speed up dramatically with experience.
Tool unlocks reshape the diagnosis strategy, since better tests skip disassembly.
Coupled with economy and workshop progression, choosing which jobs to accept becomes a planning layer.
failure_modes: When the game highlights faulty parts directly, diagnosis disappears and only the removal chore remains.
Deep disassembly for a single part becomes tedious once the novelty fades.
Faults that do not follow from symptoms make diagnosis guesswork.
mechanics.name: Diagnose and repair
open_questions: Can fault states generated from a causal model of the machine, rather than authored per job, produce varied but solvable diagnoses?
Could a language-model customer describing symptoms in their own words make diagnosis a real inference task?
mechanics.player_experience: Methodical, calm problem-solving with a clear finish. Players narrow down causes from symptoms, enjoy the order of unbolting and rebolting parts, and see a fixed machine run again. Learning the real structure of an engine or PC is part of the appeal.
mechanics.summary: The player inspects a machine, finds faulty parts with tools and tests, disassembles in order to reach them, and repairs or replaces them.

synergy.note: Breakdowns create the repair work; repair makes wear a skill problem rather than a tax.

mechanics.definition: Owns, per patient, a hidden condition, a set of symptoms (some visible, some revealed only by examinations), a diagnosis certainty or candidate list, and a deterioration timer. Each examination reveals symptoms or raises certainty at a cost in time and capacity; once certainty passes a threshold or one candidate remains, the patient goes to the matching treatment, whose success depends on staff skill or equipment. Untreated or mistreated patients worsen or die. Theme Hospital sends patients from a GP's office to diagnosis rooms, lets policy raise the required diagnosis level, and can kill patients when a guessed cure is wrong; Project Hospital has examinations uncover symptoms drawn from real medicine, tunes symptom overlap so one examination rarely settles a case, and requires finding dangerous hidden symptoms in time. Inputs are arrivals and examination capacity; outputs are cures, deaths, and throughput.
design_levers: number of conditions and the overlap of their symptom sets
information gained per examination and its time, cost, and capacity
certainty threshold for treatment and whether the player can override it
deterioration rate of untreated patients and the cost of misdiagnosis
staff skill and equipment effects on test accuracy and treatment success
dynamics: Diagnosis capacity becomes a bottleneck that creates queues, so room layout and staffing drive outcomes.
Guessing cures to clear queues trades throughput against deaths and reputation.
Contagious conditions couple diagnosis speed to outbreaks inside the facility.
failure_modes: Distinctive symptom sets let one examination solve every case, removing the uncertainty that defines the mechanic.
Opaque certainty math leaves players unable to tell whether a death was bad luck or bad policy.
Conditions are expensive to author, so case variety runs out and players memorize answers.
mechanics.name: Diagnosis and treatment
open_questions: Can language-model patients that describe symptoms in their own words make history-taking a real diagnostic channel?
Can generated cases keep symptom overlap tuned so diagnosis stays uncertain but solvable?
mechanics.player_experience: Detective work under time pressure. The player weighs another test against the risk of the patient worsening and decides when certainty is good enough to act. In management games the same choice becomes a policy over many patients: how much diagnosis to buy before treating.
mechanics.summary: Patients present symptoms, examinations reduce uncertainty about a hidden condition, and the correct treatment cures it while wrong or late treatment harms.

synergy.note: Patients queue at each diagnostic step, so hospital layout is queue design (Theme Hospital).

mechanics.definition: A card holds a prompt, two to four options, and per-option effects on meters, resources, relationships, or flags, sometimes with hidden or delayed outcomes. A deck sampler draws the next card by weights conditioned on state and history. In Reigns, advisors present cards that the player swipes left or right; each choice moves some of four meters (church, people, army, treasury), and the reign ends if any meter becomes completely full or empty, after which a successor continues with newly unlocked cards. FTL beacon events, This War of Mine encounters, and Paradox event pop-ups use the same option-and-effect format inside larger simulations. Inputs: current meters and flags. Outputs: meter deltas, flag changes, and the next card's eligibility.
design_levers: number of options per card and whether one is a safe default
how much of each option's effect is shown in advance (which meters, direction, magnitude)
effect magnitudes and whether meters fail at one bound or both
deck weighting, repetition limits, and state conditions for eligibility
delayed consequences that resolve cards later
dynamics: Two-sided meters push players to keep every value near the middle, which creates oscillation as they correct overshoots.
When eligibility depends on earlier flags, players steer toward or away from card lines across runs.
Inside a larger sim, choice effects feed other systems, so a cheap answer can surface as a crisis many turns later.
failure_modes: Repeated cards expose a small deck and turn dilemmas into memorized answers.
A dominant option on common cards removes the tradeoff.
Fully hidden effects make outcomes feel random; fully shown effects make them arithmetic.
Without a simulation underneath, choices do not interact and the format becomes a sequence of isolated quizzes.
mechanics.name: Dilemma cards
open_questions: Can a language model write cards conditioned on live simulation state while keeping effects inside a balanced, typed budget?
How much effect preview maximizes deliberation time without reducing choices to arithmetic?
mechanics.player_experience: Quick, weighty decisions where every answer costs something. Players weigh which meter can absorb the hit, try to predict hidden effects, and learn the deck over many runs. Two-sided limits, as in Reigns, make even popular choices dangerous.
mechanics.summary: Discrete choice events present a situation with a few options that each shift meters, values, or flags in tradeoff.

synergy.note: Laws presented as dilemmas make policy a moral choice with permanent consequences (Frostpunk).

mechanics.definition: The player maps controller or keyboard input to one character's locomotion (walk, run, jump, swim, fly) and interactions (pick up, use, attack, build) in real time. State owned: the avatar's position, velocity, facing, stance, and interaction target. Update rule: each frame, read input, apply a movement controller (kinematic or physics-based) subject to collision and terrain, and resolve interaction requests against objects in range. The world simulation runs around the avatar, often with only the area near it simulated in detail. It contrasts with overseer control, where the player commands at a distance. Canonical forms: Minecraft, Stardew Valley, The Long Dark, Subnautica, Valheim, and the farmer in Harvest Moon; hybrid games such as Satisfactory and Factorio put a factory builder in an avatar.
design_levers: movement speed, traversal options, and fast travel, which set how large the world feels
interaction reach and whether actions take time or animate
physics-based versus kinematic controller
whether the avatar has needs or survival meters
camera: first person, third person, or top-down
how much of the world simulates outside the avatar's vicinity
dynamics: The avatar's travel time becomes the hidden limiting resource, pushing players to build transport and automation.
Embodied presence makes environmental systems such as weather, temperature, and day-night directly threatening.
Avatar location sets what is simulated, so player movement shapes world state in games that simulate only loaded chunks.
failure_modes: Large worlds with slow movement turn logistics into walking chores until fast travel or automation unlocks.
Simulation limited to the avatar's surroundings freezes distant systems, breaking the illusion that the world runs without the player.
Avatar control competes with overseer tools in hybrid games, forcing awkward building from a character's viewpoint.
mechanics.name: Direct avatar control
open_questions: Can learned motion models (physics-based character controllers trained by RL) give avatars natural interaction with arbitrary simulated objects without per-object animation?
In generative world models where the world is rendered from the avatar's action stream, what simulation persistence can survive outside the view?
mechanics.player_experience: The player is in the world rather than above it. Scale, distance, and danger are felt in the body: a long walk to a resource, a fall, darkness. Systems are learned by touching them, and attachment shifts from managed agents to one's own character.
mechanics.summary: The player directly controls one embodied character's movement and actions in the simulated world.

mechanics.definition: Owns a lineage graph over characters, a succession law, and the mapping from the player's identity to a living character. When the player character dies, the law ranks eligible heirs by kinship, age, gender rules, or election; titles and assets are assigned, possibly split among several heirs; and control passes to the designated player heir. If no valid heir exists, the run ends. Crusader Kings III offers primogeniture, ultimogeniture, house seniority, three partition variants, and elective laws for feudal titles; the player continues as the player heir, normally the primary heir, and partition splits realms among siblings; with no valid heir titles pass to the liege, and the run ends without a playable heir. Reigns (2016) continues with a successor monarch who keeps unlocked cards. Inputs: lineage, laws, deaths. Outputs: the new player character, title distribution, opinion resets, claimants.
design_levers: succession law catalog and how players can change laws
what carries over to the heir: wealth, titles, opinions, skills, unlocks
partition versus single-heir distribution
opinion penalties and claimant uprisings at succession
game-over condition when no heir exists
dynamics: Rulers invest in heirs' education and marriages, coupling succession to lifecycle and romance.
Succession crises spawn claimant wars, connecting lineage to diplomacy and conflict.
Long runs become multi-generation stories that players chronicle as family histories.
failure_modes: Partition fragments a large realm into small pieces, which players experience as punishment and work around with exploits.
Successors who inherit everything make death meaningless.
Heir-killing exploits (arranging deaths to reach a better heir) become optimal play.
Sudden game over from a missing heir feels arbitrary if eligibility rules are opaque.
mechanics.name: Dynasty succession
open_questions: Can generated character arcs give each heir a distinct reign narrative while succession rules stay mechanical?
How much should the heir inherit to keep death meaningful without punishing long-term investment?
mechanics.player_experience: Death becomes a chapter break. The player plans for succession by raising, educating, and marrying heirs, fears the untested successor, and feels continuity through the dynasty rather than one person. Partition laws make every death a crisis of fragmentation.
mechanics.summary: When the player character dies, play continues as an heir chosen by inheritance rules.

synergy.note: Inherited traits make succession a long-term breeding and planning problem (Crusader Kings).

mechanics.definition: Owns an education level per citizen or the population's distribution over levels, and school capacity and coverage. Each period, school-age or eligible citizens with access and seats advance a level after a study period; capacity and budget limit throughput, and aging and migration change the mix. Jobs and buildings require minimum levels, so the distribution decides which industries can be staffed. Cities: Skylines uses uneducated, educated, well educated, and highly educated, with elementary schools of 300, high schools of 1,000, and universities of 4,500 seats; jobs carry education requirements, higher building levels need more educated workers, and citizens take lower jobs when nothing else is open. Victoria 3 moves literacy toward education access and grants pops qualifications for professions each month. Inputs: seats, budget, age structure. Outputs: the qualified worker distribution that labor matching reads.
design_levers: number of levels and job requirements per level
school capacity, upkeep, and study duration
who studies: age gates, coverage radius, cost to citizens
whether over-educated citizens accept lower jobs
side effects of education on crime, garbage, or consumption
dynamics: Education shifts the industry mix toward offices and high tech, changing pollution and land value.
Generational lag: the education mix follows age structure, so baby booms create later waves of graduates.
Mismatches between education and jobs produce unemployment and shortages simultaneously.
failure_modes: Over-education: when educated citizens fill matching jobs first, basic industry reports worker shortages while graduates compete for offices.
Long study times hide the lag between investment and effect, so players misread cause and effect.
Single-step jumps with large schools make education a one-time checkbox.
mechanics.name: Education and workforce
open_questions: Can agent-level career choice and schooling decisions by learned agents replace fixed education ladders without losing planning legibility?
Which matching rule between education and jobs avoids both over-education collapse and meaningless education?
mechanics.player_experience: The player invests now for a different city later: schools cost upkeep for years before industry can upgrade. Players watch over- and under-education and adjust capacity, policies, and job mix to avoid unemployable graduates or empty offices.
mechanics.summary: Education levels gate job types, and schooling converts the labor pool into higher levels over time.

synergy.note: Education reshapes which jobs can be filled.
Children age into a workforce whose skills depend on schooling.

mechanics.definition: Owns an election calendar, an electorate (simulated voters, voting blocs, or real players), candidates or parties, and a counting rule. At each election every voter's choice is computed from satisfaction, group membership, and campaign effects, or cast by a real player; the counting rule (plurality, threshold, single transferable vote) picks the winner, which sets tenure, a ruler, or party strength. Losing can end the game or remove the player's powers. Democracy 4 (2020) gives each simulated citizen membership in several overlapping voter groups, so elections depend on keeping enough groups content; before each election the player makes two promises, and broken promises raise cynicism. Frostpunk 2 (2024) has a council of 100 faction delegates vote on each proposed law, needing 51 votes, or two thirds for laws that expand the Steward's power. Tropico lets El Presidente hold or rig elections. EVE Online has real players elect the Council of Stellar Management, using single transferable vote since the eighth council.
design_levers: election frequency and whether the player can call, delay, or cancel elections
voter model: aggregate approval, blocs, or individually simulated voters with overlapping groups
franchise rules that decide who votes and with what weight
counting rule and thresholds
consequence of losing (game over, loss of office, reduced powers)
manipulation options such as rigging, promises, or campaign spending, and their costs
dynamics: Election cycles create policy rhythms: unpopular measures early in a term, giveaways before the vote.
Overlapping voter groups make every policy please someone and anger someone, which pushes players toward coalition math.
Promise systems couple short-term electoral gain to long-term credibility.
failure_modes: Elections that only test approval above 50% add a pass or fail check without strategy.
Cheap rigging or postponement removes the threat, so elections become a formality.
Real-player elections with low turnout let organized blocs capture outcomes, which can be accepted as play or felt as unfair.
mechanics.name: Elections
open_questions: Can LLM-driven voters and rival candidates respond to the player's actual speeches and platform, so campaigning is persuasion rather than slider tuning?
How should simulated electorates balance realism (stable partisanship) against responsiveness to player choices?
mechanics.player_experience: A deadline for popularity. The player tracks polls, times unpopular reforms for just after an election, courts swing groups, and feels the stakes rise as election day nears. In player-run elections the experience shifts to campaigning and alliance-building.
mechanics.summary: Periodic votes by simulated or real voters determine tenure or policy.

mechanics.definition: The player's continuous inputs (stick, wheel, pedals, mouse, motion controllers) drive the control surfaces or actuators of a physically simulated mechanism, and the challenge is the skill of producing good inputs, not choosing goals. State owned: mapping from input devices to actuator commands, including curves, deadzones, and assists. Update rule: each physics step, read inputs, apply response curves and optional assists (stability control, auto-trim, autopilot), and send commands to the mechanism model, such as flight aerodynamics or vehicle dynamics. Skill emerges because the mechanism has inertia, delays, and nonlinearities the player must learn to anticipate. Canonical forms: hand-flying in Microsoft Flight Simulator, X-Plane, and DCS World; driving in iRacing, Gran Turismo, and BeamNG.drive; and deliberately clumsy hand control in Surgeon Simulator.
design_levers: fidelity of the underlying mechanism model
assist layers that can be turned on or off (traction control, stability assist, auto-rudder, autopilot)
input device support and response curves
feedback channels: force feedback, motion, sound, and visual cues
deliberate awkwardness of control mapping for comedy, as in Surgeon Simulator
consequences of error: reset, damage, or permanent loss
dynamics: Skill becomes a personal progression system independent of unlocks, sustaining long-term play in racing and flight communities.
Hardware investment (wheels, HOTAS, VR) forms around the mechanic and reinforces community identity.
Combined with damage models, small control errors cascade into dramatic, unscripted failures.
failure_modes: Keyboard or gamepad play of a mechanism tuned for wheels or sticks is nearly impossible, splitting the audience by hardware.
Missing tactile and vestibular cues make real-world techniques fail on screen.
Assists that are all or nothing leave no learning ramp between novice and full simulation.
mechanics.name: Embodied skill control
open_questions: Can learned coaching models watch input traces and teach technique the way an instructor does?
Can adaptive assists, trained to keep the player near the edge of competence, replace fixed difficulty toggles?
mechanics.player_experience: Competence lives in the hands. The player practices, crashes, and gradually internalizes how the mechanism responds until difficult maneuvers feel fluid. Mastery is personal and hard-won, and assists let novices participate before they have the skill.
mechanics.summary: Real-time motor skill operating a simulated mechanism, such as hand-flying, driving, or surgery, is the main challenge.

synergy.note: Detailed handling models reward motor skill and hardware like wheels and pedals.

tension.note: Real-time motor skill and time compression are hard to offer together.
Turns remove the real-time pressure motor skill depends on.

mechanics.definition: Owns each company's share count, share price, and ownership table. Share price is recomputed from company value (cash, assets, earnings, debt) and moved by trading pressure, so purchases raise it and sales lower it. Players buy and sell shares in their own and rival companies for dividends or gains. Crossing an ownership threshold, usually a majority, transfers control: the target is merged, its assets absorbed, or its owner eliminated. Railroad Tycoon (1990) starts each railroad with $1 million split between equity and a loan and lets players trade shares in themselves and rivals in a miniature stock market. Offworld Trading Company (2016) makes buyouts the win condition: a player who loses majority control of their own company is eliminated, and the game warns a player when a rival can afford to buy them out without telling the rival. Capitalism (1995) makes being bought out by a competitor a loss, and Transport Tycoon sells rival company shares in 25% blocks.
design_levers: share price formula (book value, earnings multiple, dividend yield, recent trading pressure)
price impact per share bought or sold
control thresholds and their consequences (merger, elimination, board control)
restrictions on buying, such as minimum company age or share blocks
dividends and buybacks as defensive tools
visibility of who owns what and warnings before a takeover
dynamics: Owning shares of rivals turns their success into the player's dividends, softening competition into partial alliance.
Late-game cash races emerge as players hoard money for buyouts instead of investing in production.
Buying back one's own stock converts operating profit into takeover defense, starving expansion.
failure_modes: A leading player can buy out weaker rivals early, ending the game before economic play matters.
AI companies that do not defend their float become free takeover targets.
Share prices driven only by book value can be gamed by moving cash into assets before a buyout.
mechanics.name: Equity and buyouts
open_questions: Can learned or LLM-driven investor agents produce believable sentiment (bubbles, panics) without a hand-tuned price formula?
What takeover thresholds keep buyouts a threat without ending multiplayer games early?
mechanics.player_experience: Reading a rival's balance sheet as a target. The player buys a rival's stock while it is cheap, defends their own float by buying back shares, and feels dread when a competitor's cash nears the price of a takeover. Endgames become races to accumulate cash.
mechanics.summary: Companies issue shares whose price tracks performance, and players buy them for profit or accumulate a majority to take control of rivals.

synergy.note: Buyouts give competition a decisive end state (Offworld Trading Company, Capitalism).

mechanics.definition: Owns a compute budget and the cost charged against it: a per-tick allowance with an optional carryover bucket, a time cost per operation, or a fixed capacity such as instruction slots or memory. Each run or tick the game charges each operation or program its cost; when the budget runs out the program is terminated, throttled, or simply takes longer in game time, and unused allowance may accumulate. Screeps gives each player a CPU limit per tick (20 without CPU Unlock), banks unused CPU in a bucket of up to 10,000, lets a tick draw up to 500 from it, and terminates scripts at the limit. The Farmer Was Replaced charges simulated ticks per operation: literals and assignment are free, arithmetic costs 1, and a successful move() costs 200. Autonauts caps each bot's program at 12 to 32 instructions by its head part. Bitburner charges each script a RAM cost that must fit on the server running it. Player-programming owns the language and interpreter; this mechanic owns only the metering, so one language can run under tight, loose, or no budgets.
design_levers: budget type: real CPU time, simulated tick cost per operation, instruction count, or memory
size of the per-tick allowance and of a carryover bucket that allows bursts
per-operation cost table, especially the ratio between cheap computation and expensive actions such as moves
overrun consequence: termination, throttling, or slower simulated time
how the budget grows: progression, hardware parts, or payment
dynamics: Players adopt caching, memoization, and scheduling patterns that resemble real systems engineering.
Expensive actions relative to computation push players toward code that plans a lot and acts rarely.
Communities share profilers and optimized libraries, spreading efficient patterns across players.
failure_modes: Budgets measured in real CPU time vary with server load, so the same code can pass or fail unpredictably.
Budgets that are too tight make debugging feel like fighting the platform rather than solving the problem.
When budget increases are bought, as with Screeps' CPU Unlock, competitive outcomes mix code quality with spending.
Cost tables that charge almost nothing for computation let players brute-force problems the budget was meant to constrain.
mechanics.name: Execution budget
open_questions: When AI assistants write working code from a description, does the budget become the main remaining challenge, and does that keep programming games interesting?
Which budget types (time per tick, cost per operation, memory) teach the most transferable efficiency skills?
mechanics.player_experience: Optimization becomes the game once the code works. Players profile, cache paths, batch work, and count moves, because the same behavior written more cheaply runs more units, farms faster, or fits on the bot. A routine that finally fits under the cap, or a tick that stops overrunning, feels like a real engineering win.
mechanics.summary: Player-written programs are metered against a simulated compute budget, such as CPU per tick, tick cost per operation, instruction slots, or RAM, which makes efficiency the scarce resource.

mechanics.definition: Owns a relation value for each pair of factions, the modifiers feeding it, and agreement states such as war, peace, truce, alliance, and vassalage. Events (trade, gifts, border friction, attacks, broken treaties) change the value, and many games drift it toward a baseline. A proposal is accepted when an AI evaluation combining relation, interests, relative power, and reputation passes a threshold. RimWorld faction goodwill runs -100 to 100: hostile at -75 or below, allied at 75 or above until it falls to 0; civil outlanders drift back into -50..50; trade gives +1 per 500 silver and returning a prisoner +12, while pirates stay at -100. Europa Universalis IV caps opinion at +200 and -200 with itemized reasons, adds 5 to alliance acceptance per point of diplomatic reputation, and allows a base of 4 diplomatic relations. Inputs: events, interests, power. Outputs: war declarations, trade access, military aid, coalitions.
design_levers: relation scale, thresholds for state changes, and baseline drift
modifier catalog and decay per event type
AI acceptance formula (relation, power, interests, reputation) and how much of it is shown
agreement types and their obligations, such as alliance calls to arms and truce lengths
limits such as relation slots or diplomat counts
dynamics: Coalitions against an expanding player form from shared grievances, a balancing loop on growth.
Alliance chains pull factions into wars they did not choose, producing cascading conflicts.
Trade raises goodwill, which opens more trade, a reinforcing loop between economy and diplomacy.
failure_modes: Gift exploits: money converts linearly into friendship, so diplomacy becomes a purchase.
AI that ignores its own interests or the balance of power feels suicidal, while AI that refuses for unshown reasons feels arbitrary.
Factions locked at permanent hostility remove diplomacy from most of the threat model.
Coalitions that form against the leader regardless of context read as rubber-banding.
mechanics.name: Faction diplomacy
open_questions: Can language-model negotiators bargain, bluff, and keep commitments with players in ways players accept as fair and legible?
How should opinion and interest be separated so AI factions betray for reasons players can foresee?
mechanics.player_experience: The player manages a web of relations as a resource: buying goodwill with gifts, timing betrayals, and reading acceptance breakdowns to see what a deal needs. Wars feel like consequences of accumulated grievances rather than random events.
mechanics.summary: Factions hold relations with each other, and treaties, alliances, and wars follow from interests and opinion.

synergy.note: Standing with a faction gates treaties and trade.

mechanics.definition: The world is a 2D grid where each cell stores a material id and sometimes temperature, velocity, or lifetime. Each update a cell applies its class rule: powders fall straight or diagonally, liquids fall then spread sideways and swap with lower-density neighbors, gases rise then spread, and solids stay. Reaction rules convert cells, such as fire igniting flammable neighbors and water turning to steam. In Noita (2019) liquids compare densities to swap, wood burns for a set time and is destroyed, and explosions turn pixels into collapsing sand. The world is split into 64x64 chunks with dirty rectangles, updated bottom-up across threads in four checkerboard passes, with each pixel able to move 32 pixels beyond its chunk. Rigid bodies made of pixels (Box2D) recompute their shape and split as pixels are destroyed. The Powder Toy (2008), with 258 elements as of 2025, is the long-running sandbox in this lineage.
design_levers: material catalog and per-material density, flammability, and melting point
update order and randomization, such as alternating left and right scans
reaction table between materials
simulation region: whole world or only near the player
whether mass is conserved
dynamics: Hazard chains such as oil fires spreading, steam forming, and floors collapsing.
Players engineer traps and terrain with the same rules that threaten them.
The level is permanently reshaped by play, so no two runs stay alike.
failure_modes: A fixed scan order biases movement in one direction unless it alternates or randomizes.
Compute limits restrict simulation to areas near the player, so distant regions freeze.
Chain reactions kill the player suddenly, which can read as unfair.
Rules that duplicate or delete material break conservation and enable exploits.
mechanics.name: Falling-sand materials
open_questions: Can neural cellular automata or learned rules produce new materials with plausible behavior at runtime?
Can GPU compute extend per-pixel simulation to whole persistent worlds instead of the area near the player?
mechanics.player_experience: Everything is simulated, so play becomes experiment. Players pour, burn, flood, and dig, and they die to chain reactions they set off themselves. Wonder and danger come from the same rules.
mechanics.summary: Every pixel or cell holds a material whose class rule makes it fall, flow, or rise by swapping with neighbors, with reactions layered on top.

synergy.note: Per-pixel materials with reaction rules produce chemistry players can exploit (Noita, Powder Toy).

mechanics.definition: Owns a burning state per cell, tile, or object (unburnt, burning, burnt), often with fuel and heat values. Each tick a burning unit consumes fuel and tries to ignite neighbors with a chance or rate scaled by their flammability, moisture, and wind direction; it goes out when fuel runs out or when water, rain, or firefighters remove it. Inputs are material flammability, weather, and suppression; outputs are destroyed structures and terrain, heat, and sometimes smoke or updrafts. SimCity spreads fire between flammable tiles and fire stations put it out; Breath of the Wild's chemistry engine lets fire change the state of materials such as grass, whose burning creates updrafts, and rain stops it; Far Cry 2 and Dwarf Fortress propagate fire through grass and trees.
design_levers: ignition sources and their rates: lightning, overheating, arson, player tools
flammability, fuel load, and burn duration per material
spread probability per neighbor and the wind bias on it
moisture and weather modifiers, such as rain suppressing ignition
suppression tools: water, firefighters, fire station coverage, firebreak materials
dynamics: Players build firebreaks and separate flammable storage, which changes settlement layout.
Fire couples with weather and terrain: dry seasons and wind produce larger fires, and rain ends them.
Players repurpose fire as a weapon or tool, such as burning grass under enemies or clearing forest.
failure_modes: Spread tuned slightly too high burns the whole map before the player can react; slightly too low makes fire a nonevent.
Fire that ignores construction choices, such as stone burning like wood, removes the decision space.
Large burning areas in cell-based implementations cost noticeable frame time during big fires.
mechanics.name: Fire spread
open_questions: Can learned combustion and smoke surrogates make fire visually rich while its spread stays readable and controllable?
mechanics.player_experience: A small spark becomes an emergency. The player races to contain fire before it reaches stockpiles or homes, or uses it as a tool: burning a field to clear it, lighting grass to drive enemies, or riding the updraft. Fire teaches the player to read the map as fuel and firebreaks.
mechanics.summary: Fire ignites and spreads across flammable cells or objects at rates set by fuel, wind, and moisture, consuming what it burns.

synergy.note: Wind and dryness govern fire spread.

mechanics.definition: The aircraft state holds position, attitude, linear and angular velocity, control-surface deflections, and engine state. Each physics step computes aerodynamic forces from airspeed, angle of attack, sideslip, and air density, adds thrust and gravity, and integrates six-degree-of-freedom rigid-body motion. Two families exist. Coefficient-table models look up lift, drag, and moment coefficients per flight condition. Blade element models, as in X-Plane, divide wings, control surfaces, and propellers into small elements, compute forces on each from aircraft geometry rather than relying only on performance tables, and sum them, so stalls, spins, and ground effect arise from the geometry. Arcade games use simplified models that keep the aircraft stable. Outputs are aircraft motion and instrument readings.
design_levers: model fidelity: arcade, coefficient tables, or blade elements
assists such as auto-trim, stability augmentation, and stall protection
stall and spin behavior near the edge of the envelope
weather and turbulence coupling
control response curves and input filtering
dynamics: Weather and terrain create emergent challenges such as crosswind landings and mountain wave turbulence.
System failures interact with aerodynamics to produce scenarios no one scripted.
Energy management becomes the core tactical resource in air combat.
failure_modes: Over-stable models feel on rails and remove the skill.
Without assists, high fidelity makes flight unflyable for new players.
Table-driven models misbehave in regimes outside their data, such as spins or ground handling.
Each new aircraft needs costly per-model tuning before it feels right.
mechanics.name: Flight aerodynamics
open_questions: Can learned surrogates trained on computational fluid dynamics give accurate flight models for aircraft without hand tuning?
Can an AI instructor read the flight model state and coach novices through stalls and landings?
mechanics.player_experience: Hands-on control with real consequences. Players learn energy management, trim, stall warnings, and landings, and skill grows visibly over hours. Arcade variants keep the feeling of speed without the workload.
mechanics.summary: Lift, drag, thrust, and control-surface forces computed from airspeed and attitude govern aircraft motion.

synergy.note: A faithful flight model makes real procedures necessary rather than ceremonial.

mechanics.definition: Fluid state is stored per cell (mass, depth, pressure, element) or as velocity and density fields. Cellular games move mass between neighbor cells in proportion to height or pressure differences and sort elements by density, as in Oxygen Not Included, where each cell holds one gas or liquid element with a mass, and Dwarf Fortress, where water depth runs from 1 to 7 per tile. Continuous solvers follow Jos Stam's Stable Fluids for games (2003): add sources, diffuse implicitly with Gauss-Seidel relaxation, advect semi-Lagrangian by tracing cells back through the velocity field, and project velocity to be divergence-free by solving a Poisson equation, which stays stable at any time step. Outputs feed breathing, flooding, pressure damage, and heat transport.
design_levers: representation: cellular mass transfer, particles, or velocity fields
grid resolution and update rate
one element per cell or mixtures
compressibility and pressure limits
viscosity and flow speed per fluid
whether mass is strictly conserved
dynamics: Leaks contaminate connected spaces and couple room layout to air quality.
Floods spread through open layers and paths and reshape priorities across a colony.
Coupled with heat, fluids carry temperature and drive phase changes.
failure_modes: Non-conserving rules let players delete or duplicate fluid, which becomes an exploit.
Fluid simulation dominates compute and forces small maps or reduced update rates.
Semi-Lagrangian solvers lose detail to numerical dissipation, so flow looks thick and smoothed.
Gases are unreadable without overlays, so players misjudge spreading hazards.
mechanics.name: Fluid and gas simulation
open_questions: Can learned fluid simulators run 3D liquids at game budgets while conserving mass well enough for gameplay?
What overlays make invisible gas flow legible without constant mode switching?
mechanics.player_experience: Managing something that spreads on its own. Players seal leaks, vent gases, pump floods, and plan around pressure they can only see through overlays. Small mistakes spread slowly, then all at once.
mechanics.summary: Liquids and gases stored per cell or as fields flow, mix, and pressurize across space according to pressure and density differences.

synergy.note: Gases and liquids carry heat, so thermal management becomes plumbing (Oxygen Not Included).

mechanics.definition: Pipes connect producers, consumers, tanks, and pumps into networks that carry one fluid type per segment. The update rule ranges from discrete packets to pooled segments to pressure solvers. Oxygen Not Included moves one packet of up to 10 kg per pipe segment per second, giving 10 kg/s per line, and exchanges heat between the liquid, the pipe, and its tile. Factorio 1.x simulated flow between adjacent pipes, so throughput fell with distance and depended on build order; Factorio 2.0 merges connected pipes into segments where producers push freely, consumers pull at a rate proportional to the fill ratio, and fluid does not propagate. SimCity games treat water and sewage as coverage networks; GlassBox modeled units of water as agents moving through pipes. Inputs: producer output, consumer demand, topology, pumps. Outputs: fluid delivered per consumer and stored per segment or tank.
design_levers: flow model: packets, pooled segments, or pressure simulation
throughput limits per pipe and whether distance matters
fluid mixing rules and penalties
pumps, valves, and priority controls
thermal and phase-change behavior in pipes
dynamics: Fluid networks couple to thermal systems, as when hot pipes in Oxygen Not Included cook a base or freeze lines.
Shared networks create priority conflicts between consumers.
Tanks act as buffers, changing timing behavior across networks.
failure_modes: Distance-dependent throughput with no in-game feedback, as in Factorio 1.x, made long pipelines fail mysteriously; the developers rewrote the system for predictability.
Accidental fluid mixing can contaminate a network permanently if cleanup is costly.
Pressure models that are realistic but invisible make players guess.
mechanics.name: Fluid pipe networks
open_questions: Could learned fluid surrogates give pipe networks pressure realism at low compute while keeping behavior predictable?
Which fluid behaviors (pressure, mixing, heat) add decisions rather than confusion?
mechanics.player_experience: Plumbing problems. Players learn that fluids behave differently from items: they mix, back up, and run out at the far end. When the model is predictable, routing is satisfying; when it is not, pipes become a source of mysterious shortages.
mechanics.summary: Fluids such as water, oil, sewage, or gas flow through pipes with pressure or throughput limits between producers and consumers.

claims.text: Walter Bright's 1977 game Empire is credited as the earliest video game use of fog of war, and Warcraft and StarCraft keep previously seen areas visible as terrain while hiding changes to enemy units.

mechanics.definition: For each player the world holds a visibility state per cell or entity, usually three-valued: unexplored, explored but not currently visible, and visible. Each tick visibility is recomputed from the sight radius of the player's units, buildings, and sensors, optionally modified by line of sight, elevation, weather, and target stealth. Visible cells show live state; explored cells show the last observed snapshot, so changes there go unseen. Inputs are observer positions and sensor ranges; outputs are a per-player view and a hidden-information gap between true and known state. Walter Bright's Empire (1977) is credited as the earliest use; Warcraft and StarCraft used the explored-but-stale shroud. In simulation games: Factorio's radar charts distant chunks slowly and keeps nearby ones live, unexcavated tiles in Dwarf Fortress stay unknown, and Against the Storm keeps forest glades hidden until opened.
design_levers: two-state (unexplored or visible) versus three-state with stale memory
sight radius per unit or building and terrain, elevation, and weather modifiers
radius check versus true line-of-sight raycasts
whether remembered cells show last-seen enemies or only terrain
reveal tools: scouts, radar, satellites, traded maps
whether the AI obeys the same fog or has full knowledge
dynamics: Hidden information enables ambushes, bluffs, and a scouting economy where information has a price.
Stale memory produces errors such as attacking a base that has since been reinforced.
Coupled with procedural terrain, fog turns every map into an exploration problem rather than a known layout.
failure_modes: An AI given full map knowledge to compensate for weak reasoning feels like cheating once players notice.
Fog that hides only static terrain becomes a one-time clearing chore with no lasting tension.
Cheap, fast scouts make fog trivial and reward spamming them.
In simulations whose threats are systemic rather than adversarial, fog adds travel tedium without decisions.
mechanics.name: Fog of war
open_questions: Can learned opponents that keep beliefs about unseen state replace AI map-hacking without losing challenge?
If a generative world model creates unobserved regions only when observed, does fog become a generation trigger rather than concealment?
mechanics.player_experience: The edge of the known map pulls the player outward. Scouting becomes a decision with costs, darkness reads as threat, and finding a resource deposit or an enemy base feels like discovery rather than lookup.
mechanics.summary: Parts of the world stay hidden or stale until observed by the player's units, structures, or sensors.

synergy.note: Sensor coverage and concealment are central to operational play.

mechanics.definition: Owns population counts per species (aggregate) or individual animals (agent-based) and a directed feeding graph of who eats whom. Each tick prey grow toward a carrying capacity set by plants or habitat, predators remove prey in proportion to encounters, and predators reproduce from food eaten and starve without it. The Lotka-Volterra form, published by Volterra in 1926, has prey growing at rate a and consumed at rate b times predators, and predators converting prey into growth while dying at a constant rate; the result cycles without damping. Games add carrying capacity, starvation, migration, and respawn so species do not drift to extinction. SimLife and Species: Artificial Life, Real Evolution let creatures eat each other on a shared map; Eco simulates plant and animal populations that players can overhunt; Viva Pinata attracts visitors and predators according to garden contents. Inputs are species, habitat, and harvesting; outputs are population trajectories.
design_levers: feeding graph topology: number of species, diet breadth, and omnivores
prey growth rate and carrying capacity from plants or habitat
predation efficiency and conversion of food into offspring
starvation and natural death rates, and the minimum population before extinction
immigration or respawn rules that rescue extinct species
aggregate populations versus individually simulated animals
dynamics: Trophic cascades: removing a top predator lets herbivores strip vegetation, which lowers carrying capacity for everything.
Player hunting or harvesting acts as an extra predator and can tip a stable cycle into collapse.
Coupled with habitat or climate change, species ranges shift and new feeding links form.
failure_modes: Undamped predator-prey cycles drift until a population hits zero, so ecosystems collapse without any player error.
Hidden population floors or respawns added to prevent extinction make overhunting consequence-free.
Long delays between action and population response hide cause and effect, so players read crashes as random.
mechanics.name: Food web
open_questions: Can learned behavior models give individually simulated animals plausible foraging and avoidance at ecosystem scale without hand-written AI?
Which visualizations make delayed predator-prey feedback legible without population graphs?
mechanics.player_experience: Tending a system the player cannot command. Adding a predator to fix overgrazing can crash the herbivores and then starve the predator a few generations later. The player learns to act through balance and delay, watches population graphs, and feels responsible when a species disappears.
mechanics.summary: Species eat and are eaten along a feeding graph, so populations rise, crash, and oscillate under predator-prey dynamics.

synergy.note: Predation supplies selective pressure; selection reshapes the food web over generations.
Habitat defines which species can co-occur, which sets the possible food webs.

mechanics.definition: A forecaster computes and displays projected future values of selected variables: days of food left at current consumption, next period's budget balance, upcoming temperature or storms, population trend, or completion time for a project. It owns a forecast method, a horizon, and a refresh interval, but no simulation state. Common methods are runway (stock divided by net rate), linear extrapolation of recent trend, lookup of an authored or pre-rolled schedule of events, and rarely a short simulated lookahead. Outputs are numbers, countdowns, or projected curves. Canonical forms: Frostpunk's temperature forecast showing cold snaps days ahead, budget projections in SimCity and Cities: Skylines, turns-to-complete counters in Civilization, and Football Manager's projected finances.
design_levers: forecast method: runway, extrapolation, authored schedule, or simulated lookahead
horizon length
accuracy and whether uncertainty is shown, such as ranges or confidence that improves with upgrades
which variables get forecasts
whether forecasts include the player's queued actions
proactive display versus on demand
dynamics: Players stock to the forecast horizon, so a forecast that underestimates causes synchronized shortfalls.
Forecast crises create preparation sprints followed by slack, a characteristic rhythm in survival city builders.
Shifting play from reactive to anticipatory raises the value of storage and buffers relative to throughput.
failure_modes: Linear extrapolation misleads when rates are seasonal or batched, producing false alarms or false security.
Perfect forecasts of every threat turn disasters into checklists with no uncertainty.
Noisy forecasts with no stated error teach players to ignore them.
mechanics.name: Forecasting
open_questions: Can a learned surrogate of the full simulation give cheap probabilistic forecasts (a 70 percent chance of famine within two seasons) for coupled systems that games now only extrapolate?
What forecast accuracy maximizes preparation decisions without removing surprise?
mechanics.player_experience: Monitoring turns into planning. The player sees the cliff before reaching it and acts early, buffers to the forecast horizon, and feels dread when the projection is grim. Surprise drops; preparation becomes the challenge.
mechanics.summary: The interface projects future states such as resource runway, budget balance, or upcoming weather.

mechanics.definition: The player picks a structure type, position, and usually rotation. The game tests the footprint against occupancy, terrain slope, required neighbors (road access, a water tile, an ore patch), and cost. A valid placement writes the structure into the occupancy grid or spatial index and deducts cost; demolition reverses it, often with a partial refund. Tile grids (SimCity, Factorio, RimWorld) make footprints exact; gridless placement (Manor Lords, Foundation) allows arbitrary angles and curved streets. A ghost preview tinted valid or invalid is the standard interface. The occupancy map is the input to pathing, coverage, adjacency, and room detection.
design_levers: grid, offset grid, or gridless placement, with or without snapping
footprint sizes and shapes, and whether rotation changes them
terrain rules: slope tolerance, water, and foundations
requirement rules such as road adjacency or resource tiles
demolition refund and rebuild cost, which set how much commitment a placement carries
dynamics: Early placements constrain later ones, producing path-dependent layouts and eventual rebuilds.
Space becomes a resource that players trade against throughput or beauty.
Players converge on standard modules, which leads to blueprint copying and sharing.
failure_modes: Gridless placement leaves slivers and gaps that waste space and look untidy.
Free demolition and full refunds remove commitment, so placement stops being a decision.
A red ghost with no reason given makes hidden placement rules feel arbitrary.
Permissive rules with abundant space make layout trivial.
mechanics.name: Building placement
open_questions: Can natural-language or sketch placement ("put a market near the docks") keep the puzzle while removing the click cost?
Which footprint rules make gridless placement as plannable as a grid?
mechanics.player_experience: A spatial puzzle with immediate feedback. Players plan space, fit footprints together, and live with early decisions as the layout fills. Gridless placement adds expressive freedom but also the chore of aligning things by eye.
mechanics.summary: The player places discrete structures on a grid or freely, and placement constraints turn layout into a spatial puzzle.

mechanics.definition: Player input (free text, a combination of objects, or a request) plus selected game context is sent to a generative model, usually a large language model, and the output is either shown as content or parsed into game state such as a new item, a combination result, or a rule change. AI Dungeon continues a story from Do, Say, Story, and See inputs, first on GPT-2 (1.5 billion parameters in AI Dungeon 2, 2019) and later GPT-3, with a player-editable memory field. Infinite Craft asks a model to name the result of combining two elements and records first discoveries. Suck Up! and Whispers from the Star use models to drive character responses. Key parts: a context builder, an output schema or parser, a cache that may make results deterministic, and moderation. Inputs: player request and context window. Outputs: text or structured content.
design_levers: what the model may change: presentation only, or typed game state through a constrained schema
caching and determinism: fresh generation per request versus a shared global cache
context and memory construction, such as summaries, retrieved facts, and player-pinned memory
moderation filters and their false-positive rate
model size, latency budget, and per-request cost
authored seeds, examples, and rules that anchor tone and balance
dynamics: Players treat the model as a system to probe, sharing prompts that produce surprising or broken outputs.
A shared global cache turns generation into a discovery race, with first discoveries as social status.
When outputs are typed into game state, they combine with other systems and can unbalance economies or progression.
failure_modes: Models forget earlier content beyond their context, so stories contradict themselves (a criticism of AI Dungeon).
Unprompted inappropriate output, and broad filters that flag harmless text, both damaged AI Dungeon's community in 2021.
Output that does not alter simulation state feels weightless, because nothing it says has consequences.
Per-request inference cost and latency limit how often generation can run and push it to servers.
mechanics.name: Generative content on demand
open_questions: What output schemas let a model add items or rules to a running simulation without breaking its balance?
Can on-device models make generation cheap enough to run per tick rather than per player request?
How should generated content be persisted and versioned so that worlds stay consistent across sessions?
mechanics.player_experience: Open-ended curiosity. Players try things no designer anticipated to see what the model will produce, and part of the fun is probing its boundaries. When the output changes game state, finds feel personal; when it is only text, players notice that nothing is remembered or consequential.
mechanics.summary: A generative model creates new content such as text, items, recipes, or rules at runtime in response to player input.

synergy.note: Language input invites generated responses; generated content invites further language input.

tension.note: Generated content resists the authored preconditions event chains rely on.

claims.text: In Populous, raising and lowering land is the most basic power, mana comes from followers building houses, and increasing mana unlocks earthquakes, floods, swamps, and volcanoes.
In Black & White, villagers worshipping around the Temple generate power for miracles, which can be cast by gestures with the Hand.

mechanics.definition: The player is an external force that cannot command agents directly but can cast powers on the world. State owned: a power pool (mana, belief, prayer power) and the set of unlocked powers with costs and cooldowns. The pool fills from a simulation quantity, typically the number or devotion of followers, and casting spends it to apply an effect at a target: raise or lower land, flood, earthquake, swamp, volcano, rain, lightning, heal, or summon. Effects then propagate through the other systems (terrain, hydrology, population). Canonical forms: Populous, where raising and lowering land is the basic power, mana comes from followers building houses, and more mana unlocks earthquakes, floods, swamps, and volcanoes; Black & White, where worshipping villagers generate power for miracles cast by gesture; From Dust; WorldBox.
design_levers: power source: followers, belief, devotion, or time
cost, area, and cooldown per power
unlock order of powers
whether powers are destructive, constructive, or both
casting input: menu, gesture, or physical manipulation
how much the world's systems amplify or resist each power
dynamics: Follower-funded power creates a reinforcing loop: help followers grow to gain power to help them more.
Terrain-altering powers chain into hydrology and settlement systems, such as floods that relocate a whole population.
In competitive god games, power denial (reducing enemy followers) matters as much as casting.
failure_modes: One dominant power used repeatedly trivializes opponents.
Gesture recognition that misreads input makes casting frustrating and unreliable under pressure.
Powers with fixed scripted effects feel like animations rather than interventions in a simulation.
mechanics.name: God powers
open_questions: Can players describe a miracle in language and have a generative system produce effects grounded in the world's physics rather than from a fixed list?
How do learned agents that react to miracles, such as fear or worship, change the follower loop?
mechanics.player_experience: The player feels large and indirect. Problems are solved by reshaping the world rather than ordering people, and destruction is satisfying. The loop of growing followers to earn more power to help or punish them gives a sense of patronage.
