mechanics.summary: The player spends a power resource on miracles that alter terrain, weather, or creatures.

synergy.note: Miracles that raise land or move water are terraforming delivered as power.

mechanics.definition: Each household, residence, or population tier consumes a basket of goods at fixed per-capita or per-residence rates. Consumption draws from a market, warehouse, or delivered stock; the satisfied fraction of each need feeds population size, satisfaction, tax income, or eligibility to upgrade. Anno 1800 splits needs into basic needs, which raise inhabitants per house, and luxury needs, which raise taxes and happiness, and requires full houses before residents advance a tier. Caesar III houses evolve only when supplied with several food types and goods such as pottery, furniture, oil, and wine, and devolve when supply lapses. Victoria 3 pops buy goods from a market to meet their needs. Inputs: population counts and supplied goods. Outputs: stock drawdown, fulfillment ratios, and growth or downgrade signals.
design_levers: consumption rate per capita for each good and how it scales with tier
which needs are mandatory for population or upgrades versus optional bonuses
substitutability between goods (any of several food types) versus strict requirements
penalty curve for unmet needs: lost population, lower taxes, unrest, or downgrade
delivery path from stock to consumer: global pool, market radius, or walker delivery
dynamics: Population growth raises consumption, which requires more production, which requires more workers: the expansion loop of Anno-style builders.
Tier requirements create layered dependency trees that couple distant islands or regions through trade.
Shortages propagate to labor because unhappy or downgraded populations work less or leave.
failure_modes: Fixed rates make ideal ratios solvable once, after which consumption becomes a spreadsheet exercise.
Downgrade cascades, where one lapsed good devolves a district and collapses its labor supply, feel disproportionate.
Too many required goods per tier create micromanagement that crowds out spatial decisions.
mechanics.name: Goods consumption
open_questions: Can learned demand models give populations preferences that shift with culture and events instead of fixed baskets?
What is the smallest basket that still produces interesting supply-chain planning?
mechanics.player_experience: The population is a mouth the player must keep feeding at scale. Players compute production ratios, such as producers per hundred residents, and expand supply ahead of demand. Each tier upgrade raises income but adds new goods to the basket, so success creates the next shortage.
mechanics.summary: A population consumes goods at per-capita rates; unmet consumption lowers satisfaction or blocks advancement.

synergy.note: Each tier consumes new goods, so advancement drives production expansion (Anno).

mechanics.definition: Owns per-agent knowledge sets (facts, rumors, beliefs about events or other agents), optionally with source and confidence, and the social graph they travel over. When two agents interact, each fact the speaker holds passes with a probability set by salience, relationship, and personality, possibly distorted; receiving a fact can trigger opinion or memory updates. Most games skip this and treat events as known to all: Comme il Faut's social facts database in Prom Week records every event as known to every character. Generative Agents (2023) shows diffusion through language-model conversation: over two game days, awareness of a Valentine's Day party grew from 1 to 13 of 25 agents and of a mayoral candidacy from 1 to 8. Inputs: interactions, event salience, the social graph. Outputs: who knows what, reputation and opinion effects that lag the event, misinformation.
design_levers: transmission probability per interaction and decay of salience over time
graph structure: who talks to whom in households, workplaces, and gathering places
distortion rate and whether sources are tracked
which facts are worth gossip and how they change opinions
player tools to plant, suppress, or trace rumors
dynamics: Information cascades through social hubs such as innkeepers and leaders, so centrality determines influence.
Lagged knowledge lets players act before consequences arrive, enabling crime, deception, and damage control.
Distorted rumors create conflicts over events that did not happen as told.
failure_modes: Slow or patchy propagation makes consequences feel disconnected from actions.
Untraceable chains make reputation changes look random.
Tracking every fact for every agent costs memory and update time in large populations.
Language-model gossip can invent facts that never happened and corrupt game state.
mechanics.name: Gossip propagation
open_questions: Can language-model gossip be constrained to facts in the simulation log while keeping distortion as a designed, tunable variable?
What propagation speed makes consequences feel both earned and suspenseful?
mechanics.player_experience: Actions have a spreading radius: a crime matters once someone talks, so the player manages witnesses, timing, and who to tell. Watching news reach a rival late creates suspense and room for deception.
mechanics.summary: Information about events spreads through social contacts, changing what agents know and believe.

synergy.note: Reputation travels through gossip, so deeds have audiences.
What agents hear about each other changes how they feel.

mechanics.definition: Owns a preference profile per species or crop (acceptable ranges or targets for terrain type, temperature, humidity, water, foliage, space, and company) and computes a suitability score for each tile, region, or enclosure by comparing local conditions to the profile, often as a weighted sum or as the worst single factor. The score gates where things can be placed or survive and scales growth, yield, welfare, or breeding. Zoo Tycoon and Planet Zoo grade each enclosure on terrain mix, foliage, area, and biome for each animal; Anno 1800 gives each island fertilities that decide which crops it can farm; Viva Pinata spawns a species only when the garden meets its requirements. Inputs are terrain and climate state; outputs are a scalar per location used by other systems.
design_levers: number of factors in the profile and how narrow each acceptable range is
combination rule: weighted average, product, or worst single factor
hard gate on placement versus soft multiplier on growth or welfare
how the score is shown: checklist, percentage, overlay, or only through outcomes
whether conditions change at runtime through seasons, climate, or terraforming
dynamics: Different profiles force specialization by location, which drives trade between regions or islands.
Coupled with climate or seasons, suitable areas move and populations must migrate or be relocated.
Players terraform to manufacture suitability, creating demand for terrain tools and materials.
failure_modes: Checklists with exact percentages become form-filling once the player knows the threshold values.
Averaging factors lets a perfect score on one factor hide a fatal mismatch on another.
Static suitability makes each location solved once, removing reasons to revisit it.
mechanics.name: Habitat suitability
open_questions: Can species distribution models learned from ecological data generate plausible, varied requirement profiles for procedurally generated species?
mechanics.player_experience: Matching puzzles on the map. The player reads a species' or crop's profile, then sculpts terrain, plants foliage, or picks locations until the indicator turns green. Unmet requirements show up as unhappy animals or missing harvests, so the player iterates on the place rather than on the creature.
mechanics.summary: Species or crops thrive only where conditions such as terrain, temperature, water, and cover match their needs, scored per location.

synergy.note: Terrain edits change biome conditions, letting the player engineer habitats (Terra Nil, Equilinox).

mechanics.definition: The player holds an inventory of components and a set of known recipes, each mapping an input multiset to an output item. A craft checks that inputs are present, any required station (workbench, forge, furnace) is nearby, and the recipe is unlocked, then consumes the inputs and produces the output instantly or after a short delay. Minecraft uses a 2x2 grid in the inventory and a 3x3 grid at a crafting table, with shaped recipes keyed to spatial arrangement; Don't Starve, Valheim, and Subnautica use menu lists gated by stations and blueprints; Ultima Online ties success to a crafting skill. Infinite Craft replaces the recipe table with a language model (Llama 2, later Llama 3.1) that generates the result of any new pair and stores it so every player gets the same answer. Inputs: carried items, station proximity, unlock state. Outputs: new items and consumed components.
design_levers: recipe count and depth of intermediate components
discovery model: all visible, unlocked by research or blueprints, or found by experimentation
station gating and whether stations must be nearby
craft time and whether crafts can be queued or batched
spatial grid versus list interface
inventory limits that bound how much can be carried to a station
dynamics: Tool tiers gate access to materials, which gate the next tool tier, producing a progression ladder from rules alone.
Inventory limits couple crafting to base building and storage chests.
In multiplayer worlds players specialize in crafting lines and trade, as Ultima Online crafters did.
failure_modes: Hidden recipes without in-game discovery aids push players to wikis, as in early Minecraft before its recipe book.
Long chains of trivial intermediates turn crafting into inventory sorting.
Crafting that is strictly better than found loot, or strictly worse, makes one of the two systems irrelevant.
mechanics.name: Hand crafting
open_questions: Can generative models produce open recipe spaces like Infinite Craft whose outputs also have balanced, mechanically meaningful stats rather than only names?
How should discovery be explained to players when a model rather than a table decides what a combination yields?
mechanics.player_experience: Gathering with intent. The player looks at a desired item, works back to its components, and goes out to collect them, so the recipe list becomes a shopping list that structures exploration. The first craft of a new tool is a small power spike that opens the next zone or task.
mechanics.summary: The player or avatar combines carried components into items from a recipe list, gated by workstations and known recipes.

mechanics.definition: Items on the ground or in the wrong storage generate hauling jobs that name a source item and a destination with space. Idle agents with hauling enabled pick jobs by priority and distance, path to the item, carry up to their capacity, and deliver. Throughput is bounded by the number of haulers, walking distance, carry capacity, and competing work. RimWorld haulers move items to the highest-priority stockpile with space, even out of lower-priority stockpiles; Dwarf Fortress splits hauling into labors for stone, wood, food, refuse, and furniture; The Settlers passes every good from flag to flag along roads, with one carrier per road segment; Banished and Timberborn rely on laborers or haulers whose numbers set delivery speed. Inputs: item locations, destinations, agent availability. Outputs: item movement and a job backlog.
design_levers: carry capacity per agent and the effect of tools such as wheelbarrows or carts
job selection rules: priority, distance, or reservation
how many agents haul and whether hauling is a separate role
stockpile priorities and filters that generate jobs
whether production buildings have local storage or need pickup
dynamics: Distance between production and storage becomes a hidden cost, rewarding compact layouts.
Hauling competes with every other job, so labor shortages appear as slowdowns everywhere at once.
Coupled with needs, haulers take breaks, creating rhythmic dips in throughput.
failure_modes: Hauling backlogs are hard to diagnose because the bottleneck is spread across many agents.
Item ping-pong between stockpiles with similar priorities wastes agent time.
Agents abandoning urgent work to haul low-value items reads as AI stupidity.
mechanics.name: Hauling jobs
open_questions: Could learned job dispatch reduce visible AI stupidity while keeping hauling a resource the player manages?
How should backlogs be visualized so players can find the true constraint?
mechanics.player_experience: Watching the colony carry its own weight. Players notice that new production does not help when no one is free to carry it, then shorten distances, build local stockpiles, or assign more haulers. The constraint is visible on screen as piles of goods and idle workbenches.
mechanics.summary: Agents pick up and carry items between locations via a job queue, making hauling capacity a hidden throughput constraint.

synergy.note: Where stockpiles sit determines how much hauling labor the colony spends.

mechanics.definition: Each cell, room, or object holds a temperature and often mass, specific heat capacity, and thermal conductivity. Each tick heat flows between neighbors in proportion to the temperature difference and a conductance from both materials, and temperature changes by heat divided by mass times heat capacity. Thresholds trigger melting, boiling, freezing, damage, and effects on agents. In Oxygen Not Included a tick is 0.2 s; cell-to-cell transfer uses q = dT x dt x k x 1000, multiplied by 25 between solids and gases and 625 between liquids; transfer stops below a 1 C difference or 0.1 DTU, and one tick may close at most a quarter of the difference. Insulated tiles divide conductivity heavily. RimWorld holds one temperature per room that equalizes with outdoors through walls and doors and is driven by heaters and coolers.
design_levers: per-material specific heat capacity and conductivity
phase-change temperatures and their consequences
transfer multipliers between solids, liquids, and gases
tick length and per-tick caps for stability
insulation strength and environmental heat sinks
damage and agent thresholds
dynamics: Machines emit heat as a byproduct, so a growing industrial base slowly overheats itself.
Seasons, fire, and magma couple to temperature and drive phase changes and evacuations.
Heat moved by fluids links plumbing layout to thermal management.
failure_modes: Rounding and phase-change edge cases let players create or delete heat, which becomes a standard exploit.
Per-cell diffusion across a large map becomes a late-game performance cost.
Without overlays, rising temperature is invisible until a threshold fails.
If equilibrium takes far longer than a session, heat stops mattering; if it is fast, it becomes noise.
mechanics.name: Heat transfer
open_questions: Can forecasting tools that project temperature trends turn slow thermal failure into a readable planning problem?
mechanics.player_experience: Thermal engineering. Players insulate, vent, and cool, and they watch overlays for creeping heat. Late failures arrive slowly: a base heats a fraction of a degree per cycle until crops die or machines stop.
mechanics.summary: Temperature diffuses between cells, materials, and objects by conductivity and heat capacity, and thresholds trigger phase changes and damage.

synergy.note: Temperature thresholds trigger material state changes and reactions.
Temperature drives rot rates.

mechanics.definition: A recorder subscribes to simulation events, filters them by significance, and stores structured records (actor, action, target, place, time, cause) indexed by entity. Browsers present the records as biographies, site histories, and timelines; some games feed records back into play. Dwarf Fortress Legends mode lists historical figures, sites, artifacts, written works, regions, and civilizations, with Chronicles by Age, records the player's own fortress and adventurer achievements, and exports XML that can reach about a gigabyte for long histories. RimWorld records tales that its art system uses to describe what a sculpture depicts. Inputs: the event stream. Outputs: a queryable archive, generated descriptions, and knowledge that agents or items can carry.
design_levers: significance filter: which event types and thresholds get recorded
record granularity and causal links between records
retention policy and summarization as the archive grows
presentation: raw log, templated prose, timeline, or map
feedback paths: art, books, rumors, or agent knowledge drawn from the archive
export formats for external tools
dynamics: Players reconstruct and embellish stories from sparse records, and communities share them as written retellings.
Fed back into the world, records let artworks, books, and rumors reference real past events.
Third-party legends viewers and map tools grow around exported data.
failure_modes: Recording everything floods the archive with trivial entries and very large files.
Templated, tabular text is dry, so most players never open the browser.
Records without causal links list events but do not explain why they happened.
mechanics.name: History chronicle
open_questions: Can language models turn structured event logs into faithful narrative summaries that do not invent causes?
Which significance measures best predict the events players later retell?
mechanics.player_experience: Looking back over a run turns scattered events into a story. Players browse to find out who caused what, discover that a minor figure had a long history, and retell their runs to others. When chronicles feed art or rumors, players see their own history reflected inside the world.
mechanics.summary: The game records significant simulation events into a structured history that players can browse and other systems can reference.

synergy.note: Directed incidents become chronicle entries, so pacing produces a retellable history.
Pre-play generated history populates the same archive that records play (Dwarf Fortress legends).

mechanics.definition: After terrain and biomes exist, a coarse simulation runs the world forward for a chosen number of years: civilizations found sites, grow, migrate, trade, make war, and found religions, and a subset of individuals is tracked as historical figures with families, titles, kills, and relationships. The final state is the starting map for play, and the event log feeds a chronicle. In Dwarf Fortress the player sets history length (worlds of 1,000 or 10,000 years are possible), populations and deaths counters rise during generation, only part of each site's population becomes historical figures (nobles, megabeasts, villains, their families), and a cap with optional culling limits their total. Caves of Qud generates sultan histories and Crusader Kings seeds dynasties from authored history instead. Inputs: map, races, parameters. Outputs: sites, factions, figures, artifacts, and an event archive.
design_levers: history length in years
number and type of civilizations and their behavior rules
which individuals are tracked as historical figures and the cap on their count
abstraction level of populations, battles, and trade during generation
event types simulated (wars, migrations, religions, artifacts, monsters)
how much of the generated history is revealed versus discoverable in play
dynamics: Generated grudges and alliances set the political situation the player starts in, so two seeds play differently.
Historical figures and artifacts become quest targets, visitors, and threats during play.
Players share notable generated histories as stories in their own right.
failure_modes: Long histories take a long time to generate and produce very large saves.
Coarse rules can produce degenerate worlds, such as one civilization conquering everything or all civilizations dying out.
History that never surfaces in play is invisible effort.
mechanics.name: Simulated history generation
open_questions: Can language models turn coarse simulated histories into readable myths and chronicles without contradicting the record?
What is the cheapest history abstraction that still yields grudges and relationships players recognize in play?
mechanics.player_experience: The world feels older than the player. Ruins, feuds, and legendary artifacts have causes the player can look up, and players discover that the world they inherited contains specific grudges, heroes, and lost wars. Long generation times build anticipation.
mechanics.summary: World generation simulates years to centuries of civilizations, figures, and events before play begins, producing the starting world.

synergy.note: Generated terrain constrains where simulated civilizations settle, fight, and leave ruins.

mechanics.definition: Owns water depth per cell on a terrain heightfield, often with source and sink rates, flow velocity, and soil moisture. Each tick water moves from higher to lower surface height between neighboring cells, evaporates, and is added by springs, rain, or rivers; moisture spreads from water to nearby land and gates crop growth. Timberborn links each tile to its four neighbors by virtual pipes, ticks every few hundred milliseconds, evaporates water, and runs recurring droughts that switch sources off and grow harsher; dams, levees, and floodgates regulate flow, and moisture falls off with distance and sharply uphill. From Dust and Cities: Skylines also simulate terrain water, while Pharaoh schedules a yearly Nile flood that waters floodplain farms. Inputs are terrain, sources, weather, and player structures; outputs are water levels, floods, and moisture.
design_levers: grid resolution and tick rate of the flow solver
source strength schedules, including drought and flood cycles and how fast they ramp
evaporation rate, seepage, and moisture spread distance
structures: dams, levees, floodgates, pumps, canals, and their flow controls
whether water erodes or deposits terrain
dynamics: Upstream structures change downstream conditions, creating spatial dependencies across the map.
Reservoir capacity becomes a stock that buffers seasonal or drought variability.
Flooding couples with building placement, farmland, and disasters such as dam failure.
failure_modes: Fixed flow values on structures cause oscillations and waves; Timberborn's developers avoided hard-coded dam values for this reason.
Abrupt switching of water sources makes water slosh unrealistically; Timberborn ramps source strength down before a drought starts.
Water that leaks through gaps or ignores terrain edits reads as a bug and breaks trust in the system.
Large water grids can dominate simulation cost and cap map size.
mechanics.name: Hydrology
open_questions: Can learned shallow-water surrogates run large terrain water at interactive rates while staying predictable enough to engineer against?
mechanics.player_experience: Engineering with a moving material. The player shapes terrain and builds dams to store water for dry spells, protects low ground from floods, and watches a mistake travel downstream. Droughts turn reservoir size into the main survival question, and a dam failure is a visible, traceable disaster.
mechanics.summary: Water flows across terrain and through rivers by height differences, producing floods, droughts, irrigation, and dam management.

synergy.note: Reshaping terrain redirects water, so terrain editing becomes water engineering (From Dust, Timberborn).

mechanics.definition: Owns an attractiveness score per settlement or region, computed from jobs, housing vacancy, wages or standard of living, services, happiness, and reputation, and a flow rule that turns the score difference against an outside reference or other regions into arrivals and departures per period. Arrivals usually need free housing, and departures follow sustained low scores. In Micropolis, the SimCity engine, residential migration rises and falls with employment, the ratio of jobs to residents. Victoria 3 moves pops within a market toward states with higher migration attraction, set mainly by standard of living, while migration laws filter who may move. RimWorld instead adds colonists through storyteller events such as wanderers joining. Inputs: jobs, housing, satisfaction, policy. Outputs: population inflow and outflow by type.
design_levers: factors in the attractiveness score and their weights
reference point: a fixed outside world, competing regions, or other players
flow elasticity per unit of score difference
housing requirement and arrival batch size
selectivity: which classes, cultures, or skills migrate, and policy filters
dynamics: Growth raises demand for services and jobs, which lowers attractiveness until supply catches up, a balancing loop.
Booms and busts as migration lags job creation.
Inter-regional competition: improving one region drains its neighbors.
failure_modes: Overshoot: migration responds fast to jobs, then unemployment spikes, then emigration, oscillating.
Unconditional arrivals make population trivially easy and remove the planning puzzle.
Opaque scores leave players unable to tell why people leave.
Mass arrivals overwhelm services in one step and trigger cascades.
mechanics.name: Immigration by attractiveness
open_questions: Can migration models calibrated to real census or survey data make city builders useful for planning education without hurting playability?
How should attractiveness be explained so players can attribute departures to causes?
mechanics.player_experience: The player grows population indirectly by making the place worth moving to, and loses it the same way. Growth feels earned and fragile: a housing shortage or unemployment spike shows up as people leaving.
mechanics.summary: Population arrives or leaves based on attractiveness such as jobs, housing, and happiness relative to alternatives.

mechanics.definition: Owns, per creature, a tree of body parts with hit points, tissue layers, or functions, plus a list of conditions such as cuts, burns, fractures, bleeding, infection, scars, and missing or artificial parts. Damage lands on a sampled part; part health feeds capacities such as consciousness, moving, manipulation, sight, breathing, and blood pumping, which scale work speed, combat, and survival. Each tick bleeding drains blood, infections race against immunity, and tended wounds heal. RimWorld derives capacities from parts: consciousness below 30% keeps a pawn from waking, moving below 15% incapacitates, each arm supplies half of manipulation, blood pumping at 0% is fatal, poor tending raises infection and scarring risk, and each bionic leg adds 12.5% moving. Dwarf Fortress damages tissue layers per part; Project Zomboid tracks wounds per body region. Inputs are damage and treatment; outputs are capacity multipliers, pain, and death.
design_levers: granularity of the body tree: regions, organs, tissue layers
mapping from part damage to capacities and from capacities to actions
bleeding rate, infection chance, and healing rate, and how treatment quality modifies them
permanence: scars, lost parts, chronic pain
replacement options such as prosthetics, bionics, and transplants, and their availability
dynamics: Injured agents work slower, lowering output and raising pressure on healthy ones.
Demand for medicine, doctors, and prosthetics creates a medical economy.
Disabilities shape character identity and the stories players tell about them.
failure_modes: Too many parts and conditions make the health screen unreadable, so players cannot tell what is lethal.
Fine-grained damage with high lethality makes outcomes feel like dice rolls, such as death from one hit to a vital organ.
Permanent disabilities without replacement paths make injured characters dead weight the player discards.
mechanics.name: Injury body model
open_questions: Can language models narrate injuries and recovery so deep body models stay legible without a dense health tab?
mechanics.player_experience: Injuries become specific stories: a colonist missing a hand works slower, a hunter with a shattered leg cannot flee. The player triages by which wound threatens life first, stops bleeding before worrying about infection, and plans around lasting disabilities or replaces parts with prosthetics.
mechanics.summary: Bodies are hierarchies of parts with their own damage, and wounds, bleeding, infection, and prosthetics change capacities such as moving and manipulation.

mechanics.definition: Owns a set of groups within the polity, each with members, clout (political power), ideology or preferences over laws and policies, and approval. Clout is recomputed from members' wealth, numbers, and enfranchisement; approval from how well current laws match the group's preferences, whether it is in government, and events. Approval and clout gate what the player can do and trigger effects: favorable traits, petitions, obstruction, radicalization, or revolt. Victoria 3 (2022) is the canonical form: each pop gives political strength to the group it supports based mainly on wealth and the voting law, clout is the group's share of the national total and classifies groups as powerful, influential, or marginalized, marginalized groups cannot activate traits, and law enactment chances depend on the endorsement or opposition of groups in government. Tropico 6, Stellaris factions, and Frostpunk 2's factions are other forms.
design_levers: number of groups and how distinct their preferences are
clout formula (wealth, population, votes, offices held)
approval inputs (laws, government membership, events, promises)
effects at each approval and clout band (traits, petitions, obstruction, revolt)
how members move between groups as their economic conditions change
dynamics: Laws that empower a group raise its clout, which helps it block reforms that would weaken it, so institutions entrench.
Economic change moves people between groups, so industrialization shifts political power over decades.
Angry groups with high clout radicalize into movements that can force concessions or civil war.
failure_modes: When one group's clout dominates and nothing shifts it, politics freezes into one optimal coalition.
Approval effects that are too weak make groups ignorable, and too strong make reforms impossible.
Opaque clout and approval math makes political outcomes feel random without detailed tooltips.
mechanics.name: Interest groups
open_questions: Can LLM-driven group leaders negotiate, make demands, and remember broken deals in ways that stay consistent with the clout and approval model?
Can interest groups form and dissolve from the population's actual interests rather than from a fixed authored list?
mechanics.player_experience: Governing through coalitions. The player reads which groups are strong and what they want, brings friendly groups into government, placates or marginalizes opponents, and accepts that every reform makes someone angry. Power is never absolute.
mechanics.summary: Factions within a polity have clout and preferences over policies, and their approval gates what the player can do.

synergy.note: Policies gain or lose group approval, so lawmaking becomes coalition management.
Alienated groups radicalize into unrest.

mechanics.definition: Owns the worker supply by type (education, class, or profession) and the job slots by type that buildings offer, and matches them. Unmatched workers are unemployed; unfilled jobs leave buildings understaffed, and output scales with staffing. In Micropolis, the SimCity engine, Employment = jobs / (residents / 8) drives migration of (residents / 8) x (Employment - 1) per cycle, a labor ratio of residents to jobs clamped to 0-1.3 scales projected commercial and industrial growth, and unemployment is one of the problems citizens complain about. Cities: Skylines and Workers and Resources split workers by education, so a city without educated workers cannot staff offices or advanced plants. Victoria 3 hires pops into buildings by profession and wage, and Anno 1800 requires each residence tier to staff that tier's production buildings.
design_levers: number of worker types and whether higher types can fill lower jobs
staffing-to-output curve (linear, threshold, or minimum crew)
commute or catchment limits on which workers can reach which jobs
migration response to unemployment and vacancies
wages as a lever that shifts who takes which job
dynamics: Jobs attract migrants, migrants demand shops and services, and those create more jobs, producing boom cycles.
A large employer far from housing generates commuter traffic and congestion.
Education pays off with a long lag, so labor mismatches appear whenever the economy shifts.
failure_modes: Aggregate matching hides the cause of shortages, so players see idle buildings without knowing which worker type is missing.
Education systems that push the whole population past the available jobs can stall industry with no clear fix.
Instant matching removes the lag that makes workforce planning interesting.
mechanics.name: Labor market
open_questions: Can agent-level career choice by learned or LLM agents produce realistic structural unemployment without hand-tuned migration formulas?
How much labor detail (types, commutes, wages) can players manage before the mechanic becomes opaque?
mechanics.player_experience: Balancing homes against jobs. The player reads unemployment and vacancy numbers, builds housing or schools when factories sit idle, and learns that a new industry is useless without workers to run it.
mechanics.summary: Workers fill jobs by type and education; mismatches create unemployment or labor shortages that throttle production.

mechanics.definition: Owns a value per tile or block, recomputed periodically from distance to centers, nearby amenities and nature, and nuisances. In Micropolis, the open-source SimCity engine, each developed 2x2 block gets value = 4 x (34 - distance to the population-weighted center) + a bonus for nearby trees and water - pollution, minus 20 where crime exceeds 190, clamped to 1-250. The value then drives residential growth (value minus pollution, scaled and capped), picks which of four building quality tiers develops, raises tax revenue through the city average, and lowers crime, which is computed as 128 - land value + density - police coverage. SimCity 4 computes desirability separately for each wealth level, and Cities: Skylines levels up buildings partly on land value raised by services and parks and lowered by pollution and noise.
design_levers: components of the value formula (center distance, amenities, terrain, pollution, crime, noise) and their weights
radius and falloff of each amenity or nuisance
smoothing and update frequency of the value field
thresholds that map value to building tiers, density, or wealth class
whether value feeds taxes, rents, or residents' wealth directly
dynamics: Low value raises crime and crime lowers value, so neglected districts slide toward slums unless policing or amenities break the loop.
Rising value upgrades buildings and density, which adds traffic and noise that cap further gains.
Value-based tax revenue rewards beautification, coupling aesthetics to the budget.
failure_modes: Stacking cheap amenities such as parks in one spot maxes value and becomes a dominant pattern.
When the formula is visible only as an overlay color, players cannot tell which factor holds a block back.
A strong distance-to-center term makes every city look the same: dense core, poor fringe.
mechanics.name: Land value
open_questions: Could a learned hedonic model trained on real property data give land values that feel like real cities, and would players accept its opacity?
Can land value include speculation and expectations, not only current neighbors, without destabilizing growth?
mechanics.player_experience: Shaping neighborhoods. The player places parks, transit, and services to lift values, keeps factories away from homes, and watches shabby blocks turn into towers. Checking the land value overlay becomes a planning habit.
mechanics.summary: Each location's value is computed from nearby amenities, nuisances, and access, and it drives density and building upgrades.

synergy.note: Zones develop according to land value, so placement decisions compound over time.
Service coverage raises land value, rewarding complete coverage with density.
Pollution depresses land value, creating the industrial-residential separation puzzle.

mechanics.definition: Owns each agent's age (or an age-structured population count) and a table of life stages with durations, capabilities, needs, and mortality. Each tick age advances; crossing a stage boundary changes what the agent can do (work, marry, study), what it needs, and how it looks; mortality rises with age until death. Births add agents through reproduction rules. The Sims 2 has seven stages (baby, toddler, child, teen, young adult with University, adult, elder): babies become toddlers after 3 Sim days, children become teens after 8, teens live 15 days, adults become elders after 29, and elder lifespan depends on the aspiration meter. Victoria 3 aggregates the same idea: natural growth is birth rate minus mortality, both falling as standard of living rises. Inputs: time, health, birth rules. Outputs: workforce and dependents, deaths, succession and inheritance triggers.
design_levers: number and duration of life stages relative to the game calendar
capabilities and needs per stage, such as child labor rules or elder frailty
mortality curve and whether death is fixed-age or probabilistic
birth rules and fertility windows
player controls such as aging toggles and lifespan settings
dynamics: Age structure sets dependency ratios that throttle labor and drive housing and school demand.
Founding cohorts create waves of births, retirements, and deaths that repeat across generations.
Deaths trigger inheritance, succession, and grief, coupling lifecycle to social and dynastic systems.
failure_modes: Lifespans short relative to play pace make characters die before players attach, so games add lifespan settings or aging toggles.
Demographic echoes: one founding cohort ages together and causes a labor collapse or mass death decades later.
Children are pure cost with nothing to do, so players avoid births.
mechanics.name: Lifecycle and aging
open_questions: Can generative models keep a character recognizable across ages in appearance and personality while allowing growth?
What ratio of lifespan to play pace maximizes attachment and generational play?
mechanics.player_experience: Time becomes personal: the player watches characters grow up and grow old, plans careers and heirs, and grieves. Aging turns a static roster into a pipeline in which the player raises the next generation of workers.
mechanics.summary: Agents are born, age through life stages with different capabilities, and die.

synergy.note: Generations turn over, carrying inherited traits forward.
Families form and produce the next generation.

mechanics.definition: Owns outstanding principal, an interest rate, a repayment schedule, and a borrowing limit. Each period interest is charged to the treasury, and principal is repaid on schedule, at will, or at bond maturity. The limit and rate often depend on a credit rating, net worth, or the number of outstanding loans. Missed payments trigger penalties, forced liquidation, bankruptcy, or game over. Railroad Tycoon (1990) starts each railroad with $1 million split evenly between equity and a loan and lets players sell bonds for more capital. SimCity 2000 adds bonds to the city budget, Theme Hospital offers loans through a policy setting, and Transport Tycoon lets companies raise and repay a loan in increments up to a cap.
design_levers: interest rate and whether it rises with debt load, credit rating, or economic conditions
borrowing cap tied to net worth, rating, or a fixed limit
repayment structure (amortized, interest-only, bond maturity, repay at will)
default consequence (penalty, asset seizure, bankruptcy, game over)
priority of debt service relative to wages and services when cash runs short
dynamics: Leverage amplifies booms and busts: borrowed capital grows revenue faster but turns a demand dip into bankruptcy.
Rates that rise with debt load create spirals in which new loans pay old interest.
Interest acts as a money sink that drains surplus in the late game.
failure_modes: Cheap debt with high early returns makes borrowing the maximum at the start a dominant opening in many tycoon games.
Default with no warning or recovery path ends runs abruptly and teaches players never to borrow.
Fixed rates in a growing economy make debt irrelevant once revenue scales.
mechanics.name: Loans and debt
open_questions: Could AI lenders that assess a player's plans and history negotiate terms in language, making credit a relationship rather than a slider?
What rate curves keep leverage a real choice across a whole game rather than an opening move?
mechanics.player_experience: Betting on the future. The player borrows to build faster than income allows, watches interest eat margins, and times repayment. A downturn while leveraged turns a confident plan into a scramble to stay solvent.
mechanics.summary: Capital can be borrowed at interest with repayment schedules, so leverage accelerates both growth and failure.

mechanics.definition: Owns the rules applied to an entity's assets at death: which items are destroyed, which drop into a container (corpse, tombstone, wreck) at the death location, who may loot it and for how long, and what compensation applies, such as insurance payouts or protected items. On death the inventory is partitioned by those rules, a container entity is spawned with a despawn timer or permanence, and the character respawns elsewhere or not at all. Ultima Online left corpses lootable by other players and added item insurance in 2003; EVE Online destroys ships for good and drops part of the cargo and fittings in a wreck. Valheim leaves the player's items in a tombstone at the death site; Minecraft drops the inventory where the player died. Unlike permadeath, which removes the character, this mechanic removes or relocates possessions while the character usually continues.
design_levers: share of assets destroyed, dropped, or kept
who can loot dropped assets and for how long before they despawn
insurance or protected-slot systems and their cost
respawn location relative to the death site
additional death costs such as skill or experience loss
dynamics: Asset destruction creates steady demand for replacements, sustaining player crafting and markets.
Corpse runs become memorable expeditions, often with friends.
Players match the value of a loadout to the risk of the area, producing cheap disposable kits for dangerous trips.
failure_modes: Full loot in open player-versus-player worlds lets strong players farm weak ones, a problem Ultima Online answered by splitting off the consensual-PvP Trammel facet in 2000.
Short despawn timers turn a death far from home into an unrecoverable loss that ends play sessions.
Players hoard their best gear and never use it, so the items the loss rule protects stop being played.
mechanics.name: Loss on death
open_questions: Could AI-run recovery services or scavenger agents make dropped assets part of the world's economy rather than a pure loss?
What mix of destroyed and recoverable assets keeps risk meaningful without driving players to hoard?
mechanics.player_experience: Risk is measured in gear. The player decides what to carry into danger, keeps backups at home, and after a death makes a tense run back to recover a corpse or tombstone. In player-versus-player worlds the same rule makes every fight a gamble for the other side's equipment.
mechanics.summary: When a character or ship is destroyed, its carried or fitted assets are lost or dropped at the death site for the owner or others to recover, with insurance or retrieval rules as softeners.

mechanics.definition: Owns, for each producing machine, a set of modifier slots or settings and the effect vector they sum to: speed, productivity (extra output per cycle), energy use, and sometimes pollution or quality. Cycle time divides by one plus the speed bonus, productivity fills a bonus bar that yields free outputs, and power draw scales with the boost, often superlinearly. Satisfactory clock speed runs from 1% to 250%, each of up to three Power Shards raises the cap by 50 points, and power scales with exponent 1.321928, so 250% draws 335.77% of base power. Factorio fills module slots with speed, productivity, efficiency, or quality modules, beacons project module effects onto nearby machines, and productivity bonuses are capped at +300%. Dyson Sphere Program coats items with proliferator so machines consuming them gain extra products or speed. Captain of Industry spends Unity on building boosts. Unlike production-chain, which owns recipes and buffers, and quality-tiers, which owns item grades, this mechanic owns the cost-benefit curve of pushing a single machine harder.
design_levers: shape of the power or cost curve per unit of boost, linear or convex such as Satisfactory's exponent of about 1.32
separate effect axes (speed, productivity, efficiency, pollution) and the tradeoffs bundled into one slot
slot counts per machine and whether boosts can be shared with neighbors, as with beacons
cost of the boost itself: crafted modules, rare world pickups such as Power Shards, or a currency such as Unity
caps on stacked bonuses, such as Factorio's +300% productivity limit
which machine types accept boosts: assemblers, drills, labs, turrets
dynamics: Players trade space for power: compact boosted builds compete with sprawling unboosted ones.
Productivity bonuses on late stages save every upstream input, so players boost the end of a chain first.
Boosting a bottleneck moves the bottleneck to power generation, coupling factory design to the grid.
failure_modes: Productivity bonuses that stack without a cap create net-positive loops; Factorio caps productivity at +300% to prevent this.
One dominant configuration, such as productivity modules everywhere with beacons for speed, becomes a solved template.
Convex power costs that are not shown make overclocking feel like a sudden grid failure.
Boosts gated on rare pickups push players into exploration chores unrelated to factory design.
mechanics.name: Machine boosting
open_questions: Can planners that solve module and clock settings for a target rate coexist with players who enjoy solving them by hand?
Which cost curves keep boosted and unboosted builds both viable through the late game?
mechanics.player_experience: An optimization layer on top of ratio planning. Players decide whether to build more machines or push the ones they have, weighing floor space and materials against a growing power bill. Slotting the last productivity module or overclocking a bottleneck machine is a satisfying fix, and the power spike that follows is the bill.
mechanics.summary: Per-machine modifiers such as modules, beacons, clock speed, or coatings trade extra power, scarce items, or currency for faster or more productive machines.

mechanics.definition: Entities carry material tags (wood, metal, grass) and element states (burning, wet, frozen, electrified). A rule table maps element-material and element-element pairs to state changes applied on contact or within an area each tick. In The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, Takuhiro Dohta described a chemistry engine beside the physics engine: physics is a rule-based movement calculator and chemistry a rule-based state calculator. Elements (fire, water, ice, electricity, wind) change the states of materials and of each other, and materials do not change each other. Divinity: Original Sin uses surfaces where oil burns and water conducts lightning. Outputs are state changes that trigger damage, movement, and new elements.
design_levers: number of elements and material tags
density of the interaction table: which pairs react
propagation: contact, area, or spread rate over time
duration and decay of states
how closely rules follow real-world intuition
how strongly reactions are telegraphed visually
dynamics: Chained reactions, such as fire on grass creating an updraft for gliding in Breath of the Wild.
Environmental kills and accidents emerge from mixing combat with terrain and weather.
Players find puzzle solutions designers did not plan.
failure_modes: An interaction that works in one place but not another breaks trust in the whole system.
Combinatorial growth of pairs produces untested reactions and bugs.
One reaction combo dominates combat and flattens choice.
Authored puzzles with single intended solutions conflict with systemic shortcuts.
mechanics.name: Material interactions
open_questions: Can a language model judge interactions for arbitrary pairs of materials at runtime while staying consistent across a session?
What is the smallest rule table that still produces chains players experience as emergent?
mechanics.player_experience: Asking "what if" and having the world answer consistently. Players combine elements for creative solutions in puzzles and fights, and the satisfaction is in solutions that feel discovered rather than designed.
mechanics.summary: A rule table defines how elements such as fire, water, and electricity change materials and each other on contact.

claims.text: Satisfactory's Space Elevator has five Project Assembly phases that unlock tiers 3-4, 5-6, 7-8, 9, and the ending; phase 1 needs 50 Smart Plating, and phase 5 needs Nuclear Pasta, Biochemical Sculptors, AI Expansion Servers, and Ballistic Warp Drives.
Dyson Sphere Program solar sails are fired by EM-Rail Ejectors, last 5,400 seconds by default, and are absorbed permanently by completed shells, while Small Carrier Rockets build frames.
shapez 2 operator goal lines grow exponentially in cost per level, for example 15,000 shapes at 18% growth.

mechanics.definition: Owns one or more megaprojects, each a sequence of phases with large delivery requirements (item types and quantities, or energy), the deliveries accumulated so far, and the reward for each phase or the whole project (unlocks, power, a victory, or an ending). Delivered goods are consumed, so the project converts factory throughput into progress and gives an open-ended economy both a target and an outlet. Satisfactory's Space Elevator takes five Project Assembly phases, from 50 Smart Plating in phase 1 to Nuclear Pasta, Biochemical Sculptors, AI Expansion Servers, and Ballistic Warp Drives in phase 5, and its phases unlock tiers. Dyson Sphere Program builds its sphere from solar sails fired by EM-Rail Ejectors and frames carried by rockets, and sails expire after 5,400 seconds unless a completed shell absorbs them. shapez 2 operator goal lines grow exponentially in cost per level. Factorio's rocket silo is a similar sink for rocket parts. It differs from milestone-unlocks, which tests thresholds without consuming goods, and from goods-consumption, which feeds a population's recurring needs rather than a one-off structure.
design_levers: number of phases and the quantity curve across them (linear, geometric, exponential)
which goods are required and how deep in the production chain they sit
reward per phase (unlocks, power, cosmetics, an ending)
whether deliveries persist or expire, as Dyson sphere sails do
whether play continues after completion
shared versus individual progress in multiplayer
dynamics: Players design factories backward from the project's bill of materials, so it organizes the layout.
Exponential requirements push players to rebuild for throughput rather than add variety, as with shapez 2 operator levels.
Completed phases unlock technology that raises throughput for the next phase, a reinforcing ramp.
failure_modes: A finale that ends the game abruptly leaves large factories without purpose.
Requirements that only scale quantity turn the endgame into waiting rather than designing.
A phase gated on one bottleneck good stalls the whole project.
A sink too small to matter fails to absorb late-game surplus, so production has no outlet.
mechanics.name: Megaproject sink
open_questions: Can megaproject requirements adapt to the player's factory so the finale tests its weak points rather than a fixed list?
Does an endless exponential sink keep factory games engaging longer than a fixed finale, or does it reduce play to scaling?
mechanics.player_experience: A monument to throughput. The player reads the bill of materials, works backward through the factory to supply it, and watches a structure fill phase by phase. It turns an endless sandbox into a campaign with a finish line, or in endless versions a scoreboard of scale.
mechanics.summary: A terminal construction absorbs very large quantities of produced goods in staged phases and serves as the long-run goal and output sink of a production game.

mechanics.definition: Owns a per-agent list of memory entries, each with a type, a source (event, object, or other agent), an effect magnitude, a start time, and an expiry or decay. Events append entries; each tick expired entries drop and the active set is summed into mood or opinion, with stacking rules that cap and discount repeats. RimWorld memory thoughts list mood effect, duration, stack limit, and a stack multiplier (mostly 0.75): My son died is -20 for 30 days, Ate lavish meal +12, and some traits nullify specific thoughts. The Sims 3 and The Sims 4 show the same idea as timed moodlets. Generative Agents (2023) stores memory as a natural-language stream retrieved by the sum of normalized recency (decay 0.995 per game hour), language-model-rated importance (1-10), and embedding relevance, and writes reflections when summed importance exceeds 150. Inputs: events with sources. Outputs: mood and opinion contributions, and retrieved context for decisions and dialogue.
design_levers: magnitude and duration per event type
stack limit and multiplier for repeated events
decay shape (fixed expiry, linear, exponential) and which memories become permanent
trait filters that nullify or amplify memory types
retrieval weights (recency, importance, relevance) when memories drive decisions or dialogue
dynamics: One disaster writes negative memories into many agents at once, synchronizing their breakdown risk.
Players schedule offsetting positive events, turning mood into a budget managed against expiry timers.
Memories that name other agents seed opinions and grudges that outlive the event.
failure_modes: Long lists of small thoughts become noise that players stop reading.
Cheap positive thoughts (fine meals, art) are easy to farm and swamp negative events, draining drama.
Short durations make tragedies trivial; long ones create unavoidable spirals after a single disaster.
Natural-language memory streams grow without bound, raising retrieval cost and surfacing irrelevant memories.
mechanics.name: Memories and thoughts
open_questions: How should natural-language memory streams be compressed so retrieval stays relevant across years of game time?
Which memories should be promoted from temporary modifiers to lasting personality change, and can that rule be learned?
mechanics.player_experience: The player can read why an agent feels the way it does, line by line, and plans around expiry: a funeral penalty will pass in days, and a lavish meal can offset it now. Itemized memories turn hidden state into stories players retell.
mechanics.summary: Events create itemized, time-limited mood modifiers or lasting memories that shape later behavior.

synergy.note: Itemized, expiring thoughts give mood a history the player can read and story-tell around (RimWorld).

mechanics.definition: A milestone is a predicate over aggregate state (population at least 1,000, output of an item, cumulative revenue, a tier of residents) paired with a set of unlocks. State owned: the ordered list of milestones and which are reached. Update rule: periodically test the next milestones; on success, permanently unlock their content and notify the player. Unlike research, the player spends nothing directly; progress is a side effect of growth. Canonical forms: Cities: Skylines population milestones that unlock services, zoning types, policies, and map tiles; Anno resident tiers whose population thresholds unlock new buildings. Satisfactory names its HUB unlocks milestones, but they are paid for with item deliveries, which places them closer to a tech tree.
design_levers: threshold variable: population, output, money, or satisfaction
spacing of thresholds, linear or geometric
which content is gated and in what order
whether milestones can be lost if the variable falls back
option to disable gating for sandbox play
dynamics: Players inflate the gated variable artificially, such as dense cheap housing to reach a population tier, then rebuild.
Milestone order shapes city or factory layout, since early buildings lock in space before later ones arrive.
As a tutorial pacing tool it teaches systems in sequence; experienced players disable it.
failure_modes: Gating essential services, such as sewage or healthcare, behind milestones forces players to build broken cities before they can fix them.
Thresholds hit too quickly flood the player with unexplained tools.
Thresholds placed far apart produce long stretches of growing without new decisions.
mechanics.name: Milestone unlocks
open_questions: Can milestones be selected adaptively from what the player has not yet engaged with, rather than fixed by the designer?
Does gating by behavior (built a working transit line) teach better than gating by aggregate size?
mechanics.player_experience: Growth is rewarded with options. The player expands toward the next threshold, gets a burst of new tools, and learns systems in the order the designer chose rather than all at once.
mechanics.summary: Reaching thresholds such as population, output, or score unlocks new buildings, areas, or features.

mechanics.definition: Each unit is an agent with a platform record (speed, endurance, signatures), sensors with detection models against target signatures, weapons with ranges and hit or kill probabilities, and a doctrine or rules-of-engagement profile that governs when it fires and emits. The simulation advances in continuous or stepped time with acceleration; contacts are detected, classified, and engaged under that doctrine, often without per-shot player input. Command: Modern Operations, from Warfare Sims, gives operational control of units on a map of Earth through missions or direct orders, runs scenarios lasting hours to days with time acceleration, and draws platforms and weapons from databases such as DB3000; a Professional Edition adds database editing and Monte Carlo analysis for defense customers. Harpoon is the lineage ancestor. Inputs: orders, missions, doctrine settings. Outputs: detections, engagements, losses, and mission outcomes.
design_levers: fidelity of sensor and signature models
kill probabilities and countermeasure effects
doctrine, rules-of-engagement, and emission-control settings available to the player
database breadth and accuracy
time acceleration and command granularity (mission versus direct orders)
dynamics: Emission control creates cat-and-mouse play, because radiating sensors reveal the radiating unit.
Munitions and fuel limits turn engagements into logistics problems over long scenarios.
Monte Carlo repetition shows outcome distributions, so planning targets probabilities rather than certainties.
failure_modes: High fidelity buries the player in parameters, and new players cannot tell why an engagement failed.
Database errors or outdated data undermine credibility with expert players.
Automated unit behavior that ignores doctrine settings reads as the simulation disobeying orders.
mechanics.name: Military operations
open_questions: Can reinforcement-learning opponents trained in operational simulators provide credible adversaries without scripted behavior?
Can language interfaces let players issue operational orders at the level of commander's intent?
mechanics.player_experience: The player is a commander, not a pilot. They plan patrols, set emission and engagement rules, manage fuel and munitions, and watch detections develop, so most decisions concern information and timing. Success comes from planning; failure arrives as a missile on the screen that should have been detected earlier.
mechanics.summary: Units with modeled sensors, weapons, platforms, and doctrine conduct operations at operational fidelity, mostly under player orders and automated behavior.

synergy.note: Operations stall when supply is cut.

mechanics.definition: The game exposes two surfaces: data definitions for entities, recipes, and parameters that the engine loads at startup, and a scripting runtime that registers handlers for game events and calls an API to read and change state. Factorio mods use modified Lua 5.2 and pass through settings, prototype (data), and runtime (control) stages in a fixed lifecycle, with the runtime stage event-driven. RimWorld loads XML definitions and C# assemblies; Crusader Kings III exposes event, trigger, and effect scripting; Minecraft's Java Edition relies largely on third-party loaders. A mod manager resolves load order and dependencies. Inputs: mod files. Outputs: changed content, rules, and UI.
design_levers: surface breadth: data only, data plus scripting, or full code injection
sandboxing and determinism requirements, such as lockstep multiplayer
API stability and versioning policy
load-order and dependency management
distribution channel and discovery, such as an official mod portal or Steam Workshop
dynamics: Popular mods become de facto features, and developers later absorb them into the base game.
Moddable games keep long active communities and sales tails.
Mods expose and fix balance problems faster than official patches.
failure_modes: Game updates break mods, and players delay updating or abandon saves.
Large mod lists conflict and degrade performance in ways that are hard to diagnose.
Unsandboxed code mods carry security risk to players' machines.
mechanics.name: Modding API
open_questions: Can coding models let non-programmers write working mods from natural-language descriptions against a documented API?
What API design keeps generated mods sandboxed, deterministic, and compatible across updates?
mechanics.player_experience: Players reshape the game to their taste, from small fixes to total conversions, and the game keeps renewing years after release. Modders gain a creative outlet and an audience, and non-modders browse mod lists to assemble their own version of the game.
mechanics.summary: Official hooks for scripts and data definitions let players change and extend the simulation's content and rules.

mechanics.definition: A design is a set of parts joined at attachment points. Each part carries stats (mass, thrust, fuel, capacity, power, abilities) and sometimes a collision body. Behavior is computed either by aggregating stats or by simulating the assembled structure. Kerbal Space Program stacks tanks, engines, and decouplers into stages whose delta-v follows from mass ratios and simulates the craft as jointed parts. Besiege simulates blocks, hinges, and powered wheels as rigid bodies. Spore's creature editor grants abilities from attached parts. Armored Core assembles mechs from frame parts under weight and energy limits. Space Engineers builds small and large grids from blocks such as thrusters, reactors, conveyors, and deformable armor. Constraints such as budget, mass, power, or part count bound the design space.
design_levers: part catalog size and granularity
stat aggregation versus full physical simulation of the assembly
attachment rules: fixed nodes, free attachment, symmetry tools
constraints: cost, mass, energy, part count
test environment and how clearly failure causes are shown
dynamics: Players invent contraptions designers did not anticipate, such as flying machines in Besiege, and share them.
When parts are unlocked by progression, the assembly space widens over time and old designs get rebuilt.
Coupled with physics, small design changes produce large behavioral differences, which drives iteration.
failure_modes: Joint strength limits and physics instability in large assemblies make craft wobble or break apart; Kerbal Space Program players call unexplained destruction the Kraken.
Part count drives simulation cost, so ambitious builds slow the game down.
A dominant part combination becomes the only competitive build.
Catalog bloat buries useful parts and overwhelms new players.
mechanics.name: Modular assembly
open_questions: Can reinforcement-learned controllers make arbitrary player-built bodies walk, swim, or fly convincingly at runtime?
Can generated parts with stats derived from their geometry replace hand-authored part catalogs?
mechanics.player_experience: Tinkering and test-to-failure. Players build, watch the contraption flip, explode, or fail to lift off, diagnose why, and rebuild. A working design earns engineering pride, and many get shared.
mechanics.summary: The player builds machines, vehicles, or creatures from parts whose stats and physical arrangement determine how the result behaves.

synergy.note: Physics decides whether an assembled machine works, so building becomes experimentation (Besiege).
Rocket design is meaningful because orbits demand specific delta-v budgets (Kerbal Space Program).

mechanics.definition: Owns a per-agent mood value equal to a baseline plus the sum of active modifiers (needs, memories, environment, traits), usually smoothed toward that target, and a set of thresholds. While mood sits below a threshold a hazard rate rolls for a break whose severity rises with depth; during a break the agent leaves player control. High mood can roll for positive states. RimWorld: base mood 22 to 42 by difficulty; the bar moves toward its target at up to +12 per hour rising and -8 falling; break thresholds are 35%, 20%, and 5% (traits shift the minor one, capped 1-50%), with mean times between breaks of about 4, 0.8, and 0.5 days; above 49% mood, inspirations arrive with a mean interval of 410 - 400 x mood days and grant effects such as x1.8 work speed for 8 days. Dwarf Fortress keeps a hidden stress value, scaled by personality facets, that can end in tantrums or depression. Inputs: needs, memories, traits. Outputs: lost labor, destructive acts, temporary buffs.
design_levers: baseline per difficulty and weights of each mood input
threshold levels and trait offsets
hazard rate per band and severity table
break catalog (sad wander, binge, tantrum, violence) and whether breaks harm others
chance and size of positive states at high mood
dynamics: Breakdown contagion: breaks generate negative memories in witnesses that lower their mood, a reinforcing loop.
Players build mood infrastructure (recreation, beauty, fine meals) as defense, coupling mood to the economy.
Inspirations reward stable groups with bursts of output, so content colonies pull further ahead.
failure_modes: Cascades: one break creates negative memories in witnesses, and the group spirals beyond recovery after a random event, which feels unfair.
Mood that is easy to max removes the system from mid and late game.
Breaks that destroy hours of work feel punitive rather than dramatic.
Opaque mood sources make breaks feel random.
mechanics.name: Mood and breakdowns
open_questions: Can breaks be generated as character-specific behavior by language-model agents instead of drawn from a fixed catalog, and still be legible?
What hazard shape keeps breaks dramatic without producing unrecoverable cascades?
mechanics.player_experience: The player manages risk rather than events: watching mood bars near thresholds, removing stressors, and bracing when a disaster pushes several agents under at once. Breaks are memorable because they are partly random and partly the player's fault.
mechanics.summary: Mood aggregates needs, memories, and environment, and crossing thresholds triggers mental breaks or inspired performance.

synergy.note: Unmet needs feed mood; breakdowns make neglect dramatic instead of a silent efficiency loss.

mechanics.definition: Owns the mapping from a player utterance to a game-meaningful interpretation and the character's reply. A parser or model classifies free text or speech into intents, or produces an open reply, and the result updates character state, relationships, or plot. Facade (2005) maps typed text through about 800 hand-authored template rules (compiled to about 6,800 Jess rules) into 24 discourse act types such as agree, criticize, and flirt, plus a catch-all for non-understanding; the rules are permissive, accepting false positives to avoid non-understanding, and a drama manager sequences story beats from the result. AI Dungeon (2019) passes player text to GPT-2 and from 2020 GPT-3 to continue the story. Seaman (1999) took microphone input, and Suck Up! (2023) has players talk their way into homes of language-model characters. Inputs: text or speech, game state. Outputs: intent or discourse act, state updates, generated dialogue.
design_levers: interpretation target: a fixed intent set, discourse acts, or open generation
fallback behavior when input is not understood
grounding constraints that tie replies to game state and authored canon
input modality (typed or voice) and response latency
how strongly language outcomes change simulation state versus adding flavor only
dynamics: Players develop phrasing strategies (flattery, logic traps, role-play) that work as skill expression.
Language outcomes feed relationship and opinion systems, making conversation a primary social lever.
Players share transcripts, so interactions become community content.
failure_modes: Non-understanding loops: the system misreads input and the player rephrases repeatedly.
Open models drift from canon or game state and promise things the simulation cannot deliver; AI Dungeon was criticized for forgetting earlier content.
Players manipulate characters with meta-instructions, trivializing persuasion goals.
Moderation filters misfire; AI Dungeon's 2021 filter flagged harmless content.
mechanics.name: Natural-language interaction
open_questions: How can free-form dialogue be grounded so that what characters say always matches simulation state and what they can do?
What evaluation shows that language input adds agency rather than guesswork compared with dialogue menus?
mechanics.player_experience: The player says what they mean instead of picking from a menu, which raises both agency and anxiety: phrasing becomes a skill and characters can surprise. Misunderstandings and off-topic replies break immersion quickly, so players probe the system's limits.
mechanics.summary: The player communicates with characters by free text or voice, and the system interprets intent and responds.

synergy.note: Free-text conversation can move relationship state in ways menu choices cannot enumerate.

mechanics.definition: Owns no trait values itself; it is the rule that ties reproduction and death to how well an individual's traits fit the environment, so populations change without a designer choosing outcomes. Each generation, individuals that find food, avoid predators, and tolerate climate leave more offspring; with heritable variation the trait distribution moves toward fitter values, and when populations split by geography or genetic distance new species can form. Species: ALRE (Early Access 2018) charges energy for movement from skeleton forces and torques, lets creatures eat only within head reach, and defines species by interbreeding within a genetic distance. SimLife (1992) lets players edit genetics and environments and watch evolution. Spore (2008), by contrast, has players design creatures directly and is not natural selection. Inputs: heritable traits, environment, mortality and reproduction. Outputs: changing trait distributions, speciation, extinction.
design_levers: fitness sources (energy budgets, predation, climate tolerance, mate choice)
generation time relative to play pace
population size, which sets drift versus selection strength
speciation rule (genetic distance, geography)
player interventions such as culling, feeding, catastrophes, and nurseries
dynamics: Arms races between predator and prey traits.
Environmental shocks cause extinction and radiation into emptied niches.
Coupled with food webs, species composition and trait distributions shift together.
failure_modes: Evolution is too slow to see within a session, so players perceive nothing happening.
Degenerate optima: populations converge on one exploit body plan and diversity collapses.
Fitness hidden behind physics is opaque, so players cannot tell why traits win.
Games that call designed progression evolution set expectations they do not meet; biologists criticized Spore's model.
mechanics.name: Natural selection
open_questions: Can learned simulators or GPU-accelerated physics make open-ended evolution fast enough to watch in a session?
What visualizations let players see selection pressure acting, not just its outcome?
mechanics.player_experience: The player shifts from designer to gardener: setting conditions and watching which bodies and behaviors win. Results surprise and teach, as in finding why the long-necked line died out after an ice age.
mechanics.summary: Differential survival and reproduction by fitness shifts trait distributions across generations.

synergy.note: Selection needs heritable variation; inheritance needs selection to produce adaptation.

mechanics.definition: Each agent holds a vector of bounded need stocks (typically 0-100). Every tick each stock decays at a per-need rate, optionally modified by traits, activity, and environment. Actions or objects restore specific needs by fixed or quality-scaled amounts. Low values feed downstream systems: mood, action selection priority, health, or death.
design_levers: number of needs and which are lethal versus mood-only
decay rate per need and modifiers by trait, age, or activity
restoration amount and duration per action or object quality
threshold values that trigger warnings, priority overrides, or breakdowns
whether needs are shown as raw meters, icons, or only through behavior
dynamics: Synchronized decay creates rush hours at kitchens, beds, and bathrooms.
Needs compete for agent time, so throughput falls as needs rise, coupling productivity to comfort.
Better objects restore more per use, creating an upgrade treadmill.
failure_modes: Too many needs turn play into chore management with no strategic choice.
Uniform decay rates make every agent identical and remove personality.
Fast decay with slow restoration produces unavoidable death spirals early in a run.
Hidden needs read as random misbehavior when agents act on them.
mechanics.name: Needs decay
open_questions: Can needs be inferred from behavior by learned agents rather than declared as fixed meters?
What is the minimal need set that still yields distinct personalities?
mechanics.player_experience: Constant low-grade triage. The player reads meters, anticipates which need will bottom out first, and arranges the environment or schedule so agents can meet needs without supervision. Neglect is visible and personal.
mechanics.summary: Each agent has needs such as hunger, energy, social, and fun that decay over time and are restored by actions.

synergy.note: Objects advertising need restoration turn decaying needs into autonomous, legible daily behavior (The Sims).

claims.text: Theme Park includes wage and supply negotiations.

mechanics.definition: Owns a negotiation session: the terms on the table (wage, fee, price, length, bonuses, clauses), the counterpart's reservation value and preferred terms, a patience or round budget, and the outcome. Each round the player proposes terms; the counterpart accepts if the offer clears its reservation value and otherwise counters toward its preference, and patience falls with each round or with offers far from acceptable. When patience runs out talks end, sometimes with a consequence such as a strike, a lost transfer, or damaged goodwill. Reservation values come from simulation state such as the counterpart's ability, reputation, market rates, alternatives, and relationship with the player. Theme Park (1994) has wage negotiations with staff and supply negotiations, where failure brings strikes or lost shipments; sports management games run contract and transfer talks with players, agents, and clubs. It differs from staff-hiring, which owns the roster and wages once agreed, and from faction-diplomacy, which owns standing relations and treaty acceptance rather than a bounded bargaining session over terms.
design_levers: spread between the counterpart's reservation value and its opening demand
number of rounds or patience, and what drains it
how much of the counterpart's position is revealed (hints, agent comments, mood)
which terms can be traded against each other (wage, length, bonuses, clauses)
consequence of failure (walkout, strike, lost deal, damaged relationship)
whether rival bidders negotiate at the same time
dynamics: Reservation values tied to reputation and form make success raise future wage demands, a balancing loop on dominant teams.
Competing bidders turn talks into auctions that push prices up for scarce talent.
Failed wage talks cascade into service failures when staff strike, as in Theme Park.
failure_modes: Fixed, discoverable acceptance rules let players always find the minimum, turning talks into a ritual.
Refusals with no visible reason feel random and push players to accept the first offer.
Long multi-clause talks repeated for every signing become busywork.
AI counterparts that accept deals clearly bad for themselves break the economy.
mechanics.name: Negotiation
open_questions: Can language-model counterparts bargain in natural language while their concessions stay consistent with a calibrated reservation value?
How much of the counterpart's position should be revealed so talks reward reading people rather than brute-force probing?
mechanics.player_experience: A small poker game inside the management sim. The player probes how low a star will go, risks a walkout or a strike by pushing too hard, and weighs a deal now against losing the target. Talks put a face on the economy's prices.
mechanics.summary: The player and an AI party exchange offers and counteroffers over wages, prices, or contract terms against the AI's hidden reservation value until a deal is struck or talks fail.

claims.text: The Sims 3 places households in a seamless open neighborhood, and its Story Progression keeps households the player is not controlling aging, working, and forming relationships.

mechanics.definition: Owns a per-period update for agents or households outside the player's active simulation: unplayed households, agents beyond a radius, or regions not loaded. Instead of running needs, action selection, and pathing, each period it rolls life events for every off-screen unit from a table (age up, take or lose a job, move in or out, start or end a relationship, marry, have a child, die) with probabilities set by coarse state such as age, relationships, money, and household size, and writes the results straight into the shared state that the full simulation reads when the unit comes back into view. Many versions also manage population, moving households in when a town is sparse and out when it is crowded. The Sims 3's Story Progression keeps unplayed households aging, working, and forming relationships across its open neighborhood.
