It differs from lifecycle-aging, which owns life stages and mortality for every agent, and from autonomy-levels, which filters the choices of agents that are fully simulated; here simulation is replaced by event rolls.
design_levers: which event types may fire off-screen (aging, jobs, moves, romance, births, deaths)
event rates relative to the pace of played households
per-household or per-world opt-outs that protect characters the player cares about
population targets that move households in or out
fidelity of the off-screen model, from pure event tables to simplified versions of the on-screen systems
how off-screen events are reported (notifications, a newspaper, or nothing)
dynamics: Neighborhoods drift into new social graphs over generations, giving long saves a history no one played.
Players protect some households and leave others to the dice, producing a two-tier world of directed and generated lives.
Players install community mods that replace The Sims 3's Story Progression with per-household controls, which shows they want the surprises on their own terms.
failure_modes: Off-screen events split families or move away characters the player was invested in, which reads as the game vandalizing the save.
The off-screen and on-screen models disagree, so an agent returns in a state the full simulation would never produce, such as a job its skills cannot support.
Unreported events leave players unsure why the town changed and push them to wikis or mods.
Unbounded population management fills a town with generated strangers and dilutes authored characters.
mechanics.name: Off-screen life progression
open_questions: Can a language model write coherent off-screen life summaries for unplayed agents that the full simulation can resume without contradictions?
How large a fidelity gap between on-screen and off-screen agents do players notice, and where does it stop mattering?
mechanics.player_experience: The world feels lived in: visiting a neighbor reveals a new spouse, a baby, or a funeral the player never saw. The same rule also takes control away, since favorite characters can marry, move away, or die off-screen, so players either embrace the surprises or switch the feature off for the households they care about.
mechanics.summary: Households or agents outside the player's active simulation advance through life events on a cheap stochastic model, so the world changes between visits.

mechanics.definition: Owns, for each observer-target pair, a list of named modifiers, each with a value, a source, and an expiry or decay rate. Opinion is the clamped sum of static modifiers (shared traits, faith, dynasty, attraction) and event modifiers (gifts, insults, broken promises), and the list is shown as a tooltip. Event modifiers decay toward zero or expire; some are permanent. Crusader Kings III: most opinion decays to 0, tyranny decays 0.25 per month, Friend gives +60 and Nemesis -120, Broke Truce -50 for 3 years, faith hostility 0 to -30, Beautiful +30 attraction, and predecessor opinion is the only inheritable kind. RimWorld pawn opinions are built the same way from social thoughts such as insulted (-15 for 20 days) and deep talk (+15). Europa Universalis IV caps nation opinion at +200 and -200 with itemized reasons. Inputs: events, traits, relations. Outputs: one opinion number for AI decisions plus its legible breakdown.
design_levers: modifier catalog and magnitudes
decay or expiry per modifier and whether repeats diminish
clamp range and thresholds that change AI behavior
balance between static and event modifiers
which modifiers are hidden from the player
dynamics: Players time requests around expiry, waiting for a negative modifier to lapse before asking a favor.
Shared static modifiers such as faith and culture create blocs whose opinions move together.
Modifier accounting turns relationships into economic decisions priced in gold or prestige.
failure_modes: Additive stacking lets players farm cheap positives, such as repeated gifts or feasts, to override severe grievances.
Long tooltip lists overwhelm, so players read only the total.
Linear sums ignore context, so a murderer can be liked if enough small bonuses stack.
Hidden modifiers that contradict the visible list break trust in the itemization.
mechanics.name: Opinion modifiers
open_questions: Can modifiers be generated from free-form events described by a language model while keeping magnitudes balanced and itemized?
Which nonlinear combination rules (per-category caps, context checks) keep opinions plausible without losing legibility?
mechanics.player_experience: The player reads exactly why someone likes or hates them and treats opinion as an account: stacking small positives, waiting out a scandal, or choosing which grudge to pay off. Itemized lists make social systems feel fair and gameable.
mechanics.summary: Opinions are sums of named, decaying modifiers from events and traits, itemized for the player.

synergy.note: Events add named modifiers, and modifiers gate later events, chaining stories.

mechanics.definition: Each body holds a position and velocity under gravity. Under the patched conic approximation, used by Kerbal Space Program, each celestial body has a sphere of influence; inside it only that body's gravity is modeled, so the trajectory is an analytic conic propagated on rails, and segments are joined at sphere boundaries by matching position and velocity. This turns the n-body problem into a chain of two-body problems and cannot represent Lagrange points. Full n-body integration, as in Universe Sandbox or the Principia mod for Kerbal Space Program, integrates every body's gravity numerically. Engine burns change velocity, the rocket equation sets the delta-v budget, and maneuver planners preview the orbit that a planned burn will produce.
design_levers: patched conics or n-body integration
scale of the system; Kerbal Space Program uses a planet with a 600 km radius
time warp limits and whether thrust is allowed during warp
maneuver planning tools and how much they automate
atmospheric drag and its coupling to orbits
dynamics: Transfer windows create timing pressure and missions that run in parallel.
Delta-v couples orbital planning to vehicle design, so mission ambition shapes the rocket.
Gravity assists and aerobraking reward players who learn the system deeply.
failure_modes: Many players never get past the learning cliff without external tutorials.
Patched conics cannot model Lagrange points or halo orbits, which surprises experienced players.
Floating-point precision at solar-system distances causes jitter unless the engine re-centers the origin.
mechanics.name: Orbital mechanics
open_questions: Can an AI mission planner that explains its burns flatten the learning cliff without removing the planning itself?
mechanics.player_experience: A counterintuitive system that becomes mastery. Players learn that speeding up raises the far side of the orbit, plan burns on maneuver nodes, and earn rendezvous and landings through precise planning.
mechanics.summary: Bodies move under gravity, and maneuvers spend delta-v to change orbits, intercepts, and transfers.

mechanics.definition: Owns a period length and a set of update functions that run only when the period elapses. Between ticks the simulation runs continuously or not at all; at the tick, accumulated quantities settle: tax income and upkeep are booked, population grows, crops are harvested, research advances, or reports are produced. Hamurabi resolves a whole year per round: harvest, rats, immigration, plague, and starvation; SimCity books taxes and service funding at each year's budget; Paradox grand strategy games apply income and many modifiers on a monthly tick inside a daily simulation. Different systems can run on different periods in the same game. Inputs are activity accumulated during the period; outputs are discrete jumps in stocks and a report.
design_levers: period length, and whether different systems use different periods
which quantities settle at the tick and which change continuously
what the player sees at the tick: reports, prompts, or a forced pause
whether actions just before the tick can game the settlement
dynamics: Batched income creates sawtooth cash curves, so players keep buffers to survive between ticks.
Synchronized ticks across many agents produce simultaneous demand spikes.
Reports at each tick become the main legibility tool for slow variables.
failure_modes: Players time actions around a tick to exploit settlement rules, such as building just after upkeep is charged.
Large batched computations at the tick cause visible stutter in late game.
Long periods delay feedback until players cannot connect a decision to its result.
mechanics.name: Periodic ticks
open_questions: Can learned surrogates settle long periods in one step so players can skip ahead without simulating every day?
mechanics.player_experience: Bookkeeping beats. The player watches the date approach the next settlement, makes changes just before it, and reads the report afterward to judge the period. Ticks create small moments of anticipation and give a long continuous game recurring checkpoints.
mechanics.summary: Some state changes, such as budgets, harvests, or growth, resolve in batches at fixed intervals like a month or a year rather than continuously.

mechanics.definition: Death is an absorbing state: when an entity's health or survival condition fails, the entity and its accumulated state (skills, gear, relationships) are removed with no reload. Enforcement lives in the save system: Rogue deleted the save file when it was loaded, and modern ironman modes keep a single autosave. Two scopes exist. Avatar permadeath ends the run, as in FTL, which deletes the save when the ship is destroyed or all crew die, and Project Zomboid. Agent permadeath removes a member from a continuing game, as with RimWorld colonists, Dwarf Fortress dwarves, and Fire Emblem units. Softeners include FTL's clone bay, which revives crew with a skill penalty, downed states before death, and meta-progression that survives the run. Inputs: lethal events from combat, injury, or survival systems. Outputs: entity removal, run termination, or succession.
design_levers: scope: avatar death ends the run versus agent death inside a continuing game
save policy: single autosave, optional ironman toggle, or tolerated save scumming
what persists past death: unlocks, world state, heirs, or nothing
recovery tools such as revival with penalties, downed states, or medical rescue windows
replacement cost and time for lost agents
dynamics: Losing a key specialist cascades: a colony without its only doctor loses more colonists to untreated wounds.
Attachment plus loss produces the personal stories players share from colony sims and roguelikes.
Combined with procedural generation, it makes each run a fresh attempt rather than a retry of the same state.
failure_modes: A single high-variance event ends a long run, which reads as unfair rather than consequential.
Players back up and restore save files (save scumming), bypassing the design.
Fear of loss pushes players into slow, repetitive grinding instead of bold play; Richard Bartle's analysis of virtual worlds notes most MMORPGs avoid permadeath for this and retention reasons.
Bugs or connection drops that kill characters become catastrophic.
mechanics.name: Permadeath
open_questions: Does making lost agents persist as memories, ghosts, or chronicle entries change how much risk players accept?
What variance profile of lethal events keeps permadeath consequential without making long runs feel like lotteries?
mechanics.player_experience: Every risky decision carries weight because losses cannot be reversed. Players grow attached to named survivors, play more cautiously, and remember specific deaths as the turning points of a run. A loss late in a long run is the most memorable and the most frustrating moment the mechanic produces.
mechanics.summary: Death of agents or the avatar is permanent, and the save system prevents undoing it.

synergy.note: Unique generated characters make permanent loss felt.

mechanics.definition: Authoritative world state lives on servers that advance it continuously in real time; clients submit actions and receive updates, and changes such as built structures, market orders, territory, and destroyed assets persist for everyone. Design choices are shard topology and what the world does while a player is away. Eve Online runs one universe on the Tranquility server rather than parallel copies, takes it offline daily for maintenance, trains character skills in real time while players are logged out, and slows the server clock in crowded systems (time dilation) so large fights stay simulated; the Bloodbath of B-R5RB ran 21 hours. Ultima Online (1997), A Tale in the Desert, Second Life, and Eco are other persistent worlds. Inputs: concurrent player actions and world rules. Outputs: shared, durable state and history.
design_levers: shard topology: one universe, many parallel shards, or instanced zones
offline progression: what continues for absent players (skills, production, decay)
persistence scope: which changes are permanent versus reset
server tick rate and overload handling such as time dilation or queues
world resets, seasons, or wipes
rules for asset loss and protection of offline players
dynamics: Player-driven economies, wars, and politics emerge because consequences persist and accumulate.
Time-zone coverage becomes a strategic resource for groups that hold territory.
Persistent history makes notable events into community lore and news.
failure_modes: Early arrivals accumulate wealth and territory, and new players find no room to matter.
Load spikes in popular locations degrade simulation for everyone present.
Abandoned structures and items clutter the world without decay rules.
The world dies when concurrency falls below what its systems assume.
mechanics.name: Persistent shared world
open_questions: Can AI agents that stand in for absent players keep a persistent world active at low concurrency without dominating it?
What offline progression rules keep a persistent world fair to players with little play time?
mechanics.player_experience: Actions matter to strangers, and the world changes while the player sleeps. Players log in to see what happened, plan around other time zones, and take part in events, such as wars or market crashes, that no single player or designer controlled.
mechanics.summary: A server-side world keeps running and keeps its state for many players, whether or not any one player is logged in.

synergy.note: A persistent world lets player markets accumulate history, monopolies, and scams (EVE Online).
Laws only matter where the world persists long enough to need governance (Eco, A Tale in the Desert).

tension.note: A shared persistent world cannot be paused or sped up by one player.

mechanics.definition: Owns a small per-agent set of discrete traits or continuous personality dimensions, assigned at generation or during development. Traits hold no dynamics of their own; other systems read them as modifiers: they scale need decay, shift utility scores and break thresholds, nullify or add memories, change opinions of others, and unlock or forbid actions. The Sims (2000) uses points in opposing pairs such as nice/grouchy and active/lazy that scale object advertisements (Feed Fish gives 1-11 Fun by Playful); The Sims 3 lets adults hold up to five traits; RimWorld traits such as Steadfast and Nervous shift the mental break threshold, and Psychopath nullifies several death thoughts. Crusader Kings III characters tend to hold three personality traits gained through childhood events at ages 9, 11, and 13, opposites are excluded, and stress breaks can change them. Inputs: generation or life events. Outputs: differentiated behavior from shared rules.
design_levers: trait count per agent and exclusivity rules
magnitude of each trait's modifiers and which systems it touches
discrete traits versus continuous dimensions
acquisition: fixed at birth, childhood events, life events, or stress
visibility of traits to the player
dynamics: Traits that affect opinion create recurring frictions and friendships between particular pairs.
Players build around trait combinations, so traits become strategy as well as flavor.
Inherited or culturally transmitted traits drift across generations, coupling personality to lineage.
failure_modes: Strictly positive traits make recruitment a search for the same few, flattening variety.
Flavor traits with no mechanical effect feel fake; traits with huge effects dwarf player choices.
Too many traits per agent average out into bland behavior.
mechanics.name: Personality traits
open_questions: Can a natural-language persona replace a trait list while keeping behavior predictable enough for players to plan around?
What is the smallest trait set that still produces distinct, recognizable characters?
mechanics.player_experience: Traits are the shorthand by which players recognize and cast characters. The player reads a trait list, predicts behavior, and assigns roles; contradictory combinations become memorable, and players chase or avoid specific traits when recruiting.
mechanics.summary: Fixed or slow-changing traits change each agent's needs, preferences, and available actions.

mechanics.definition: Owns a small set of planet-scale stocks such as atmospheric gas fractions, greenhouse level, mean temperature, ice cover, sea level, and biomass, sometimes resolved on a coarse map grid. Each tick emissions, volcanism, and life change the gases, temperature follows radiative balance and albedo, and temperature moves ice, sea level, and where life can grow. SimEarth, advised by James Lovelock, shows gas levels as percentages, melts ice caps and raises seas under warming, cools the planet with volcanic dust, and offers a Daisyworld mode based on Watson and Lovelock's model, in which daisies of different albedo regulate temperature. Civilization added global warming from unchecked pollution; Surviving Mars: Green Planet terraforms by raising planetary parameters toward habitable targets; Eco lets player emissions raise sea level. Inputs are emissions and player projects; outputs are habitability and disasters.
design_levers: which planetary stocks exist and how many feedbacks link them (albedo, greenhouse, biosphere)
time constants between emissions and temperature or sea-level response
presence of tipping points or runaway regimes versus smooth response
player levers: emissions policy, terraforming buildings, direct parameter sliders
spatial resolution: single global numbers or a gridded map
dynamics: Biosphere-climate feedback can stabilize temperature, as in Daisyworld, or amplify change when it breaks down.
Climate shifts move habitat suitability, crop yields, and coastlines, forcing migration or rebuilding.
Shared emissions in multiplayer worlds such as Eco create commons problems between players.
failure_modes: Many coupled variables with long delays make cause and effect opaque, so players change sliders without learning what moved the planet.
Linear, delay-free responses reduce climate to a single meter to keep below a line.
Runaway feedback with no recovery path ends runs because of early mistakes the player could not see.
mechanics.name: Planetary climate
open_questions: Can learned climate emulators give fast, plausible regional responses to player emissions without hand-tuned equations?
How short can feedback delays be made before climate stops reading as climate?
mechanics.player_experience: Slow consequence at the largest scale. The player makes small persistent changes, such as emissions or terraforming projects, and watches planet-wide numbers creep toward thresholds where oceans boil, ice advances, or the planet becomes habitable. Success feels like stewardship; failure arrives long after its cause.
mechanics.summary: Planet-scale variables such as atmospheric composition, temperature, sea level, and biosphere evolve under coupled feedbacks and can be deliberately altered.

mechanics.definition: Owns per-market order books. Each order has an item, a price, a quantity, a location or range, and an expiry. A new buy order fills against the cheapest compatible sell order and vice versa; any remainder rests in the book. Transaction fees and sales taxes remove currency while NPC bounties and sales add it, so the operator manages faucets and sinks rather than prices. Players make nearly all goods, so prices emerge from their mining, manufacturing, hauling, and speculation. EVE Online (2003) is the canonical form: regional markets where players gather most raw materials and build nearly all ships, price history charts, and large-scale manipulation such as ramping and bear raids; its developer hired an economist in 2007 to monitor the economy. Ultima Online's player vendors and Albion Online's player-crafted gear economy are other forms.
design_levers: market topology: one global book, regional books, or local station markets with hauling between them
fees, sales tax, and order modification costs as sinks and anti-spam measures
how much NPC supply or demand exists to anchor prices
order range, duration, and how much order-book depth is visible
currency faucets (bounties, NPC sales) relative to sinks
dynamics: Trade hubs form where liquidity concentrates, as at EVE's Jita, which concentrates trade further.
Wars destroy goods and raise demand, coupling combat to manufacturing prices.
Speculators anticipate patches and events, so prices move before a change ships.
failure_modes: Faucets that outpace sinks inflate prices and devalue new players' earnings.
Low population leaves thin books where one player sets prices or nothing sells.
Bots and automated relisting dominate when order updates are free and fast.
Manipulation and scams drive away players who did not opt into that kind of play.
mechanics.name: Player-driven markets
open_questions: Can LLM or RL trader agents supply liquidity for small servers or single-player worlds without becoming exploitable market makers?
Which sink and faucet controls keep a long-running player market stable without visible developer intervention?
mechanics.player_experience: Being one trader among thousands. The player hunts arbitrage between regions, undercuts by a fraction of a unit, posts low buy orders and waits, and reads price charts like a real trader. Wealth comes from information and patience as much as production.
mechanics.summary: Players post buy and sell orders in shared order books, and prices emerge from player behavior.

mechanics.definition: Owns a set of player-authored laws, each a condition and an effect expressed in a structured rule language (for example: when a player fells a tree in district X, charge a tax or block the action), a proposal and voting procedure, and an enforcement hook that checks every relevant action against the active laws. A law passes when its vote meets the threshold set by the world's constitution or government type, after which the simulation enforces it automatically. Eco (early access 2018) lets players form governments and propose and vote on laws that restrict what other players can do or apply taxes and grants to specific actions, to manage an ecosystem that overharvest and pollution can damage. A Tale in the Desert (2003) let players petition and vote on laws that the developers then implemented.
design_levers: expressiveness of the rule language (which triggers, conditions, and effects are available)
voting thresholds, quorum, and who can propose
constitutional limits on what laws may do
enforcement mode: hard blocks, automatic fines, or reports for players to act on
how government offices are filled and how long laws persist
dynamics: Ecological or economic crises create pressure for regulation, and regulation shifts which professions are profitable.
Laws generate evasion strategies and loophole-seeking, which prompts amendments.
Factions form around legislative interests, producing persistent political rivalries.
failure_modes: A small active group can pass laws that grief or exclude other players.
A rule language too limited to express what players want pushes politics into informal agreements the game cannot enforce.
Low participation makes votes meaningless, and governance becomes the hobby of a few players.
mechanics.name: Player legislation
open_questions: Can LLMs compile natural-language laws into enforceable rules faithfully enough that players trust the translation?
What constitutional constraints prevent minority capture without making legislation toothless?
mechanics.player_experience: Politics with real teeth. Players argue about what should be allowed, draft rules, lobby for votes, and then live under the result. A logging ban or a carbon tax becomes a social contract that some players obey, some evade, and some campaign to repeal.
mechanics.summary: Players author, propose, and vote on rules that the game then enforces inside a shared world, such as taxes, bans, and permits.

synergy.note: Organized player groups are the constituencies that write and enforce laws.

mechanics.definition: An organization entity holds a membership list, a role table that maps roles to permissions (hire, spend, access storage, declare war), shared assets such as a treasury, hangars, or land, and optional revenue rules such as a tax on members' income. Organizations can nest into federations and act as parties to diplomacy and war. In Eve Online, a CEO runs each corporation and assigns roles such as director and accountant, corporations can tax members' earnings, declare war on other corporations for a weekly fee, and join alliances that claim sovereignty over null-sec star systems. Ultima Online guilds, Eco governments, and A Tale in the Desert's guilds are other forms. Inputs: membership and role changes, member income. Outputs: shared pools, permissions, and collective standing.
design_levers: role and permission granularity
shared asset types and access controls
organization taxes and costs of founding or upkeep
size caps and federation rules
war and diplomacy rules between organizations
protection against theft by members with access
dynamics: Specialization inside organizations, with miners, haulers, fighters, and diplomats, creates internal economies.
Coalitions form and split, producing large-scale political history.
Organizations act as onboarding for new players and as a reason veterans stay.
failure_modes: Coarse permissions let a single member empty shared storage; Eve Online has a history of such corporate thefts.
Large blocs coordinate so well that they lock smaller groups out of contested territory.
Leaders who quit leave organizations, and their assets, stranded.
mechanics.name: Player organizations
open_questions: Can AI officers or members fill organizational roles in small groups without crowding out human players?
Which permission and asset rules best reduce insider theft while preserving trust-based play?
mechanics.player_experience: Players belong to something larger than their own account. They take on roles such as leader, logistician, or recruiter, coordinate on projects too big for one person, and argue about governance. Betrayal and politics become play.
mechanics.summary: Players form corporations, guilds, or governments with membership, roles, permissions, and shared assets.

claims.text: In Screeps each player's main module runs once per tick against a fixed game state, and queued commands are applied together at the end of the tick.
Screeps limits CPU per tick (20 without CPU Unlock), with unused CPU accumulating into a bucket of up to 10,000 that allows bursts up to 500 per tick.

mechanics.definition: The player authors programs in a textual or visual language that the game interprets each tick to drive entities. State owned: program source, interpreter state (instruction pointer, registers, memory), and an execution budget. Update rule: each tick, run each program for up to a budget of instructions or CPU time, read sensors through an API, and issue commands that the simulation resolves. Languages range from real ones (JavaScript in Screeps and Bitburner, Python-like code in The Farmer Was Replaced) to assembly-like puzzle languages (TIS-100, Shenzhen I/O, Exapunks) and visual instruction tracks (SpaceChem waldos, Opus Magnum arms). Screeps is canonical for a persistent world: each player's main module runs once per tick against a fixed state, commands are applied together at tick end, and a CPU limit with a carryover bucket constrains computation.
design_levers: language: real general-purpose, constrained assembly, or visual
execution budget per tick (instructions or CPU milliseconds)
sensor and actuator API surface
debugging tools: stepping, logs, breakpoints, visualization
persistence: programs keep running while the player is offline
scoring of programs by size, speed, or cost
dynamics: Automation through code lets players operate at scales no one could control by hand.
In shared worlds, players' programs compete directly, producing an arms race of strategies and exploits.
Code sharing builds communities around libraries and frameworks.
failure_modes: A steep entry cost excludes players who cannot already program.
A real language with a rich API lets players import libraries and copied code, so the community's code replaces the puzzle.
Execution budgets set too tight make debugging feel like fighting the platform.
Weak debugging tools turn failures into opaque guessing.
mechanics.name: Player programming
open_questions: When code assistants can write competent bots from a description, what remains of the programming puzzle, and does play shift to specification and review?
Can games teach programming effectively by letting AI assistants scaffold and then withdraw?
mechanics.player_experience: The player designs behavior rather than performing it. Writing, running, and debugging a program that then works unattended is satisfying in a way direct control is not, and failures are logic errors the player can find and fix.
mechanics.summary: The player writes code in a language the game executes to control units, machines, or the world.

synergy.note: Both express automation as logic; games that offer both span visual and textual programming.

mechanics.definition: Owns a directed graph whose nodes are policies (with slider levels), simulation values (crime, GDP, pollution), situations, and voter groups, and whose edges are weighted effect equations. Each turn every node's value is recomputed as a function of its weighted inputs, bounded to a fixed range, and effects can be lagged or averaged over several turns; situations switch on and off when their input values cross thresholds. Voter-group happiness at the end of the chain sets approval and election results. Positech's Democracy series (2005-2022) is the canonical form: its designer describes it as a homebrew neural network in which voters, voter groups, policies, ministers, and events are neurons capped to 0..1 or -1..+1, with most logic in editable CSV files. Democracy 4 added fixed-income neurons that can exceed 1 because percentage effects on a 0-1 income scale gave wealthy voters more than poor ones.
design_levers: graph density: how many effects each policy and value has
effect equation forms (linear, power, threshold) and weights
delays and averaging per edge
value bounds and normalization
situation trigger and clear thresholds with hysteresis
how much of the graph is shown to the player
dynamics: Feedback loops between values (unemployment, crime, GDP) produce virtuous or vicious cycles across several turns.
Situations appear and vanish as values cross thresholds, creating emergent crises from slow drifts.
Overlapping voter-group memberships turn every policy into a tradeoff among coalitions.
failure_modes: Percentage effects on bounded values distort distribution, the problem that led Democracy 4 to add fixed-income values.
Dense graphs with small weights make most policies feel inert while a few dominate.
Long delays without visible pending effects make players misattribute causes.
mechanics.name: Policy influence network
open_questions: Could learned causal models fit to real policy data replace hand-authored effect equations, and would players accept the loss of authored intent?
Can an LLM generate new policies and situations with consistent graph effects from a text description?
mechanics.player_experience: Pulling one thread and watching the web move. The player hovers a policy to see lines to everything it touches, raises a tax and sees the deficit shrink while a voter group sours, and plans reforms in sequence because effects arrive with delays.
mechanics.summary: Policies, indicators, and voter groups connect through a weighted causal graph with delays.

mechanics.definition: Owns a catalog of policies, each with an active flag or a choice among mutually exclusive options in a group, prerequisites, an enactment cost (money, political capital, influence, or time), upkeep, and a cooldown. Enacting a policy applies modifiers or changes rules: it unlocks an action, alters a rate, or changes how agents behave, with a stated benefit and a stated cost. Frostpunk (2018) has a Book of Laws in which similar laws are sequenced so later ones are harsher, and accepting early compromises makes later ones likelier. Victoria 3 groups laws into mutually exclusive sets and, since update 1.3, requires each law to pass three enactment phases whose success chances depend on interest-group support, with up to three setbacks before failure. SimCity 2000 introduced city ordinances, and Civilization civics and Cities: Skylines district policies are other forms.
design_levers: number of policies and how many can be active at once (slots, groups, budget)
enactment cost, delay, and cooldown
size and visibility of side effects
reversibility: free to revoke, costly, or permanent
prerequisites and sequencing (escalating law chains)
dynamics: Escalating law chains pull players toward harsher policies one reasonable step at a time.
Policies that change agent behavior ripple into economic and social systems in ways their tooltips do not state.
Mutually exclusive groups create identity: a society defined by its chosen laws.
failure_modes: Policies with no real downside become always-on, leaving a menu of mandatory picks.
Too many small modifiers make each choice unnoticeable.
Free revocation lets players toggle policies around events, undermining the tradeoff.
mechanics.name: Policy toggles
open_questions: Could players draft bespoke policies in language and have an LLM translate them into balanced, consistent rule changes?
Which explanations of second-order policy effects keep surprises interesting rather than unfair?
mechanics.player_experience: Choosing which tradeoff to live with. The player browses a menu of laws, weighs their benefits against costs and side effects, and commits. In Frostpunk each signature feels like a moral line crossed; in grand strategy, passing a law is a political campaign.
mechanics.summary: Enactable laws or policies change simulation rules with explicit tradeoffs.

claims.text: Democracy 4 constrains the player with political capital.
Europa Universalis IV uses administrative, diplomatic, and military monarch power to buy technology, and Hearts of Iron IV uses political power for laws and ministers.

In Captain of Industry each fully satisfied settlement need yields about 1-2 Unity per month, spent on edicts, outposts, quick trades, contracts, quick-build, vehicle recovery, emergency repairs, and building boosts.

mechanics.definition: Owns one or more non-monetary stocks or capacities, each with a per-period income, an optional cap, and a price list of state actions. Income comes from the skill or loyalty of rulers and ministers, faction support, prestige, or satisfied population needs; spending buys discrete actions such as enacting or repealing a policy, issuing an edict, researching, raising stability, claiming territory, or rushing construction. Unlike a treasury, the stock usually cannot be borrowed or traded and its income comes from political or welfare state rather than economic activity, so it rations institutional change per period. Democracy 4 charges political capital, earned through loyal ministers, to introduce or cancel policies. Europa Universalis IV pays administrative, diplomatic, and military monarch points set by the ruler's skills, which buy technology among other things. Hearts of Iron IV spends political power on laws and ministers. Captain of Industry yields about 1 to 2 Unity per fully satisfied need per month, spent on edicts, outposts, quick builds, and emergency repairs. Policy-toggles owns the policies; this mechanic owns the currency that rations them.
design_levers: income sources (ruler skill, minister loyalty, faction approval, satisfied needs) and their weights
cap on the stock and whether overflow is lost
one pool versus several (administrative, diplomatic, and military points)
action prices relative to income, and whether prices scale with realm size or development
banked stock versus a capacity that ongoing commitments draw against
whether the currency converts to or from money
dynamics: Spending on stability or welfare raises future income, a reinforcing loop for well-run states.
Players time large reforms for when income peaks, such as after a strong heir succeeds or the cabinet is loyal.
Saving for expensive actions creates long-term plans that compete with spending to answer crises.
failure_modes: Hitting the cap with nothing worth buying wastes income and makes the currency invisible.
Several parallel currencies with separate shops become spreadsheet optimization detached from the fiction.
Income tied to leader skill makes one bad succession a long drought with few meaningful choices.
Cheap actions let players toggle policies every period, undoing the rationing.
mechanics.name: Political capital
open_questions: Could political capital be replaced by negotiated backing from simulated ministers or factions without losing the clarity of a single number?
Does currency earned from welfare, as in Captain of Industry, make players value population needs differently from currency earned from leaders?
mechanics.player_experience: Every turn or month has a political budget. The player decides which reform is worth this period's points, saves up for a large one, and feels the quality of the ruler or cabinet as a faster or slower clock of change. Weak leaders and unhappy populations show up as a shortage of options rather than only as a penalty.
mechanics.summary: An abstract governing currency accrues each period from leaders, factions, or population welfare and is spent on policy changes, edicts, and other state actions.

mechanics.definition: Owns a pollution value per cell or chunk. Each update, emitters add pollution, a fraction diffuses to neighboring cells, and terrain, vegetation, or water absorb some; other systems read the local value as a penalty to health, land value, crop growth, or happiness. Factorio stores pollution per 32x32-tile chunk, updates every 64 ticks, diffuses 2% to each cardinal neighbor once a chunk holds 15 or more, absorbs it by tile type and trees (trees are damaged above 60), and lets enemy spawners absorb it to fund attack waves. SimCity computes a pollution map from industry and traffic that depresses land value; Cities: Skylines separates ground, noise, and water pollution, and sewage released upstream contaminates water intakes downstream. Inputs are emitter locations and rates; outputs are a spatial field read by other systems.
design_levers: emission rate per source and modifiers such as efficiency upgrades or filters
diffusion fraction, minimum amount before diffusing, and grid resolution
absorption by terrain, water, and vegetation, and whether absorbers are damaged
what pollution affects: health, land value, crops, happiness, enemy aggression
cleanup tools and their cost
dynamics: Zoning separates polluting and sensitive uses, which lengthens commutes and adds traffic.
In Factorio pollution couples production scale to attack size, so efficiency becomes a defense strategy.
Absorbers degrade under load, so a polluted region can tip into faster spread as forests die.
failure_modes: Pollution that only lowers land value is solved once by zoning distance and then ignored.
Fine-grained diffusion with no threshold or chunking costs compute and produces smeared, unreadable fields.
Effects carried by hidden channels, such as water contamination far downstream, read as unexplained sickness.
mechanics.name: Pollution spread
open_questions: Can learned dispersion surrogates make air and water pollution fields physically plausible while staying cheap and legible?
mechanics.player_experience: Growth leaves a visible stain. The player separates factories from homes, plants green buffers, and watches the overlay creep outward; in Factorio a bigger factory directly invites bigger attacks. Cleanup competes with expansion for the same resources.
mechanics.summary: Pollution emitted by sources accumulates and diffuses across land, water, or air cells and harms health, land value, or growth, or provokes threats.

mechanics.definition: Owns population counts by stratum and the per-stratum tables of needs, consumption rates, labor roles, taxes, and promotion requirements. Each period residences or pops whose stratum's needs are met may advance to the next stratum, and unmet needs can stall, demote, or anger them; production buildings require workers of specific strata. Anno 1800 residences advance from Farmers through Workers, Artisans, and Engineers to Investors (with Jornaleros and Obreros in the New World) when the house is full, basic needs are met, and construction materials exist; luxury needs raise taxes and happiness, and island level follows the highest tier, such as 1,750 Investors for a metropolis. Victoria 3 groups professions into classes and strata whose standard-of-living expectations drive radicalism. Inputs: goods, services, construction materials. Outputs: workforce by tier, tax revenue, demand for higher goods.
design_levers: number of strata and promotion requirements
per-stratum needs, consumption rates, and tax yields
workforce requirements per building by stratum
demotion or unrest rules when needs fail
whether promotion is player-triggered or automatic
dynamics: Each new tier lengthens production chains, so economic complexity grows with population.
Inequality between tiers creates political pressure when strata link to interest groups or unrest.
Promotion and demotion cycles oscillate around supply shortfalls.
failure_modes: Upgrading drains lower-tier workers, collapsing basic production; Anno players learn to keep a surplus of each worker type.
Top-tier demand chains become so long that one missing good stalls the economy.
Strata as pure progression gates feel like a checklist rather than a society.
mechanics.name: Population strata
open_questions: Can strata emerge from agent wealth and occupation dynamics rather than authored tiers, and remain legible?
How should mobility between strata be modeled so inequality has political consequences without becoming a death spiral?
mechanics.player_experience: Growth is climbing: each tier unlocks goods and buildings but also new demands, so the player keeps lower tiers staffed while serving the elite. Unmet needs at the top cost revenue, and neglect at the bottom stalls production.
mechanics.summary: The population is divided into classes or tiers with distinct needs, roles, and upgrade paths.

mechanics.definition: Owns a total budget B (reactor bars, distributor pips) and an allocated level a_i for each subsystem, with sum(a_i) <= B and each a_i capped by the subsystem's installed level. Each subsystem's output is a step or linear function of its allocation: shield layers, weapon charge rate, evasion, oxygen production. The player moves units between subsystems at any time, often while paused, and the effect applies at once or through a charge rate. FTL's reactor supplies bars that the player assigns to shields, engines, weapons, oxygen, and the medbay; each shield layer takes two bars, and the reactor and each system are upgraded separately with scrap. Elite Dangerous splits distributor pips among systems, engines, and weapons capacitors, which sets each capacitor's recharge rate, while a separate priority list decides which modules shut down when the power plant is overloaded. Unlike power-grid, there is no network topology and no automatic shortfall rule: the split itself is the decision. Inputs: budget, subsystem caps, damage to the reactor or subsystems. Outputs: per-subsystem effectiveness.
design_levers: total budget relative to the sum of subsystem caps, which sets how often the player must choose
cost per subsystem level and step thresholds such as two units per shield layer
reallocation speed: instant, only while paused, or through capacitor recharge rates
how damage reduces the budget or a subsystem's cap, and how repair restores it
which subsystems draw from the budget and which run without it
upgrade path for the budget versus the subsystems
dynamics: Opponents target the reactor or a key subsystem to force bad splits, coupling allocation to subsystem damage.
Players shift power in phases of a fight (shields early, weapons once enemy shields drop, engines to escape), giving combat a rhythm.
Upgrade choices become a question of which subsystems the budget can actually feed at once.
failure_modes: A budget large enough to max every subsystem removes the decision; one too small leaves a single viable split.
A dominant split, such as maximum shields at all times, turns allocation into a one-time setup step.
Real-time reallocation without pause rewards input speed over judgment in games that are otherwise tactical.
Hidden thresholds, such as a shield layer needing two units, make partial allocations look like wasted power.
mechanics.name: Power allocation
open_questions: Could an AI crew officer that proposes splits from the tactical situation keep allocation a decision rather than a reflex?
What ratio of budget to total subsystem cap keeps allocation meaningful across a whole campaign of upgrades?
mechanics.player_experience: A running triage under pressure. The player pulls power from oxygen to charge one more weapon, moves it all into engines to escape, or holds shields high while waiting for a volley. Each reallocation is a small bet about what the opponent will do next, and a damaged reactor turns a comfortable budget into a painful choice.
mechanics.summary: The player splits a fixed power budget among a vehicle's subsystems in real time, trading shields, weapons, engines, and life support against each other.

mechanics.definition: Generators, consumers, and optional storage are joined by poles, wires, or adjacency into connected components. Each tick each component sums generation and demand; if supply covers demand every consumer runs, otherwise a shortfall rule applies: proportional slowdown, priority shedding, or outages in some order. Factorio spreads power evenly so machines slow proportionally (a 300 kW load on 180 kW of solar runs at 60%), dispatches solar first, then steam engines, turbines, and fusion, discharges accumulators only when other sources fall short, and charges every connected machine an idle drain. Micropolis, the released SimCity engine, walks conductive tiles outward from each plant, spends one unit of capacity per tile (700 per coal plant, 2,000 per nuclear plant), and when capacity runs out reports brownouts and leaves the remaining tiles unpowered. Oxygen Not Included gives wires a load capacity and damages overloaded wires. Inputs: generator output (fuel, weather, time of day), consumer demand, topology. Outputs: a satisfaction ratio per component and the operating state of each consumer.
design_levers: shortfall rule: proportional slowdown, priority tiers, or hard outages
connection model: pole radius, wires with capacity, or adjacency
generator variability by fuel, time of day, and weather, plus storage buffers
idle drain and standby consumption
wire or transformer capacity limits and overload consequences
dynamics: Growth outpaces generation in steps, so power becomes a recurring stop-and-fix cadence.
Variable sources such as solar and wind plus storage create daily cycles of surplus and deficit that decide what runs when.
Grid topology sets the blast radius of failures: one broken link can isolate a district.
Circuit or priority controls let players build load shedding, coupling power to automation.
failure_modes: A single global power pool without topology reduces the mechanic to a number to keep positive.
Proportional slowdown can cause a death spiral when brownouts slow the miners and inserters that fuel the generators, a known trap in early Factorio steam power.
Overload damage without clear warnings reads as random breakage.
mechanics.name: Power grid
open_questions: Would learned grid operators that forecast demand and weather turn power from a capacity check into a dispatch problem players manage?
How much electrical realism (voltage, phase, line losses) can players absorb before the grid stops being legible?
mechanics.player_experience: A clear supply-demand puzzle with a visible penalty. Players watch the satisfaction bar, add generation ahead of growth, and learn that a fuel shortage at the plant can slow the very machines that supply its fuel. Night, weather, and storage add a timing layer to an otherwise static capacity problem.
mechanics.summary: Generators produce energy that is distributed over a connected network to consumers; shortfalls cause brownouts or shutdowns.

synergy.note: Machines draw power, so production throughput becomes coupled to generation capacity.

mechanics.definition: The player supplies coarse intent (add or remove a block, drag a wall or path) and local rules pick the detailed geometry for the affected cells and their neighbors. In Townscaper each click adds or removes a block on an irregular quad grid made by subdividing a hex grid and jittering points; corner modules are chosen with a marching-cubes-style lookup and a real-time wave function collapse that narrows valid modules per cell, then decorations such as windows, chimneys, and bushes are added, and gardens appear only in enclosed areas. Each change ripples through connected cells, so delay grows with structure size, and the solver may fail silently. Tiny Glade (2024) turns drawn walls and paths into detailed castles and gardens. State: a coarse occupancy grid; output: derived geometry, recomputed locally on edit.
design_levers: input granularity: blocks, strokes, or brushes
size of the module library and number of variants per configuration
constraint priorities, such as which modules win when several fit
determinism: whether the same input always yields the same output
how much manual override the player gets
dynamics: Builds spread through screenshots and social media more than through gameplay goals.
Rules produce context-sensitive surprises, such as stairs, arches, or gardens appearing where the player did not place them.
Shipped examples rarely couple the output to a simulation; when they do, agents must interpret generated spaces.
failure_modes: After hours of play the module library repeats and outputs start to look the same.
Players cannot get the exact shape they want because the rules decide the detail.
Silent solver failures leave odd fragments; Townscaper can leave loose structures where no module fits.
Recalculation delay grows on large builds.
mechanics.name: Procedural build assist
open_questions: Can generative 3D models replace hand-built module libraries while keeping the instant, local response players expect?
Can build-assist output feed a simulation (rooms, pathing, structural load) without the player losing track of what they built?
mechanics.player_experience: Low effort, high expressiveness. A few clicks yield something that looks hand-made, which feels like collaborating with a builder. There is no failure state, so play is calm, exploratory, and screenshot-driven.
mechanics.summary: Coarse player input such as a block or a drawn wall is turned into detailed, organic structures by procedural rules.

tension.note: Assisted organic building favors freedom; strict structural rules punish it.

mechanics.definition: A generator samples a character record from tables and rules: name from culture-specific lists or grammars, age, appearance parameters, traits under compatibility constraints, skills, and backstory fragments that modify the other fields. RimWorld gives every pawn a childhood backstory and, if generated at 20 or older, an adulthood backstory; each adds flat skill bonuses, disables or enables work types, and grants or forbids traits, and 25% of regular pawns and all faction leaders first try a fixed player-made bio before falling back to shuffled ones. Dwarf Fortress generates personalities, preferences, and appearance; The Sims and Crusader Kings generate townies and courtiers. Inputs: faction or culture, role requirements, random seed. Outputs: a character record consumed by needs, skills, and social systems.
design_levers: number of trait, skill, and backstory fragments, and their compatibility constraints
how strongly backstory fragments change mechanics such as skills and disabled work
share of fixed, hand-written or community-written characters versus fully generated ones
name and appearance generators per culture
player rerolls and edits at game start
dynamics: Disabled work types and traits force colony role planning around the people who arrive.
Generated quirks seed conflicts once relationships and mood systems act on them.
Community-submitted fixed characters appear across many players' games, creating shared recognizable figures.
failure_modes: Small fragment pools repeat, and players recognize the same backstories across runs.
Incompatible combinations produce incoherent characters, such as a pacifist whose backstory is soldier.
Mechanically weak characters feel like dead weight, which drives heavy rerolling.
mechanics.name: Procedural characters
open_questions: Can language models generate backstories that stay consistent with the mechanical traits and skills they imply?
How many independent fragments are needed before players stop recognizing repeats?
mechanics.player_experience: Each new arrival is a small unwrapping. Players read the backstory and traits, decide whether to recruit, and form a picture of the person that makes later events personal. Rerolling starting characters is itself a common ritual.
mechanics.summary: Characters are generated with names, backstories, traits, skills, and appearance sampled from constrained tables or grammars.

mechanics.definition: Equipment is modeled as interacting subsystems (electrical, fuel, hydraulic, engines, avionics) whose states are changed through individually operable controls. A procedure is an ordered sequence of control actions with preconditions on subsystem state; doing steps out of order produces the physical result of that order, such as a failed engine start, rather than an error message. DCS World models aircraft from real-world data, with clickable cockpit switches and subsystems such as engines, fuel, electrical, hydraulics, and radios, and the U.S. Air Force's 355th Training Squadron uses it as an A-10C instrument and weapons-systems trainer. Microsoft Flight Simulator offers interactive checklists with optional copilot assistance. Inputs: control manipulations. Outputs: subsystem states and operational readiness.
design_levers: number of modeled subsystems and controls
strictness: whether wrong orders fail realistically or are forgiven
assists such as auto-start, checklist overlays, or copilot automation
manual and tutorial depth
failure injection during procedures
dynamics: Communities share checklists, tutorials, and training videos, and some organize realistic group operations.
Injected failures turn memorized procedures into troubleshooting.
Assists create a ladder from casual to study-level play inside one product.
failure_modes: Long procedures before any action exclude newcomers unless an auto-start or assisted mode is offered.
When the underlying systems are not simulated, steps become arbitrary button sequences.
Missing feedback leaves players unable to tell which step went wrong.
mechanics.name: Procedural checklists
open_questions: Can a voice-driven AI instructor or crew member coach procedures adaptively from the live subsystem state?
Can procedure models be extracted from real manuals automatically to cut the cost of new equipment?
mechanics.player_experience: Mastery through ritual. Players study manuals, practice startup sequences until they are reflexive, and feel competence when a complex machine comes alive under their hands. Mistakes teach how the systems connect.
mechanics.summary: Operating simulated equipment requires performing ordered steps on modeled controls that mirror real procedures, with system states gating each step.

mechanics.definition: A seeded pipeline builds layered fields over a grid or chunks: elevation from fractal noise or midpoint displacement, then derived temperature, rainfall, drainage, and biome classification, then rivers, ores, vegetation, and points of interest placed by rules. Perlin gradient noise (1985) is the basis of most heightmaps; Minecraft samples noise per chunk on demand for an effectively endless world. Dwarf Fortress starts from a randomized fractal elevation map, adds temperature, rainfall, drainage, vegetation, and salinity layers, traces rivers by erosion from mountains to oceans, and models rain shadows. Inputs: seed, size, and parameters such as sea level or mineral frequency. Outputs: terrain, biome, and resource maps used by construction, pathfinding, and ecology systems.
design_levers: noise type, octaves, frequency, and amplitude
erosion and hydrology passes
climate model for temperature, rainfall, and biome thresholds
resource and point-of-interest placement rules and guaranteed fairness constraints
world size and whether generation is finite or chunked on demand
player-exposed parameters and seed sharing
dynamics: Terrain shapes where settlements, roads, and defenses go, so map features drive later strategy.
Communities trade seeds and rank them, turning generation into shared content.
Resource scarcity set at generation time determines the pace of mid-game economies.
failure_modes: Pure noise produces terrain with no recognizable structure that players stop finding interesting after a few runs.
Unconstrained placement yields unfair or unplayable starts, such as no water or no ore near the spawn point.
Version updates that change the generator break seed sharing and older saves at chunk borders.
mechanics.name: Procedural terrain
open_questions: Can generative models trained on real elevation data or player-favored maps produce terrain with more recognizable structure than noise?
How should learned generators keep fairness constraints, such as guaranteed resources near spawn, that rule-based pipelines enforce directly?
mechanics.player_experience: Each start is new ground to read: players scout for flat land near water, ore, and defensible chokepoints, and share seeds with unusual landforms. Exploration means something because no guide has mapped this world.
mechanics.summary: Maps are generated from a seed through noise, erosion, climate, and placement rules.

mechanics.definition: Owns a product in progress: chosen attributes (topic, genre, features, components), an allocation of effort across development areas, quality points accumulated from staff skill and time, and a cost. On release a market evaluator scores the product against hidden or partly revealed ideals (good attribute combinations, the right effort balance), against current trends, and against rivals or the player's own past work, then turns the score into reviews and a sales curve. Game Dev Tycoon (2012) is the canonical form: topic and genre pairs and per-stage effort sliders are rated for fit, and review scores depend on beating the player's earlier releases. Big Pharma (2015) has players build machine lines that refine ingredients and combine their effects into drugs, and Capitalism raises product quality through research projects.
design_levers: size of the attribute space and how many combinations score well
how much of the scoring rule is revealed through reports or reviews
rising quality bar (relative to past work or rivals) versus fixed standards
trend volatility, so last year's best combination fades
how staff skill, time, and money convert into quality points
dynamics: Players converge on a few proven formulas until trends or a rising bar force variation.
Revenue from hits funds better staff and technology, which raises quality and the bar together.
Rival releases in the same category split sales, encouraging release timing.
failure_modes: Once players look up the best combinations on a wiki, the mechanic collapses into executing a table.
Scoring relative to the player's own best punishes experimentation, since a novel but weaker product reviews badly.
Opaque evaluators make poor reviews feel random when the cause is hidden.
mechanics.name: Product development
open_questions: Could generative models let players make an actual product artifact (a game concept, a recipe, a design) that a learned critic scores, replacing slider allocations?
Can a learned market evaluator stay consistent enough that players can still learn its preferences?
mechanics.player_experience: Iterating on recipes for success. The player picks combinations, adjusts sliders, ships, reads reviews, and infers the hidden scoring rules over many releases. Each product is a hypothesis about what the market wants.
mechanics.summary: The player configures a product's features, and a simulated market scores it against trends, quality, and competition.

mechanics.definition: Each producer holds a recipe (input amounts, output amounts, cycle time), an input buffer, an output buffer, and a progress timer. Each tick, if inputs and power or labor are present and the output buffer has room, progress advances; on completion inputs are consumed and outputs added. Chained producers form a directed graph from raw resources to finished goods whose steady-state throughput is set by recipe ratios and the slowest stage. The Settlers (1993) chains wheat through a mill to a bakery; Anno 1800 gives each building a fixed cycle time so players build in ratios; Factorio and Satisfactory expose rates directly and add alternate recipes, modules, and productivity bonuses. GlassBox, the SimCity (2013) engine, expresses production as rules that move or combine resources held in a unit's bins. Inputs: raw goods, labor, energy. Outputs: intermediate and final goods, plus a blocked or starved state per producer.
design_levers: recipe depth and branching factor of the dependency tree
cycle times and ratios, and whether they are round numbers players can compute
alternate recipes and multi-output recipes that create choices
buffer sizes at inputs and outputs
modifiers such as modules, worker skill, or productivity bonuses
how chains are displayed: hidden, per-building stats, or a full production overview
dynamics: The slowest stage sets throughput, so the bottleneck moves each time players fix one, creating a chase loop.
Shared intermediates create contention between chains and force priority decisions.
Coupled with logistics, layout distance becomes part of the recipe cost.
Machines that build machines produce exponential factory growth, capped by inputs, space, or threat.
failure_modes: A single optimal ratio per product, once solved, turns play into copying calculator output.
Deep trees of single-use intermediates add layout work without adding decisions.
Starvation far upstream is hard to diagnose without flow statistics, so players blame the wrong building.
mechanics.name: Production chains
open_questions: Can AI generate recipe graphs that are solvable, non-degenerate, and on-theme, cutting content cost for factory games?
Do players learn chain design faster from flow visualizations or from AI explanations of bottlenecks?
mechanics.player_experience: Building machines that build things. The player traces a desired product back through its tree, sizes each stage, and watches for the stage that starves or backs up. Satisfaction comes from a balanced line running unattended; tension comes from every new product adding a branch to an already crowded layout.
mechanics.summary: Buildings or machines convert input goods into output goods via fixed recipes and cycle times, forming multi-step dependency trees.

synergy.note: Buffers decouple steps of a chain; their fill levels reveal bottlenecks.

mechanics.definition: Owns a recording session (the agent being taught and the sequence of player actions or positions captured so far) and the resulting routine. While recording, each player action is generalized into a step that names an action and a target class or place rather than one specific object; the agent then replays the routine, often in a loop, and the player may edit it. Autonauts bots watch the player perform a task and record it as blocks in a Scratch-style visual language, which the player wraps in repeat loops and conditions, and the bot's head caps program length. Satisfactory trucks and tractors repeat a route the player records by driving it once, stopping at truck stations. Unlike player-programming, the player does not write code to create the routine; unlike blueprints, which snapshot a spatial layout, a recording captures a sequence over time. Inputs: player actions while recording and later edits. Outputs: an autonomous routine, and its failures when the world no longer matches the recording.
design_levers: how actions are generalized: exact positions, nearest object of a type, or named areas
whether recordings become editable programs with loops and conditions or stay opaque replays
program length caps and how agent upgrades raise them
recovery behavior when a step fails: skip, wait, or stop
whether one recording can be copied to many agents
dynamics: Each taught agent frees player time to teach the next, so automation grows quickly once the first routine works.
Players pick up programming concepts such as loops and conditions by editing what they demonstrated.
Fleets of copied routines amplify any flaw in the original recording.
failure_modes: Over-literal recording replays positions after the world has changed, so routines break silently.
Opaque replays with no editing force players to re-record a whole routine for one small change.
Recorded vehicle routes drift or collide when terrain or traffic differs from the recording run.
mechanics.name: Programming by demonstration
open_questions: Can learned imitation policies generalize a single demonstration to new layouts while staying predictable and editable?
Does editing a demonstrated routine teach programming better than writing code from a blank page?
mechanics.player_experience: Teaching instead of coding. The player shows a bot how to chop a tree or drives a delivery once, then watches it repeat the job, which makes automation approachable for players who have never programmed. The surprise comes when the routine generalizes the wrong thing, such as returning to a spot where the resource is already gone.
mechanics.summary: An agent or vehicle learns a routine by recording the player performing it, and the recording becomes a replayable, sometimes editable, program.

mechanics.definition: Owns, per fired projectile, position, velocity, and type data (mass, drag or ballistic coefficient, guidance if any, and penetration or warhead parameters). Each physics step integrates gravity, drag, and wind (or propulsion and guidance for torpedoes and missiles), tests for intersection with targets or terrain, and on impact resolves penetration against the struck material's thickness and angle, then passes damage to the target. Arma 3 weapons are affected by external ballistics and recoil, so shooters must account for drop and travel time at range; Silent Hunter III torpedoes run at a set speed, depth, and gyro angle toward a computed intercept; DCS World flies missiles, bombs, and gun rounds as projectiles; Command: Modern Operations lists ballistics among its modeled effects. Unlike rigid-body-physics, the projectile is a point mass or simple body integrated at high speed with no contact solver; unlike military-operations, this mechanic owns only the shot's flight and impact, not detection or doctrine.
design_levers: which forces are integrated: gravity only, drag, wind, Coriolis, or guidance
penetration model: none, thickness and angle tables, or material-based energy loss
projectile speed relative to engagement ranges, which sets how much lead and drop matter
dispersion and weapon accuracy versus player aim
aids that show the solution, such as ranging reticles or automatic firing solutions
dynamics: Engagement ranges spread out as skilled players exploit long-range accuracy, changing how teams move across terrain.
Cover becomes material-dependent, so the environment's construction feeds tactics.
Aids such as rangefinders and fire-control computers become valuable equipment, coupling ballistics to loadouts and procedures.
failure_modes: Ballistics fidelity beyond what players can perceive costs compute and data without changing decisions.
Fast projectiles tunnel through thin geometry at low step rates and register no hit.
Penetration tables that disagree with visible armor make hits and non-hits feel arbitrary.
Networked games must reconcile projectile flight across clients, and disagreements show as hits that did not happen.
mechanics.name: Projectile ballistics
open_questions: Can learned surrogate models of penetration and fragmentation replace hand-built tables while staying consistent with what players see?
Which aids keep long-range ballistics learnable for new players without removing the skill?
mechanics.player_experience: Hitting a target is a skill or a calculation rather than a cursor placement. The player estimates range, holds over for drop, leads a moving target, or computes a torpedo solution, and a long-range hit feels earned. Misses teach the model; cover that stops some rounds and not others teaches materials.
mechanics.summary: Shots are simulated as projectiles in flight with velocity, gravity, drag, and penetration, so range, angle, and lead decide hits rather than an instant trace or a dice roll.

mechanics.definition: The player defines lines as ordered stop sequences and assigns vehicles with a capacity. Passengers spawn with origins and destinations and choose a route that may include transfers; vehicles load at stops up to capacity and unload at destinations. Ridership depends on stop catchment, frequency (vehicles per line), transfer penalties, and travel time compared with other modes. Mini Metro spawns passengers as shapes that travel to any station of a matching shape, lets about six wait before a station overcrowds, ends the game when a station stays overcrowded too long, and hands out new rolling stock weekly. Cities: Skylines II citizens weigh transit against driving and walking using travel time, comfort, and money costs. Inputs: lines, vehicles, passenger demand. Outputs: ridership, waiting times, overcrowding, and changes in mode share.
design_levers: vehicle capacity and count per line
passenger route choice model: matching shapes, shortest time, or utility with transfer penalties
stop capacity and overcrowding consequences
line constraints such as river crossings, line count, or budget
fares, subsidies, and operating costs
dynamics: Hub-and-spoke versus grid patterns emerge from transfer penalties.
New lines shift demand rather than add it, moving overcrowding elsewhere.
Coupled with land value and zoning, stations attract density, which raises ridership further.
failure_modes: Passengers taking implausible routes because the route-choice model ignores transfer cost.
Lines that run full or empty without explanation because demand is hidden.
In city builders, transit that cannot reduce traffic because citizens' mode choice is too sticky.
mechanics.name: Public transit lines
open_questions: Can agent route choice that is learned from real transit data be made legible enough for players to design against?
What is the minimal passenger model that still punishes bad transfer design?
mechanics.player_experience: Network design with immediate feedback. Players draw a line, watch riders pile up or flow, and redraw. Good transfer points and frequency matter more than raw coverage, and in Mini Metro the game is about deciding which stations can wait.
mechanics.summary: Player-drawn lines with stops and vehicles carry passengers whose ridership depends on coverage, frequency, and transfers.

synergy.note: Transit is the relief valve for congestion; congestion is what makes transit worth building.

mechanics.definition: Owns a security rating or ruleset per zone (star system, region, server facet) and each player's standing, such as security status or criminal flags. When one player attacks another, the zone's rules decide whether the attack is allowed, whether NPC enforcers respond and how fast, and how much standing the attacker loses; standing then limits where the attacker can travel safely. EVE Online rates each system from 1.0 to -1.0, with the CONCORD police destroying unprovoked aggressors in high-security space while low- and null-security space leaves fights to players, and the most profitable activities sit in the less secure zones. Ultima Online split its world in 2000 into Trammel, where player-versus-player combat is consensual, and Felucca, where it is open. Unlike persistent-world, which owns continuity of the shared world, this mechanic owns the spatial rules for aggression inside it.
design_levers: number of security tiers and how rewards scale with risk across them
enforcement: instant destruction, delayed police response, flags that make the aggressor attackable, or none
standing penalties for aggression and how they recover
whether players can choose a ruleset at entry, as with separate facets
map layout of tiers, including chokepoints between safe and dangerous space
dynamics: Gate camps form at chokepoints where safe space meets dangerous space.
Players stage risky ventures from safe hubs, creating hub-and-frontier geography in the economy.
Groups organize escorts, scouts, and intelligence networks to operate in dangerous zones.
failure_modes: Safe zones that cover everything valuable empty the dangerous zones, and the player-versus-player design withers.
Delayed enforcement allows suicide attacks on rich targets in safe space when the loot exceeds the attacker's loss.

Offering a consensual ruleset beside an open one lets most players choose safety, which can leave the open ruleset thinly populated; Ultima Online's Felucca after the Trammel split is the usual example.
mechanics.name: PvP security zones
open_questions: Could AI enforcers that respond to context, rather than fixed rules, curb exploits such as suicide attacks without blocking legitimate play?
What reward gradient across tiers keeps both safe and dangerous zones populated?
mechanics.player_experience: The player chooses a risk level by choosing where to go. Safe zones let new and cautious players work and trade; dangerous zones promise better rewards and real fights. Crossing a border with valuable cargo is a decision, and an attacker in safe space knows the police are coming.
mechanics.summary: A shared world is divided into zones whose rules set whether players may attack each other and what an aggressor pays, such as NPC police response or lost standing.

mechanics.definition: Each produced item carries a discrete grade drawn when it is made. The draw depends on input quality, worker or player skill, tool or module bonuses, and a random roll; the grade then multiplies the item's value, durability, or effect. Factorio: Space Age has five levels (normal, uncommon, rare, epic, legendary) with bonuses from +30% to +150%; a quality module 1 adds a +1% chance of a higher grade, each further step is ten times less likely, and a recycler returning 25% of ingredients lets players reroll. RimWorld grades crafted items from awful to legendary by crafter skill, and Dwarf Fortress grades by skill up to masterful items. Stardew Valley crops come in normal, silver, gold, and iridium quality depending on farming level and fertilizer. Inputs: ingredient grades, skill, modifiers, random draw. Outputs: graded items whose stats scale by tier.
design_levers: number of tiers and the stat multiplier per tier
base chance and how skill, inputs, or modules raise it
whether rolls can skip tiers and how steeply odds fall per step
reroll or recycling paths and their loss rate
whether low-grade items have a use or are pure waste
dynamics: Players build sorting and filtering stages, adding logistics complexity that scales with tier count.
Skill coupling makes specific workers valuable, so losing a master crafter is a real setback.
Higher-grade machines and modules work faster or roll better, so quality compounds once established.
At scale, reroll loops convert a random mechanic into a predictable expected-value pipeline.
failure_modes: Many tiers multiply item variants and storage slots, cluttering logistics.
Reroll loops without enough loss become net-positive generators; Factorio sets recycler returns at 25% and caps productivity at +300% to prevent this.
Low tiers with no use make most production feel wasted.
mechanics.name: Quality tiers
open_questions: Could quality be judged by a learned model of an item's form and function, for example a player-designed object, instead of a hidden roll?
What tier count keeps grades meaningful without overwhelming storage and sorting?
mechanics.player_experience: A gamble layered on production. Players chase rare outputs, sort and filter by grade, and decide whether to sell, use, or recycle low rolls. In colony sims a legendary item from a favored crafter is a memorable event; in Factorio quality becomes an expected-value problem of reroll loops.
mechanics.summary: Produced items carry quality grades derived from inputs, worker skill, or chance, scaling their value or effect.

mechanics.definition: An attack generator spawns hostile groups at map edges, by drop, or by tunneling, sized by a threat budget; attackers path toward targets such as colonists, valuables, or polluting buildings, and resolve combat against walls with hit points, turrets with range and ammunition, traps, and defenders. RimWorld raids arrive by walking, drop pods, sappers who dig through walls, or sieges, sized by raid points; Factorio biters attack polluting structures and evolve stronger forms; Dwarf Fortress has goblin sieges; Mindustry and They Are Billions use scheduled waves. Inputs: threat budget, attacker types, map. Outputs: damage, casualties, loot, and the defensive layout's measured strength.
design_levers: attack frequency and size, often from adaptive threat scaling
attacker types that bypass static defense, such as sappers, flyers, or drop pods
pathing rules and how attackers choose targets
defense costs, maintenance, and ammunition supply
warning time before arrival
player control of fighters during the fight
dynamics: Defense layout constrains the whole settlement plan, pulling walls, chokepoints, and storage together.
