Wounded defenders strain medical and food systems after each fight, so raids cascade into other systems.
Arms races appear as attacker variety forces layered defenses.
failure_modes: A single killbox design defeats every raid, so defense stops being a decision; RimWorld's sapper and breach raids counter this by digging or blasting through walls.
Pathfinding exploits let attackers be lured into infinite loops.
Raids that interrupt every build session feel like chores rather than tests.
mechanics.name: Raid defense
open_questions: Can attacker AI that learns the player's defenses across raids prevent dominant killbox designs without feeling unfair?
What raid frequency keeps defense meaningful in games whose main loop is building?
mechanics.player_experience: Long build phases punctuated by short, tense fights. The player designs killboxes and chokepoints, stocks ammunition and medicine, and learns each attacker type's counter. A breached wall is a crisis that tests the whole colony.
mechanics.summary: Settlements defend against periodic attacks with walls, turrets, traps, and fighters placed and commanded by the player.

mechanics.definition: Signals placed on track divide it into blocks or guard reservable paths. A block signal admits a train only if the next block, meaning all track reachable up to the next signal, is empty. A path signal admits a train once it reserves a route through to the next signal, so trains on non-conflicting paths can share a block. Transport Tycoon (1994) had only bi-directional block signals, and Deluxe added one-way signals. OpenTTD adds pre-signals, where an entry signal opens only if an exit is green, plus path signals, and since version 12 shows only path signals by default. Factorio pairs rail signals with chain signals that mirror the state of the signals ahead. Inputs: signal placement, train positions and routes. Outputs: per-signal open or closed states, train waits, and network throughput.
design_levers: available signal types: block, one-way, pre-signal, path, or chain
default signal behavior and which types are exposed to new players
train braking distance and the resulting minimum signal spacing
whether trains reroute around blocked paths
visual debugging aids such as block coloring and reservation display
dynamics: Junction design becomes a shared craft, and community blueprints of standard intersections spread.
Throughput limits push players toward one-way double track and dedicated stations.
Adding trains raises throughput until signal capacity binds, after which waits and gridlock grow quickly.
failure_modes: Rules learned mainly from community guides, such as Factorio's chain-in, rail-out convention, block new players.
Deadlocks that occur long after a junction is built are hard to trace.
Block signals that are too coarse cut throughput, and pre-signal logic can trigger on exits a train cannot reach.
mechanics.name: Rail signaling
open_questions: Can an assistant explain a specific deadlock in plain language from the signal states, removing the wiki dependency?
What minimal signal vocabulary still supports high-throughput designs?
mechanics.player_experience: Traffic engineering on rails. Players learn why trains stop, then redesign junctions, stations, and signal spacing until flow is smooth. Deadlocks, with trains frozen in a loop that blocks itself, are a vivid and instructive failure, and fixing one is a satisfying puzzle.
mechanics.summary: Block and path signals partition track so trains can share it without collision; throughput depends on signal design.

synergy.note: Circuit-controlled train stops and signals turn logistics into programmable dispatch.

mechanics.definition: A hazard process samples each tick or cycle whether a disaster occurs, picks a type from a weighted table that may be conditioned on state, picks a location, and applies a damage template such as destroying tiles, starting fires, or flooding. In the SimCity engine (Micropolis), doDisasters fires with probability 1/481, 1/241, or 1/61 per cycle depending on difficulty, then chooses among fire, flood, tornado, earthquake, or nothing, and spawns a monster only if average pollution exceeds 60. Cities: Skylines Natural Disasters adds early-warning buildings and shelters; RimWorld adds short circuits, solar flares, and toxic fallout; Banished has tornadoes and fires. Unlike a crisis countdown, timing is unknown in advance. Inputs: difficulty, optional state conditions. Outputs: damage events and secondary hazards passed to fire, flood, or health systems.
design_levers: base frequency per difficulty level and whether the player can disable or manually trigger disasters
type weights and state conditions, such as monsters tied to pollution or fires tied to dry weather
magnitude distribution and area of effect
warning time and mitigation tools (shelters, firefighters, seawalls, insurance)
secondary effects that hand off to fire spread, flooding, or disease
dynamics: Players disperse and duplicate critical services so one hit cannot cripple the system.
Disaster damage reduces income and service coverage, which can cascade into abandonment if reserves are thin.
State-conditioned disasters turn neglected variables, such as pollution, into delayed risks.
failure_modes: Large unmitigable disasters erase hours of building and read as arbitrary rather than as a test of preparation.
Frequent small disasters turn into repetitive cleanup chores.
If disasters are rare and easily disabled, the mechanic adds content that most players never see.
mechanics.name: Random disasters
open_questions: Can learned physical simulators make disaster damage depend on how the player actually built, rather than on fixed templates?
What warning lead time makes disasters feel like a test of preparation rather than bad luck?
mechanics.player_experience: Background dread and sudden recovery work. The player builds redundancy, spreads out critical infrastructure, keeps cash in reserve, and then scrambles to rebuild when a disaster hits. Players who want a calm build often disable disasters, which shows how much they change the tone.
mechanics.summary: Stochastic disasters such as fires, floods, earthquakes, storms, or meteors strike at random times and places and damage the system.

mechanics.definition: Owns three demand valves (residential, commercial, industrial) updated from the balance of population, jobs, and outside trade, and read by zone growth. In Micropolis, the SimCity engine, projected residents = residents + migration (proportional to jobs per resident - 1) + 2% births; projected commerce = total population / 3.7 x a labor ratio capped at 1.3; projected industry = industry x labor ratio x an external market factor (1.2, 1.1, or 0.98 by difficulty). Each valve moves by (projected / actual - 1) x 600 plus a tax offset (+200 at 0% tax, 0 at 7%, -600 at 20% on easy), is clamped to +/-2000 (residential) or +/-1500, and is held at 0 until a needed stadium, seaport, or airport exists. A zone grows when valve + a local score (land value for homes) passes a random test. SimCity's RCI bar and Cities: Skylines' demand bars display these valves.
design_levers: inputs to each valve (jobs per resident, internal market size, external trade, taxes)
gain and clamp on each valve, which set how fast demand swings
caps that hold demand at zero until a specific building is placed
how much local factors (land value, traffic, pollution) add to the global valve
whether demand is split further by wealth or density tier
dynamics: Residential and job growth chase each other, producing alternating waves of house and workplace construction.
Raising taxes depresses all three valves at once, so tax policy shows up as slower development rather than a direct penalty.
Valve caps create milestone moments when one building unlocks a growth spurt.
failure_modes: Players treat the bar as an instruction and zone mechanically, so the city grows without plan or tradeoff.
Hidden caps (needing a stadium or port) freeze growth with no explanation unless an advisor says why.
High gain makes demand oscillate between booms and abandonment.
mechanics.name: RCI demand
open_questions: Would demand derived bottom-up from simulated households and firms be more interesting than a three-valve controller, and could players still read it?
Can an AI advisor turn valve inputs into a plain causal explanation of why demand is low?
mechanics.player_experience: A steering signal. The player glances at three bars, zones whatever is in demand, and learns that homes need jobs, jobs need workers, and industry needs outside trade. When a bar stays pinned despite growth, the player hunts for the missing stadium, port, or tax cut.
mechanics.summary: A demand signal for residential, commercial, and industrial land derived from the balance of jobs, workers, and goods.

synergy.note: The demand meter tells the player which zone to paint next; zoning answers it.

mechanics.definition: Owns a mapping from the device or server clock to game time plus the last-seen timestamp. On launch or each tick, the real time elapsed since the last update is computed and the simulation catches up: needs decay, crops grow, timers finish, or a capped amount of progress is granted. Calendar dates trigger holidays and seasonal events. Tamagotchi (1996) ages its pet through life stages in real time; Animal Crossing uses the console's internal clock and calendar so time of day, seasons, holidays, and tree growth follow the real date, with music that changes each hour; mobile builders and idle games run construction timers and offline earnings on the device or server clock. Inputs are real elapsed time; outputs are catch-up updates and dated events.
design_levers: ratio of game time to real time, 1:1 or compressed
catch-up rule for absence: full simulation, capped progress, or frozen
penalties or rewards for absence
calendar-tied events and how often content changes
handling of player clock changes
dynamics: Daily check-in habits form, and with streak rewards they produce strong retention.
Offline catch-up must be computed in bulk, pushing designs toward simple closed-form growth.
Real-time waits become a resource that free-to-play games sell speed-ups for.
failure_modes: Players change the device clock to skip waits (Animal Crossing players call it time travel), which breaks event pacing and timer economies.
Harsh absence penalties punish ordinary life events and drive players to quit after a missed week.
Content tied to real dates excludes players in other time zones or hemispheres unless the game adapts it.
mechanics.name: Real-time clock
open_questions: Can generated daily content keep a real-time world changing enough that daily visits stay worthwhile for years?
mechanics.player_experience: A world that lives alongside the player's own day. Visiting at different hours shows different scenes, shops open and close, and holidays arrive with the real calendar. The player builds a daily habit, and absence has consequences, from weeds to a sick pet, so returning feels like coming home or like guilt.
mechanics.summary: Game time follows the real-world clock and calendar, so the world advances, ages, and holds events while the game is closed.

tension.note: Binding time to the wall clock removes player control of pacing.

mechanics.definition: Owns a mapping from external datasets to simulation state, a refresh schedule, a cache, and fallback rules. At world creation or on a schedule it fetches data (imagery, elevation, building footprints, star catalogs, weather observations, aircraft positions), converts it into terrain tiles, objects, weather fields, or agents, blends it with procedural or authored content where data is missing, and falls back to cached or generated state when offline. Microsoft Flight Simulator (2020) streams Bing Maps imagery updated every 28 days and AI-generated 3D content from more than two petabytes in the cloud, and feeds in Meteoblue live weather and live air traffic. Elite Dangerous blends real astronomical catalog systems into its procedural galaxy, and Aurora 4X can build systems from real star data. Unlike procedural-terrain, which generates from a seed, and weather, which owns weather state and its effects, this mechanic owns the import of outside data into the simulation.
design_levers: which subsystems are fed: terrain, buildings, weather, traffic, catalogs
refresh rate: one-time import, periodic updates, or live streaming
blending rules with procedural or authored content where data is missing or poor
offline fallback and caching
player choice between live data and preset conditions
dynamics: Real events such as storms enter play, and players fly into them as they happen.
Communities fix and supplement data with handcrafted add-ons, building an ecosystem around the gaps.
Players use the sim as a reference for real places, raising expectations of accuracy.
failure_modes: Errors in source data appear in the world as artifacts; a widely shared example is a lone skyscraper in Melbourne in Microsoft Flight Simulator (2020), traced to a mistyped building height in OpenStreetMap data.
Dependence on servers makes the game fragile; Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 launched with server problems that caused long loads and missing content.
Licensing or service changes can remove a data feed after release.
mechanics.name: Real-world data feeds
open_questions: Can generative models fill gaps in real-world data, such as inferring 3D buildings from imagery, without introducing visible errors?
Could learned weather models fed by live observations give small studios accurate global weather at low cost?
mechanics.player_experience: Recognition. Players fly over their own house, check the sim against the sky outside, or navigate to a star they can see. Live data makes every session a little different and ties the game to the present day, while gaps and errors in the data are noticed and shared as quickly as its successes.
mechanics.summary: Simulation state is initialized or driven at runtime by external real-world data such as map imagery, elevation, star catalogs, live weather, or live traffic instead of authored or procedural content.

mechanics.definition: Owns a weighted, often directed graph over agent pairs holding one or more scalar affinities (friendship, romance, respect) and labels derived by threshold (friend, rival, lover). Interactions add or subtract amounts that depend on the action, personalities, and the current value; many games decay values toward neutral without contact. Agents read the values to decide whom to approach, help, or attack. RimWorld opinion runs -100 to 100 with rival below -20 and friend above 20; chitchat adds about 0.66 up to +10, while insults, up to 6 times likelier at -100 opinion, can start social fights. Prom Week keeps three bidirectional networks: buddy, romance, and cool. The Sims: Hot Date introduced separate short-term and long-term relationship scores. Inputs: interactions, traits, events. Outputs: social choices, cooperation, romance eligibility, conflict.
design_levers: number of dimensions per pair (single affinity versus friendship, romance, respect)
change per interaction and its dependence on the current value
decay toward neutral and its rate
label thresholds such as friend, rival, and partner
symmetry: directed or mutual values
dynamics: Agents with compatible traits cluster into friend groups, producing cliques within a colony or town.
Insults at low opinion push values lower, a reinforcing loop into feuds and fights.
Deaths and breakups spread grief along the graph, coupling relationships to mood.
failure_modes: One-dimensional affinity conflates liking with respect or attraction, so relationships feel thin.
Positive feedback drives every long-standing pair to best friends or mortal enemies.
Repeating one friendly action maxes a relationship with no story behind it.
Pairwise storage grows with the square of population, so large games restrict it to notable characters.
mechanics.name: Relationship values
open_questions: Can relationship state be inferred from language-model agent conversations rather than incremented by fixed amounts, and stay stable?
How many relationship dimensions do players track before additional meters stop adding meaning?
mechanics.player_experience: The player watches friendships and feuds form, reads relationship meters, and engineers meetings to repair or create bonds. Relationships make losses personal and give characters reasons to act together.
mechanics.summary: Pairwise numeric affinity between characters changes with interactions and drives social choices.

synergy.note: Completing requests raises friendship, giving the social meter a concrete verb (Animal Crossing, Stardew).

mechanics.definition: A harvestable stock (trees on tiles, fish in a zone, animals in a region, soil fertility) regenerates each tick at a rate that depends on its current level: often logistic growth, sometimes a fixed respawn timer or seed spread to neighboring cells. Harvesting removes stock at the rate set by extraction; if harvest exceeds regrowth the stock falls and, below a threshold, can collapse or stop regenerating. Banished foresters replant cut trees around their lodge; Eco tracks plant and animal populations that players can overharvest; Minecraft saplings regrow trees only where players plant them. Inputs: harvest rate, current stock, environmental modifiers. Outputs: stock level and yield available per tick.
design_levers: regrowth curve shape (logistic, linear, or timer) and its maximum rate
collapse threshold below which a stock stops recovering
whether regrowth is automatic or needs planting or breeding
spatial spread from neighboring cells versus regrowth in place
visibility of stock levels and sustainable yield
dynamics: Overharvesting produces boom-bust cycles in yield, the classic tragedy of the commons in shared or multiplayer worlds such as Eco.
The maximum sustainable yield of a logistic stock is at half capacity, so optimal play keeps stocks at partial depletion.
Coupled with predator-prey or habitat systems, harvest pressure ripples through an ecosystem.
Rotating among harvest sites becomes a spatial schedule.
failure_modes: Fast regrowth makes stocks effectively infinite and removes the tradeoff.
Collapse thresholds that are hidden make extinction feel like a sudden bug.
Replanting that is free and instant reduces stewardship to placing one building.
mechanics.name: Renewable regrowth
open_questions: Can learned ecological models give regrowth realistic spatial patterns while keeping sustainable yield readable?
Does shared regrowth in multiplayer reliably produce cooperative norms, or only collapse?
mechanics.player_experience: Stewardship under temptation. Players can take more now and pay later, so they learn to harvest at a pace the land can sustain, replant deliberately, or move on. Watching a forest or fishery recover after a pause makes the system's memory visible.
mechanics.summary: Harvested stocks such as forests, fish, game, and soil regenerate over time at density-dependent rates, allowing sustainable yield or overexploitation.

mechanics.definition: Owns a scalar or small vector (fame, infamy, honor) for the player or an organization, held per faction or globally, that rises and falls with witnessed or reported acts and often decays toward neutral. Unlike pairwise relationships it is the many-to-one view others hold of one actor, read by rules that gate access (quests, ranks, shops), set prices or acceptance odds, and change NPC reactions. Crusader Kings III tracks character prestige and dynasty renown as standing currencies; Europa Universalis IV diplomatic reputation adds 5 to alliance acceptance per point; RimWorld faction goodwill doubles as reputation by gating trade, caravans, and military aid. Inputs: acts and who observed them. Outputs: modifiers on prices, recruitment, acceptance, aggression, and unlocks.
design_levers: per-faction versus global scope, and whether there are separate fame and infamy axes
magnitude per act and whether acts need witnesses or reports
decay toward neutral and its rate
threshold tiers and what each unlocks or blocks
spillover between allied or rival factions
dynamics: Good standing opens trade and quests that further raise standing, a reinforcing loop.
Opposed factions turn every gain with one into a loss with the other, forcing alignment choices.
When reputation spreads by gossip, information lag creates windows for crime before word gets out.
failure_modes: Reputation grinding: repeating cheap acts maxes standing without meaningful choices.
Global reputation without witnesses means everyone knows everything instantly, which breaks plausibility.
Tiers that only unlock shops make reputation a currency, not an identity.
Irreversible collapse locks players out of content with no repair path.
mechanics.name: Reputation
open_questions: Can reputation be carried in language-model NPCs' remembered accounts of the player rather than in a number, and still gate content predictably?
Should reputation be a property of the actor or of each observer's beliefs about the actor?
mechanics.player_experience: The player cultivates a public identity and feels its weight when doors open or close. Reputation makes past choices follow the player into new encounters and creates tension between profitable acts and standing.
mechanics.summary: A standing value with a faction or the public changes access, prices, and how others respond.

mechanics.definition: Owns a set of logistic containers, each with a role (provider, requester, storage, buffer) and per-item request amounts or supply and demand settings, plus a fleet of carriers with speed, cargo size, and range or charge, and the stations that define coverage and recharge carriers. Each update the dispatcher computes open demand (requested minus held minus in transit), picks a provider holding the item by priority and distance, and assigns an idle carrier in coverage, which travels directly and delivers. Factorio roboports define logistic zones in which robots move items among active provider, passive provider, storage, buffer, and requester chests in priority order, carrying 1 item at 3 tiles per second before research. Dyson Sphere Program interstellar logistics stations set each item slot to local or remote supply, demand, or storage and send up to 100 drones within a planet and 10 vessels between planets, pairing stations by priority. Unlike conveyor-transport, the player routes nothing; unlike hauling-jobs, carriers are dedicated machines rather than agents with other work; unlike vehicle-route-scheduling, there are no order lists.
design_levers: carrier speed, cargo size, and energy or charging model, and how research upgrades them
coverage model: roboport zones, station range sliders, or minimum trip distances
container roles and the priority order among them
request thresholds and minimum load settings that batch trips
carrier count limits per station and the cost of each carrier
unlock timing relative to belts and trains
dynamics: Factories split into belt-fed bulk lines and robot-fed low-volume or mixed-item stations.
Coverage gaps and charging capacity become the new bottleneck, so players build infrastructure for the carriers themselves.
Supply and demand settings across planets or outposts produce hub-and-spoke shipping patterns no one drew.
failure_modes: A cheap, unconstrained robot network makes belts and layout obsolete once unlocked, removing the earlier puzzle.
Charging queues at a few stations leave swarms of idle carriers that are hard to diagnose.
Large carrier counts become a late-game compute cost in very large factories.
Priority rules that send carriers to distant providers when near ones exist make the network look broken.
mechanics.name: Request-provider logistics
open_questions: Could learned dispatch policies cut idle trips and charging queues while staying predictable to players?
How should a game show open requests, in-transit items, and carrier states so the network can be debugged at a glance?
mechanics.player_experience: Logistics stops being a layout puzzle and becomes a declaration of intent. The player sets what each chest wants and has, then watches a cloud of robots or a stream of vessels move goods, adding roboports, chargers, or carriers where the swarm thins out. It arrives as a late-game reward that dissolves earlier belt problems while creating new coverage and throughput ones.
mechanics.summary: Containers declare per-item requests and supplies, and a dispatcher sends drones or robots from providers to requesters without fixed routes.

mechanics.definition: Map nodes (ore patches, trees, fishing spots, oil wells) hold a resource type and a richness or purity value. An extractor, which is a placed machine, an assigned worker, or the avatar with a tool, produces units at a base rate multiplied by tool tier, worker skill, richness, and modifiers. Output goes to an adjacent buffer or is carried away by hauling. Satisfactory multiplies extraction by node purity (impure 0.5x, normal 1.0x, pure 2.0x); Factorio drills mine a fixed rate per tile with productivity research; RTS games such as Age of Empires assign villagers who gather by walking to nodes and back; Minecraft and Valheim gate which blocks can be mined by tool tier. Inputs: node, extractor, labor or power. Outputs: a stream of raw materials and, where depletion exists, a decrement to the node.
design_levers: base rate per extractor and tool or tier multipliers
richness or purity variation across nodes
labor model: machine, assigned worker, or avatar action
node placement and distance from base
whether extraction depletes the node (see deposit depletion) or is infinite
dynamics: Rich nodes far from base create a tradeoff between yield and logistics cost.
Contested nodes become flashpoints in multiplayer and RTS maps.
Extraction is the root of every production chain, so its rate caps the whole economy.
failure_modes: Uniform nodes make location choice irrelevant.
Extraction rates far above processing capacity create endless stockpiles and remove pressure.
Avatar gathering that never automates becomes grind late in a run.
mechanics.name: Resource extraction
open_questions: Could procedural geology tied to visible terrain features make extraction sites a matter of inference rather than icons?
mechanics.player_experience: The first link in every chain. Players scout for rich nodes, claim them, and judge how many extractors a site justifies. In avatar games, swinging a tool at a rock is a tactile, repeatable earning loop; in factory games, placing drills on the best patch is an early, high-leverage decision.
mechanics.summary: Workers or machines harvest raw materials from map nodes (ore, trees, fish, oil) at rates set by tools, labor, and node richness.

mechanics.definition: Each body holds mass, an inertia tensor, position, orientation, and linear and angular velocity. Each step the engine applies forces and gravity, finds colliding pairs with a broad phase and contact points with a narrow phase, solves contact and joint constraints iteratively (sequential impulses or projected Gauss-Seidel), and integrates positions; resting bodies sleep to save compute. Engines include Havok, used for Half-Life 2's gravity gun puzzles in 2004, PhysX, and Box2D by Erin Catto. Dennis Gustafsson's voxel physics engine after Teardown uses substeps instead of more solver iterations, in the style of temporal Gauss-Seidel, with a parallel solver for large piles. Outputs are motion, contact events, and impact forces that other systems read as damage or sound.
design_levers: solver iterations or substeps per frame
friction and restitution per material
allowed mass ratios between interacting bodies
joint types and limits
sleep thresholds and active simulation range
determinism requirements for replays and networking
dynamics: Contraptions, chain reactions, and Rube Goldberg machines arise in sandboxes such as Garry's Mod, whose tool gun welds and constrains props.
Impact forces feed damage, sound, and destruction systems.
Ragdoll physics turns failure into comedy and shareable clips.
failure_modes: Large mass ratios and stiff joints cause jitter or explosive separation.
Fast small objects tunnel through thin walls without continuous collision detection.
Non-deterministic solvers desynchronize multiplayer sessions and replays.
Players exploit clipping and stacking to launch themselves or bypass level geometry.
Body count caps scale and causes late slowdowns in sandbox play.
mechanics.name: Rigid-body physics
open_questions: Can learned simulators handle thousands of interacting bodies more cheaply than iterative solvers while staying stable?
Can deterministic GPU solvers make large rigid-body worlds practical in multiplayer?
mechanics.player_experience: Tactile and playful. Objects behave as expected, so players stack, throw, and build contraptions, and failures turn into slapstick. Physics puzzles feel solved by understanding rather than by finding the intended key.
mechanics.summary: Objects with mass and inertia move under forces and collide, constrained by contacts and joints solved each step.

mechanics.definition: Owns one or more competitor companies, each with cash, assets, market presence, and strategy parameters such as aggressiveness, expansion rate, and pricing policy. Each turn or tick a rival evaluates opportunities, builds or buys capacity, sets prices, and competes for the same customers, so market share splits by relative price, quality, coverage, and brand. Rivals can go bankrupt, be bought, or buy the player. Railroad Tycoon (1990) has rival railroad barons who try to drive the player out through stock dealings and rate wars. Capitalism (1995) lets the player set rivals' competence and managerial style from very aggressive to conservative and makes being bought out a loss. Transport Tycoon's AI companies build competing routes, and Offworld Trading Company's rivals contest the same resources and prices.
design_levers: number of rivals and their strategy profiles (aggressive, conservative, specialist)
whether rivals obey the same rules and economics as the player or receive bonuses
responsiveness: how quickly rivals react to price cuts or new entrants
interaction channels: price, location, stock, sabotage, poaching staff
bankruptcy and merger rules for rivals
dynamics: Price wars drive margins toward zero until one firm exits, after which prices rebound.
Market leaders gain economies of scale that compound their lead.
Rivals entering a player's niche push the player to diversify into new markets.
failure_modes: Passive AI that never contests markets turns competition into decoration.
AI that receives hidden resource bonuses feels unfair once players notice it.
Rivals that keep building in unprofitable markets go bankrupt early and leave the player alone.
mechanics.name: Rival firms
open_questions: Can LLM or RL-driven firms pursue legible strategies (cornering a supply, undercutting, collusion) that players can read and counter?
How should rival competence scale with difficulty without hidden bonuses?
mechanics.player_experience: Having someone to beat. The player watches rivals enter their markets, cuts prices or raises quality to hold share, and sometimes waits for a rival to overextend before striking. Victory becomes relative, which gives the sandbox a scoreboard.
mechanics.summary: AI or player competitors contest markets, prices, and assets; market share decides who wins.

synergy.note: Competitors move prices, turning a market into a strategic game.

mechanics.definition: Road tiles or segments form a graph whose nodes are intersections and building access points. Each building checks for a road connection; unconnected buildings do not function, grow, or receive services. Travel along the graph has a cost per segment set by road type, speed limit, and length, used by pathfinding and trip generation. In Micropolis, the released SimCity engine, a zone scans its perimeter for a road; if none exists the traffic test fails and residential and commercial zones shrink. Caesar III walkers move only on roads, so road shape determines service coverage. Cities: Skylines adds a road hierarchy with lanes and capacities. Banished treats roads as a speed boost rather than a requirement. Inputs: player-placed road segments. Outputs: connectivity per building and travel costs between points.
design_levers: whether connection is required or only speeds movement
road types with different speeds, capacities, and costs
placement freedom: grid-locked, free curves, or segments
intersection rules and traffic controls
cost per segment and upkeep
dynamics: Road layout determines which areas are reachable and therefore where growth happens.
Hierarchies of arterials and local streets emerge under congestion pressure.
Coupled with walker or coverage systems, road shape becomes a service-distribution tool.
failure_modes: Grid-only placement makes every city look the same.
Free placement without snapping guides makes clean layouts hard.
Dead-end tolerance that is too forgiving removes any layout pressure.
mechanics.name: Road networks
open_questions: Could procedural road generation that follows terrain and demand make player road-drawing optional without losing authorship?
mechanics.player_experience: Drawing the city's skeleton. Players lay roads first and fill blocks after, so road layout fixes later possibilities. Disconnected buildings are an immediate, readable failure, while inefficient geometry shows up slowly as long trips and congestion.
mechanics.summary: Roads and paths define connectivity; buildings must connect to function, and travel cost depends on network geometry.

mechanics.definition: Owns relationship-status edges (crush, lover, fiance, spouse, ex) and family links (parent, child, sibling) plus the rules that move pairs between statuses. Attempts such as flirting, proposals, and breakups succeed with probabilities from attraction, opinion, age, traits, and existing commitments; partnered pairs gain bonuses and can produce children, linking to lifecycle and inheritance. RimWorld pawns over 16 can attempt romance every 12 days; success depends on beauty (Ugly x0.3, Pretty x2.3), relative age, and existing relationships; a rebuff gives -10 and -15 opinion; lover is +35, spouse +30, ex -15, breakup -50, and kin get base opinions such as parent +30. Stardew Valley has 12 marriage candidates courted through a heart-based friendship meter (250 points per heart). Crusader Kings III makes marriage a political act that links dynasties. Inputs: relationship values, traits, ages. Outputs: couples, households, children, grief, jealousy.
design_levers: attraction model (traits, beauty, orientation, compatibility) and attempt cooldowns
status ladder and requirements for each step
jealousy, cheating, and breakup rules
whether relationships are player-directed, autonomous, or both
fertility and household formation rules that link to lifecycle
dynamics: Couples anchor households and change migration, mood, and grief networks.
Love triangles and rivals produce recurring social conflicts and fights.
In dynastic games, marriage creates alliance and inheritance claims across factions.
failure_modes: Romance spam: compatible agents pair off immediately and the system stops generating story.
Autonomous affairs and breakups wreck carefully built families, which feels like the game punishing the player.
Narrow attraction rules repeat the same few pairings every run.
Ignoring orientation or consent in autonomous romance produces behavior that players report as harmful.
mechanics.name: Romance and family
open_questions: Can language-model characters carry courtship as dialogue with consistent preferences, and how should that be constrained for safety and consent?
What autonomy level for romance maximizes story without making players feel they lost control of their families?
mechanics.player_experience: Romance gives characters personal goals and the player a matchmaking game. Players engineer meetings, celebrate weddings, and deal with affairs and breakups; children turn a run into a family saga.
mechanics.summary: Agents court, partner, marry, and form families according to compatibility and relationship state.

mechanics.definition: When walls, doors, or floors change, a flood fill over passable tiles bounded by impassable structures finds enclosed regions. Each region is scored against role templates by its furniture and size; the best match becomes the room type, and room stats feed effects. In RimWorld rooms are bounded by walls, doors, and natural rock; roles are scored from contents (12 per table for a dining room, 27 per workbench for a workshop, and a room with more than one unassigned human bed scores as barracks rather than a bedroom); rooms are capped at 36 map regions or 5,184 tiles; and wealth, beauty, space, and cleanliness combine into impressiveness that sets mood thoughts. Oxygen Not Included recognizes rooms such as barracks and mess halls by enclosure, size limits, and required buildings. Theme Hospital and Prison Architect instead have the player designate the room type and validate its requirements.
design_levers: enclosure rule: what counts as a wall, whether doors and vents close a room, diagonal gaps
minimum and maximum room size
role templates, their scores, and tie-breaking
whether one room can hold several roles
effects granted per role and stat tier
dynamics: Raid or disaster damage breaks enclosures and triggers mood or productivity drops across the base.
Rooms double as thermal and atmospheric zones, coupling layout to temperature and gas systems.
Room upgrades become a progression track toward higher stat tiers.
failure_modes: Invisible enclosure breaks, such as a destroyed wall or an opened gap, silently change room roles and their effects.
Role conflicts surprise players; in RimWorld a second unassigned bed turns a bedroom into barracks.
Tiny or multipurpose rooms that satisfy templates cheaply become the optimal design.
Very large open spaces exceed size limits and stop counting as rooms.
mechanics.name: Room recognition
open_questions: Can a vision or language model classify rooms by what they are used for rather than by fixed furniture templates?
How should recognition explain to the player why a space failed to qualify?
mechanics.player_experience: Walls acquire meaning. Players build a room, watch it get its label, and upgrade it to earn bonuses. A broken wall or an extra bed silently downgrades the room, which teaches players to read enclosure carefully.
mechanics.summary: Enclosed spaces are detected by flood fill and classified into room types by their size and contents, and the type grants effects.

mechanics.definition: A generator produces cases (travelers, documents, cargo) with attributes, some injected with discrepancies at a configured rate. A rulebook of predicates defines valid cases and grows or changes each day. The player inspects, cross-references, uses tools to reveal hidden attributes, and issues a verdict; errors produce penalties and correct verdicts produce pay, within a fixed time per shift. In Papers, Please each day sets documentation requirements that grow over time, tools include interrogation, fingerprinting, and body scans, citations for protocol violations cut daily earnings, and wages must cover rent, food, and heat. Contraband Police applies the loop to cargo and vehicles. Inputs: case attributes and rules. Outputs: verdicts, earnings, penalties, and story flags.
design_levers: rule count and the rate at which rules are added
discrepancy injection rate and subtlety
time per shift and pay per correct case
penalty structure for errors
inspection tools and their cost in time
authored cases with moral stakes mixed into generated ones
dynamics: Time pressure trades accuracy against throughput, and income pressure pushes players to cut corners.
Bribes and sympathetic cases set economic incentives against moral judgment.
Rule growth makes earlier skill obsolete, renewing difficulty every day.
failure_modes: Too many concurrent rules overload working memory and become frustrating.
Purely generated cases without authored stakes reduce play to a matching task.
Binary penalties with no explanation leave players unsure which rule they broke.
mechanics.name: Rule-checking inspection
open_questions: Can language models generate cases and dialogue whose discrepancies are subtle yet verifiable against a formal rulebook?
What rule-addition rate keeps load challenging without exceeding working memory?
mechanics.player_experience: Rising cognitive load and moral pressure. Players scan for mismatches against a growing rulebook, race the clock to earn enough for their family, and face cases where following the rules is cruel. Rule changes keep competence from settling into routine.
mechanics.summary: The player checks documents, people, or cargo against a rulebook that changes over time, under time pressure, with penalties for errors.

claims.text: SimCity (1989) included goal-oriented, time-limited scenarios that end in win or loss; Broderbund suggested scenarios to make SimCity more like a traditional game.
RollerCoaster Tycoon, designed and programmed by Chris Sawyer, shipped with 21 scenarios in which completing one unlocks the next.

mechanics.definition: A scenario bundles an initial state (map, buildings, budget, population, problem) with a goal predicate, optional constraints (banned buildings, fixed budget, no loans), and a deadline. State owned: the scenario definition and evaluation status. Update rule: each evaluation interval, test the goal and failure predicates; on the deadline or a failure condition, end with win or loss and often unlock the next scenario. Canonical forms: SimCity (1989), whose goal-oriented, time-limited scenarios were added at Broderbund's suggestion to make the toy more like a traditional game; RollerCoaster Tycoon, whose 21 base scenarios each unlock the next on completion, typically requiring a guest count and park rating by a date; Railroad Tycoon II's bronze, silver, and gold goal tiers; and Theme Hospital levels and Planet Coaster career scenarios.
design_levers: goal type: target value, survival, or rescue
deadline length
constraints and starting resources
single goal versus tiered bronze, silver, gold goals
scenario ordering and unlocks
whether play continues after the goal is met
dynamics: Scenarios function as structured tutorials for systems hidden in sandbox mode.
Hard scenario lines become community challenges with shared strategies.
Inherited problem cities expose systemic interactions the player did not cause.
failure_modes: Goals that reward a degenerate strategy, such as a guest count met by trapping guests in the park.
Deadlines that leave no room for experimentation make scenarios feel like puzzles with one answer.
Initial states that are trivially fixable or hopeless.
mechanics.name: Scenario objectives
open_questions: Can scenarios be generated by searching initial states and constraints for a target difficulty using automated RL playtests?
Can a language model generate a scenario brief and constraints from a real-world event that the simulation can actually evaluate?
mechanics.player_experience: The sandbox gets a question. The player studies an inherited mess, plans against the clock, and feels accomplishment rather than open-ended satisfaction. Constraints force use of systems the player would otherwise ignore.
mechanics.summary: Preset maps or situations come with explicit goals, constraints, and often a deadline.

mechanics.definition: Each entity attribute has a true hidden value and, per player, a knowledge level or confidence interval. Scouting actions (assigning a scout, watching matches, spending time or money) raise knowledge for specific entities or regions; knowledge may decay. The display shows a masked value, a range, a noisy point estimate, or a star rating whose noise scales with the scout's judging skill and the knowledge level. State owned: (player, entity, attribute) knowledge and the current estimate. Update rule: knowledge increases with effort and observer skill; estimate = true value plus noise scaled by remaining uncertainty, or hidden until a threshold. Canonical forms: Football Manager attribute masking, regional scouting knowledge, and scout ability and potential star ratings; Out of the Park Baseball, where displayed ratings are your scouting staff's opinion and accuracy is a setting.
design_levers: representation of uncertainty: masked, range, noisy estimate, or rating
scouting cost and speed per entity or region
scout skill as the noise level of reports
whether knowledge decays over time
whether true values are ever fully revealed, for example after signing
separate uncertainty for current ability and future potential
dynamics: Information asymmetry creates market behavior: overpaying for hyped players and bargains in under-scouted regions.
Uncertain potential couples with skill growth to make youth signings speculative bets.
Rival AI clubs with better knowledge outbid the player, making scouting investment competitive.
failure_modes: Third-party editors and database tools reveal true attributes, collapsing the mechanic for players who use them.
Cheap, complete scouting turns uncertainty into a delay rather than a decision.
Uncertainty that persists after acquisition and long observation feels arbitrary.
mechanics.name: Scouting knowledge
open_questions: Can language-model scouts write reports whose hedges and biases track their numeric noise, so reading reports is itself a skill?
Does Bayesian updating from observed performance, shown to the player, make uncertainty feel fairer than fixed masking?
mechanics.player_experience: Recruitment becomes investment under uncertainty. The player decides where to send scouts, weighs a cheap unknown against a known star, and feels vindicated or burned when performance reveals the true value.
mechanics.summary: Entity attributes are known only with uncertainty that scouting effort reduces.

mechanics.definition: Owns the season's state: start date, an end condition (fixed duration, a scheduled wipe, or a world-level goal or catastrophe), and the carryover rules that say what survives into the next season (nothing, account-level unlocks, records, or changed rules). When the end condition fires, world state is archived or deleted, a new world is generated or loaded, and carryover is applied. A Tale in the Desert runs in Tellings that average about 18 months and end in a wipe, with rule changes for the next Telling shaped by what players achieved. Eco gives each world a meteor due in thirty days, so a server's run is bounded by stopping it or suffering the impact, and servers are commonly restarted as new worlds. Unlike persistent-world, which assumes continuity, this mechanic owns the bounded lifetime of a shared world and the transition between lifetimes.
design_levers: season length or end condition
carryover: nothing, cosmetics, account unlocks, records, or rule changes
rule variation between seasons, including player-proposed changes
whether players can migrate between seasonal and permanent worlds
announcement lead time before a wipe
dynamics: Activity surges at season start and fades toward the end, giving the population a cycle.
Players refine openings across seasons, and community guides target the first days of a wipe.
Rule changes between seasons let designers and players treat each season as an experiment.
failure_modes: Wipes erase work players were attached to, and some quit rather than start over.
Short seasons reward a known opening rush, so seasons play out the same way.
Carryover that is too generous rebuilds the early-arrival advantage the reset was meant to remove.
mechanics.name: Seasonal world reset
open_questions: Could AI summaries and chronicles of past seasons preserve their history so wipes feel less like loss?
Which carryover rules keep returning players motivated without restoring early-arrival dominance?
mechanics.player_experience: Fresh starts on a schedule. Everyone begins equal at the start of a season, so new players can matter, and the end date gives the season an arc of land rush, consolidation, and final push. Players plan around the wipe, deciding what is worth building when it will not last.
mechanics.summary: A shared world runs for a bounded season and is then wiped and restarted, often with rule changes carried into the next season.

mechanics.definition: Owns a calendar position that advances by day and maps to a season index, usually four. Each season sets parameters other systems read: which crops can grow, temperature, day length, weather odds, animal behavior, demand for heat or food, and scheduled events. Stardew Valley has four 28-day seasons, and seasonal crops must generally be harvested before the next season arrives; Don't Starve's base cycle alternates 20 summer days and 16 winter days and changes the day, dusk, and night split with them; Banished and Farthest Frontier force food stockpiling for winters without harvests. Inputs are elapsed days; outputs are season flags and parameter sets. Some games make season length a setting.
design_levers: number and length of seasons, and whether lengths vary or can be set
which systems each season modifies: growth, temperature, weather, events, prices
severity of the harshest season and how much stockpiling it demands
transition rules, such as crops dying at the change or gradual change
season-unique content: crops, festivals, creatures
dynamics: Seasonal production with year-round consumption creates demand for storage, preservation, and trade.
Combined with a crisis countdown, the approach of winter structures the year as preparation.
Labor shifts between seasonal tasks, creating idle periods and peaks.
failure_modes: Seasons that only swap textures add art cost without changing decisions.
A harsh season survivable only with one known stockpile size becomes a checklist.
Season-gated content locks players out for long stretches when they miss a window.
mechanics.name: Seasons
open_questions: Can generative asset models make seasonal variants of every asset cheap enough that seasons become a default rather than a budget decision?
mechanics.player_experience: Planning in cycles. The player plants for this season while saving for the next, treats the end of a season as a deadline, and gets a fresh start each spring. Winter tests the year's preparation, and the cycle gives long games a felt rhythm.
mechanics.summary: A seasonal calendar cycles conditions such as temperature, daylight, and growing windows that govern growth, demand, and risk.

mechanics.definition: Each service building writes an effect value onto a coverage map, within a radius, a network distance, or by dispatching vehicles. Covered cells or buildings read that value to reduce a risk or raise a satisfaction term. In Micropolis each fire or police station adds an effect equal to 1000 times funded over requested budget, halved if unpowered and halved again without road access, to an 8x8-tile block map; the map is smoothed three times, and the smoothed police map is subtracted from each cell's crime score and the smoothed fire map sets fire protection. SimCity 2000 shows coverage as a radius; Cities: Skylines uses network distance and dispatches service vehicles. Capacity limits how many buildings or residents one facility can serve. Inputs: service building locations, funding, power, access. Outputs: per-cell coverage values and the downstream risk or happiness change.
design_levers: coverage shape: Euclidean radius, network distance, or vehicle dispatch
capacity per building and falloff with distance
funding and power effects on strength
how coverage maps to outcomes such as crime, fire risk, health, or education
overlap rules: additive, maximum, or diminishing
dynamics: Coverage shapes city form, rewarding compact grids around service hubs.
Budget cuts weaken coverage everywhere at once, causing simultaneous crises.
Coupled with land value, coverage raises desirability, which raises density, which raises demand for more services.
failure_modes: Radius coverage that ignores the road network lets buildings across a river count as covered.
Overlapping coverage with no capacity limit makes one building per district enough.
Hidden funding multipliers make coverage seem to drop at random.
mechanics.name: Service coverage
open_questions: Can facility-location solvers act as advisors that suggest placements without removing the planning decision?
Does vehicle dispatch produce more interesting failures than radius coverage at equal legibility?
mechanics.player_experience: Filling the map with circles. Players place services to cover populated areas, check overlays for gaps, and balance coverage against budget. Uncovered districts show up as fires, crime, or unhappy residents, so the overlay becomes a to-do list.
mechanics.summary: Service buildings such as police, fire, clinics, and schools satisfy demand within a radius or network distance, up to a capacity.

mechanics.definition: Each service point (a ride, a clinic room, a checkout) has a service rate and a queue of waiting agents. Arriving agents join if the queue is not too long by their own tolerance; while waiting, their needs keep decaying and their satisfaction falls with waiting time; served agents leave and free the slot. RollerCoaster Tycoon builds explicit queue paths for rides, and guests think aloud about long waits. Theme Hospital and Two Point Hospital queue patients outside rooms; while they wait their health keeps falling, so long queues produce departures and deaths that lower the hospital's reputation. Inputs: arrival rate, service rate, capacity, tolerance. Outputs: queue length, waiting times, and satisfaction changes.
design_levers: service rate per point and number of parallel points
queue capacity and agents' tolerance before they balk or leave
satisfaction decay while waiting
queue discipline: first-in-first-out, priority, or player reordering
information shown about wait times
dynamics: Utilization near 100% causes waiting times to explode, the core queueing-theory result, so players learn to keep slack.
Coupled with needs decay, long waits create secondary demand at food and toilet facilities.
Demand shifts toward shorter queues, balancing load across service points.
failure_modes: Fixed tolerance across all agents makes queues predictable and dull.
Queues that grow without bound because agents never leave freeze the simulation.
Invisible queues inside buildings hide the bottleneck.
mechanics.name: Service queues
open_questions: Could generative agents with learned patience models make queues produce more varied and memorable behavior?
mechanics.player_experience: Visible lines are an instant read on capacity. Players add service points, lengthen or shorten queue paths, and redistribute demand, learning from the line itself where the bottleneck is.
mechanics.summary: Agents wait in lines for limited-capacity services; waiting time feeds back into satisfaction and throughput.

claims.text: Factorio introduced arithmetic, decider, and constant combinators on a circuit network where red and green wire signals entering one entity are summed.
Factorio developers stated a design principle of not adding dedicated logic, bit, or timer combinator types during the 0.13 circuit network work.
Factorio 2.0 added a selector combinator and decider combinators with multiple AND/OR conditions, multiple outputs, and per-wire input selection.

mechanics.definition: The player places wires between entities and logic elements to build control systems inside the world. State owned: the wire graph, signal values on each network, and logic element configuration. Update rule: each tick, sensors and connected entities write signals (item counts, fluid levels, power, conditions) onto their networks; logic elements read input networks and write outputs, often with a one-tick delay; actuators enable or disable themselves or change settings by condition. Canonical form: the Factorio circuit network, where red and green wires carry item-count signals, signals from both wires entering one entity are summed, and arithmetic, decider, and constant combinators operate on them; Factorio 2.0 added a selector combinator and multi-condition deciders. Others: Minecraft redstone, Oxygen Not Included automation wires with sensors and logic gates, Stationeers logic and IC chips, and Mindustry logic processors.
design_levers: signal type: binary, integer, or multi-channel item vectors
logic primitives provided and whether higher-level elements are deliberately withheld
timing: propagation delay per element and tick order
which entities can read and write signals
debugging aids: signal readouts, wire visualization, element descriptions
physical cost of wires and logic elements
dynamics: Turing-complete primitives lead players to build CPUs, displays, and games inside the game.
Demand-driven control (produce only when stock falls) dampens the oscillations and gluts of always-on production.
Shared circuit designs spread as blueprints, coupling this mechanic to community design culture.
failure_modes: Invisible signal values and per-tick delays make circuits hard to debug without readouts.
Circuit control is optional in many games, so most players never engage and designers cannot build challenges around it.
Missing primitives force contraptions for simple tasks, while too many make the logic trivial.
mechanics.name: Signal circuits
open_questions: Can a model synthesize circuit layouts from a behavior spec (keep 2,000 plates buffered) and explain existing circuits to newcomers?
What minimal primitive set gives the widest range of player designs without making simple tasks contraptions?
mechanics.player_experience: The player turns a passive factory into one that senses and responds: lamps that show stock, trains that go where they are needed, power that switches on demand. Building memory, timers, or displays from parts feels like engineering, and the most ambitious players build computers inside the game.
mechanics.summary: In-world wires, sensors, and logic elements carry signals that read machine state and control machines.

mechanics.definition: Owns per-object interaction definitions: each interaction carries advertisements (which needs it satisfies and by how much), availability checks, distance attenuation, and the behavior script the agent runs. Agents carry no knowledge of how to use things; when choosing, an agent gathers advertisements from reachable objects, scales them by its needs, personality, and distance, selects one, and runs that object's script. In The Sims, per Forbus and Wright's notes, advertisements cover nine motives, can scale with personality points, attenuate with distance through high, moderate, low, or none presets, and check trees hide unavailable interactions; a toilet advertises 0-70 Bladder. Because behavior lives in objects, new objects add new behaviors without changing agent code, which suits expansion packs and mods. Inputs: objects in range, agent needs. Outputs: candidate actions, need restoration, animations.
design_levers: advertised magnitude per need and whether it scales with personality or object quality
distance attenuation curve per interaction
advertised versus delivered value, which allows deceptive or broken objects
availability and permission checks such as ownership, age, and room
how many agents one object can serve at once
dynamics: Each new object adds behaviors, so the behavior space grows with content packs, which is how The Sims expansions extended play.
Players use objects as lures to route agents, coupling placement to behavior.
Scarce objects create queues and conflicts when several agents select the same one.
failure_modes: An over-tuned advertisement makes one object a magnet that agents queue for regardless of need.
Assuming honest advertisements breaks when objects fail, producing loops of agents repeatedly using broken objects.
Attenuation errors make agents walk past nearby options to distant ones.
Behavior spread across hundreds of objects is harder to debug than one agent controller.
mechanics.name: Smart objects
open_questions: Can generative models author new objects with consistent advertisements, scripts, and animations, turning content packs into runtime generation?
Should language-model agents read object affordances as numeric advertisements, as text descriptions, or both?
mechanics.player_experience: Buying or placing an object changes what agents want to do, so the player designs behavior through the environment. Players learn that a better object pulls agents across the room and use placement to steer them.
mechanics.summary: Objects advertise the need satisfaction they offer, and agents query nearby objects to decide what to do.

mechanics.definition: Owns a library of social exchange definitions, each with an intent, preconditions on the social state, initiator and responder desire rules, and effects for acceptance and rejection on relationships, statuses, and history. Each cycle an agent scores the exchanges it could start with each other agent, picks one, the responder evaluates acceptance, and the outcome is written to state and history. Comme il Faut in Prom Week defines exchanges with one intent, hard preconditions, initiator and responder influence rule sets, and at least accept and reject instantiations; volition sums the weights of over 5,000 influence rules across 34 statuses and 44 traits. RimWorld rolls chitchat, deep talk, slights, and insults with weights from opinion and compatibility; The Sims 3 defined hundreds of interactions from thousands of production rules (Evans, GDC 2010). Inputs: social state, traits, history. Outputs: relationship and status changes, logged events.
design_levers: size of the exchange library and intents covered
precondition strictness and which norms or statuses gate moves
volition rule weights for initiators and responders
effect magnitudes for accept and reject outcomes
player control: choose moves, suggest, or only watch
dynamics: Logged exchanges become history that later rules reference, so past insults enable future revenge moves.
Status effects spread socially, so one embarrassing exchange changes how a group treats a character.
Exchange outcomes drive relationship values, which change the next exchange's odds, producing escalating arcs.
failure_modes: Small libraries repeat the same exchanges until characters feel scripted.
Rule weights interact unpredictably across thousands of rules, so authors cannot predict outcomes.
Exchanges change numbers without visible performance, so moves feel interchangeable.
Spam: repeating the best-scoring move maxes relationships.
mechanics.name: Social exchanges
open_questions: Can language models generate performances and new exchange types on the fly while a symbolic layer keeps preconditions and effects consistent?
Can influence-rule weights be learned from player judgments of plausibility rather than authored?
mechanics.player_experience: The player chooses moves in a social puzzle, or watches agents make them, and learns the norms that make a move land. Rejections and backfires are part of the fun, and players develop social strategies such as softening a target before the big ask.
mechanics.summary: Discrete social moves such as flirt, insult, or apologize have preconditions on social state and norms, and they update relationships.

mechanics.definition: An object is a network of nodes (point masses) linked by beams (massless springs with damping). Each step every beam applies force from its length deviation and damping, nodes integrate, and collisions push nodes. A beam whose force passes a deform threshold permanently changes its rest length, and one that passes its strength breaks, so parts detach. In BeamNG.drive vehicles are authored in JBeam: nodes have weight, beams have beamSpring (stiffness), beamDamp, beamDeform, and beamStrength. Beams do not resist bending or twisting, so cross braces are needed for rigidity, and stiff beams on light nodes vibrate or explode (the documentation's example stabilizes a structure by raising nodes from 6 kg to 7 kg). Finite-element and position-based methods are alternatives.
design_levers: node density and placement
beam stiffness and damping per part
deform and break thresholds
physics step rate
which parts are soft and which are rigid or cosmetic
coupling of deformation to function, such as steering or engine damage
dynamics: Damage changes handling, which changes driving, which causes more damage.
Crash testing becomes its own play style and community genre.
Deformed tires and suspension couple to grip and vehicle dynamics.
failure_modes: Stiff beams on light nodes vibrate or explode, so every structure needs stability tuning.
CPU cost per vehicle limits how many soft bodies can run at once.
Hand-building node-beam structures for every vehicle is a large authoring cost.
Too-soft settings make solid objects look like jelly.
mechanics.name: Soft-body deformation
open_questions: Can node-beam structures be generated automatically from a visual mesh and material labels?
Can learned deformation surrogates run many soft bodies at once on consumer hardware?
mechanics.player_experience: Visceral, readable damage. Crashes crumple metal where they hit, and the damage changes how the vehicle drives. Players experiment with crashes as much as they drive.
mechanics.summary: Objects built from mass nodes and spring beams bend, crumple, and break under stress, and deformation persists.

synergy.note: Deforming chassis change handling after impacts (BeamNG.drive).

mechanics.definition: Each perishable item or stack carries a freshness value or age that advances each tick at a rate set by item type and storage conditions; at a threshold it becomes rotten, converts into a spoiled item, or is destroyed. RimWorld stops rot for food kept at or below 0 C, so walk-in freezers are standard; Don't Starve moves food from fresh to stale to spoiled and finally to rot, with ice boxes slowing the clock; Factorio: Space Age gives biological items spoil times from about two hours down to a few minutes, cannot be delayed, turns spoiled items into Spoilage, and passes ingredient freshness on to recipe outputs. Inputs: item type, time, storage environment. Outputs: current freshness, value or effect scaling, and spoil events.
design_levers: spoil time per item type
storage modifiers such as temperature, containers, and preservation methods
whether freshness is binary (fresh or rotten) or continuous and scales value
what spoiled goods become: nothing, a waste item, or a useful input such as fertilizer
freshness inheritance across recipes
dynamics: Shifts optimal play from stockpiling to just-in-time throughput; Factorio's developers state that buffering is not helpful under spoilage.
Cold storage couples food to power and temperature systems, so a power failure becomes a famine risk.
Seasonal harvests plus spoilage create a winter preservation problem.
Freshness-priority handling (pick freshest or oldest first) creates new logistics rules.
failure_modes: Spoilage that is cheap to stop, such as one freezer that halts all decay, becomes a one-time build tax.
Short spoil times on items with long logistics routes make some chains impossible without explanation.
Hidden freshness values make sudden losses feel unfair.
mechanics.name: Spoilage
open_questions: What spoil-time distribution across goods produces interesting routing without making long chains infeasible?
mechanics.player_experience: A clock on every stockpile. Players stop hoarding and start thinking in flow: produce close to consumption, build cold storage, preserve food, or accept waste. Opening a storeroom to find a harvest rotted is a sharp, memorable loss.
mechanics.summary: Perishable goods lose value or rot over time depending on storage conditions such as temperature and containers.

synergy.note: Storage conditions decide spoilage rates, making cold storage valuable.

mechanics.definition: Owns an unrest or radicalism stock per region, group, or nation. Each period grievances (unmet needs, opposed laws, taxes, war exhaustion, occupation) add to it and suppression (police, garrisons, concessions, propaganda) subtracts. Crossing thresholds triggers escalating events: protests, strikes, riots, rebel spawns, secession, revolution, or game over. Civilization (1991) puts a city into disorder, halting production, when unhappy citizens outnumber happy ones. Europa Universalis IV accumulates rebel progress in provinces with positive unrest until rebels rise. Victoria 3 starts a revolution clock when a political movement's radicalism is high enough that it turns to revolt, and each time the clock fills the revolution advances through events. Frostpunk (2018) ends in revolt when discontent stays too high or hope too low for an extended period.
design_levers: grievance sources and their weights
suppression tools, their costs, and side effects such as increasing long-term grievance
threshold ladder and escalation speed
spatial scope: per province, per group, or national
warning visibility, such as clocks, meters, and forecasts
dynamics: Disorder halts production, which worsens shortages and raises grievances, a death spiral.
Suppression buys time but raises long-term grievances, deferring rather than resolving crises.
Unrest in one region can spread or inspire neighboring regions.
failure_modes: Cheap suppression makes unrest trivial, as with stacking garrisons or police.
Instant revolt at a threshold feels arbitrary without visible warning.
Revolts that only spawn more units to fight turn politics into whack-a-mole combat.
mechanics.name: Stability and unrest
open_questions: Can agent-based protest dynamics (social contagion, leaders) replace scalar unrest meters while staying readable?
Can LLM-generated demands make movements negotiable rather than just threats to suppress?
mechanics.player_experience: A pressure cooker. The player watches unrest rise, decides whether to concede, suppress, or wait it out, and feels the cost of each option. Thresholds create anxious countdowns and dramatic turning points.
mechanics.summary: Grievances accumulate into unrest that triggers protests, strikes, or revolt.

mechanics.definition: Owns a candidate pool and a roster. Each candidate has skills or attributes, traits, and a wage demand; hiring moves them to the roster at a recurring wage. Rostered staff are assigned to rooms, roles, or positions, and their skill sets the speed or quality of work there; fatigue, morale, and pay satisfaction change over time and can trigger rest, raise demands, or quitting. Training spends money and time to raise skills. Theme Hospital (1997) has the player hire doctors, nurses, handymen, and receptionists with performance statistics, train doctors, require specialist skills for rooms such as the operating theatre, send staff to rest, and dismiss staff who argue about pay. Football Manager builds a whole game around player and staff attributes, contracts, and wages, and Two Point Hospital follows Theme Hospital's model.
design_levers: number of staff types and skill dimensions
candidate pool size, refresh rate, and quality distribution
wage curve relative to skill and how raises are demanded
fatigue, morale, and quitting rules
training cost, duration, and skill ceilings
how much candidate information is hidden until hired or scouted
dynamics: Strong staff raise income, which funds better hires, so facilities snowball toward elite rosters.
Fatigue and rest create capacity dips that ripple into queues.
Losing a star employee causes a sudden performance drop and a recovery arc.
failure_modes: When one stat dominates, hiring becomes sorting a list and staff stop feeling like individuals.
Raise demands that grow too fast make experienced staff a liability and push players to churn employees.
Generic stats without traits make staff interchangeable and remove attachment.
mechanics.name: Staff hiring and rosters
open_questions: Can LLM-generated candidates with backstories, interviews, and evolving workplace relationships make rosters as memorable as authored characters?
What is the smallest set of staff attributes that keeps hiring a real decision?
mechanics.player_experience: Assembling a team. The player compares candidates' stats against their wages, places the best people where they matter most, and nurses tired or unhappy staff. Names and faces make the facility feel staffed by people rather than counters.
mechanics.summary: The player hires individual staff with skills, traits, and wages to operate a facility or team.

mechanics.definition: Owns, per engaged unit or stack, strength pools (hit points, manpower, organization, morale) and a vector of combat stats, and, per engagement, a round counter and modifiers from terrain, commanders, and supply. Each round, each side's damage is computed from its attack against the opponent's defense, scaled by modifiers and a random draw, and subtracted from the opponent's pools; a side whose morale or organization breaks retreats or is destroyed. Sid Meier's Civilization compares a unit's attack with the defender's defense under terrain and fortification modifiers and a random draw. Europa Universalis IV rolls dice in alternating fire and shock phases modified by general skill and terrain, and morale damage usually ends the battle. Hearts of Iron IV compares divisions' attack against defense or breakthrough, draining organization. FTL rolls each shot against the target's evasion and absorbs shots with shield layers. Unlike military-operations, there are no modeled sensors, signatures, or flight paths; unlike attribute-match-engine, the output is attrition of unit pools rather than a stream of sports events.
design_levers: stat set: attack and defense only, or separate stats for different damage types and targets
randomness: dice range per round versus deterministic expected values
morale or organization as a separate pool that ends battles before units are destroyed
terrain, river crossing, fortification, and commander modifiers
round length and the number of rounds before a battle resolves
how much of the formula and odds the game previews
dynamics: Players optimize army compositions and commanders around the formula, producing a meta that patches revise.
Morale breaking before units die produces retreats and pursuits, giving campaigns a rhythm of decisive and indecisive battles.
Terrain modifiers make certain regions natural defensive lines, shaping fronts and borders.
failure_modes: One unit composition or stat dominates once players find the formula's best ratio, a recurring issue in strategy communities.
High variance lets a weak unit defeat a much stronger one, which reads as unfair when the odds were not shown.
Opaque modifier stacks make losses impossible to diagnose without community spreadsheets.
mechanics.name: Statistical combat resolution
open_questions: Can generated battle narration explain why a stat-resolved battle went as it did, so players can separate luck from preparation?
Could learned surrogate models of tactical combat give abstract resolution more of the texture of simulated battles at low cost?
mechanics.player_experience: Battles are prepared rather than performed. The player stacks advantages (terrain, a better general, the right unit mix, a fresh army) and then watches the bars move, knowing the dice can still go against them. Reading a combat preview and deciding whether the odds justify an attack is the core skill.
mechanics.summary: Battles between units resolve from attack, defense, morale, terrain, and random rolls in rounds rather than from physics or modeled sensors and weapons.

mechanics.definition: The game samples aggregate variables (population, money, production and consumption per item, prices, power, happiness, crime) at fixed intervals into time series and renders them as line graphs, stacked areas, tables, or pies. State owned: ring buffers of samples per variable, usually at several resolutions with older data downsampled. Update rule: each sample period, append the aggregate; when a buffer fills, merge samples into a coarser tier. The player picks variables, windows, and breakdowns. Canonical forms: the SimCity graphs window, Factorio production statistics per item across windows from seconds to hundreds of hours, Transport Tycoon company graphs for income and cargo delivered, Oxygen Not Included's daily colony report, and market price history in EVE Online and Victoria 3.
design_levers: which variables are logged and at what granularity (per item, per region, per agent class)
time windows and downsampling scheme
comparison views: against rivals, against previous periods, production versus consumption
drill-down from an aggregate line to its contributors
trend-based alerts and export of data
dynamics: Visible production and consumption rates make ratio optimization possible, as in finding Factorio bottlenecks from item statistics.
Trend reading supports experimental play: change one policy, watch the curve, revert.
Public price histories in shared markets feed speculation and coordinated trading.
failure_modes: Graphs show a decline but give no path to its cause.
Coarse sampling hides short spikes or aliases oscillations into smooth lines.
Dashboards buried in menus are never opened by most players.
Long high-resolution histories bloat save files.
mechanics.name: Stats dashboards
open_questions: Can natural-language queries over logged history (why did power drop last winter) replace browsing graphs for most players?
Which few variables, logged by default, let players diagnose most failures in a given genre?
mechanics.player_experience: The player steps back from the moment to read trends, confirm a change worked, and spot slow declines that no single frame reveals. A rising curve is its own reward.
mechanics.summary: Graphs and tables show the recorded history of simulation variables over selectable time windows.

mechanics.definition: Owns a set of active stimuli, each with a source position, type (sound, light, smell, sight of the player), intensity, radius, and decay time, plus each agent's perception thresholds and current alert target. When an action fires it emits a stimulus sized by the action (gunshot, smashed window, running, a lit fire); each update, agents within range whose perception exceeds the threshold switch to an investigate state and path toward the source, and some propagate the alert to nearby agents so groups follow. Stimuli fade, and agents that find nothing return to idle or wander. Project Zomboid zombies respond to sight and hearing, and loud actions draw them from a distance; This War of Mine shows noise from scavenging actions that can alert people nearby. Unlike fog-of-war, which hides information from the player, this mechanic models what hostile agents perceive about the player; unlike adaptive-threat-scaling, it changes where threats go, not how strong they are.
design_levers: emission radius and intensity per action, weapon, and tool
perception thresholds per agent type and modifiers such as weather, time of day, and walls
stimulus decay time and how long agents investigate before giving up
alert propagation between agents, which turns individuals into crowds or hordes
player feedback: visible noise rings, audio cues, or no indication
dynamics: Players lure groups away with distractions such as alarms or thrown objects, turning the rule into a tool.
