Fighting creates noise that draws more enemies, a reinforcing loop that punishes loud tactics.
Quiet tools and routes become valuable, shaping crafting and travel choices.
failure_modes: Invisible emission rules make attacks feel random when players cannot tell what they did to cause them.
Propagation that is too strong snowballs every mistake into an unwinnable horde.
Agents that ignore walls and distance when following sound feel omniscient and break stealth.
mechanics.name: Stimulus attraction
open_questions: Can learned agents that reason about what they heard and saw produce searches that feel smarter without becoming omniscient?
Does visualizing emissions improve player decisions or remove the tension of not knowing what heard you?
mechanics.player_experience: Every action has an audience. The player weighs the speed of smashing a window against the zombies it will call, walks instead of running, and uses noise deliberately as a lure. Mistakes are legible and frightening: a gunshot that brings a crowd teaches the rule at once.
mechanics.summary: Player actions emit sound or light stimuli with a radius and decay, and agents that perceive them move toward the source, so managing emissions is part of survival.

mechanics.definition: Storage containers, warehouses, stockpile zones, and machine input or output slots each hold a capacity measured in units, stacks, slots, or volume. Producers push into storage until it is full, then stall; consumers pull from it until it is empty, then starve. Between those limits, buffer level absorbs mismatches in timing. Factorio chests have fixed slot counts and machines hold small input and output buffers; RimWorld stockpile zones accept filtered items in priority order (low, normal, preferred, important, critical) and haulers move items toward higher-priority zones with space; Anno caps each good at an island-wide storage limit that warehouses raise; GlassBox in SimCity (2013) stores everything in capacity-limited resource bins, such as a house holding 20 of 30 food and 4 of 10 people. Inputs: incoming and outgoing flows. Outputs: stock level and full or empty states that gate adjacent processes.
design_levers: capacity per container and whether it is per good, per slot, or shared
filters and priorities that decide what goes where
behavior when full: stall, overflow to the ground, or discard
local buffers on machines versus central warehouses
storage cost in space, money, or construction
dynamics: Buffers absorb shocks such as raids, winters, and broken links, trading space for resilience.
Full buffers propagate backpressure upstream, so one blocked output can stop an entire chain.
Coupled with spoilage, storage becomes a liability instead of a safe stockpile.
Players build overflow sinks or priority splits so critical chains never block.
failure_modes: Very large storage hides every imbalance, so production ratios never matter.
Tiny buffers make chains brittle and turn play into constant stop-and-go.
Full storage stalls without alerts make the cause invisible.
mechanics.name: Storage and buffers
open_questions: Can automatic buffer sizing advisors teach players about backpressure without solving the layout for them?
mechanics.player_experience: Buffers give breathing room and hide problems. Players size storage to survive supply gaps, then discover that a full warehouse has silently stopped a production line. Organizing what goes where becomes its own small design task.
mechanics.summary: Goods occupy finite storage; buffers decouple producers from consumers, and full storage blocks production.

mechanics.definition: A director process tracks a pacing signal and runs a cycle that selects incidents from a catalog. Left 4 Dead's AI Director keeps an emotional intensity value per survivor that rises with damage, incapacitation, and nearby infected deaths and decays when not engaged; it cycles through Build Up (full threat until peak intensity), Sustain Peak (3-5 s), Peak Fade, and Relax (30-45 s of minimal spawns), spawns mobs every 90-180 s on Normal, and deals boss events (Tank, Witch, nothing) along the route. RimWorld storytellers weigh colony wealth, colonists, recent deaths or wounds, and time since the last major event; incident chance is a base chance times a population-intent factor, and presets differ (Cassandra escalates in cycles, Phoebe leaves long gaps, Randy is irregular). The director decides when and what; magnitude usually comes from adaptive threat scaling. Outputs: incident firing, spawn populations, item placement, music cues.
design_levers: pacing signal: per-player intensity, time since last threat, or colony state
phase thresholds and durations for build-up, peak, and relaxation
incident catalog, base weights, and state conditions such as population intent
selectable presets that change cycle shape and randomness
randomness floor and mercy rules after heavy losses
dynamics: Pressure and relief cycles create natural story beats that players retell as chapters.
Combined with persistent injuries and permadeath, a poorly timed second incident starts cascades that become memorable runs.
Players manipulate the director's inputs, such as population or wealth, to shape which incidents it can choose.
failure_modes: Fixed cycles become predictable, and players learn to exploit relax windows.
Irregular presets can stack several hard events, which feels unfair when combined with permadeath.
Heavy rubber-banding makes skill feel irrelevant because the director compensates for good play.
mechanics.name: Storyteller director
open_questions: Can a language-model director author new incidents conditioned on colony state and characters, not just select from a catalog?
Can learned models of player stress from play telemetry replace hand-built intensity formulas?
How should a director balance dramatic pacing against fairness when deaths are permanent?
mechanics.player_experience: Play has a rhythm of pressure and relief that feels authored even though it is generated. Players use calm windows to build and heal, brace when calm runs long, and talk about storytellers as personalities with moods and grudges.
mechanics.summary: A director AI chooses which events to fire and when, pacing them by a model of tension and the current state.

claims.text: Dwarf Fortress keeps a hidden stress value from -1,000,000 to +1,000,000 with effects from +10,000, +25,000, and +50,000; emotions add or subtract stress and facets such as bravery, stress vulnerability, and anxiety scale it.
In Crusader Kings III, acting against personality traits adds stress that can be lethal, and stress breaks at level 2 or higher can change traits.

mechanics.definition: Owns a per-agent stress value with slow decay and a ladder of levels. Each experience adds or removes an amount scaled by personality, and the value relaxes toward zero only slowly, so stress is an integral of history rather than a snapshot of current conditions. Crossing a level triggers a break event, a coping trait, a lasting change in behavior, or death at the extreme. Dwarf Fortress keeps a hidden stress value from -1,000,000 to +1,000,000 with effects from +10,000, +25,000, and +50,000: emotions add or subtract stress, facets such as bravery, stress vulnerability, and anxiety scale it, long-term memories keep adding to it, and high stress leads to tantrums, depression, obliviousness, or insanity. Crusader Kings III adds stress when a character acts against its personality traits, fires mental-break events as stress levels are crossed, lets breaks at level 2 or higher change traits, and can kill at extreme stress, all without a mood meter. It differs from mood-breakdown, whose mood is a near-instant sum of current modifiers, and from memories-thoughts, which owns the event entries that can feed it.
design_levers: stress per event type and the personality scaling applied to it
decay rate toward zero and whether relief needs active coping (feasts, hobbies, vices)
level thresholds and what each level triggers
break catalog: tantrums, coping traits, personality change, death
visibility of the value, hidden as in Dwarf Fortress or shown as in Crusader Kings III
dynamics: A shared tragedy stresses many agents at once, so breaks cluster weeks or months after the event.
Breaks generate new stressors for witnesses, a reinforcing cascade, as in Dwarf Fortress tantrum spirals.
Coping traits acquired through breaks permanently change characters, turning stress history into identity.
failure_modes: Hidden stress makes breakdowns look random, since the cause may be months old.
Slow decay plus frequent stressors leaves a population chronically stressed after one disaster, with no recovery path.
Cheap relief actions such as a feast or a vice reduce stress management to a periodic chore.
Lethal stress at the top of the ladder can end a character or dynasty through bookkeeping rather than drama.
mechanics.name: Stress accumulation
open_questions: Does showing the stress value make breaks feel fair at the cost of drama, or can partial signals give warning without a meter?
Can language-model agents express accumulated stress in dialogue and behavior before a threshold break, so players see it building?
mechanics.player_experience: The player manages a slow-burning account of bad experiences rather than a moment-to-moment mood: a character can look fine while carrying stress from months ago. In Crusader Kings III this makes roleplay a resource decision, since acting against a character's traits costs stress that must later be shed; in Dwarf Fortress a fortress's past tragedies become a hidden debt that comes due.
mechanics.summary: A slow per-agent stress stock integrates negative experiences scaled by personality and, as it crosses levels, triggers breaks or lasting changes.

mechanics.definition: Structural elements form a connectivity graph rooted at grounded elements. Three update rules are common. Connectivity only: an element with no path to ground falls, as in Dwarf Fortress cave-ins and in Teardown, where disconnected voxel pieces become physics bodies. Decaying support: support propagates outward and drops by a material-specific amount per connection, and pieces past the limit collapse; Valheim shows this with a color scale from blue (grounded) to red (at the limit) while the hammer is equipped, and stone and core wood carry farther than wood. Load and stress: a physics solve computes member forces and breaks members past their strength, as in Poly Bridge. Collapse removes elements, spawns debris or rigid bodies, and re-checks dependents, which can cascade.
design_levers: propagation model: connectivity only, per-step decay, or physical stress
per-material strength, maximum span, and support loss per connection
what counts as ground or an anchor
collapse resolution: instant removal, debris, or simulated rigid bodies
visualization of support before failure
dynamics: Attackers and players target supports, turning integrity into a combat and demolition system.
Material limits shape architectural styles, such as regular pillars and stone bases in Valheim halls.
Fire, explosions, and digging couple into chained collapses.
failure_modes: Connectivity-only models let large structures stand on a few voxels; reviewers noted Teardown does not model compressive stress.
Per-step decay limits feel arbitrary when they do not match the visual mass of the structure.
Cascading collapse destroys hours of player work with no warning or undo.
Large collapses cause frame-time spikes.
mechanics.name: Structural integrity
open_questions: Can learned surrogates of finite-element stress make physically plausible load paths affordable in large player-built structures?
What collapse warnings preserve tension without making failure trivial to avoid?
mechanics.player_experience: Building with gravity in mind. Players add pillars, braces, and stronger materials, read the support overlay, and feel tension when extending a span. Collapses are spectacular, and demolition becomes a tactic.
mechanics.summary: Structures carry support values or loads propagated from the ground, and elements that lose support or exceed their limits collapse.

synergy.note: Destruction matters when removing a piece can collapse what it supported (Teardown).

mechanics.definition: Owns, per vehicle, a list of components (reactor, engines, shields, weapons, sensors, oxygen, hydraulics, individual blocks or parts), each with integrity, a capacity that depends on integrity, and a repair state. Incoming damage is routed to a component by hit location, a targeting choice, or a random draw; the component's capacity falls in steps or to zero, and the vehicle's derived abilities update at once. Repair restores integrity over time, through crew or damage-control teams, or at a dock. FTL ships are rooms holding systems whose power bars are disabled by hits until crew repair them, and players aim weapons at specific enemy systems. Elite Dangerous tracks integrity per module; Space Engineers functional blocks stop working when damaged below a threshold; Kerbal Space Program parts are destroyed by impact or overheating. Unlike wear-breakdown, damage comes from events rather than use and age; unlike injury-body-model, components are machines with capacities, not organisms with wounds and healing.
design_levers: component granularity: a few named systems, dozens of modules, or every block or part
damage routing: hit location, player-targeted subsystems, or random allocation
capacity curve: binary loss, stepped loss, or proportional degradation
repair model: crew time, consumable parts, damage-control assignments, or docking only
cascades such as fires, breaches, or power loss that spread damage to other components
dynamics: Targeting the opponent's key system first becomes a standard opening, such as disabling weapons or shields.
Damage to one component cascades into others: a lost reactor removes power, a lost oxygen system suffocates crew.
Repair crews and damage control become a resource that competes with combat roles.
failure_modes: Random allocation of critical hits ends fights on a single roll, which reads as unfair.
Fine granularity without clear status displays leaves players unsure which component failed.
Repair that is too fast or free removes the decision; repair that requires a dock makes one hit end a mission.
mechanics.name: Subsystem damage
open_questions: Can AI opponents choose subsystem targets based on a model of the player's ship and plan rather than fixed priorities?
What granularity of components keeps damage readable during real-time combat?
mechanics.player_experience: Damage is specific and tactical. Losing shields, engines, or oxygen each forces a different response, so the player triages repairs, reroutes power, and targets the enemy's weapons or shields first. A fight can turn on one lucky hit to a key system, and limping home with half a ship working is a story in itself.
mechanics.summary: A vehicle or ship is a set of named components with their own integrity, and damage to one removes its capacity, such as power, thrust, shields, or sensors, until it is repaired.

mechanics.definition: Owns a price per good per market, anchored to a base price. Each tick the rule compares demand (consumption, buy orders) with supply (production, stock, sell orders) and raises the price when demand exceeds supply and lowers it otherwise, usually within a band around the base. Common forms are a stock-based price, p = base x f(stock / target stock), and an incremental update, p += k x (demand - supply) / supply. Prices feed back into production profitability and consumption. Victoria 3 (2022) sets each good's national market price from the balance of buy orders from consumption and sell orders from production relative to a base price, scales each state's orders by its market access, and blends local and market prices for poorly connected states. Offworld Trading Company moves prices continuously with every player's purchases and sales.
design_levers: price sensitivity (gain) and the band around base price
base price per good, which sets the default value hierarchy
whether the player's own trades move prices (price impact)
smoothing, inertia, and update frequency
how far price signals propagate between markets
dynamics: High prices attract new producers whose output then pushes prices down, producing cobweb cycles.
Producers crowd into the most profitable good, so profit migrates between goods over time.
Shortages of an input propagate down production chains as price spikes.
failure_modes: High gain causes price oscillation and boom-bust cycles that players read as random.
When the player's trades do not move prices, a single arbitrage loop can be exploited indefinitely.
Tight bands make prices too sticky to signal shortages; loose bands let goods become worthless.
mechanics.name: Supply-demand pricing
open_questions: Can demand models calibrated on real market data give games more believable price dynamics without making them unreadable?
How much player price impact keeps markets responsive without enabling degenerate exploits?
mechanics.player_experience: Buy low, sell high, and watch your own trades move the market. The player spots shortages, rushes production to profit from high prices, and sees margins collapse as they and rivals flood the market. Prices become a readout of what the economy lacks.
mechanics.summary: Prices adjust to supply and demand, so scarcity raises prices and gluts lower them.

synergy.note: Price differentials are what make routes profitable; trade flattens them.

mechanics.definition: Units or outposts draw supply from sources (hubs, depots, capitals, ports) through a connected path of controlled territory, rail, roads, or sea lanes. Each tick, supply delivered falls off with distance and is capped by the weakest link; units below a supply threshold lose strength, organization, or health. Hearts of Iron IV routes supply from the capital by railway to supply hubs, with hub capacity from 15 to 35 by railway level and capped by the weakest link; supply falls off per province from the hub, and attrition starts at 35% supply or less. Unity of Command makes supply range central to its operational puzzle, and Company of Heroes yields resources only from territory connected to the player's base. Inputs: source capacity, network connectivity, distance. Outputs: per-unit supply level and attrition.
design_levers: falloff curve with distance from source
network carriers: territory, rail, roads, or sea
attrition thresholds and penalties
buffers such as stored supply or foraging
visibility of supply levels and routes
dynamics: Encirclement emerges as the main operational goal.
Infrastructure investment becomes a military priority.
Fronts stall when supply limits are hit, producing realistic operational pauses.
failure_modes: Opaque supply calculations make attrition feel arbitrary.
Supply too forgiving makes logistics irrelevant.
Supply too harsh makes offensives impossible and pins the front.
mechanics.name: Supply lines
open_questions: Could an AI opponent that reasons about supply networks produce more convincing operational play than current scripted AIs?
mechanics.player_experience: Strategy at the level of the map. Players plan advances along supply routes, pause to bring up hubs, and seek to cut enemy lines. Encircling an enemy and watching it starve is a strong, systemic win.
mechanics.summary: Remote units or outposts need a continuous connection to a supply source; cutting the connection causes attrition.

mechanics.definition: Each surface carries a coverage mask (a texture or vertex grid) storing remaining dirt, paint, or material per cell, sometimes in several layers with different hardness. The tool casts a footprint with radius, falloff, and strength, and each frame it reduces or adds coverage under the footprint, scaled by distance, angle, and tool type versus layer type. Objects report the percentage done and count as complete past a threshold. PowerWash Simulator has four nozzles with different power and spray width, dirt types (dirt, grime, lichen, moss, rust), surface-specific soaps, progress bars per object and level, and a highlight for remaining dirt. House Flipper uses the same pattern for cleaning and painting walls; Hardspace: Shipbreaker's laser cutter is a cutting variant in which cutting electrical wires or coolant pipes can cause an explosion. Inputs: tool parameters and aim. Outputs: coverage state and completion events tied to payment.
design_levers: tool footprint size, strength, and falloff
layer types and which tools or consumables work on them
completion threshold per object
remaining-coverage highlighting and other assists
texture resolution of the coverage mask
tool upgrades and their price
dynamics: Players develop efficient sweep patterns, a real coverage-path optimization.
Tool upgrades change which strategy is efficient, renewing early levels on replay.
Completion feedback rewards perfectionism, which is the core motivation loop.
failure_modes: High completion thresholds turn the last few percent into a hunt for invisible specks; PowerWash Simulator added a highlight for this.
Weak tools or huge areas make sessions drag.
Consumables with unclear benefits feel pointless; reviewers criticized PowerWash Simulator's soap system.
mechanics.name: Surface work tools
open_questions: Can generative texture models produce varied dirt and wear layouts on arbitrary scanned objects to cut level-authoring cost?
Which feedback cues sustain the relaxation loop across long sessions?
mechanics.player_experience: Calm, absorbing, visibly productive work. Players sweep a tool across grime and watch clean surface appear, chase the last stubborn patches, and feel satisfied when an object pings complete. The appeal is relaxation and order, not challenge.
mechanics.summary: The player applies a tool to surfaces to clean, paint, or strip them, and a per-surface coverage state shows visible progress toward completion.

mechanics.definition: Owns a few bounded stocks on the avatar or party, such as hunger, thirst, body temperature, fatigue, and sometimes sanity or calories. Each tick each stock falls at a base rate modified by activity, weather, and clothing; eating, drinking, resting, or standing near heat restores it. At zero or past a threshold the stock drains health, applies penalties, or kills. Don't Starve uses a default maximum hunger of 150 that drains 75 per game day, and at zero health drains 1.25 per second; The Long Dark tracks calories, body temperature, fatigue, and hunger against cold nights and weather; The Oregon Trail asks each round how much food to eat and kills the party through starvation, cold, or untreated illness. Roguelikes such as Rogue and NetHack use a food clock. Inputs are time, environment, and consumption; outputs are health drain and penalties.
design_levers: which meters exist and which are lethal versus only penalizing
base drain rates and modifiers from activity, temperature, and gear
restoration value of each consumable and its availability in the world
consequence at zero: health drain rate, penalties, or instant death
difficulty presets that scale drain and resource scarcity
dynamics: Low meters reduce the ability to gather, which accelerates decline into a death spiral.
Meters couple the avatar to weather, day-night temperature, and cooking or crafting systems.
Players build bases and routes around reliable sources of food, water, and heat.
failure_modes: Fast drain with scarce restoration forces repetitive eating and drinking that crowds out exploration.
Abundant food trivializes meters by midgame, so they become noise.
Several meters with overlapping warnings overload attention without adding decisions.
mechanics.name: Survival meters
open_questions: Can drain rates adapted by a learned player model keep survival pressure steady from early to late game without feeling rubber-banded?
mechanics.player_experience: Constant pressure to keep moving. The player plans every trip around food, water, and warmth, weighs risky exploration against returning to safety, and feels relief at a full stomach by a fire. The meters make the world feel hostile and give mundane items life-or-death value.
mechanics.summary: The avatar's bodily stocks such as hunger, thirst, warmth, and fatigue deplete over time and, if unmanaged, drain health and kill.

mechanics.definition: Owns one or more tax rates (global, by zone type, by class, or by good) and converts a tax base into revenue each accounting period, while applying a growth or satisfaction penalty that rises with the rate. In Micropolis, the SimCity engine, revenue = population x average land value / 120 x tax rate x a difficulty factor; the rate (0-20%) indexes a table that offsets all three RCI demand valves by +200 at 0%, 0 at 7%, and -600 at 20% on the easiest level, enters the citizens' problem list as rate x 10, and is subtracted from the city score. SimCity 2000 lets players set separate residential, commercial, and industrial rates. Democracy 4 ties tax policies to voter-group happiness and makes very high taxes cause evasion. Victoria 3 derives the tax base from a taxation law and lets the player set an overall tax level.
design_levers: tax base (population, land value, income, trade, goods) and how many separate rates exist
shape of the penalty curve (linear, threshold, accelerating) and where the neutral rate sits
lag between a rate change and its effect on growth or approval
avoidance responses such as evasion, emigration, or capital flight
who bears the tax and which groups react
dynamics: Revenue funds services that grow the tax base while high rates suppress growth, so a revenue-maximizing rate emerges.
Different rates by zone or class let players steer development, such as cutting industrial taxes to attract jobs.
Tax hikes during a crisis can trigger emigration that shrinks the base and deepens the deficit.
failure_modes: A fixed neutral point (Micropolis' 7%) becomes a memorized constant, so the lever is set once and forgotten.
When revenue uses the rate at the moment of collection, as in Micropolis, players can keep taxes low most of the year and raise them just before collection.
A single global rate removes distributional choices and the politics around them.
mechanics.name: Taxation
open_questions: Could AI-simulated households and firms respond to tax changes with realistic avoidance and migration, making tax design a policy puzzle rather than one slider?
How should tax effects be lagged so the tradeoff is felt without enabling raise-before-collection exploits?
mechanics.player_experience: Turning a dial between money now and growth later. The player raises taxes to fund services or pay debts, then watches demand or approval sag and searches for the rate the economy will bear.
mechanics.summary: Player-set tax rates convert economic activity into revenue at the cost of growth, happiness, or competitiveness.

claims.text: A technology tree is a directed acyclic graph; Francis Tresham's 1980 board game Civilization is generally credited with introducing it, and Sid Meier's Civilization (1991) is the iconic video game example.

Stellaris replaces a fixed tree with three semi-random research options per area, weighted by empire ethics, scientist traits, and known techs, plus rare techs and procedurally generated improvement techs.

mechanics.definition: Technologies are nodes in a directed acyclic graph; each has prerequisites, a research cost, and unlocks. State owned: which techs are researched, current research progress, and queued research. Update rule: each tick or turn, research output (from labs, scientists, or consumed science items) accumulates toward the selected tech; when it reaches the cost, the tech is researched and its unlocks apply. Variants: complete trees where everything is reachable (Civilization), branching trees with exclusive choices, and weighted random draws (Stellaris). Francis Tresham's 1980 board game Civilization is generally credited with introducing the tree, and Sid Meier's Civilization (1991) carried it into video games. Factorio consumes science packs as research input; Stellaris offers three semi-random options per research area, weighted by ethics, scientist traits, and known techs.
design_levers: graph shape: linear, branching, web, or random draws
cost curve per tier
research input: abstract points, science items, or scientists
exclusivity: mutually exclusive branches versus all reachable
repeatable infinite techs for the late game
visibility of future nodes
dynamics: Research pace couples to the economy, so economic snowballing compounds into technological leads.
Exclusive branches create faction or playstyle identity and replay value.
In factory games, science items make research a production target, linking progression to logistics throughput.
failure_modes: A dominant path that every player follows removes strategic choice.
Late-tree techs that do nothing useful leave research facilities idle; some players dismantle labs to save upkeep.
Top techs so strong that the game ends quickly once they are researched, as with the final technologies in Rise of Nations.
Fully random draws frustrate players who plan, since a needed tech may not appear.
mechanics.name: Tech tree
open_questions: Can a tech tree be generated from the simulation's own physics or chemistry so that research discovers real affordances rather than authored unlocks?
Can RL agents search tree costs and structures for balance faster than human playtesting?
mechanics.player_experience: A visible map of future capability. The player plans paths, makes long bets on branches, anticipates key unlocks, and feels progress as a chain of small upgrades toward transformative ones.
mechanics.summary: A research or unlock graph gates buildings, recipes, or abilities behind prerequisites and accumulated research.

mechanics.definition: Terrain is a height field, often with surface material and water layers. A brush raises, lowers, levels, smooths, or paints cells under the cursor; slope limits propagate the edit to neighbors, and a cost is charged per cell or per volume moved. Downstream systems read the new heights: buildability, water flow, pathing, and views. In Populous (1989) raising and lowering land is the basic divine power, used mainly to give followers flat land for houses, which grows followers and mana. SimCity 2000 and RollerCoaster Tycoon charge money for land edits. Planet Coaster uses voxel terrain that also allows tunnels and overhangs. From Dust moves sand, water, and lava as simulated materials rather than as height edits.
design_levers: brush shapes and sizes
slope limits and how edits spread to neighbors
cost per cell or per volume, and whether material must be conserved
whether terraforming is available in play or only in an editor
how water, pathing, and buildings respond to edited terrain
dynamics: In Populous, flattening land leads to more houses, more followers, and more mana for more powers, a reinforcing loop.
Coupled with hydrology, terrain edits create dams, floods, and reservoirs.
Terraforming against an opponent, such as sinking their land, turns it into a weapon.
failure_modes: Cheap unlimited terraforming flattens the map and removes terrain as a design constraint.
Edits silently break water flow or paths and cause floods or stranded buildings.
Fiddly brush controls make precise shaping tedious.
mechanics.name: Terraforming
open_questions: Can semantic terrain brushes ("carve a canyon here") backed by generative terrain models keep edits predictable?
How should material conservation be enforced so terraforming stays a resource decision rather than free sculpting?
mechanics.player_experience: Shaping the world directly. Players prepare sites, carve scenery, and sometimes wield terrain as a weapon. The pleasure is tactile and godlike; the constraint is cost and the knock-on effects on water and access.
mechanics.summary: The player raises, lowers, flattens, or repaints terrain, usually at a cost, to make land usable or to reshape water and paths.

mechanics.definition: Ground is a height field with a soft-material layer. Contacts displace material by pressure, wheel slip, and softness; the displaced height persists and changes contact and traction on later passes. In Spintires: MudRunner, according to its lead developer Pavel Zagrebelny, terrain is a regular vertex grid displaced by a height map and covered by a mud layer that artists paint, with a second higher-resolution grid for the mud; when a wheel is in mud or spins too fast, the game computes forces approximating mud physics, and mud displacement runs entirely on the GPU. SnowRunner (2020) extends the approach to snow. Many games deform terrain cosmetically, leaving tracks that do not affect physics.
design_levers: material softness and depth by terrain type
rut depth, persistence, and recovery over time
coupling strength between ruts and traction
simulation resolution and whether it runs on the GPU
how deformation is synchronized in multiplayer
dynamics: Spinning wheels dig deeper and lose traction, a stuck spiral that rewards slow throttle and winching.
Earlier vehicles' ruts change the route for convoy members that follow.
Weather that softens ground couples terrain deformation to route planning.
failure_modes: Cosmetic deformation that does not affect handling creates a mismatch between what players see and feel.
Permanent deep ruts can make a route impassable for the rest of a session.
Deformation state is large and hard to keep synchronized across networked players.
mechanics.name: Terrain deformation
open_questions: Can learned granular-material models make mud, sand, and snow respond more physically at game frame rates?
mechanics.player_experience: Struggle and patience. Players read the ground, pick lines, rock the vehicle, and winch out. Every crossing feels earned, and the track left behind tells the story of the trip.
mechanics.summary: Wheels, feet, and impacts displace soft ground such as mud and snow, and the persistent ruts change traction for later passes.

synergy.note: Ruts and mud change traction, making route reading a skill (SnowRunner).

mechanics.definition: Owns, per map region (province, county, state, star system, city), an owner, a controller, and an integration state such as core, claim, incorporated, or newly conquered, plus claims that other factions hold on it. Military presence or a completed siege sets the controller; ownership changes only through a peace settlement, inheritance, purchase, or capture rule; and a newly owned region ramps from low to full integration over time or for a price, yielding less and generating more unrest until then. Europa Universalis IV separates owner from controller, makes new provinces costly to core with administrative power, and counts uncored land toward overextension, which raises unrest. Crusader Kings III ties counties to titles and de jure claims and adds a county control value that drops after conquest. Victoria 3 incorporates states over time; Hearts of Iron IV separates core from occupied states; Stellaris takes systems by building outposts and spends influence on claims against rivals. Unlike faction-diplomacy, which owns relations between factions, this mechanic owns who holds each piece of the map.
design_levers: separation of owner and controller, and what occupation alone grants
integration path: time, a currency such as administrative power or influence, or culture and religion matching
penalties for unintegrated land: reduced output, unrest, overextension, or rebel spawns
claim types and how claims are created, fabricated, inherited, or expire
region granularity: provinces, counties, states, systems, or cities
dynamics: Conquest snowballs because new land adds resources and manpower, while integration costs and unrest apply the brake.
Claims and de jure boundaries steer wars toward historically plausible borders.
Occupation without ownership creates leverage for peace negotiations, coupling the map to war score.
failure_modes: Integration costs too low make snowballing conquest the only strategy; too high and expansion stops being worth it.
Border gore and fragmented holdings from inheritance or peace deals become tedious to manage without consolidation tools.
Players treat the map as a coloring exercise and ignore the systems that integration was meant to engage.
mechanics.name: Territorial control
open_questions: Could AI factions that reason about claims and integration costs expand in ways players read as purposeful rather than greedy?
What integration model keeps conquest consequential without becoming a waiting timer?
mechanics.player_experience: Expansion has a shape and a hangover. The player plans conquests around claims, watches borders shift as sieges complete, then spends years digesting new land before it pays off. The map itself becomes the scoreboard, and an overstretched realm with restless new provinces is a visible warning to slow down.
mechanics.summary: Map regions have an owner and a current controller; occupation flips control in war, and peace, purchase, or integration transfers ownership at a cost in time, unrest, or political currency.

mechanics.definition: Owns a set of track pieces joined end to end, each with a type (straight, curve, slope, switch, bridge, tunnel, or special element such as a loop), an entry and exit position and heading, and a cost. Construction extends an open endpoint with a piece whose entry matches it; the game checks grade and curvature limits, terrain clearance, and collisions with other structures, then charges a cost that depends on terrain (slopes, water, demolition) and piece type. Railroad Tycoon and Transport Tycoon lay track on a tile grid, with slopes, bridges, and tunnels in Transport Tycoon; RollerCoaster Tycoon builds coasters piece by piece on a tile grid by direction, height, steepness, and elements such as loops and corkscrews; Planet Coaster adds spline editing; Factorio places straight and curved rail pieces. Outputs: a track graph that vehicles traverse, used by scheduling, signaling, and ride rating. Unlike free-placement, the unit of building is a connected chain rather than a footprint; unlike road-network, it owns segment geometry and its constraints rather than building connectivity; unlike modular-assembly, the result is a path.
design_levers: grade and curve radius limits and their effect on vehicle speed
terrain cost model for slopes, water, tunnels, and demolition
piece set: fixed tiles, free splines, or both
auto-routing tools that pick a path between endpoints
special pieces such as switches, loops, lifts, and brakes
dynamics: Terrain shapes networks and rides: lines follow valleys, and coasters use hills for drops.
Junction and switch layouts couple track design to signaling and throughput.
Track geometry feeds ride ratings and train speeds, so building quality shows up in revenue.
failure_modes: Tile-locked pieces make every layout look the same; free splines without snapping make clean joins hard.
Construction controls that need many precise clicks per segment make building tedious.
Costs too low make terrain irrelevant, so lines ignore the landscape.
mechanics.name: Track laying
open_questions: Can route-finding assistants that propose track under grade and cost constraints keep the craft while removing click work?
Could generative models propose coaster layouts that hit target ratings for players to refine?
mechanics.player_experience: Drawing a line through the world under constraints. Players hunt for the gentle grade around a hill, decide whether a bridge is worth its price, and fit a coaster's drops and turns into a cramped park. A clean line that vehicles run smoothly on is a craft object players admire and share.
mechanics.summary: The player builds rail or coaster track segment by segment under grade, curvature, terrain, and cost constraints, and vehicles then run on the resulting path.

mechanics.definition: Owns a set of routes, each linking a source market to a destination market for a good, with a volume level or capacity, a transport cost or transit time, and tariffs. Each period profit per unit = destination price - source price - transport cost - tariffs; volume grows when profitable and shrinks when not, which narrows the price gap. In Victoria 3 (2022) routes start at level 1 and change level weekly mainly by profitability, purchase and sale prices are the midpoints of each market's pre- and post-trade prices, tariffs are charged per unit on the base price, sea routes depend on convoys, and each route has a fixed bureaucracy cost that replaced an earlier cap on route count. Civilization's caravans set up routes whose income depends on distance and the cities involved, and Railroad Tycoon pays for delivering goods to stations that demand them.
design_levers: how volume responds to profit (player-set, automatic growth, or capped by vehicles)
transport cost model (distance, time, convoys, ships)
tariffs, trade agreements, embargoes, and their calculation basis
fixed costs per route versus per-unit costs, which decide whether many small or few large routes win
how much information about remote prices the player gets
dynamics: Arbitrage narrows price gaps, so the most profitable routes erode over time.
Trade makes markets interdependent, so a war or blockade in one region causes shortages elsewhere.
Per-unit tariffs on base price hurt high-volume, low-margin routes most, shaping which goods are traded.
failure_modes: Static price gaps that trade does not close create permanent money loops.
With no fixed cost per route, many tiny routes become optimal and flood the interface.
Automated routes that never fail or need attention become set-and-forget income.
mechanics.name: Trade routes
open_questions: Can AI merchant agents discover and contest routes on their own, giving players competition for arbitrage instead of a static spreadsheet?
What route cost structure keeps trade decisions meaningful without micromanagement?
mechanics.player_experience: Connecting surplus to scarcity. The player finds where a good is cheap and where it is dear, opens routes, and watches the gap close as the trade succeeds. Tariffs, embargoes, and blockades make trade a lever in diplomacy and a target in war.
mechanics.summary: Goods are exchanged between settlements, regions, or foreign markets along routes with price differences, tariffs, and transit time.

mechanics.definition: Trips generated by zones or agents travel over a road network; each segment has a capacity, and travel time rises as volume approaches or exceeds it. Micropolis, the released SimCity engine, has no vehicles: a zone tries a random walk of up to 30 steps along roads until it is adjacent to a destination zone of the required type, and success adds 50 to the traffic density at saved points on the path. Density decays each scan by 34 above 200 and by 24 above 24, and is otherwise reset to zero. Cities: Skylines simulates individual vehicles on lanes. Cities: Skylines II agents choose routes by a combined cost of time, comfort, money, and behavior, spread across lanes, and can be stopped by accidents checked per segment. Inputs: trips, network capacity, route choice. Outputs: per-segment volume, travel times, and delays to services.
design_levers: capacity per lane or road type
route choice model: random walk, shortest path, or cost-based with re-routing
trip generation rate and timing
consequences: lower desirability, delayed services, or lost deliveries
stuck-vehicle handling such as despawning
dynamics: Induced demand: new capacity attracts more trips.
Congestion delays emergency services, so fires spread and crime rises.
Players build hierarchies and transit to shift demand.
failure_modes: Vehicles that crowd into one lane while parallel lanes sit empty, a common complaint about the first Cities: Skylines, produce jams that better road design cannot fix.
Despawning stuck vehicles, as the first Cities: Skylines does by default, hides real congestion problems.
Opaque route choices make traffic feel random.
mechanics.name: Traffic congestion
open_questions: Could learned driving policies trained on real traffic data make in-game congestion match real-world patterns at city scale?
What level of traffic fidelity improves design decisions rather than just spectacle?
mechanics.player_experience: Watching gridlock form. Players see jams, trace them to bad intersections or missing routes, and redesign. Congestion is the most visible symptom of a city's structure, and fixing one jam often moves it elsewhere.
mechanics.summary: Trips route over a capacitated network; volume beyond capacity raises travel time and delays services and deliveries.

mechanics.definition: Owns a genome per agent (gene list, trait set, or continuous parameters) and the reproduction operator that builds a child's genome from its parents: per-gene selection or crossover, optional dominance, and mutation with set rate and size. The genome then sets appearance, capabilities, or behavior parameters read by other systems. Creatures (1996) uses a haploid genome of about 320 genes coding receptors, reactions, and brain lobes, with crossover at gene boundaries, omissions, duplications, mutations, and genes that switch on at set ages. The Sims 2 passes appearance and personality with dominant and recessive genes; Crusader Kings III passes genetic traits; Planet Zoo genomes set lifespan, size, health, and fertility with an inbreeding penalty; Species: ALRE adds random values to numeric genes. Inputs: parent genomes, mutation parameters. Outputs: offspring traits and variation for selection or breeding.
design_levers: genome representation (discrete traits, numeric genes, structural genes)
inheritance rule (averaging, per-gene selection, dominance, linkage)
mutation rate and size
inbreeding penalties and diversity rewards
visibility of genotype versus phenotype
dynamics: Selective breeding by the player concentrates traits across generations.
With natural selection, inheritance lets populations adapt to environments.
Inbreeding in small populations produces defect clusters that force outbreeding or trade for new stock.
failure_modes: Averaging inheritance regresses everything to the mean and removes surprise.
Eugenic optimization: players breed for top traits and the system becomes a stat grind, with uncomfortable framing in human-character games.
High mutation rates produce non-viable offspring that read as broken.
Hidden genetics with no inspection make breeding feel random.
mechanics.name: Trait inheritance
open_questions: Can generative models map genomes to coherent novel appearances and behaviors rather than to a fixed set of parts?
Which inheritance models keep breeding surprising without becoming a pure stat grind?
mechanics.player_experience: Breeding becomes a long game of chance: the player pairs parents for desired traits, gambles on outcomes, and watches family resemblance and surprises appear. Lineages carry identity.
mechanics.summary: Offspring inherit traits or genes from their parents with recombination, variation, or mutation.

mechanics.definition: Owns, per trip or agent, the set of available modes (walk, bicycle, car, taxi, transit), the cost weights used to compare them, and car ownership and parking state. For each trip it computes a generalized cost per mode, such as weighted travel time plus money (fares, fuel, parking fees) plus discomfort (transfers, waiting, crowding, walking distance), and picks the cheapest mode or samples one with logit-style probabilities. Cities: Skylines II combines time, comfort, money, and behavior into its route cost, adds parking fees to driving, and has citizens compare driving, transit, and walking. Outputs are mode shares that load trips onto roads, transit lines, and paths. Unlike public-transit, which owns lines and vehicles, traffic-congestion, which owns per-segment volume, and agent-pathfinding, which searches routes within one network, this mechanic owns the choice between networks.
design_levers: weights on time, money, comfort, and transfers, and whether they vary by age, wealth, or household
car ownership rates and parking supply and pricing
deterministic cheapest-mode choice versus probabilistic choice that spreads demand
transfer and waiting penalties for transit
whether choice is recomputed per trip or fixed per agent
dynamics: Congestion raises driving cost and pushes riders to transit, a balancing loop between roads and lines.
Parking pricing becomes a policy lever that moves demand without building anything.
Dense mixed-use districts shorten trips enough that walking takes a large share, coupling zoning to traffic.
failure_modes: Sticky or opaque choice models keep transit from relieving traffic, so players stop investing in it.
Deterministic choice flips whole populations between modes after a small change, producing oscillating congestion.
Cost terms the player cannot see make empty transit lines look like a bug.
mechanics.name: Travel mode choice
open_questions: Can discrete-choice models estimated from real travel surveys be simplified enough for players to design against?
Would letting players inspect a citizen's per-mode cost breakdown make transit planning feel fair rather than random?
mechanics.player_experience: The player shapes behavior indirectly. Instead of ordering citizens onto buses, they raise parking fees, add frequency, or shorten walks to stops, then watch mode share shift in the info views. Success shows up as emptier roads; failure as a new metro line nobody rides.
mechanics.summary: Agents choose among walking, cycling, driving, and transit for each trip by comparing time, money, and comfort costs, which sets how demand splits across networks.

mechanics.definition: Each template holds a trigger predicate over state, a selection weight or mean time to happen, an immediate effect block, options with effects, and calls that schedule follow-up events with delays. Hooks such as yearly pulses, births, or deaths evaluate eligible templates and fire them. In Crusader Kings III, events do not fire on their own: on_actions, decisions, or interactions call them; an on_action can fire a list of events, weighted random_events, or the first valid one; and trigger_event schedules a follow-up such as days = { 7 14 } later, so a chain carries saved scopes and flags across months. Europa Universalis IV and Stellaris use the same Paradox script family; Frostpunk and Banished use simpler condition-fired events. Unlike a storyteller director, which paces generic incidents, chains carry authored story state forward. Inputs: state predicates and flags. Outputs: effects, flags, and scheduled events.
design_levers: trigger specificity: broad pulses versus narrow state predicates
weights, mean time to happen, and random delay ranges between links
branching factor and how many chain steps carry state forward
whether follow-ups re-check conditions so chains can fail when the world changes
cooldowns and once-per-game flags that limit repetition
dynamics: Chains link otherwise separate systems, such as health, inheritance, and war, into multi-year storylines.
Overlapping chains on the same characters produce compound situations that no single template described.
Modders extend event pools until mods conflict on shared hooks.
failure_modes: Players see the same chains every playthrough once the event pool is exhausted.
Chains ignore world changes made between links, producing contradictions such as an event about a ruler who has died.
Broad iteration in frequent pulses (the CK3 modding wiki warns against every_living_character in pulse on_actions) causes late-game slowdown.
Authored text quality caps depth, because each branch must be written by hand.
mechanics.name: Triggered event chains
open_questions: Can a language model write follow-up links conditioned on the actual state reached, keeping chains coherent with world changes?
What fraction of authored chain content could be replaced by generated text while keeping effects hand-tuned?
mechanics.player_experience: The simulation seems to notice what the player did. A rival's illness leads to a succession dispute, which leads to a war invitation. Players feel stories unfolding from their situation, learn to set up conditions for chains they want, and dread chains they recognize.
mechanics.summary: Authored event templates fire when state conditions hold, and their outcomes schedule follow-up events that chain into multi-step stories.

mechanics.definition: Owns the turn counter, the current phase, and the order of actors. Within a turn players act in sequence or submit orders simultaneously; then the world resolves production, growth, movement, combat, and events, and the next turn begins. A turn stands for a fixed span of game time, from a year in Hamurabi to two weeks in The Oregon Trail. Phased variants split a turn into stages, as in Agricola's work and harvest phases or Imperium Romanum II's taxation every third turn; simultaneous variants, called WEGO, such as Diplomacy and Combat Mission, collect all orders and then execute them together. Civilization is the canonical sequential form in strategy simulation. Inputs are player orders; outputs are the resolved world state each turn.
design_levers: game time per turn and whether it changes over the game
sequential, simultaneous, or mixed actor order
phase decomposition and which systems update in which phase
per-turn action limits or action points
time limits on turns in multiplayer
dynamics: Players optimize per-turn efficiency, making the turn itself the unit of strategy.
Batched world resolution makes chains of consequences visible as discrete steps.
Simultaneous orders create bluffing and prediction between players.
failure_modes: Late-game turns with many units or cities take long to play and process, producing micromanagement fatigue.
Sequential order gives first-mover or last-mover advantages that need compensation.
Waiting for other players' turns makes multiplayer sessions long and idle.
mechanics.name: Turn structure
open_questions: Can learned opponents that negotiate in natural language make phase-based diplomacy viable against AI rather than only humans?
mechanics.player_experience: Unlimited time to think. The player studies the state, plans, and commits, then watches the consequences resolve at once. Turns make cause and effect easy to trace and support a 'one more turn' rhythm, while simultaneous turns add the tension of predicting what others will do.
mechanics.summary: The simulation advances in discrete turns, each divided into ordered phases in which players decide and the world then resolves.

mechanics.definition: The player selects one or more units and gives explicit orders (move here, attack this, use that, stay, guard) that take precedence over the units' autonomous decision making. State owned: per-unit order queue and override flag. Update rule: when an order is present, the unit's action selection is bypassed or constrained to executing it; on completion or cancellation, autonomy resumes. Orders can be queued and may be refused if impossible. In simulation games it often sits beside autonomy: RimWorld's drafting switches a colonist from autonomous work to direct control for combat; The Sims lets the player queue actions for a Sim who otherwise acts on free will; Dwarf Fortress squads take orders while civilians do not. Strategy games make it the default control mode.
design_levers: scope: any unit, only military units, or only drafted units
how long overrides last and how autonomy resumes
order queue length and shift-queue support
whether units can refuse or delay orders based on morale or needs
group orders and formations
what autonomous behavior continues under orders, such as eating or fleeing
dynamics: A dual mode emerges: autonomy in peace and direct command in crisis, giving play a rhythm of calm and intensity.
The cost of micromanagement pushes players to improve autonomy-affecting systems such as priorities and schedules.
Override on one agent shifts load to others, revealing hidden dependencies in job systems.
failure_modes: Orders are needed constantly because autonomy is weak, turning play into micromanagement.
Drafted or ordered agents ignore needs and starve or collapse, producing deaths players blame on the interface.
Unclear return-to-autonomy rules leave units idle after an order completes.
mechanics.name: Unit commands
open_questions: Can units interpret high-level natural-language orders (hold the bridge until the medic arrives) and decompose them, and how should they report failure?
When agents have language-model reasoning, how should they negotiate or refuse orders without frustrating the player?
mechanics.player_experience: When autonomy fails or stakes are high, the player takes the wheel. Drafting colonists into a defensive line or forcing a Sim to bed is precise and reassuring, but heavy use turns agents into puppets and the player into a micromanager.
mechanics.summary: The player issues direct orders to specific units or agents, overriding their autonomous behavior.

mechanics.definition: Owns per-agent scoring weights and response curves rather than world state. Each decision cycle it enumerates candidate actions, scores each from inputs such as need levels, distance, personality, risk, and context passed through response curves and combined by product or weighted sum, then selects the top action or samples among high scorers. Dill and Mark (GDC 2010) present response curves, population distributions, and weighted random selection as a fix for the abrupt switches of if-then logic. The Sims picks the behavior that most increases happiness from object advertisements; The Sims 3 (Richard Evans) samples with a modified Boltzmann distribution whose temperature rises when a Sim is doing poorly; the Infinite Axis Utility System (Mark and Lewis, GDC 2015) multiplies normalized considerations. Inputs: candidate actions and their considerations. Outputs: the chosen action and, if exposed, a ranked list of reasons.
design_levers: response curve shape per consideration
combination rule (product, sum, max) and normalization
selection rule: argmax, random among the top N, or softmax with a temperature
inertia or commitment bonus that prevents switching between close options
per-agent personality weights
dynamics: Priorities emerge from scores rather than authored order, so new situations get plausible, unscripted responses.
Coupled with needs decay, agents cycle through activities in rhythms that read as routines.
Small weight changes ripple across a population, so balance patches visibly change agent culture.
failure_modes: Dithering: two actions with close scores alternate, so agents start and abandon tasks.
One consideration dominates the product or sum, and agents ignore everything else.
Choices are hard to explain because each score is the product of many curves, so players see randomness.
Weight tuning grows with the number of actions times considerations and resists local fixes.
mechanics.name: Utility action selection
open_questions: Can language-model agents propose candidate actions that a utility layer then scores, combining open-ended options with predictable tuning?
Can scoring functions learned from player-labeled preferences replace hand-built response curves?
mechanics.player_experience: Agents look like they are weighing options: they handle the urgent thing first but sometimes surprise. The player steers them indirectly by changing inputs such as needs, objects, and priorities, and reads odd choices as personality.
mechanics.summary: Agents choose actions by scoring options against needs and context, then picking the highest or sampling among high scores.

mechanics.definition: Owns a time scale, paused or one of several multipliers, and the rule that converts real time into simulation ticks. At higher speeds the loop runs more ticks per real second up to hardware limits; while paused no ticks run but the player can still give orders. Some games pause or slow automatically on events. RimWorld runs 60 ticks per second at normal speed and multiplies that by 3, 6, or 15, the last only in development mode, and runs as close to the target as the machine allows; SimCity and Paradox grand strategy games offer pause and several speeds; flight simulators call it time compression. Inputs are the player's speed choice and event triggers; outputs are the tick rate of every other system.
design_levers: number of speeds and their multipliers
whether orders can be given while paused
auto-pause and auto-slowdown triggers, such as raids or letters
speed restrictions in multiplayer or during events
whether higher speeds change simulation fidelity, such as larger time steps
dynamics: Players alternate between paused planning and fast-forward waiting, creating a two-tempo play pattern.
Fast-forward exposes the compute cost of every other system, making simulation performance a gameplay issue.
Auto-pause rules decide which events players notice.
failure_modes: High speeds the hardware cannot sustain silently run slower than shown, so late-game fast-forward feels broken.
Larger time steps at high speed can destabilize physics or give different outcomes than normal speed.
Multiplayer games must reconcile players' speed preferences, often by host control or voting.
mechanics.name: Pause and speed control
open_questions: Can learned surrogate simulators let players skip long quiet stretches without running full-fidelity ticks?
mechanics.player_experience: Control over attention. The player slows down or pauses for crises and detailed orders, then fast-forwards through quiet stretches such as waiting for crops or construction. Pause makes real-time games playable at a thoughtful pace, and fast-forward removes dead time.
mechanics.summary: The player pauses the simulation and switches between speed multipliers, trading attention against elapsed game time.

mechanics.definition: The vehicle state holds the chassis rigid body, wheel angular speeds, suspension compression, engine speed, gear, and often tire temperature and wear. Each physics step routes engine torque through the drivetrain, computes each tire's longitudinal and lateral force from slip ratio, slip angle, and vertical load, applies suspension forces that transfer weight under braking, acceleration, and cornering, and integrates. A common tire model is Hans Pacejka's semi-empirical Magic Formula, which fits force against slip as y = D sin(C arctan(Bx - E(Bx - arctan Bx))). Simulators such as iRacing and Gran Turismo use detailed tire and suspension models; arcade racers simplify grip into tunable curves. Assists such as ABS and traction control act on the same quantities.
design_levers: tire model fidelity: simple grip curve to full Magic Formula
driving assists and their strength
physics step rate relative to frame rate
setup parameters exposed to the player
surface grip by material and weather
force feedback and camera cues that communicate grip
dynamics: Setup choices create a tuning meta per track and car.
Tire wear and temperature create race strategy over a stint.
Changing weather and surfaces force mid-race adaptation.
failure_modes: Grip that falls off too sharply produces snap oversteer that feels unfair.
Tire models become unstable at very low speeds, causing jitter at standstill.
Too little detail feels like ice skating; too much excludes players without wheels.
Physics tied to frame rate makes handling change with performance.
mechanics.name: Vehicle dynamics
open_questions: Can tire models learned from real telemetry replace hand-fitted coefficients for each car?
mechanics.player_experience: Feel and control. Players sense grip through the screen or wheel, learn to balance the car at the limit, and tinker with setups. Mastery is slow and physical, and small improvements feel large.
mechanics.summary: Tire, suspension, drivetrain, and weight-transfer models compute vehicle handling from forces at each wheel.

mechanics.definition: Each vehicle holds an order list: an ordered sequence of stops, each with load and unload rules and optional wait conditions. The vehicle travels to each stop in turn, applies its rules, and continues. OpenTTD offers full load of any or all cargo, unload, transfer with partial payment for feeder services, no loading, go-via waypoints, timetables, conditional jumps, and shared orders across vehicles. Transport Tycoon pays by delivery time, distance, and quantity, so mail must be fast while coal tolerates long routes. Factorio train schedules use wait conditions such as full cargo, inactivity, or circuit signals. Inputs: orders, vehicles, cargo at stops. Outputs: cargo movement, revenue, and station service frequency.
design_levers: available order types and wait conditions
payment model by distance, time, and cargo type
shared orders and fleet management tools
vehicle capacity, speed, and reliability
station ratings that respond to service frequency
dynamics: Feeder and trunk networks emerge from transfer orders.
Station competition between companies or players shifts cargo flows.
Fleet growth eventually saturates track or roads, coupling routing to signaling and congestion.
failure_modes: Full-load orders at low-supply stations park vehicles forever.
Complex order systems without templates make fleet changes tedious.
Revenue models that ignore time make every route identical.
mechanics.name: Vehicle routes and schedules
open_questions: Could natural-language order entry ("keep this mine's output moving to the steel mill") replace order lists without losing player control?
mechanics.player_experience: Programming a fleet. Players design routes, tune load rules, and watch vehicles run. Well-tuned routes make money unattended; badly tuned ones leave vehicles waiting at empty stations.
mechanics.summary: Vehicles are assigned ordered stops with load and unload rules to move goods or passengers between nodes.

mechanics.definition: The map is a stack of layers indexed by depth or named by function. Each layer holds its own grid, and cross-layer rules link them: stairs and ramps for movement, support from below, fluids and objects falling through openings, and utilities in a hidden layer serving the surface tiles above. Dwarf Fortress models a full 3D map of z-levels where dwarves dig down, build stairs and channels, and water and magma flow downward through openings. SimCity 2000 adds an underground view for water pipes and subways under the surface grid. Cities: Skylines places metro tunnels and pipes underground, and Factorio: Space Age adds elevated rails over ground tracks. State: per-layer grids plus inter-layer links; update: per-layer rules plus transfer rules at the links.
design_levers: number of layers and whether they are uniform or functionally distinct
what crosses layers: movement, fluids, support, light, utilities
visibility tools: cutaways, layer toggles, isometric views
cost and hazard gradient with depth
dynamics: Digging into water or magma floods layers below or above, a classic Dwarf Fortress disaster.
Vertical separation lets transit and utilities cross without conflicts, relieving surface congestion.
Defenses gain a vertical dimension through chokepoints, drops, and layered walls.
failure_modes: Legibility collapses when players must mentally stack many layers; Dwarf Fortress players used third-party visualizers to see their fortresses in 3D.
A utility layer that mirrors the surface grid becomes a chore with no decisions of its own.
Pathfinding and fluid updates across many layers become a major performance cost.
mechanics.name: Vertical layers
open_questions: Can automatic camera and cutaway selection make deep 3D colonies as legible as a single-layer map?
mechanics.player_experience: Depth and hidden infrastructure. Players dig toward risk and reward, route utilities out of sight, and switch camera layers to manage what they cannot see at once.
mechanics.summary: The world has stacked layers such as z-levels, floors, or underground networks, and rules connect what happens between them.

mechanics.definition: A generator periodically picks a requester, a template (fetch an item, deliver a gift, clear pests, make a visit), and parameters drawn from current state, such as an item in season or a nearby location. It posts the request with a reward, often relationship points or money, and a deadline. Completing it applies the reward; expiry may cost relationship. Stardew Valley's Help Wanted board posts item delivery and gathering requests from villagers; Skyrim's radiant quests fill templates with locations and targets; Animal Crossing villagers ask small favors; Mount and Blade lords issue procedural tasks. Inputs: requester state, inventory and season, relationship. Outputs: posted tasks and reward deltas.
design_levers: template set and how parameters bind to live state
posting frequency and number of concurrent requests
reward type and size relative to effort
deadlines and penalties for expiry
requester selection by need, relationship, or location
dynamics: Requests pull players across map areas and seasonal resources they would otherwise skip.
Rewards in relationship points couple requests to romance and social progression.
When requests read live scarcity, they double as a signal of what the economy lacks.
failure_modes: Template repetition makes requests read as generic chores; radiant quests in Skyrim drew this criticism.
Requests that ignore state ask for impossible items or locations already cleared.
Low rewards teach players to ignore the system entirely.
mechanics.name: Villager requests
open_questions: Can requests generated from a character's actual needs and memories, with language-model dialogue, avoid template fatigue?
What request rate keeps them meaningful without crowding out self-directed play?
mechanics.player_experience: A light stream of small goals that gives daily play direction and makes characters feel like they have needs. Requests nudge players toward activities they might skip and reward them with friendship. Players learn which requests are worth it and ignore the rest.
mechanics.summary: Characters generate small requests or quests from templates whose parameters are filled from simulation state, with rewards and deadlines.

mechanics.definition: The world is stored as voxels with a material per cell, sometimes in several separate volumes. Tools, explosions, and fire remove or convert voxels; the engine then recomputes connectivity, and pieces cut loose either become rigid bodies or stay in place. In Teardown every level is built from destructible voxels; each voxel's material comes from an 8-bit palette setting color, roughness, emissiveness, reflectivity, and physical type; the world is split into several voxel volumes; and the engine does not model compressive stress. Minecraft breaks blocks after a mining time set by tool and material, and only some blocks, such as sand and gravel, fall when unsupported. Outputs are the edited world, debris bodies, and new paths.
design_levers: voxel size relative to the player
material hardness and which tools break which materials
connectivity and support rules for loose pieces
debris lifetime and cleanup
fire and explosion coupling
unbreakable materials that preserve level structure
dynamics: Players cut their own routes, turning levels into planning puzzles, as in Teardown's heist missions.
Fire and collapses chain through flammable and weakened structures.
Persistent edits accumulate, so the world reflects a session's history.
failure_modes: Level design is hard because walls and doors cannot block players; Teardown relied on elevation, distance, water, and unbreakable objects.
Synchronizing voxel physics over a network is hard; Teardown's team originally judged multiplayer infeasible, and co-op arrived only in a 2026 update.
Structures stand on implausibly little support when only connectivity is checked.
Destruction at scale caps performance and map size.
mechanics.name: Voxel destruction
open_questions: Can generative models author voxel levels whose structure holds up to arbitrary destruction?
Can learned fracture models give voxel destruction plausible stress without full physical simulation?
mechanics.player_experience: Total freedom of route. Any wall can become a door, so players plan paths through buildings and enjoy demolition for its own sake. The world remembers what they broke.
mechanics.summary: The world is built from small destructible units that can be removed, broken loose, and burned anywhere.

mechanics.definition: Each service building periodically spawns a walker that follows roads; as it passes, it writes a coverage value to nearby houses, which decays over time until the next visit. In Caesar III, as reproduced by the Julius reimplementation, a roaming walker first heads for a road point about 8 tiles out in a cardinal direction that rotates with each spawn, then wanders, turning pseudo-randomly at intersections and ending its walk at dead ends. Culture, health, and religion walkers set a per-service house value to 96, which decays by 1 on each periodic update; prefects reset fire risk to zero and engineers reset collapse risk to zero. Pharaoh and Zeus keep the model, and Pharaoh added roadblocks that turn roaming walkers back; Augustus, a Julius fork, brings roadblocks to Caesar III. Inputs: building location, road network, random turns. Outputs: per-house coverage values that gate housing evolution and prevent fires or collapses.
design_levers: walker roaming range and spawn interval
turn rule at intersections: random, biased, or destination-based
coverage radius around the walker and decay rate on houses
roadblocks or other routing controls
number of walker types and services per type
dynamics: Standard block layouts (looped housing blocks with services inside) become community conventions.
Coverage gaps produce local fires and collapses that spread.
Road changes can suddenly strand houses by changing walker routes.
failure_modes: Randomness that leaves some houses uncovered causes devolve-evolve flicker.
Walker logic that needs community analysis to understand frustrates players.
Too many walker types multiply layout constraints until blocks become formulaic.
mechanics.name: Walker service delivery
open_questions: Would walkers with learned or goal-driven routes make coverage more legible or less?
mechanics.player_experience: Designing for wanderers. Players build looping road blocks so walkers cover the right houses, use roadblocks where available, and watch for houses that a walker never reaches. Knowing that coverage depends on chance makes layout feel like guiding a crowd.
mechanics.summary: Services are delivered by agents walking routes from their building, so coverage depends on where walkers actually go.

mechanics.definition: Owns, for each active war, a score per side (or a shared balance) and the list of war goals, plus a menu of peace terms with a cost in score. Each update, battles won, regions occupied, and time spent holding the war goal add score, and casualties and occupation add exhaustion. A peace offer is accepted when its total cost is within the winner's score or when the loser's exhaustion or support crosses a capitulation threshold; otherwise the AI weighs score against demands. Europa Universalis IV prices each demand (provinces, gold, vassalage) in war score. Crusader Kings III lets an attacker enforce the war goal at full war score and allows white peace. Victoria 3 tracks war support that falls with exhaustion until a side capitulates. Hearts of Iron IV holds a peace conference in which winners spend points on demands in turns. In Stellaris a side at maximum war exhaustion can be forced into a status quo peace. Unlike faction-diplomacy, which decides whether factions go to war, this mechanic owns how a war ends and what the winner may take.
design_levers: score sources and their weights: battles, occupation, blockades, holding the war goal
cost table for each peace term, and whether costs scale with the target's size
exhaustion accumulation and its domestic effects such as unrest or lower production
capitulation or forced-peace thresholds, and whether third parties join the settlement
truce length after peace
dynamics: Players carry out limited wars that take exactly what the score allows, then wait out the truce and return.
Exhaustion couples military campaigns to stability and the economy, so long wars bleed the home front.
Multi-party peace conferences produce partitions that set up later conflicts.
failure_modes: Score dominated by occupation rewards sieging empty land over defeating armies.
AI that refuses reasonable terms because of hidden acceptance factors makes wars drag on.
Capitulation thresholds that trigger too early end wars before the strategic situation is resolved.
mechanics.name: War score and peace terms
open_questions: Can language-model negotiators bargain over peace terms in ways players find legible and hard to exploit?
Would score models that weigh strategic outcomes rather than counts of occupied regions produce more plausible peace deals?
mechanics.player_experience: Wars become negotiations with a running tally. The player fights for score as much as for ground, deciding when a battle or a siege is worth the cost and when to cash in. Bargaining over which provinces fit within the score turns the end of a war into a planning problem, and exhaustion forces the question of whether to sue for peace before the home front breaks.
mechanics.summary: Each war tracks a score or exhaustion level from battles, occupation, and war goals, and that value caps what a peace settlement can demand or forces capitulation.

mechanics.definition: Each asset holds a condition or reliability stock. Each update it decays by a base rate scaled by usage, age, and environment, and a breakdown is drawn with probability that rises as condition falls. A broken asset stops or malfunctions until a repair job, often done by a maintenance agent, restores it. In RollerCoaster Tycoon 2 (as reimplemented in OpenRCT2), reliability starts at 100% and drops every 256 ticks by the ride's unreliability factor plus an age penalty that grows from one-eighth of that factor in year one to double after eight years; breakdown types are weighted, brake failure is likelier in rain, players set inspection intervals for mechanics, and a repair restores reliability in proportion to the deficit. Transport Tycoon vehicles lose reliability between depot services; Theme Hospital machines explode if handymen do not repair them. Per-use item durability, as in Minecraft tools, is a variant without maintenance.
design_levers: decay rate per asset class and its usage and weather modifiers
age penalty curve that forces eventual replacement
breakdown probability as a function of condition, and the menu of breakdown types and severities
maintenance interval, labor required, and repair restoration amount
repair versus replacement cost
a global breakdown setting (off, reduced, normal)
dynamics: Aging fleets and rides create replacement waves that strain budgets years after the original build-out.
Mechanic coverage becomes a routing and staffing problem coupled to park or network layout.
Breakdowns create service queues and satisfaction drops that spread to nearby systems.
failure_modes: Maintenance with no tradeoffs becomes a chore; OpenTTD exposes a setting to reduce or disable breakdowns, and many players use it.
Too few maintenance workers lets breakdowns pile up faster than repairs, a spiral that is hard to diagnose.
