Hidden condition values make breakdowns feel random even when the player could have prevented them.
mechanics.name: Wear and breakdown
open_questions: Can predictive maintenance tools that forecast failure from condition history become part of play instead of a hidden optimization?
When does per-use durability add decisions rather than inventory chores?
mechanics.player_experience: A steady background of upkeep decisions. The player schedules inspections, staffs mechanics, and decides when an aging asset should be replaced instead of repaired. Breakdowns are visible interruptions with queues of angry customers or stalled trains.
mechanics.summary: Assets lose condition with use and age, breakdown risk rises as condition falls, and maintenance or repair restores it.

mechanics.definition: Owns a current weather state, and sometimes a forecast, drawn each day or interval from season-dependent probabilities or evolved as a Markov chain or noise field across the map. The state sets modifiers other systems read: rain waters crops or puts out fire, storms bring lightning that damages things, cold lowers body temperature, wind changes travel or spread, and fog cuts visibility. Stardew Valley picks daily weather, shows tomorrow's forecast on the TV, never rains in winter without a Rain Totem, and lets lightning destroy crops unless lightning rods intercept it; The Long Dark's blizzards and cold nights drive its survival loop; Microsoft Flight Simulator 2020 can stream real-world weather. Inputs are season, location, and random draws; outputs are condition flags and values such as temperature and wind.
design_levers: set of weather states and their transition probabilities by season and region
duration and spatial extent of weather events
which systems each state modifies and by how much
forecast availability and accuracy
protection tools: shelter, lightning rods, clothing, irrigation
dynamics: Weather couples many systems at once: crops, fire, travel, mood, and body temperature.
Forecasts turn weather from noise into a planning input, rewarding flexible schedules.
Rare extreme weather becomes a memorable event that players prepare for.
failure_modes: Purely cosmetic weather costs effects budget without changing decisions.
Severe weather with no forecast or counterplay feels like an unfair random penalty.
Weather rolled independently each day can flip implausibly between extremes.
mechanics.name: Weather
open_questions: Can learned global weather models supply spatially coherent, plausible weather for procedural worlds at low runtime cost?
mechanics.player_experience: Adapting plans to conditions outside the player's control. The player checks the forecast, moves tasks indoors on stormy days, waits out a blizzard, or takes advantage of rain. Weather makes days feel different and gives the world a mood.
mechanics.summary: Weather states such as rain, storms, snow, wind, and temperature change over time and modify activities and other systems.

mechanics.definition: Owns a matrix of agents by job types holding enabled flags or priority numbers, plus a fixed ordering of job types. When an agent is idle it scans job types in priority order, breaking ties by column order, and takes an available job of the highest priority it can do, usually the nearest. RimWorld's work tab has a standard mode (checkmarks, columns further left more important) and a manual mode with priorities 1 (highest) to 4; all available work at one priority is done before the next, blank cells are never done, incapable work types are excluded, and allowed areas restrict where jobs are taken. Dwarf Fortress uses per-dwarf labor toggles, and Oxygen Not Included combines per-duplicant errand priorities with 1-9 priorities on individual buildings. Inputs: the job queue, skills, distances. Outputs: who does what, and how fast the group responds to new work.
design_levers: granularity of job types
number of priority levels and tie-break rules
global agent-by-type priorities versus per-task or per-building overrides
interaction with distance: nearest job first versus highest priority first
automatic suggestions based on skill
dynamics: Fixing one starved job type exposes the next bottleneck, so the table evolves as the group grows.
Priorities aligned with skills create specialists, which reinforces skill gaps.
Emergencies force temporary reshuffles or direct control, producing spikes of micromanagement.
failure_modes: Priority inversion: an agent hauls a distant item at priority 1 while a patient bleeds, because all priority-1 work is done before the next level.
Large matrices become spreadsheet management that players solve once with a template and stop engaging with.
Poor tie-breaking sends agents across the map for low-value tasks.
Hidden ordering within a job type surprises players.
mechanics.name: Work priorities
open_questions: Can a manager agent translate high-level intents (keep everyone fed, prioritize medicine) into the priority table and explain its settings?
Does automatic assignment remove the managerial decision or only the spreadsheet tedium?
mechanics.player_experience: The player acts as a manager, matching people to jobs by skill and interest, then debugging the table when hauling never happens or the doctor is busy cooking. The table is where strategy is expressed without micromanaging each task.
mechanics.summary: The player sets which agents do which job types in what order, and agents self-assign from that priority table.

mechanics.definition: The player paints a land-use type, often with density, onto tiles or lots. A zone places nothing by itself. Each update the simulation checks zoned lots and grows, upgrades, downgrades, or abandons buildings based on demand, access, utilities, services, pollution, crime, and nearby uses. In SimCity (1989) players zone residential, commercial, and industrial land, and the Sims choose what to build and upgrade based on traffic, power, crime, and proximity to other buildings, so homes next to a power plant seldom reach the highest grade. Cities: Skylines grows buildings in low- and high-density zones along roads. Games without zoning, such as Anno, have the player place every house directly. State: zone type per tile plus building level per lot.
design_levers: zone categories and density tiers
development rule: growth probability, thresholds, and upgrade conditions
hard requirements such as road access, power, and water
lot size and shape rules
abandonment and decline rules
whether the player can also place specific buildings directly
dynamics: City form emerges from the interaction of zones, transport, and land value rather than from direct design.
Nuisance uses push residential away, producing segregated districts and commute traffic.
Successful zones raise demand and land value, which invites more zoning, a growth loop until services saturate.
failure_modes: Zones fail to develop with no visible reason, forcing players to hunt through overlays and demand meters.
Cheap zoning paint encourages over-zoning, leaving large empty tracts.
Uniform growth rules produce monotonous cities with little local character.
mechanics.name: Zoning
open_questions: Can LLM-driven developer agents make zoned growth explain itself and vary by local character?
Can generated building assets end the repetition of growable buildings across a large city?
mechanics.player_experience: Indirect control. Players paint intent and watch a city grow into it, like gardening. The main skill is diagnosing why a zone stalls or decays and fixing the conditions rather than the buildings.
mechanics.summary: The player paints land-use zones, and the simulation decides whether and what to build, upgrade, or abandon on each zoned lot.

opportunities.design_sketch: The player appoints an envoy with a mandate (export grain, import steel, never sell land). Envoys meet other envoys in a shared hub, negotiate deals constrained by mandates, and report back with transcripts and outcomes the player can ratify.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Store page or documentation describing autonomous AI envoys acting between players.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A released game will let players' AI representatives trade or negotiate with other players' worlds asynchronously.

key_risks: Agents exploited by adversarial players.
Mandate violations create disputes.
Server cost of agent negotiation.
opportunities.name: Agent ambassadors between player worlds
opportunities.summary: Let each player's simulation send language-agent representatives that trade and negotiate with other players' worlds while they are offline.
opportunities.thesis: Asynchronous shared regions (SimCity 2013) and visits (Animal Crossing) connect players thinly because the other player is absent. Agents that represent a player's interests, constrained by the player's standing instructions, can conduct trade and diplomacy between worlds asynchronously, turning a set of single-player games into a living network.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Run 100 simulated player worlds with envoy agents under mandates for 30 days; measure mandate violations, trade volume, and player-rated fairness in a pilot. Success: zero hard mandate violations and positive fairness ratings.

opportunities.design_sketch: Each market has a population of agent traders with budgets, risk profiles, and information limits matching human traders, operating under the same order-book rules. Their share of volume is capped and published. Designers tune agent populations to target liquidity and volatility bands.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Developer announcement or documentation of AI traders in a player-driven market.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A persistent online game will announce AI market participants calibrated to player behavior.

key_risks: Players perceive bots as unfair competition.
Agents can be exploited for arbitrage.
Calibration drift as the human population changes.
opportunities.name: AI liquidity in player markets
opportunities.summary: Keep player-driven markets liquid on small servers with model-driven traders whose behavior is calibrated to human trading and constrained by market rules.
opportunities.thesis: Player-driven economies need large populations; EVE Online works because it has them, and smaller persistent worlds stagnate. Agents calibrated to human trading behavior, and analyzed with mean-field methods for stability, can supply liquidity and price discovery without dominating. Mechanism design keeps them from front-running humans.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Simulate a 200-player market with and without calibrated agents using logged order data from a public game economy; measure spread, depth, volatility, and human profit share. Success: tighter spreads and lower volatility with human profit share unchanged within 5 percent.

opportunities.design_sketch: A bottleneck lens colors every producer by how much one more unit of it would raise the selected output, and a sentence explains the top constraint ('circuits are limited by copper cable, which is starved because the smelter column shares a belt with iron'). Clicking jumps to the machine.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Shipped feature described in patch notes or developer blog of a released title or official mod tool.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A factory or city-building game will ship a feature that identifies the binding constraint in the player's production network by simulation sensitivity rather than static ratio display.

key_risks: Players who enjoy diagnosis lose the puzzle; must be optional or costly.
Nonlinear buffers make one-step sensitivity misleading.
Explanations wrong in edge cases erode trust.
opportunities.name: Bottleneck explainer for production networks
opportunities.summary: Explain where and why a production network is starved or blocked by combining sensitivity analysis of the actual simulation with grounded language explanations.
opportunities.thesis: No technique in the dataset is linked to production chains, yet the mechanic's main documented failure is diagnosis: starvation far upstream is hard to see, so players blame the wrong building. Differentiable or finite-difference sensitivity of output to each machine, buffer, and route identifies the binding constraint exactly; a constrained language layer turns that into a short explanation with links to the machines involved. The same tool supports designers checking recipe balance.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Implement sensitivity analysis over a factory prototype's production graph and test whether players fix an injected bottleneck faster with the lens. Success: 50 percent faster fixes with no drop in reported satisfaction among experienced players when the lens is optional.

opportunities.design_sketch: Before enacting a policy the player opens Preview: the game forks 32 to 256 copies from the current tick with stochastic seeds, fast-forwards each one in-game year on spare cores (or a learned surrogate), and shows fan charts for key indicators plus the two most divergent futures as short replays. Preview costs an in-game resource so it remains a decision.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Store page, patch notes, or developer talk describing multi-run forward simulation of the live game state shown to players.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: At least one commercial city builder, colony sim, or grand strategy game will ship a feature that simulates multiple stochastic futures of the player's current state before a decision.

key_risks: Previews reveal hidden randomness and can make play feel solved.
Simulations with large state may not fork cheaply on consumer hardware.
Surrogate predictions that disagree with the real run break trust.
opportunities.name: Branch preview of policy futures
opportunities.summary: Fork the simulation in the background and show the player likely futures of a decision before committing, using parallel or surrogate simulation.
opportunities.thesis: Forecasting in shipped games is shallow: a runway counter, a weather icon, a predicted approval delta. Accelerated and learned simulators make it cheap to run many short futures of the actual game state. Showing a distribution of outcomes for a pending law, budget, or layout change turns opaque coupling into a visible tradeoff and makes long feedback delays playable. Deterministic, event-sourced simulations can fork from any tick, so the preview runs the real rules rather than a hand-built predictor.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Take a deterministic city or colony prototype, implement state snapshot plus N-way fork, and measure fork-and-simulate cost for one in-game year at mid-game scale. Playtest with preview off and on; measure decision regret (outcome versus best available) and session length. Success: preview of 64 branches under 5 seconds on a mid-range PC and a measurable drop in regret without lower engagement.

opportunities.design_sketch: A contagion sim offers a 'calibrated scenario' mode where parameters come from posterior distributions fitted to historical outbreaks. Outcomes show credible intervals; a fit report explains what data the model matches and where it is unreliable.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Release notes or paper accompanying a playable simulation that reports calibration method and fit.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A serious-game or educational simulation will publish posterior-calibrated parameters with fit metrics as part of its release.

key_risks: Users over-trust calibrated outputs.
Data availability limits domains.
Calibration may reduce play value.
opportunities.name: Calibrated serious simulations
opportunities.summary: Use simulation-based inference and differentiable simulators to calibrate game-grade models of epidemics, traffic, and markets to real data, with published fit metrics.
opportunities.thesis: Plague Inc. and Rebel Inc. are used in classrooms and briefings despite stylized models. Simulation-based inference and differentiable simulation make it practical to fit agent-based and compartment models to observed data and quantify uncertainty. Shipping calibrated parameter sets with published fit metrics lets game interfaces carry real insight while keeping play.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Fit a game-grade SIR network model to a public historical outbreak with simulation-based inference and report posterior predictive coverage. Success: 90 percent interval coverage on held-out weeks.

opportunities.design_sketch: A query box and a right-click 'why?' on any entity. The answer is three to six sentences, each linked to log events the player can jump to on the timeline, plus a small causal graph. Answers that cannot be grounded say so. Advisors use the same pipeline proactively when a key indicator crosses a threshold.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Official release notes or store page describing a player-facing feature that answers causal questions about the player's own game state in natural language.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A simulation or strategy title in Steam's top 100 by concurrent players will ship a natural-language why-query grounded in game state.

key_risks: Ungrounded but fluent answers teach players wrong models of the system.
Event logs in shipped engines often lack cause links; instrumenting them is real work.
Explanations can make optimal play too easy, flattening difficulty.
opportunities.name: Why-query over the simulation log
opportunities.summary: Let players ask why something happened and answer from the simulation's own event log, making deep systemic games legible without simplifying them.
opportunities.thesis: The strongest constraint on simulation depth has been legibility: players abandon systems they cannot diagnose, so designers cap coupling. Overlays and causal tooltips help with current values but not with histories ('why did the hospital close?'). If the simulation records an event log with causes, a language model can retrieve the relevant chain and narrate it with citations to specific events, and a constrained output format can force every claim to point at a logged record. This turns the event log, which many engines already keep for replays and debugging, into a player-facing explanation layer.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Instrument an open-source simulation (a city or colony sim) to log events with parent-cause ids. Give two player groups the same failing save; one gets the why-query. Measure time to correct diagnosis and the share of answer sentences whose cited events actually support them (human audit). Success: 40 percent faster diagnosis with at least 95 percent supported sentences.

opportunities.design_sketch: Designers write 200 event templates with preconditions, effects, and tone notes. At build time or runtime, a generator instantiates variants that reference specific characters, places, and history from the save, emits schema-valid events, and passes them through a validator that rejects anything whose effects violate invariants. Generated events are tagged so players can filter them.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Steam AI disclosure or developer documentation describing runtime-generated events in a released title.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A grand strategy, life sim, or narrative management game will ship runtime-generated events constrained by an event schema, disclosed on its Steam page.

key_risks: Generated text quality below authored text lowers perceived quality.
Disclosure and player backlash against AI-generated writing.
Validation catches logic errors but not tone errors.
opportunities.name: Content-elastic event systems
opportunities.summary: Remove the authoring ceiling on event chains, requests, and dilemmas by generating schema-constrained variants from designer templates and validating them against game state.
opportunities.thesis: Event chains, villager requests, and dilemma cards are capped by writing budgets: players exhaust the deck and recognize repeats. Language models can generate variants, but unconstrained text breaks game logic. Templates with typed slots, constrained decoding into the event schema, and automated checks against preconditions let a small team ship a deck that keeps producing valid, state-aware events.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Take 50 authored events from an existing design, generate 500 variants, have blind raters compare authored and generated events on quality, and run a validator on every variant. Success: generated events rated within 0.5 points of authored ones with 99 percent passing validation.

opportunities.design_sketch: Each candidate incident from the authored deck is scored on threat budget plus a narrative score: which characters it involves, whether it resolves or escalates an open thread, and whether it pays off a setup. The chosen incident is logged with the narrative reason, readable in the chronicle.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Developer documentation describing model-based narrative scoring in event selection.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A colony sim or survival management game will ship an event director that uses a language model to evaluate narrative state when choosing authored events.

key_risks: Players perceive arc-shaped events as rigged.
Narrative scoring adds latency at incident time.
Arcs can repeat across runs if scoring is too deterministic.
opportunities.name: Drama-aware storyteller
opportunities.summary: A storyteller that models characters' arcs and relationships, not only threat budgets, choosing authored incidents that create meaningful stakes for specific colonists.
opportunities.thesis: RimWorld's storytellers select incidents mostly by threat budget and timing. They create tension but not arcs: they do not know that two colonists are estranged siblings or that the doctor is the colony's only hope. A model that reads relationship and memory state can score candidate incidents by narrative relevance while the incidents themselves stay authored and rules-bound, adding arc awareness without surrendering control to generation.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Add narrative scoring to an incident deck in a colony prototype; run blind playthroughs and ask players to recount their run a week later. Success: players recall more named characters and causal links with the narrative storyteller.

opportunities.design_sketch: Clicking a memory in a colonist's inspector plays a few seconds of generated footage conditioned on the logged event and the colonist's mood. Rumors render with distortions proportional to how many retellings they passed through. Ruins found in worldgen offer a short generated vision of their past from history-generation records.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Store page, trailer, or patch notes describing generated memory or history visualizations.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A shipped game will use a generative video or world model to show character memories or in-world histories.

key_risks: Generation latency breaks the inspection flow.
Generated imagery of violent events needs content controls.
Players may read subjective views as ground truth.
opportunities.name: Generated dream and replay views
opportunities.summary: Use generative world models for non-authoritative views such as memories, rumors, and alternate histories, where drift is acceptable and variety is the point.
opportunities.thesis: The weaknesses of generative world models (short consistency horizon, no exact state) disqualify them as engines but suit a different role: showing things that are supposed to be subjective. A colonist's memory, a rumor that changed in the telling, a forecast that might not happen, or the history of a ruin are views where approximation reads as character rather than bug.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Prototype generated memory clips from 50 logged events in a colony sim using an available video model; measure generation time and ask players whether clips increased attachment. Success: under 10 seconds per clip and a majority reporting increased attachment.

opportunities.design_sketch: Developers use a runtime where every state change, including those decided by a model, is an event with inputs, outputs, and causes. Replays and multiplayer clients consume logged outputs instead of re-calling models. Tools offer fork-from-here, diff-between-branches, and cause tracing.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Public release from Unity, Epic, a major middleware vendor, or an open-source project with documented adoption in a shipped game.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A game engine or middleware vendor will ship an event-log-based replay and determinism layer designed for generative AI components.

key_risks: Log size grows quickly in large simulations.
Retrofitting existing engines is costly.
Privacy and storage of logged player text.
opportunities.name: Event-sourced simulation runtime
opportunities.summary: An engine layer that records simulation and model calls as an append-only event log, giving replay, forking, explanation, and determinism for games with AI components.
opportunities.thesis: Most AI-component risks in simulation games are determinism risks: model outputs are not reproducible, so replays, lockstep multiplayer, bug reports, and save integrity break. Recording every model call and its output as an event, and treating the log as the source of truth with state as a projection, restores reproducibility: replays read cached outputs, forks branch from any event, and explanations cite events. The same log feeds why-queries, branch previews, and chronicles.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Wrap the model calls of an AI-agent prototype in an event log, then replay 100 sessions and verify byte-identical state reconstruction and fork divergence only after the fork point. Success: 100 percent reproducible replays with log overhead under 20 percent of save size per hour.

opportunities.design_sketch: Hand a region, department, or supply chain to a manager. It proposes actions with reasons referencing indicators and the player's past choices; the player can approve, veto, or adjust standing preferences. A weekly report summarizes what changed.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Developer documentation describing per-player preference learning for delegated subsystems.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A grand strategy or management game will ship AI managers that learn from the individual player's past decisions.

key_risks: Imitating a novice player perpetuates mistakes.
Explanations that rationalize rather than explain.
Late-game play becomes approval clicking.
opportunities.name: Explained delegation to AI managers
opportunities.summary: Subsystem managers that learn the player's preferences from their past decisions and explain each action, so delegation scales play without hiding it.
opportunities.thesis: Delegation exists (Stellaris sectors, Football Manager staff, automated trade routes) but managers are weak and opaque, so players either micromanage or tolerate bad decisions. Imitation of the player's own past choices plus explanation grounded in game state makes delegation trustworthy: the manager does what you would do and tells you why.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Train a manager by imitation on a player's first 10 hours of decisions in a strategy prototype, then measure agreement with the player's choices in held-out situations and player trust ratings. Success: 75 percent agreement and higher trust than the baseline AI manager.

opportunities.design_sketch: Each day introduces rule changes written as formal predicates and rendered as in-world memos. Applicants, documents, and stories are generated to exercise boundary cases of the current rules. The game knows the correct ruling for every case and scores accordingly.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Store page or developer statement describing generated cases scored against formal rules.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A released inspection or bureaucracy job sim will use runtime generation of documents or applicants with a rule-derived answer key.

key_risks: Generated text leaks the answer or contradicts the formal case.
Repetitive tone across generated applicants.
opportunities.name: Generated inspection shifts
opportunities.summary: Rule-checking job sims with generated documents, items, and rule changes each shift, verified against an answer key so infinite variety stays fair.
opportunities.thesis: Papers, Please and its successors are limited by hand-built document sets that players memorize. Constrained generation can produce documents, forgeries, and edge cases from a formal rule set, and because the rules are formal, every generated case has a computable correct answer. That combination gives endless fair variety, which ordinary procedural generation struggles to make interesting and unconstrained generation cannot make fair.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Generate 1,000 inspection cases from a 30-predicate rule set and have a checker and two humans verify the answer key on a sample of 200. Success: 99 percent agreement between generated answers and human rulings.

opportunities.design_sketch: Designers set a theme, resource set, and target depth; the tool proposes recipe graphs with cycle times and alternates, simulates optimal and novice factories, and returns an archive ranked by depth, branching, and degeneracy checks. Designers edit and lock items they like.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Developer or mod author statement crediting algorithmic or model-based generation of the shipped recipe graph.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A factory or crafting game or major overhaul mod will credit a generative tool for its recipe graph or tech tree.

key_risks: Generated graphs feel arbitrary without thematic logic.
Agents optimize for metrics that miss what makes a recipe satisfying.
opportunities.name: Generated recipe graphs
opportunities.summary: Generate solvable, non-degenerate, on-theme production recipe graphs and tech trees, verified by agents, to cut content cost for factory and crafting games.
opportunities.thesis: Recipe graphs and tech trees are among the most prevalent content structures in the catalog, and their design is slow: each new item must be reachable, useful, and not dominated. Automated rule generation and quality-diversity search can propose graph variants, and agent playtests can check reachability, ratio complexity, and whether alternate recipes create real choices. Modding communities could use the same tool for overhaul mods.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Generate 100 recipe graphs for a fixed resource set and have experienced factory players rate a sample against an authored graph blind. Success: top-decile generated graphs rated equal to the authored one.

opportunities.design_sketch: A generate button in build mode takes a prompt or sketch, produces three candidates in the game's style, auto-fits collision and placement metadata, and assigns gameplay tags (seating, light, beauty value) from a classifier. Players share pieces with provenance labels.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Shipped feature in a title from EA/Maxis, Frontier, Krafton, Paradox, or a peer studio.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A major life or management sim will ship player-facing generation of placeable 3D objects.

key_risks: Copyright and trademark in generated pieces.
Player and press backlash against generated assets.
Gameplay tags misassigned to generated objects.
opportunities.name: Generative decoration catalogs
opportunities.summary: Let players generate furniture, scenery, and building pieces from text or sketches within a game's style and technical budgets, removing the cap on creative-mode catalogs.
opportunities.thesis: Creative-mode sims (The Sims build mode, Planet Coaster scenery, Townscaper-likes) live on catalog breadth, which is bounded by art budgets and DLC schedules. Text-to-3D asset generation reached production use in 2025, and style-constrained pipelines can enforce polygon budgets, collision, and art direction. Generated pieces then feed decoration scores and sharing.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Generate 200 decor items from player prompts within a game's style guide; have artists rate style match and check technical budgets. Success: 80 percent pass technical budgets and a majority rated on-style.

opportunities.design_sketch: Guest archetypes are generated offline from a human-behavior model conditioned on demographics; each archetype yields compact preference parameters the runtime uses. Players see segment-level reasoning ('families find this ride too intense for the price'). A sandbox mode lets designers test offerings against segments.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Developer blog, talk, or store text attributing in-game demand or preference parameters to a behavioral or language model.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A commercial management or tycoon game will state that its customer or citizen preferences were derived from a learned model of human behavior.

key_risks: Models encode demographic stereotypes that are offensive or wrong.
Calibration to real data may make the game less fun than hand-tuned curves.
Claims of realism invite scrutiny the model cannot survive.
opportunities.name: Human-calibrated customers
opportunities.summary: Replace hand-tuned customer and crowd preference curves with models that predict human choices, so tycoon markets respond like real populations.
opportunities.thesis: Customer behavior in management games is a set of hand-tuned curves: price tolerance, ride intensity preference, satisfaction decay. Research in 2024 and 2025 showed language-model agents and choice models trained on large behavioral datasets predicting individual human responses with useful accuracy. Using such models to generate preference distributions, offline, gives tycoon games demand that behaves like real segments and lets players learn transferable intuitions. The same machinery serves product and policy research outside games.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Generate preference parameters for a theme-park prototype from a behavior model, then compare predicted segment choices with a small real survey (n>=300) on the same priced options. Success: rank correlation above 0.6 between predicted and surveyed choices, and playtesters rate guest behavior as more plausible than the hand-tuned baseline.

opportunities.design_sketch: At the end of each in-game year, the chronicle drafts a chapter: key events, characters, turning points, written in a selectable voice and illustrated with generated images grounded in the logged entities. Every sentence links to its source events. Players edit and publish chronicles to a shared library.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Shipped feature in a released title or official expansion, described in patch notes or store text.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A systemic simulation game will ship an automatic, player-shareable narrative summary of a run's history.

key_risks: Summaries invent drama the log does not support.
Generated art quality and disclosure.
Players who enjoy writing their own stories may feel replaced.
opportunities.name: Illustrated chronicles
opportunities.summary: Turn a run's event log into a readable, illustrated saga that players can share, making emergent stories legible and portable.
opportunities.thesis: Players of systemic games already write their runs up as stories (Boatmurdered, colony diaries). Dwarf Fortress's legends mode stores the raw material but presents it as a database. Summarization over event logs, with grounding to cited events and generated illustrations, can produce shareable chapters automatically, which also markets the game.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Generate chronicles for 30 logged colony runs and have their players rate accuracy and whether they would share them. Success: average accuracy above 4 of 5 and more than half willing to share.

opportunities.design_sketch: An orders panel accepts sentences; each becomes a standing rule shown as a card with the exact priority changes, conditions, and expiry it compiled into. Rules can be edited in the classic UI. Conflicts between rules are flagged with an explanation.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Patch notes, store page, or developer statement describing the feature in a shipped title or official expansion.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A released colony or management sim will let players issue standing natural-language orders that compile into its job and priority systems.

key_risks: Ambiguous intents compile to surprising rules.
Hides the very systems some players enjoy mastering.
Conflicting standing rules produce opaque behavior.
opportunities.name: Intent-level orders
opportunities.summary: Players state goals in plain language and the game compiles them into priorities, designations, and schedules, cutting micromanagement in colony and management sims.
opportunities.thesis: Colony and management sims hit a micromanagement wall: the work-priority grid, stockpile filters, and schedules grow until play becomes clerical. Players think in intents ('keep the clinic staffed through winter', 'stop hauling during raids'). Constrained decoding can translate intents into the game's existing control primitives, and the result stays inspectable because it compiles into the same grids the player already understands.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Collect 200 player-stated intents from colony sim forums, compile them into a prototype's control primitives, and have players judge fidelity; measure clicks per in-game day with and without intents. Success: 80 percent judged faithful and a 30 percent drop in management clicks.

opportunities.design_sketch: An in-game mod workshop: the player describes the change, the system proposes a diff to data and scripts, runs a headless test scenario with agents to check for crashes and the intended effect, and shows before and after metrics. The player names and shares the mod; the description, code, and test results travel together.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Official tool or partnership announced by the developer of a simulation game with an active modding scene.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A popular moddable simulation game will ship or officially endorse a natural-language mod creation tool.

key_risks: Generated mods with subtle bugs corrupt saves.
Security of executing generated code.
Flood of low-quality mods drowns curation.
opportunities.name: Mechanic modding by description
opportunities.summary: Players describe a rule change in plain language; a model writes the mod against the modding API and automated agents test it before it is shared.
opportunities.thesis: Modding is how simulation games stay alive for decades, but scripting mods requires programming skill and engine knowledge. Code-generating models write working code against documented APIs, and automated playtesting agents can smoke-test results. Making 'wolves avoid fire' or 'trains prefer cheaper routes' a sentence rather than a project would enlarge the modding population by orders of magnitude.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Collect 100 mod requests from a modding community, generate mods against a documented API, and measure the share that compile, pass a headless scenario, and are judged by the requester to do what they asked. Success: at least 60 percent fully accepted.

opportunities.design_sketch: The player paints a rough block outline and selects intent (dense market street, quiet residential). The assist proposes building footprints and lanes using a learned prior constrained by WFC rules; the simulation scores walkability, land value, and traffic, and the player accepts or tweaks.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Developer documentation naming a learned or data-driven layout model in a shipped feature.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A commercial city builder will ship a learned layout generator that converts player gestures into detailed districts.

key_risks: Assist removes the planning players enjoy.
Learned priors import real-world layout biases.
Unclear ownership of generated layouts.
opportunities.name: Learned build assist for cities
opportunities.summary: Extend Townscaper-style procedural assist to full city builders with learned style priors, so rough strokes become plausible districts the simulation then evaluates.
opportunities.thesis: Townscaper, Tiny Glade, and Manor Lords showed that assisted building (the game completes detail around the player's gesture) is joyful. Constraint solving such as wave function collapse covers local consistency; learned layout generators add district-level plausibility. Feeding the result back into the simulation makes assist a gameplay tool rather than only an aesthetic one.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Train a layout generator on open street-network data and compare player-built districts with and without assist on build time and simulated performance. Success: 50 percent less build time at equal or better simulated metrics, with players preferring assist.

opportunities.design_sketch: A colony or sandbox world where water, heat, gas, and structural stress are simulated everywhere at coarse resolution by a learned surrogate and exactly within a radius of active play, with consistent hand-off at the boundary. Players can flood a valley or collapse a mountain and see effects propagate realistically across the map.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Developer documentation or technical talk confirming a trained neural model simulating physical materials during play.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A commercial game will use a learned surrogate for fluid, gas, or destruction simulation at runtime.

key_risks: Surrogates break conservation laws, producing exploitable infinite water or energy.
Boundary artifacts between surrogate and exact zones.
Determinism across GPUs for multiplayer.
opportunities.name: Learned material surrogates at world scale
opportunities.summary: Use learned and GPU-parallel physics surrogates to bring per-particle fluids, gases, and destruction from small arenas to large persistent worlds.
opportunities.thesis: Noita, Teardown, BeamNG, and Oxygen Not Included show players love worlds where every particle or voxel is simulated, but compute caps these simulations to small areas or 2D. Graph-network simulators and neural operators learn fluid, cloth, and deformation dynamics at large speedups, and GPU-parallel simulators make the remaining numerical work cheap. Combining a learned surrogate for the far field with exact simulation near the player could extend material simulation to whole maps.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Train a graph-network surrogate on a 2D falling-sand fluid simulator and measure mass conservation error and speedup over 10,000 steps at four times the training domain size. Success: mass error under 1 percent with a speedup above 10 times.

opportunities.design_sketch: A farm sim ships a small emulator per biome that rolls forward daily fields (temperature, precipitation, wind) from a seed and a climate scenario. Crops, fire spread, and hydrology read those fields. Players can choose a historical climate or a warming scenario and see droughts and storms arise at realistic frequencies.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Documentation or developer statement describing an ML weather emulator in the shipped game.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A commercial farming, flight, or city sim will ship weather generated by a learned emulator rather than scripted states or live forecast feeds.

key_risks: Global models are too large for clients; distillation to regional scale may lose coherence.
Realistic weather can be less fun than authored seasons.
Licensing of model weights and training data.
opportunities.name: Learned regional weather
opportunities.summary: Use machine-learned weather emulators to give farming, flight, and city sims realistic, cheap, regionally coherent weather and climate variability.
opportunities.thesis: Game weather is a Markov chain of states or a replay of real forecasts. ML weather models from 2023 to 2025 produce physically coherent global fields orders of magnitude cheaper than numerical prediction, and ensemble methods sample plausible variability. Distilled regional emulators can drive crop growth, fire risk, flooding, and flight conditions with correlated, believable weather, including climate-shift scenarios that sims could never author.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Distill a public ML weather model's outputs into a sub-100 MB regional emulator for one biome; compare statistics (drought frequency, storm clustering) against reanalysis data and run it inside a farming prototype at under 1 ms per in-game day. Success: matched variability statistics within 20 percent and no measurable frame cost.

opportunities.design_sketch: Machines need operators with trained skills; skilled workers age and retire; children of workers attend schools the player builds; housing, food, and morale affect shift output. A bottleneck can be a missing machine or a missing mentor. Generational play replaces the usual tech-tree endgame with succession planning for the workforce.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Steam page describing generational workforce mechanics in a factory or automation game with at least 1,000 reviews.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A factory or automation game where workers age, train, and are replaced by a simulated next generation will reach 1,000 Steam reviews.

key_risks: Workforce management can bury the logistics puzzle players came for.
Agent counts at factory scale strain compute.
Two audiences (automation and life-sim) may each find half the game unwanted.
opportunities.name: Factories with a living workforce
opportunities.summary: Automation games whose workers age, learn, form families, and retire, so a production network is also a society that must be sustained across generations.
opportunities.thesis: The white-space analysis shows production chains and agent lifecycles are both common yet almost never combined: factory games are run by machines or faceless workers, and games with aging, family-forming agents rarely have deep production. Colony sims and Workers & Resources sit closest. A factory whose throughput depends on a workforce with skills, schooling, households, and turnover couples the most-used rule-system in the catalog to the most attachment-generating ones. Salience-gated language agents make that workforce individually legible without per-tick cost.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Prototype a small automation map where each machine needs a skilled operator drawn from a simulated population with aging and schooling; compare session length and self-reported attachment with a machines-only control. Success: longer sessions and higher attachment without lower throughput-puzzle ratings.

opportunities.design_sketch: The player picks a map, founding traits, and scarcity levels, then seeds 50 to 500 agents. Interventions are god-scale and rare: a drought, a prophet, a trade caravan. A chronicle tool summarizes eras, factions, and turning points; players share worlds and replay them from saved event logs.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Steam page confirming LLM-driven agent society as the core loop and a review count of at least 1,000.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A commercially released game whose core loop is observing and nudging a society of at least 50 language-model agents will reach 1,000 Steam reviews.

key_risks: Inference cost for hundreds of agents over long runs.
Agent societies may converge to bland or repetitive behavior without engineered diversity.
Emergent content safety in open-ended social simulation.
opportunities.name: Language-agent society terrarium
opportunities.summary: An observer-gardener genre where players seed and nudge a persistent society of language-model agents and watch institutions, cultures, and histories form.
opportunities.thesis: Generative Agents (2023) and Project Sid (2024) showed that populations of language-model agents produce recognizable social structure: parties, roles, rules, shared beliefs. These are research demos, not games, but the experience they produce resembles the Game of Life and Dwarf Fortress legends: watching a world write its own history. With cheaper inference and chronicle tooling, a terrarium genre becomes viable where the player sets initial conditions and intervenes sparingly, and the product is the history.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Run 100 agents for 30 simulated days on a small local model with a chronicle summarizer; have readers rate 20 generated histories against Dwarf Fortress legends excerpts for interest and coherence. Success: comparable interest ratings at under 1 dollar of inference per simulated day.

opportunities.design_sketch: The game ships a quantized model for dialogue, event generation, and explanation, with a schema-constrained interface. Higher-quality cloud calls are optional and clearly metered. Mods can swap models.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Store pages or documentation confirming local model inference for runtime features, and review counts over 1,000.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: At least five Steam games with over 1,000 reviews will ship an on-device language model used at runtime without requiring an internet connection.

key_risks: Hardware minimums shrink the audience.
Model quality gap versus cloud models.
Download size and VRAM competition with rendering.
opportunities.name: Local-first AI simulation games
opportunities.summary: Ship small language and generative models inside the game so AI features run offline with no per-hour inference bill, changing the economics of AI-native simulation.
opportunities.thesis: Cloud inference makes AI features a variable cost per player-hour, which conflicts with the one-time-purchase model of most simulation games and their very long play sessions. Small models running on consumer GPUs and NPUs reached usable quality for constrained tasks in 2025 (inZOI's on-device characters are an example). Local-first design bounds cost, works offline, protects privacy, and survives the vendor's model deprecations.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Benchmark a 1 to 4 billion parameter quantized model on the median Steam hardware survey GPU for schema-constrained NPC dialogue, measuring latency, VRAM, and frame-time impact. Success: under 500 ms first token with less than 10 percent frame-time impact.

opportunities.design_sketch: Traffic and pedestrian flows are fields updated each tick from a mean-field equilibrium solver on the GPU; visible cars and citizens are samples drawn from those fields, so congestion is consistent at scale while inspection still shows individuals with plausible trips.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Developer documentation naming a mean-field, continuum, or equilibrium-field method used at runtime.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A commercial city builder will document a mean-field or continuum crowd model as its primary traffic or population simulation.

key_risks: Players notice when sampled individuals behave inconsistently with fields.
Equilibrium solvers can be slow to converge under rapid change.
Engineering cost to retrofit existing engines.
opportunities.name: Mean-field crowds and traffic
opportunities.summary: Simulate hundreds of thousands of agents with equilibrium-consistent route and choice behavior by combining mean-field approximations with sampled individuals.
opportunities.thesis: City builders face a ceiling where individually simulated agents cap population and aggregate models feel lifeless. Mean-field game theory describes how large populations of optimizing agents reach equilibrium, and GPU-parallel simulation makes iterating those fields cheap. A hybrid where the mean field sets congestion and choice probabilities and a sample of visible individuals follows them gives large populations that behave coherently.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Implement a mean-field traffic solver on a 100,000-trip city network and compare travel-time distributions with a full agent-based baseline. Success: within 10 percent on mean and 90th percentile travel times at a tenth of the compute.

opportunities.design_sketch: A designer selects a base simulation and a family. The system mutates rule code, runs agent populations, scores emergent variety, strategic depth, and legibility proxies, and returns an archive of diverse candidates with replays and plain-language descriptions, deduplicated against the existing taxonomy.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Developer statement or paper attributing a shipped mechanic's origin to automated search.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A shipped commercial game will credit a mechanic to an automated rule-discovery system.

key_risks: Proxies for fun are weak; search optimizes the proxy.
Discovered mechanics may be illegible to humans.
Compute cost of agent evaluation.
opportunities.name: Automated mechanic discovery
opportunities.summary: Search the space of rule programs with language-model-guided evolution and agent playtests to propose new mechanics that are learnable, deep, and unlike existing ones.
opportunities.thesis: Automated game design has produced board-game rules (Ludii and GAVEL) and levels, and LLM-guided evolutionary search (FunSearch, AlphaEvolve) has found new algorithms and constructions. Simulation mechanics are small rule programs over state; a search that proposes rule variants, evaluates them with agent populations for depth and learnability proxies, and keeps a diversity archive could surface mechanics designers have not tried. The taxonomy in this repository is a candidate search space and novelty reference.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Run LLM-guided evolution over rule variants of a small production-chain sim with a quality-diversity archive, then have designers rate the top 20 candidates for novelty and promise. Success: at least three candidates rated novel and worth prototyping by a majority of designers.

opportunities.design_sketch: The player drafts 'Ban coal plants within 2 km of housing; subsidize heat pumps by 30 percent.' The compiler returns a structured policy card listing the parameters it maps to and anything it could not map. Interest groups (miners, residents, industrialists) post positions computed from projected welfare changes and voiced by a model. Votes and compliance follow simulation state, not rhetoric.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: A shipped title (early access counts) whose documentation shows free-text law input mapped to simulation rules.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A released political or city-building game will let players enact free-text laws that change simulation parameters.

key_risks: Players write laws the simulation cannot represent; the unmapped remainder must be visible.
Group rhetoric can diverge from the computed welfare that actually drives votes.
Politically sensitive content needs moderation.
opportunities.name: Natural-language legislation
opportunities.summary: Players write laws in plain language that are compiled into typed policy parameters, while simulated interest groups argue, lobby, and comply.
opportunities.thesis: Policy mechanics have been menus: a fixed list of toggles chosen by designers. Constrained decoding can compile free-text proposals into a typed policy object over the simulation's actual parameters, and language-model interest groups can respond in character with positions grounded in how the policy affects their simulated welfare. Player-written law moves governance games from choosing among authored options toward authoring rules, which A Tale in the Desert and Eco explored with players as legislators and humans as the parsers.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Build a policy compiler over a 40-parameter city model. Collect 300 player-written laws, have the compiler map them, and have two humans judge mapping fidelity. Success: 85 percent of laws mapped faithfully or with clearly flagged gaps, and playtesters prefer authoring to menus in a within-subjects test.

opportunities.design_sketch: AI rulers send and answer proposals in text; each message is backed by an intent object (offer, demand, threat, promise) that the planner evaluates. Broken promises create named opinion modifiers visible to every faction. Players can still use classic proposal menus; text adds nuance such as conditional offers and side deals.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Developer statement or documentation describing language-based AI diplomacy in a title from Paradox, Firaxis, Amplitude, or a peer studio.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A major grand strategy or 4X release will ship AI opponents that negotiate through free-text or generated-language diplomacy backed by a planner.

key_risks: Planner cost scales badly with many factions.
Players exploit language models with persuasion that the planner should ignore.
Long campaigns exceed the consistency horizon of dialogue memory.
opportunities.name: Negotiating faction AI
opportunities.summary: Grand strategy rivals that negotiate in language and plan around their promises, combining strategic search with dialogue.
opportunities.thesis: Diplomacy in grand strategy is reduced to acceptance scores on fixed proposals. Cicero showed in 2022 that grounding dialogue in a planner that predicts others' moves lets an agent negotiate and keep useful commitments in a seven-player game. Applying the pattern to faction diplomacy makes alliances, betrayals, and bargains first-class play, and opinion modifiers give the model a structured memory of who kept their word.
opportunities.validation_experiment: In a five-faction diplomacy sandbox, compare menu-only AI with planner-plus-dialogue AI on player-rated plausibility, commitment-keeping rate, and win rates against scripted baselines. Success: higher plausibility and a commitment-keeping rate above 80 percent without exploitable persuasion loops in red-team play.

opportunities.design_sketch: Agent animation is driven by a learned controller conditioned on body-model state, load, and mood. The inspector shows the same state the motion expresses. Crowds use cheaper approximations at distance.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Developer documentation naming learned motion control in a shipped simulation game.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A management or colony sim will ship learned physics-based motion for its simulated population.

key_risks: Runtime cost at crowd scale.
Uncanny motion worse than stylized animation.
Physics instability in edge cases.
opportunities.name: Learned motion for simulated crowds
opportunities.summary: Physics-based learned character controllers let simulated agents move and react physically, so crowds, injuries, and labor look like what the simulation says is happening.
opportunities.thesis: Simulation games describe rich internal states (injured, exhausted, carrying heavy loads) but show them with a handful of canned animations, which undermines legibility and attachment. Learned physics-based controllers can produce motion conditioned on state at scale, so an agent with a leg wound limps believably and a tired hauler slows and stumbles.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Drive 200 agents with a learned controller conditioned on three state variables; measure frame cost and whether observers can identify agent state from motion alone. Success: 80 percent identification at under 2 ms per frame.

opportunities.design_sketch: The player tunes environment parameters and selection pressures for a continuous artificial-life world. An automated discovery system scans the running world for novel forms and behaviors and bookmarks them; the player curates, names, and transplants organisms between worlds and shares discoveries.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Steam page describing a Lenia-family or NCA substrate and at least 1,000 reviews.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A commercial game built on a continuous artificial-life substrate (Lenia family or neural cellular automata) will reach 1,000 Steam reviews.

key_risks: Open-ended substrates often stagnate or explode.
Players may not read abstract organisms as creatures.
GPU requirements.
opportunities.name: Open-ended evolution sandbox
opportunities.summary: Evolution games built on continuous artificial-life substrates and automated discovery, where morphology and behavior evolve without designer-authored part catalogs.
opportunities.thesis: Evolution games either use authored parts (Spore's editor) or simple genomes (Species, The Bibites). Research on Lenia, Flow-Lenia, neural cellular automata, and foundation-model-guided search for artificial life (ASAL, 2024) produced substrates where lifelike, open-ended forms emerge and tools that find interesting ones automatically. A game can use those tools as a camera operator over an evolving world, surfacing novelty to the player.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Run a Flow-Lenia world on a consumer GPU with an automated novelty detector for 8 hours and have players rate bookmarked discoveries against random snapshots. Success: bookmarked organisms rated more interesting in at least 75 percent of pairwise comparisons.

opportunities.design_sketch: A headless build of the simulation runs on a GPU cluster. A quality-diversity search maintains an archive of strategies across behavior descriptors (expansion speed, military share, trade dependence); a tuner adjusts parameters to keep win rates and resource curves inside designer-set bands; reports flag exploits with replays.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: GDC talks, technical blogs, or papers by studio staff describing the practice for a named commercial title.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: At least two studios will publicly describe using large-scale agent search to balance a simulation or strategy game's economy before release.

key_risks: Bots find exploits humans never would and miss ones humans find.
Headless builds of legacy engines are expensive to make.
Over-balancing removes interesting asymmetries.
opportunities.name: Parallel autobalancing of economies
opportunities.summary: Run thousands of scripted, learned, and diversity-seeking agents through a game's economy at accelerated speed to find degenerate strategies and tune parameters before players do.
opportunities.thesis: Production chains, markets, threat scaling, and tech trees have many interacting parameters and are tuned by small QA teams and patches after launch. GPU-parallel simulation and quality-diversity search make it practical to run very large populations of strategies and to search parameter space for regions with no dominant strategy. This shifts balance work from reactive patching to pre-launch search.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Run a MAP-Elites search over strategies in an open-source economy game for one GPU-day and compare discovered exploits with the game's historical patch notes. Success: at least half of historically patched economic exploits rediscovered.

opportunities.design_sketch: A neighborhood is loaded from open data. Participants zone, budget, and route transit; overlays show calibrated effects; simulated residents from different groups react, each tied to the data that grounds them. Sessions export a report of options and tradeoffs.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Public planning document or press release naming the tool and its use in consultation.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A city government will publicly use a game-style calibrated simulation with simulated resident feedback in a formal planning consultation.

key_risks: Simulated residents substitute for real community input.
False precision of calibrated models.
Political misuse.
opportunities.name: Participatory planning sandboxes
opportunities.summary: City-builder interfaces over calibrated urban models with simulated resident voices, used by communities and planners to explore tradeoffs together.
opportunities.thesis: Planners already use city builders to communicate, but the games' models are not calibrated to real cities and residents are absent. Simulation-based inference can calibrate traffic, housing, and service models to local data; language-model residents grounded in survey data can voice how proposals affect them. The city builder becomes a deliberation interface, with game mechanics (overlays, budgets, forecasts) as the legibility layer.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Calibrate a traffic and housing model for one district, run three participatory sessions, and measure whether participants' understanding of tradeoffs (pre and post quiz) improves relative to a slide presentation. Success: significant improvement with participants rating the tool as fair.

opportunities.design_sketch: When the player places or removes a building, the event system evaluates templates against neighbors, inhabitants, and history; a few fire as short vignettes with choices whose effects are typed (happiness, faction, resource). The chronicle records them so a district accumulates a history.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Store page or developer material describing events triggered by player placement decisions and affecting named inhabitants.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A released city builder will advertise placement-triggered narrative events tied to specific inhabitants as a core feature.

key_risks: Event frequency that interrupts building flow.
Players gaming layout for favorable events.
Generated vignettes repeat in tone.
opportunities.name: Placement that tells stories
opportunities.summary: City builders where where and what the player builds triggers specific, state-aware story events about the inhabitants of those buildings.
opportunities.thesis: Building placement and triggered event chains are both common but rarely combined: city builders tell almost no stories about what players build, and event-driven games rarely have spatial building. Events keyed to placement, adjacency, and the inhabitants affected (a tavern next to the temple, a mill that floods a farmer's field) give layout a narrative consequence. Constrained generation can instantiate such events from templates at scale while keeping effects inside the rules.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Add 50 placement-triggered event templates to a small city-builder prototype and measure whether players recall and describe their towns in narrative terms more often than a control. Success: a significant increase in narrative descriptions with no drop in building time.

opportunities.design_sketch: A scenario browser shows a grid of challenge types by difficulty; each cell holds generated scenarios that agents have solved, with par times. Players rate them; ratings retrain the generator.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Developer documentation naming quality-diversity or MAP-Elites generation for shipped content.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A released simulation or puzzle-sim game will ship a quality-diversity-generated scenario library.

key_risks: Generated scenarios feel generic.
Agent-solvable is not the same as fun.
opportunities.name: Quality-diversity scenario libraries
opportunities.summary: Generate large libraries of scenarios that cover a grid of difficulty and play style, so scenario-driven sims never run out of distinct challenges.
opportunities.thesis: Scenario modes are expensive to author and players exhaust them. Quality-diversity search can fill a map of scenario descriptors (resource scarcity, threat timing, terrain constraint) with playable, validated scenarios, and learned generators can add theming. Agent playtests confirm each is solvable and estimate difficulty.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Generate 500 scenarios for a bridge or park builder with MAP-Elites over three descriptors; have players compare random generated scenarios with authored ones. Success: generated scenarios rated at least 80 percent as enjoyable as authored ones.

opportunities.design_sketch: Colonists run a standard needs-and-utility loop. When an event crosses a salience score (death of a friend, public insult, near-starvation), the agent gets one model call with its trait list, recent memories, and the event, and must return a schema-valid object: a thought with mood value and duration, an optional relationship change, an optional one-line spoken reaction, and an optional new goal. The player sees these as ordinary thoughts in the inspector, now specific to the colonist's history.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Developer documentation, postmortems, or mod-verified behavior showing model calls triggered by discrete events, in titles with more than 1,000 Steam reviews.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: At least three commercially released colony or life sims with over 1,000 Steam reviews will use language-model calls gated by event salience rather than per-decision.

key_risks: Generated thoughts that contradict visible state erode trust faster than generic thoughts do.
Salience thresholds tuned for drama can flood the log in crisis states.
Local model quality varies by hardware tier, creating uneven experiences.
opportunities.name: Salience-gated language agents
opportunities.summary: Keep cheap utility scoring for every tick and call a language model only at salient moments, giving colony and life sims believable minds at a bounded cost.
opportunities.thesis: Rule-based utility agents are cheap and legible but repetitive; fully LLM-driven agents are expressive but cost tokens every decision and drift from game state. Most agent decisions in The Sims or RimWorld are routine (eat, sleep, haul) and need no language model. The memorable moments are rare: a breakup, a grudge, a mental break, a first meeting. A hybrid that reserves model calls for events above a salience threshold, and writes the result back as typed memories and relationship deltas, captures most of the believability at a small fraction of the cost. Small local models made this affordable in 2025; constrained decoding makes the write-back safe.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Build a 20-colonist prototype with a pure-utility baseline and a salience-gated variant capped at one model call per colonist per in-game hour. Run blind playtests (n>=30) rating believability and attachment, log tokens per player-hour, and count state-contradiction errors per hour. Success: believability gain of at least one point on a 7-point scale at under 2,000 tokens per player-hour with contradiction rate below one per hour.

opportunities.design_sketch: Each project needs a lead and collaborators; compatibility and rivalry change speed and the chance of side discoveries; scientists publish, poach, and defect. The tech graph becomes partially stochastic: what is discovered depends on who works together.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Shipped title documentation describing relationship-dependent research by named characters.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A strategy or management game will ship research performed by a simulated population of named researchers whose relationships affect outcomes.

key_risks: Stochastic research frustrates players planning builds.
Micromanaging researchers adds busywork.
opportunities.name: Research by named scientists
opportunities.summary: Replace the abstract research meter with named researchers whose skills, relationships, and rivalries determine what gets discovered and when.
opportunities.thesis: Tech trees are the most common mechanic in the catalog and among the least simulated: research is a currency spent on a graph. Relationship systems are common too, but the white-space analysis shows the two rarely meet. Research performed by a small population of named scientists with skills, collaborations, and grudges turns progression into a social system and makes breakthroughs into stories, using the same agent stack as colony sims.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Swap the research meter in a strategy prototype for a ten-scientist system and compare player-recalled research events and build-plan satisfaction. Success: more recalled research stories without lower plan satisfaction.

opportunities.design_sketch: During a landing, the instructor says 'airspeed 12 knots fast, reduce power' based on telemetry, then debriefs with a timeline of deviations. Lessons adapt to repeated errors. The player can ask questions mid-flight by voice.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Official feature in Microsoft Flight Simulator, X-Plane, DCS, iRacing, Gran Turismo, or a peer title.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A major flight or racing simulator will ship an AI voice instructor that comments on live telemetry.

key_risks: Wrong advice in safety-relevant domains if transferred to real training.
Voice latency during time-critical maneuvers.
Instructor chatter annoys experienced players.
opportunities.name: Simulator instructor coaching
opportunities.summary: Flight, driving, and procedure sims with a voice instructor that watches inputs and state, explains mistakes, and adapts lessons in real time.
opportunities.thesis: Vehicle and job simulators teach through checklists and failure. Professional training uses instructors who watch and talk. Realtime voice models, state-grounded explanation, and player modeling make an instructor that comments on what the player is actually doing, with references to the simulator's telemetry, feasible in consumer sims. The same tool serves professional training and lowers the entry barrier for the most intimidating subgenres.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Add a telemetry-grounded voice instructor to a flight sim landing lesson; compare novice landing success after five attempts with and without the instructor. Success: at least 25 percent higher success with no increase in reported frustration.

opportunities.design_sketch: A studio ships a headless build with a typed observation and action API, standard scenarios, and leaderboards for agents. Researchers measure long-horizon performance; players watch agent runs as content.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Official announcement or repository from the developer, not only a community wrapper.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A commercial simulation game developer will officially release a headless research API or benchmark for AI agents.

key_risks: Benchmarks saturate quickly.
Studios may not want agent play to define their game publicly.
Engine licensing for research use.
opportunities.name: Simulation games as agent benchmarks
opportunities.summary: Use factory, colony, and economy sims as long-horizon evaluation and training environments for AI agents, with game studios as environment providers.
opportunities.thesis: AI agents now need environments that test planning over thousands of steps, resource management, and recovery from compounding errors. Simulation games are exactly that, with measurable outcomes (throughput, survival, profit). Minecraft became a research environment through MineDojo and Voyager, and factory games have been proposed as agent benchmarks. Games with headless modes and clean observation APIs can become a licensed research category.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Wrap an open-source colony or factory sim with a typed API, define five scenarios with throughput and survival metrics, and evaluate three frontier agents. Success: scores that separate agents and do not saturate within one model generation.

opportunities.design_sketch: Each puzzle is a machine to control. The player writes a specification and test cases; a model generates implementations, some subtly wrong; the player's score counts wrong implementations caught, test cost, and spec length, plotted on histograms against other players.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Steam page describing AI-generated code that players specify, test, or verify as the main mechanic.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A commercial programming game will make specifying or testing AI-written code its core loop.

key_risks: Niche audience.
Model behavior changes over versions alter puzzle difficulty.
Players may find being a reviewer less fun than being a builder.
opportunities.name: Specification programming games
opportunities.summary: Programming puzzles where an AI writes the code and the player writes the specification and tests, scored on how precisely the spec pins down correct behavior.
opportunities.thesis: Zachtronics games and Screeps made writing code the play. Code generation changes what programming skill means: specifying behavior and catching wrong implementations. A genre built around writing specs and adversarial tests, with a model as an unreliable implementer, teaches the skill that now matters and has a natural scoring rule: how many plausible wrong programs your tests reject.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Ship a 10-puzzle web prototype where a model generates candidate implementations with injected faults; measure completion rates and whether score distributions separate skilled from unskilled testers. Success: a stable leaderboard where test-writing skill predicts score.

opportunities.design_sketch: A city builder whose simulation is a tile grid of typed buildings, agents, and fields. A renderer conditioned on the grid, time of day, and a style prompt produces the view; players restyle their city as medieval, solarpunk, or watercolor without new art. Inspection tools always read the symbolic state.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Developer documentation showing gameplay state is symbolic and the main viewport is produced by a learned generative renderer.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A released game will render its primary view with a generative model conditioned on an explicit symbolic game state.

key_risks: Rendered frames that misrepresent symbolic state confuse players (a building that looks like a hospital but is not).
Inference cost per frame on consumer GPUs.
Temporal flicker and style drift across sessions.
opportunities.name: Symbolic simulation, neural rendering
opportunities.summary: Keep gameplay in a small deterministic symbolic simulation and let a generative world model render it, decoupling visual variety from simulation cost and art budgets.
opportunities.thesis: Generative world models (GameNGen, Genie 3, Muse, Oasis) produce convincing interactive frames but drift, forget, and cannot be trusted as game state. Simulation games need the opposite: exact, persistent, inspectable state. Splitting the stack resolves the conflict: the authoritative simulation stays symbolic (grids, agents, stocks), and a conditioned generative model renders it, so visual variety becomes nearly free while rules, saves, replays, and multiplayer sync remain deterministic.
opportunities.validation_experiment: Condition an open video or image model on a 32x32 symbolic city grid and measure per-tile semantic fidelity (does a rendered tile read as its type to human raters) and frame time. Success: over 95 percent rater agreement with the symbolic type at 10 frames per second on a current consumer GPU.

opportunities.design_sketch: The player demonstrates 'set up a smelting column' once while narrating; the companion abstracts it into a named skill with parameters, shows the generated plan, and reuses it elsewhere. Skills can be edited, combined, and shared. The companion asks clarifying questions when a skill fails.

falsifiable_signal.criteria: Store page or developer documentation describing learned, reusable companion skills in a shipped title.
falsifiable_signal.prediction: A released automation or sandbox game will feature an in-game companion that learns reusable skills from player demonstration or instruction.

key_risks: Agents that play the game for you can remove the core pleasure.
