Whispers from the Star (August 2025) is built around open-ended voice, video-call, and text conversation with an AI-voiced character created with an actor, and Where Winds Meet (global November 2025) discloses real-time AI NPC text and voice chat.

ARC Raiders (November 2025) was criticized and marked down by Eurogamer for generative AI NPC voices, and the SAG-AFTRA video game strike (July 2024 to July 2025) ended with contract terms on consent for AI voice replicas.

limitations: Cost scales with talk time: at 2024 Realtime API rates, an hour split evenly between player and NPC speech is roughly $9 before context re-reads; gpt-realtime rates cut that to roughly $3 (estimates derived from list prices).
Expressive delivery and low latency trade off: context-conditioned prosody still trails humans, and the most expressive TTS was not suited to real time at launch.
Voice actor consent and compensation are now contract terms, and players have penalized AI voices in reviews.
Speech-native models are hard to constrain to game-legal actions; most games keep a text layer between speech and game state.
Microphone use and online connectivity raise privacy and access barriers (Whispers from the Star lists a broadband connection and an account).
techniques.mechanism: Two pipelines. Cascaded: streaming speech recognition, then an LLM, then streaming TTS, each optimized for time to first output. Speech-native: the model reads and writes audio tokens from a neural codec. Moshi models the user's and its own speech as parallel streams (full duplex, so it can listen while speaking) and predicts time-aligned text tokens before audio tokens. Hosted realtime APIs keep a persistent WebSocket session with voice activity detection, interruption handling, and function calls that can trigger game actions. Expressive TTS conditions delivery on context: Sesame's CSM feeds prior conversation audio and text to a Llama-style backbone over codec tokens, and Eleven v3 accepts inline tags such as [whispers] or [sighs]. Small ASR and TTS models (hundreds of millions of parameters) can run on device.
techniques.name: Realtime speech-to-speech and expressive TTS for characters
techniques.summary: Streaming speech recognition, speech-native language models, and context-aware text-to-speech that let characters hold spoken, interruptible conversations with roughly 200-250 ms response onset and generated emotional delivery.

affects.note: The world is reconstructed from real imagery instead of generated from a seed and noise; the player-facing role of an explorable map is unchanged, but its content is the real planet, with procedural filling only where imagery is missing.

Recognizable real buildings and landmarks across the planet make visual navigation by reference to the ground practicable anywhere, extending hand-flying practice beyond hand-modeled airports and cities.
Learned classification of satellite imagery turns real-world map data into simulated scenery at planetary scale (Microsoft Flight Simulator).

key_results.text: Microsoft Flight Simulator (2020) used Blackshark.ai's AI on Azure to generate 3D buildings, trees, and terrain from Bing Maps data and photogrammetry, covering about 1.5 billion buildings and 2 trillion trees from over two petabytes of streamed map data.
Blackshark.ai describes its products as turning satellite and aerial imagery into structured models of terrain, buildings, and infrastructure.
Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 carries over the satellite-derived scenery systems of the 2020 game.

limitations: Accuracy is bounded by imagery quality; blurred or pixelated areas fall back to procedural fill.
Requires cloud streaming of petabyte-scale data and a licensed imagery source.
Reconstructed buildings are generic from inferred class and height, not modeled individually, except in photogrammetry cities.
techniques.mechanism: Models trained on labeled imagery detect buildings, trees, and land cover in satellite and aerial imagery and map data and extrapolate approximate geometry; offline procedural generation then builds and dresses the buildings and places vegetation, while selected cities use photogrammetry meshes. The reconstruction runs offline in the cloud, and the result is streamed to players on demand as they fly, with procedural filling where imagery is poor.
techniques.name: ML reconstruction of the planet from aerial imagery
techniques.summary: Machine learning classifies buildings, vegetation, and terrain in satellite and aerial imagery and procedural rules rebuild them as 3D scenery, which Microsoft Flight Simulator streams for the whole Earth.

affects.note: Transmission, recovery and contact parameters can be inferred from real outbreak curves or target curves, with a posterior that shows which parameters the data cannot pin down.
Economic ABM parameters can be calibrated to price and quantity time series (Dyer et al.), grounding market sims in real data instead of hand-set elasticities.
Demand and route-choice parameters of an agent-based traffic model can be fitted to observed counts, the same likelihood-free ABM calibration applied to a city.
Match-engine parameters can be fitted so simulated score and statistic distributions match real league data, with uncertainty on each parameter.
Predator-prey rates can be inferred from target population time series, so designers state desired oscillations and the posterior returns rates that produce them.
Treating target survival-time or loss-rate distributions from playtest telemetry as the observation, the posterior gives scaling parameters that reproduce them and how sensitive each one is.

key_results.text: Cranmer, Brehmer and Louppe reviewed simulation-based inference as a general framework for inverse problems in simulators with intractable likelihoods.

Automatic posterior transformation (APT) made sequential neural posterior estimation work with arbitrary, dynamically updated proposals and flow-based estimators, including on high-dimensional time series and images.

Neural posterior and neural ratio estimation gave state-of-the-art parameter inference for economic agent-based models from multivariate time series, where older likelihood-free methods needed hundreds of thousands of simulations.
Temporal graph neural networks learned ABM parameter posteriors directly from microdata, avoiding information loss from hand-chosen summary statistics.
The open-source sbi toolkit packages these estimators with diagnostics and defaults, needing only simulator samples.

limitations: Needs many simulator runs, from thousands to hundreds of thousands depending on method and dimensionality, which is costly for slow, full-scale game simulations.
A misspecified simulator yields confident posteriors over wrong parameters; calibration fits the data and does not validate the model.
Posterior quality depends on the summary statistics or learned embeddings of noisy, high-dimensional outputs.
Matching real data or telemetry targets does not make a mechanic fun; it only removes guesswork about parameter values.
No game studio use was found in this run's sources.
techniques.mechanism: Draw parameters theta from a prior, run the simulator to get outputs x, and train a conditional density estimator, usually a normalizing flow, to approximate p(theta | x) from the (theta, x) pairs (neural posterior estimation). Conditioning on observed data x_o gives the posterior; sequential variants such as APT draw new simulations from proposals concentrated near x_o. Related variants learn the likelihood or a likelihood ratio instead. Summary statistics can be hand-chosen or learned, for example with a temporal graph neural network over agent-level microstates. The method needs only forward runs, no likelihood and no gradients, and once trained it is amortized: a new observation gets its posterior in one forward pass.
techniques.name: Simulation-based inference for calibrating simulators
techniques.summary: Neural density estimators trained on simulator runs return a posterior over a simulator's parameters given observed data, calibrating agent-based and economic models whose likelihoods cannot be computed.

affects.note: Deformation learned from an offline solver runs 300-5000x faster than that solver, putting near-offline-quality cloth and flesh response within a real-time budget.
Hands-on tasks such as surgery or handling soft objects could show tissue and cloth reacting plausibly to tools in real time, adding feedback the player reads to perform the skill.

key_results.text: Ubisoft La Forge's subspace neural physics ran interactive cloth and deformable simulation 300 to 5000 times faster than conventional simulation at a small additional memory cost (the project page states 300 to 4000).

Unreal Engine's ML Deformer trains models on externally generated deformation caches from Maya or Houdini and applies them at runtime as GPU morph targets; the Neural Morph Model is the recommended default and the cloth-oriented Nearest Neighbor Model is marked experimental.

limitations: Quality holds only near the training distribution of poses and interactions; unusual poses or collisions produce artifacts, so coverage of the offline dataset sets the limit.
Training is heavy: Unreal's documentation notes long training times and Alembic training caches of 50-100 GB.
GPU memory for morph targets is the main runtime cost, and compression settings trade memory and speed for quality.
Output is usually cosmetic; it does not feed back into gameplay physics unless the game reads the deformed state, which brings determinism and consistency issues.
No commercial title using these models at runtime was confirmed in this run's sources.
techniques.mechanism: Developers run an expensive offline simulation (cloth, soft tissue, muscle, volume-preserving flesh) over many randomized poses or interactions. Vertex positions are compressed, for example with principal component analysis, into a low-dimensional subspace. A small network is trained to predict the next subspace coordinates from the current coordinates plus external inputs such as bone transforms or collider positions (Holden et al. 2019), or to predict per-pose corrective morph-target weights applied on top of linear skinning (Unreal Engine ML Deformer, Neural Morph Model and Nearest Neighbor Model). At runtime only the network and the decode from subspace to full mesh run, on the GPU.
techniques.name: Subspace neural physics and learned deformers
techniques.summary: Small networks trained on offline cloth, flesh, or muscle simulation predict deformation in a compressed subspace or as corrective morph targets, running hundreds to thousands of times faster than the source simulation inside a game engine.

affects.note: Decor and furniture catalogs that beauty and environment scores consume can be produced from prompts or reference images in seconds per asset, so catalog size stops being bounded by modeling time.
Runtime generation extends from text and textures to placeable 3D props: inZOI players convert their own images into in-game objects.

Part-controllable generation (Roblox CubePart) produces assets split into parts intended for physics and scripts, which could supply new components for build-from-parts mechanics on request; not yet shown in a shipped assembly game.

key_results.text: TRELLIS (Microsoft, CVPR 2025) trains models up to 2B parameters on about 500K 3D objects and decodes one latent to radiance fields, 3D Gaussians, or meshes; it is MIT-licensed and needs a GPU with at least 16 GB.
TRELLIS.2 (4B parameters) outputs PBR-textured GLB assets in about 3 seconds at 512^3, 17 seconds at 1024^3, and 60 seconds at 1536^3 on an H100.
Hunyuan3D 2.0 (January 2025) released open shape and texture models; Hunyuan3D 2.1 (June 2025) added PBR texturing and training code and needs about 29 GB of VRAM for shape plus texture.
Roblox released Cube 3D text-to-shape (v0.1 March 2025, v0.5 July 2025) and CubePart part-controllable generation (May 2026) aimed at assets usable with animation, physics, and scripts.
inZOI's store page states that players can turn 2D images into in-game 3D objects, with AI tools described as auxiliary and generated content reviewed by the team.
inZOI received negative user reviews in May 2025 after Krafton announced its use of generative AI.

limitations: Hardware: 16 GB (TRELLIS) to about 29 GB (Hunyuan3D 2.1 shape plus texture) of GPU memory, so player-side generation usually runs in the cloud or on high-end PCs.
Output topology and UVs are not authored for animation or LOD; production use still needs cleanup and review, which inZOI states it applies.
Generated assets are single objects without gameplay semantics; the game must assign function, footprint, and value.
Training data provenance and licenses vary by model, and player reception of generative AI can be negative (inZOI reviews in 2025).
techniques.mechanism: Generation is split into shape and appearance. A flow-matching or diffusion transformer generates a 3D latent conditioned on an image or text: TRELLIS uses a Structured LATent (sparse voxels carrying features from a vision foundation model), Hunyuan3D-DiT a shape latent, and Roblox Cube discrete shape tokens predicted autoregressively. Decoders turn the latent into meshes, 3D Gaussians, or radiance fields. Texture is painted by a multi-view diffusion model (Hunyuan3D-Paint) or decoded directly, with 2025 versions emitting PBR maps (base color, roughness, metallic). Output is a GLB or OBJ file that drops into an engine like any other asset.
techniques.name: Text- and image-to-3D asset generation
techniques.summary: Open 3D generative models (TRELLIS, Hunyuan3D 2.x, Roblox Cube) produce textured meshes from a text prompt or image in seconds to a minute, and inZOI exposes image-to-3D object creation to players.

affects.note: The player can describe a behavior in language and the model writes, tests against the live game, and saves the program, so player code becomes a growing library of named skills rather than hand-typed scripts.
An NPC's competence can be an accumulating library of composable, verified routines it wrote itself, so skill growth adds new behaviors rather than raising a numeric speed or quality level.
A delegated controller can acquire routines for situations its designers did not code by writing and verifying new functions, instead of running the fixed opponent-AI logic restricted to a subsystem.
Exploration agents that unlock milestones 15.3x faster than earlier agents can be run as automated playtesters to measure how quickly and in what order a progression graph gets traversed.
Demonstrated routines can be stored as verified, reusable code skills that generalize to new locations.

key_results.text: Against prior LLM agents, Voyager obtained 3.3x more unique items, traveled 2.3x longer distances, and unlocked tech-tree milestones up to 15.3x faster, discovering 63 unique items in 160 prompting iterations.
The learned skill library let a fresh agent solve novel tasks in a new Minecraft world from scratch, where baselines struggled.
Code generation quality was the bottleneck: replacing GPT-4 with GPT-3.5 for code produced 5.7x fewer unique items, while GPT-4 cost 15x more per token.

In the 2025 Factorio Learning Environment, LLM agents writing code found growth strategies such as electric drilling but failed at complex automation such as electronic-circuit production, with weak spatial reasoning and error recovery.

limitations: Depends on a frontier code model; GPT-3.5 produced 5.7x fewer items and GPT-4 cost 15x more per token, so per-agent cost is high.
Hallucinated tasks and calls: the curriculum proposed items that do not exist (copper sword), and generated code used invalid inputs or functions absent from the API, causing execution errors.
Self-verification misjudges success (for example not recognizing a dropped string as proof a spider was defeated).
Needs a scripting API that exposes game actions and state as text; it does not act from pixels.
Long-horizon factory building in Factorio still fails at multi-step automation and spatial layout.
techniques.mechanism: Voyager drives a Minecraft bot through a JavaScript control API. An automatic curriculum asks GPT-4 for the next task given inventory, surroundings, and completed tasks, aiming to discover as many diverse things as possible. For each task GPT-4 writes a function that may call existing skills; the function runs, and the agent feeds back environment observations, execution errors, and a GPT-4 self-verification verdict, retrying up to four rounds before moving on. Verified functions are stored in a skill library indexed by an embedding of their description and retrieved (top-k) when writing later functions, so complex behaviors are composed from earlier ones. No model weights are trained; all learning is in the growing code library, which can be reused in a new world.
techniques.name: LLM-written skill libraries (Voyager)
techniques.summary: An LLM agent that proposes its own next task, writes executable code to do it, refines the code from execution errors and self-checks, and stores verified programs in a retrievable skill library.

affects.note: Rough player input becomes consistent detailed structure through constraint propagation over hundreds of modules: in Townscaper a click toggles one cell and the solver re-chooses compatible modules around it, so each placement reshapes its neighbors.

Tile maps can be generated from a small example or adjacency table instead of noise thresholds, giving locally coherent coastlines, cliffs, and interiors, as in Bad North's islands and Caves of Qud's areas; large-scale structure still needs another layer.
Buildings on painted zones could be assembled from modular tile sets constrained by neighbors and lot shape rather than authored per lot, varying silhouettes without new art for every building.

key_results.text: Maxim Gumin released WaveFunctionCollapse publicly on 2016-09-30 with overlapping and simple tiled models, and developers began experimenting with it within a day.
The WFC repository lists Bad North, Caves of Qud, Dead Static Drive, Townscaper, and Matrix Awakens as users, with adaptations for Unity, Unreal Engine 5, Godot 4, and Houdini.

Karth and Smith (FDG 2017) showed WFC is constraint solving with MRV ordering, frequency-weighted value choice, arc-consistency propagation, and global restarts; with an added global constraint restarts failed to finish within a minute while a backtracking solver resolved it quickly.

Townscaper runs WFC in real time on an irregular quad grid to choose building tiles from the surrounding shape and may fail silently where cells cannot fit, whereas Bad North restarts generation; Bad North uses over 300 tiles.
Caves of Qud, an early user of WFC alongside multipass generation, reached 1.0 on 2024-12-05 after early access began in 2015.
WFC constrains only nearby tiles, so it rarely produces large-scale structure without added constraints or other techniques.

limitations: Only local adjacency is enforced; reachability, room counts, or path lengths need extra constraints, and Karth and Smith found a global constraint caused hundreds of conflicts that restarts could not clear within a minute.
Contradictions are possible because the underlying problem is NP-hard; shipped systems restart (Bad North) or accept silent local failures (Townscaper).
Interactive generation delay grows with structure size, and the overlapping model is slower and can copy the example too closely.
Quality depends on an authored module set, often hundreds of tiles (Bad North uses over 300), so art cost moves into modules rather than disappearing.
techniques.mechanism: Each output cell starts with a domain of all tiles (simple tiled model) or of all N x N patterns extracted from one example image (overlapping model, typically N = 3). The solver repeatedly picks the undecided cell with the lowest Shannon entropy over its remaining options, a minimum-remaining-values heuristic, collapses it to one option sampled by that option's frequency in the example, and propagates: neighbors drop options that no longer have a compatible partner, which is arc consistency as in AC-3. If a domain empties, the attempt fails and the original algorithm restarts; later implementations add backtracking or local repair. Designers steer output with tile sets, adjacency rules, weights, pre-set cells, and extra global constraints. Townscaper runs it in real time on an irregular quad grid: the player toggles a cell's occupancy and the solver chooses compatible building modules from the surrounding shape, with decoration applied in a separate pass.
techniques.name: Wave Function Collapse and constraint-based tile generation
techniques.summary: An example-driven constraint solver that fills a grid by repeatedly collapsing the lowest-entropy cell to one tile and propagating adjacency constraints, shipped in games including Townscaper, Bad North, and Caves of Qud.

paper:
---
title: "The Grammar of Simulation"
subtitle: "A machine-readable atlas of simulation game mechanics and the mathematical, AI, ML, and LLM results that change them"
author:
  - Yohei Nakajima
  - SimGrammar contributors
date: "2026-10-23"
version: "0.1"
dataset_sha256: "9499ad51567d82756fa10261613dd985a7de2d71a0c9a6270898fdb778e90ddd"
bibliography: references.bib
---
## Abstract

Simulation games are built from a shared but undocumented vocabulary of rule-systems. This report makes that vocabulary explicit and machine-readable, then asks how mathematical, AI, ML, and LLM results from 2019 to 2026 change it. We decompose 174 simulation games (1968 to 2026, 31 subgenres) into 199 atomic mechanics, analyze each mechanic on its own (definition, levers, failure modes, dynamics, mathematical basis, and six anchored scores), map 45 techniques onto mechanics through 218 typed effect edges, and synthesize 43 design opportunities, each with a validation experiment and a dated, falsifiable prediction. All results are projections of a versioned dataset with provenance for every entity and a validator that keeps the report, wiki, tables, and graph consistent.

**Findings.**

1. **Simulation games are compositions of six layers**: substrate, dynamics, coupling, control, legibility, and pacing. Clustering games by the mechanics they use recovers design families (minds, builders, operators, planners) that cut across market subgenres; 10 of 12 clusters mix subgenres.
2. **The vocabulary was set early.** 67 percent of mechanics appear in a catalog game released by 2000. Later decades mostly deepened and recombined; 26.3 percent of possible mechanic pairs have ever co-occurred.
3. **Depth costs legibility.** Across mechanics, legibility falls as emergence potential rises (ρ = -0.42) and as compute cost rises (ρ = -0.35); emergence rises with tuning difficulty (ρ = 0.61). Legibility, more than compute, bounds how much coupling a commercial simulation can afford.
4. **AI techniques target what games show and say, not what they are built from.** Exposure concentrates in narrative, control, agent, and physics mechanics. 99 mechanics, carrying 48 percent of all mechanic uses in the catalog, are affected by no technique in the set. Explanation is the rarest effect a technique has on a mechanic (5 of 218 edges), although it addresses the binding constraint.
5. **What shipped mostly stays at the edge of simulation state.** Neural rendering, asset and motion generation, and language characters for dialogue and companionship have shipped; techniques that would replace rules or physics with learned prediction remain prototypes or research. 10 techniques in the set break reproducibility outright when used at runtime.
6. **The best near-term opportunities keep the simulation symbolic** and let learned models read, explain, decorate, and propose through validated, logged interfaces. The highest-priority opportunity is Why-query over the simulation log.

The dataset, schemas, contract, and every projection are open for extension; the procedure for contributors, human or agent, is in `AGENTS.md`.

## 1. Introduction

A simulation game is a game whose state changes by rules the player did not author and does not fully control. The player builds a road and the traffic is the city's reply; the player sets a tax and the citizens decide whether to stay. Everything distinctive about the form follows from that gap between intent and outcome: the pleasure of watching a system respond, the frustration of not understanding why it did, and the stories players tell about runs no designer scripted.

The genre is old and large. Its lineage runs from text programs on mainframes (a grain-and-population ledger in [Hamurabi](../wiki/game/hamurabi.md), a wagon party's rations in [The Oregon Trail](../wiki/game/oregon-trail.md)) through [SimCity](../wiki/game/simcity-1989.md) and [The Sims](../wiki/game/the-sims.md) to [Dwarf Fortress](../wiki/game/dwarf-fortress.md), [Factorio](../wiki/game/factorio.md), and [EVE Online](../wiki/game/eve-online.md). Its methods are less visible than its titles. Designers share a working vocabulary (needs meters, production chains, storytellers, overlays) but no common, inspectable map of which rule-systems exist, which games combine them, how each one fails, and which are near their ceilings.

That map matters now because the ceilings are moving. For forty years the depth of a simulation game was bounded by a few constraints: how much compute a consumer machine could spend per tick, how much content a studio could author, how much hidden state a player could understand, how tightly a multiplayer game had to stay deterministic, and how believable a rule-driven agent could be. Results from 2019 to 2026 in learned world models, language-model agents, learned physics, accelerated simulation, automated design, and on-device inference press on each of those constraints, unevenly and with new costs.

This report does four things:

1. **Catalogs** 174 simulation games across 31 subgenres, from 1968 to 2026, and decomposes each into the mechanics it uses (1823 typed game-to-mechanic edges, each marked core or supporting, with implementation notes for core mechanics).
2. **Analyzes** 199 mechanics one at a time: rule-level definition, player experience, design levers, failure modes, dynamics, mathematical basis, and six anchored scores (legibility, emergence potential, authoring cost, compute cost, tuning difficulty, AI leverage).
3. **Maps** 45 mathematical, AI, ML, and LLM techniques onto those mechanics through 218 typed `affects` edges that say how each technique changes each mechanic (replaces its substrate, deepens it, enables a new form, cuts its authoring cost, explains it, tunes it, or accelerates it).
4. **Synthesizes** 43 design opportunities, each with a validation experiment a small team could run and a falsifiable prediction with a resolve-by date.

Every number in this document is rendered from the dataset at build time; the dataset hash on the title page identifies the exact version. The report, the wiki, the tables, and the graph are projections of the same YAML files, so a correction to one entity updates all of them.

## 2. Method

### 2.1 Unit of analysis: the mechanic

A **mechanic** here is a rule-system that passes four admission tests (CONTRACT.md, I12):

- **Nameable.** Designers would recognize it in games other than the one being examined.
- **Atomic.** It owns one kind of state and one update rule. If it splits into two parts that each appear without the other in shipped games, it is two mechanics.
- **Tunable.** It has at least two levers.
- **Removable.** A game could drop it and keep running.

The tests exclude two common confusions. Dynamics such as "cascading failure" or "death spiral" are outcomes of coupled mechanics, so they appear in mechanics' `dynamics` fields rather than as entities. Genre-level patterns such as "colony management" are combinations, so they appear as game decompositions or opportunities. The result sits between the MDA framework's *mechanics* layer and a designer's pattern language: concrete enough to implement, general enough to recur.

Each mechanic belongs to one of 21 families, assigned by the state it owns rather than the genre it appears in: [Weather](../wiki/mechanic/weather.md) is environment, [Labor market](../wiki/mechanic/labor-market.md) is economy, [Agent inspection](../wiki/mechanic/agent-inspection.md) is information.

### 2.2 Corpus

The game catalog was built to cover every subgenre in the vocabulary, every lineage-defining title from the 1960s onward, recent releases through 2026, research demonstrations that run as interactive simulations (such as [Generative Agents (Smallville)](../wiki/game/generative-agents-smallville.md) and [Project Sid](../wiki/game/project-sid.md)), and works included for a single mechanic (marked `boundary_case`; 20 such works). The catalog is a purposive sample, not a census: prevalence figures describe this corpus, and the earliest-appearance year of a mechanic is a lower bound on its true origin.

### 2.3 Schema and scoring

Every categorical field draws from a closed vocabulary (`vocab/`), and every ordinal field names an anchored rubric (`vocab/rubrics.yaml`). Scorers match the anchor text and take the lower anchor when between two. This trades resolution for consistency across contributors: a 3 in legibility means "understood after deliberate attention and the game's info tools" whoever assigned it. Scores are expert judgments, recorded as such, and the rubric for each is reproduced in the wiki.

Relations are typed edges with one owner each (`vocab/edge_types.yaml`). Inverses (which games use a mechanic, which techniques affect it) and all aggregates (prevalence, earliest appearance, clusters, technique exposure, opportunity priority) are computed by the build and never stored, so they cannot drift from the edges they summarize.

### 2.4 Evidence

Each entity carries an epistemic status. `asserted` means written from domain knowledge without a citation; `sourced` means at least one cited source supports its factual fields; `verified` requires a second, independent run. Techniques must always cite. At this version, 388 entities are sourced or verified and 72 remain asserted; the asserted ones form a public verification queue (`dist/analysis/verification-queue.csv`).

### 2.5 Production

The dataset was produced by parallel research runs, each recorded in `log/runs/` with its operator, model, method, and the proposals it could not act on. Runs partitioned work by file, not by topic, so no two runs edited the same entity. Taxonomy runs analyzed mechanics; catalog runs verified release facts against public sources and decomposed games; technique runs searched the 2019 to 2026 literature and developer announcements. A validator enforcing the rules in CONTRACT.md §5 gated every merge. The same procedure (AGENTS.md) is what a new contributor, human or agent, follows.

### 2.6 Limitations

- **Sampling.** Commercial, English-language, PC-centric titles are over-represented; mobile management games and non-Western simulation traditions are under-represented.
- **Scoring.** Rubric scores are single-rater judgments in this version. The `verified` status and the review field exist so a second rater can confirm or contest them.
- **Decomposition depth.** A game's mechanic list records what is present and meaningful, not a complete specification. Absence of an edge is weak evidence of absence.
- **Recency.** Technique maturity and horizon are judged as of the run date and age quickly; each technique records the sources the judgment rests on.

## 4. A grammar of simulation games

### 4.1 Six layers

Decomposing the catalog suggests that every simulation game is assembled from six layers. A mechanic usually lives in one layer, and a game's character comes from which layers it invests in.

1. **Substrate: what exists.** State is held as aggregate stocks (a treasury, a population count), individual agents (a colonist with needs), fields on a grid (pollution, temperature, land value), networks (roads, pipes, social ties), or continuous bodies (a wing, a chassis). The substrate fixes the cost curve: aggregates are cheap and faceless, agents are expensive and legible, fields scale with map area, continuous physics scales with contacts and timestep. The `substrate` field on every mechanic records this (
| Substrate | Mechanics |
|---|---:|
| Rule system | 107 |
| Agent-based | 70 |
| Aggregate stocks | 69 |
| Cellular grid | 38 |
| Stochastic events | 33 |
| Network / graph | 31 |
| Continuous physics | 18 |
| Player-authored logic | 9 |
| UI layer | 9 |
| Learned model | 4 |
).
2. **Dynamics: how it changes.** Update rules form feedback loops. Most simulation games pair a reinforcing growth loop (more citizens, more taxes, more buildings) with balancing loops that resist it (congestion, pollution, unrest, raids). Difficulty is the relative strength of those loops; a death spiral is a reinforcing loop running in reverse. The `feedback` field records the dominant polarity per mechanic.
3. **Coupling: how subsystems touch.** Depth comes less from the number of systems than from how many share state. Systems couple through shared stocks (power, money, labor), shared space (a factory lowers neighboring land value), and shared agents (the same colonist hauls, eats, and grieves). [Dwarf Fortress](../wiki/game/dwarf-fortress.md) is deep because nearly everything touches nearly everything else; a game with many isolated systems feels like many small games.
4. **Control: how intent enters.** The player acts directly (an avatar, a unit), places and zones, sets parameters, issues orders that agents pick up, writes programs, or speaks. Each step away from direct control widens the *control gap*, the designed distance between what the player wants and what happens. Too narrow and the game is a toy; too wide and the player is a spectator.

5. **Legibility: how state leaves.** Overlays, inspectors, tooltips, advisors, alerts, graphs, chronicles, and forecasts expose hidden state. This layer is what lets deep simulations ship: [RimWorld](../wiki/game/rimworld.md) itemizes every mood modifier, and Paradox games nest tooltips until each number decomposes into causes. Legibility mechanics own no simulation state of their own; they are the interface between coupling and comprehension.
6. **Pacing and stakes: when the player looks and what can be lost.** Time models (pause, speed, turns, wall clock), failure models (soft setbacks, permadeath, cascading collapse), and narrative directors decide when attention is demanded and what a mistake costs.

A compact description of a simulation game is its investment profile across these layers. City builders invest in substrate (fields and networks) and legibility (overlays); colony sims in agents, coupling, and pacing (storytellers); vehicle sims in continuous substrate and direct control; programming games in control alone, with nearly no hidden state. The clustering in §5 recovers these profiles from the data without being told the subgenres.

### 4.2 The families, one at a time

Each family below is described by the state it owns, its canonical mechanics, how it characteristically fails, and what it couples to. #### Resources and production
Owns stocks of goods and the recipes that transform them. ### 5.2 How the vocabulary grew


![Cumulative count of mechanics by first appearance in the dataset. Steps mark the years a design vocabulary expanded.](figures/mechanic-accumulation.svg)

*Figure: Cumulative count of mechanics by first appearance in the dataset. Steps mark the years a design vocabulary expanded.*


67 percent of mechanics appear in at least one catalog game released by 2000. The 1980s and 1990s supplied most of the vocabulary: [SimCity](../wiki/game/simcity-1989.md) (zoning, land value, overlays, disasters), [Populous](../wiki/game/populous.md) (terraforming as a god power), [Railroad Tycoon](../wiki/game/railroad-tycoon.md) and [Transport Tycoon](../wiki/game/transport-tycoon.md) (route scheduling and competitors), [Theme Park](../wiki/game/theme-park.md) and [Theme Hospital](../wiki/game/theme-hospital.md) (crowds with preferences, queues, diagnosis), [Creatures](../wiki/game/creatures.md) (learning creatures and genetics), and [The Sims](../wiki/game/the-sims.md) at the boundary (smart objects). Later decades mostly recombined, deepened, and scaled existing mechanics; the additions after 2010 are concentrated in material simulation, programmable automation, and runtime language.

### 5.3 Which mechanics travel together

Co-occurrence lift measures how much more often two mechanics share a game than independence predicts. Several groupings are informative. Life sims, colony sims, and virtual pets share a cluster built on personality, needs, and relationships: [The Sims](../wiki/game/the-sims.md), [RimWorld](../wiki/game/rimworld.md), [Dwarf Fortress](../wiki/game/dwarf-fortress.md), and [Creatures](../wiki/game/creatures.md) are all games about minds. Physics sandboxes, construction games, programming puzzles, and hands-on job sims such as [PowerWash Simulator](../wiki/game/powerwash-simulator.md) and [PC Building Simulator](../wiki/game/pc-building-simulator.md) cluster around modular assembly and physical manipulation: they are build-or-fix-then-test games. Vehicle and flight sims form a separate cluster around embodied skill and weather. City builders, factory games, and grand strategy share the largest cluster, organized by production chains and tech trees: [Factorio](../wiki/game/factorio.md), [Anno 1800](../wiki/game/anno-1800.md), and [Europa Universalis IV](../wiki/game/europa-universalis-4.md) are all planning economies. The SimCity lineage stands apart on zoning, land value, and traffic. Inspection and dilemma games ([Papers, Please](../wiki/game/papers-please.md), [Reigns](../wiki/game/reigns.md), [Suzerain](../wiki/game/suzerain.md), [This War of Mine](../wiki/game/this-war-of-mine.md)) cluster on authored event structures despite belonging to different subgenres. The AI-native titles form their own cluster around generated content and natural-language interaction, separate from the life sims they superficially resemble.

These families correspond to the six-layer profiles in §4.1: the minds family invests in agents and social coupling; the builders in control and continuous substrate; the operators in direct control and physics; the planners in stocks, networks, and legibility.

### 5.6 The legibility frontier

Across all mechanics, legibility and emergence potential are negatively correlated (Spearman ρ = -0.42, p <0.001), and emergence potential is strongly correlated with tuning difficulty (ρ = 0.61, p <0.001). Mechanics that generate unscripted variety are harder to understand and harder to balance. Legibility also falls as compute cost rises (ρ = -0.35, p <0.001): expensive simulation tends to be hidden simulation.

These scores are expert judgments, so the correlations measure the structure of design knowledge rather than a property measured in players. They nevertheless agree with a constraint every simulation designer reports: depth, legibility, and balance cannot all be maximized with rules alone.

## 6. Five ceilings

Simulation design has been shaped less by imagination than by five constraints. Each one explains a family of conventions, and each one is the target of a different group of techniques in §7.

### 6.1 Compute per tick

A consumer machine must advance the whole simulation many times per second while rendering it. The constraint explains why city builders simulate aggregate populations with a sample of visible agents, why per-particle material simulation ([Falling-sand materials](../wiki/mechanic/falling-sand-materials.md), [Fluid and gas simulation](../wiki/mechanic/fluid-gas-simulation.md)) appears in 2D or small arenas, why late-game slowdown is a genre-wide complaint, and why [Agent pathfinding](../wiki/mechanic/agent-pathfinding.md) and [Traffic congestion](../wiki/mechanic/traffic-congestion.md) are the usual bottlenecks. Mechanics scored 4 or 5 on compute cost are the ones whose scale is capped by hardware rather than design.

**Relaxed by:** GPU-parallel and accelerated simulation, learned surrogates for physics and weather, mean-field approximations for large populations, and inference-efficient models for agent decisions.

### 6.2 Authoring cost

Every unit of variety in some mechanics must be made by hand: an animation for each interaction, a line of dialogue for each social exchange, an event for each situation, an asset for each catalog entry. Mechanics with high authoring cost are capped by budgets, and players exhaust them; this is why event decks repeat, why villagers recycle requests, and why social systems in rule-based games read as formulaic. Across mechanics, authoring cost and judged AI leverage have a Spearman correlation of 0.34 (p <0.001): the mechanics most limited by content budgets are, on expert judgment, the ones most open to generative techniques.

**Relaxed by:** constrained language generation for events and dialogue, text-to-3D and neural rendering for assets, learned motion for animation, and procedural generation with learned priors.

### 6.3 Legibility

Players must form a working model of why the simulation did what it did, or they experience the depth as randomness. Rubric scores show the tension directly: across mechanics, legibility and emergence potential correlate at -0.42 (p <0.001). The mechanics that generate the most unscripted variety are the hardest to understand.


![Each mechanic placed by rubric legibility (x) and emergence potential (y); area ~ number of games using it. Jitter is deterministic.](figures/legibility-vs-emergence.svg)

*Figure: Each mechanic placed by rubric legibility (x) and emergence potential (y); area ~ number of games using it. Jitter is deterministic.*


Designers have answered with a whole family of mechanics that own no simulation state ([Data overlays](../wiki/mechanic/data-overlays.md), [Causal breakdown tooltips](../wiki/mechanic/causal-tooltips.md), [Agent inspection](../wiki/mechanic/agent-inspection.md), [History chronicle](../wiki/mechanic/history-chronicle.md)). Legibility, not compute, is often the binding constraint on how much coupling a commercial game can afford.

**Relaxed by:** language models that read state and event logs and explain causes, forecasting by simulating futures, and learned surrogates that make expensive hidden fields cheap to visualize.

### 6.4 Determinism

Replays, lockstep multiplayer, bug reproduction, competitive leaderboards, and save integrity require that the same inputs produce the same state. [Factorio](../wiki/game/factorio.md)'s multiplayer depends on it. Determinism has kept stochastic or learned components out of authoritative game state, and it is the constraint that most runtime AI techniques violate: of the 45 techniques here, 10 break reproducibility outright when used at runtime (see `determinism_impact`).

**Relaxed by:** recording model outputs as events so replays read the log rather than re-call the model, splitting authoritative symbolic state from non-authoritative generated presentation, and constrained decoding that maps open-ended outputs into typed, validated state changes.

### 6.5 Believability of agents

Rule-driven agents are legible and cheap but shallow: their utilities are visible formulas and their speech is canned. The constraint shapes the genre's preference for many shallow agents ([Crowd preferences](../wiki/mechanic/crowd-preferences.md)) or few agents with thick systemic state ([Memories and thoughts](../wiki/mechanic/memories-thoughts.md), [Injury body model](../wiki/mechanic/injury-body-model.md)) over agents with rich minds.

**Relaxed by:** language-model agents with memory and reflection, models trained to predict human choices, and small local models that make per-agent language affordable.

### 6.6 What the ceilings imply

The five constraints do not move together. Compute and authoring cost are being relaxed fastest, with techniques already shipped. Agent believability is being relaxed at a new cost in determinism and legibility. Legibility is the constraint most worth attacking deliberately, because a deeper simulation is worthless if no one can read it, and it is also where the techniques are most mature relative to their use: explanation over structured state is an application of capabilities that already exist.

Of 45 techniques, 1 is shipped as a genre norm, 12 are shipped in at least one commercial game, 10 exist as public prototypes, and 22 are research only. The shipped ones cluster in three places: rendering and assets ([Neural rendering in the graphics pipeline](../wiki/technique/neural-rendering-shaders.md), [ML reconstruction of the planet from aerial imagery](../wiki/technique/satellite-world-reconstruction.md), [Text- and image-to-3D asset generation](../wiki/technique/text-to-3d-assets.md), [Learned kinematic motion synthesis](../wiki/technique/learned-motion-synthesis.md)), language characters ([Generative agents (memory stream, reflection, planning)](../wiki/technique/generative-agents.md), [On-device small language models for characters](../wiki/technique/on-device-language-models.md), [Realtime speech-to-speech and expressive TTS for characters](../wiki/technique/realtime-voice-models.md), [LLM game master and narrative director](../wiki/technique/llm-game-master.md), [LLM-adjudicated state transitions (LLM as game mechanic)](../wiki/technique/llm-rule-adjudication.md)), and older search and learning methods ([Monte Carlo tree search for game AI](../wiki/technique/monte-carlo-tree-search.md), [Wave Function Collapse and constraint-based tile generation](../wiki/technique/wave-function-collapse.md), [Deep reinforcement learning policies for NPC opponents and navigation](../wiki/technique/deep-rl-npc-policies.md), [Agent-based automated playtesting and balancing](../wiki/technique/automated-playtesting.md)). Almost nothing that touches the authoritative simulation state of a simulation game has shipped.

### 7.2 Adoption and reception

Generative AI has moved from novelty to a measurable share of releases. Disclosures on Steam rose from about a thousand games in April 2024 [[1](#ref-src-totallyhuman-2024-steam-genai-count)] to 7,818 Steam titles, a little under a fifth of 2025 releases, by July 2025 [[2](#ref-src-totallyhuman-2025-steam-genai-count)], and an estimate in November 2025 put games with disclosures at roughly 8 percent of the store with about 660 million dollars in combined gross [[3](#ref-src-totallyhuman-2025-steam-ai-revenue)]. Most disclosures concern pre-generated visual assets rather than runtime systems. Valve's survey distinguishes pre-generated from live-generated content and requires the latter to describe its guardrails [[4](#ref-src-valve-2026-steamworks-content-survey)].

Developer sentiment moved the other way. In GDC's 2026 survey, 36 percent of respondents used generative AI at work, while the share who believe it harms the industry rose to 52 percent from 30 percent a year earlier [[5](#ref-src-gdc-2025-state-of-industry), [6](#ref-src-gdc-2026-state-of-industry)]. Player reception has been mixed in visible cases: [inZOI](../wiki/game/inzoi.md) sold strongly at launch and drew negative reviews after announcing generative features [[7](#ref-src-wikipedia-inzoi)]; ARC Raiders was criticized for synthetic voice lines, some of which were later re-recorded by actors [[8](#ref-src-wikipedia-arc-raiders)].

Runtime language characters did ship. On-device small language models power companions and simulated people in PUBG Ally, inZOI's Smart Zoi, and NARAKA's teammate [[9](#ref-src-nvidia-2025-ace-companions), [10](#ref-src-krafton-2026-pubg-ally-beta)]; [Where Winds Meet](../wiki/game/where-winds-meet.md) discloses live NPC text and voice chat [[11](#ref-src-steam-2025-where-winds-meet)]. The cost of realtime speech fell by about a fifth between the 2024 and 2025 versions of one leading API [[12](#ref-src-openai-2024-realtime-api), [13](#ref-src-openai-2025-gpt-realtime)], and specialized text-to-speech vendors price in cents per minute [[14](#ref-src-inworld-2026-tts-1-5)]. Cost remains the stated wall for frame-generating world models: the consumer Genie product caps each world at sixty seconds of play [[15](#ref-src-techcrunch-2026-project-genie)].

Among rendering techniques, neural upscaling and frame generation are the one area where learned models are a norm, with hundreds of supported titles [[16](#ref-src-nvidia-2026-dlss-4-5)]. They never touch simulation state, which is why they could spread.

### 7.3 Seven clusters

**Frame-generating world models.** [Diffusion and autoregressive neural game engines](../wiki/technique/diffusion-game-engines.md), [Genie foundation world models](../wiki/technique/genie-world-models.md), [Muse World and Human Action Model (WHAM)](../wiki/technique/muse-wham.md), and [Open real-time interactive video world models](../wiki/technique/open-interactive-video-models.md) learn to predict the next frame from recent frames and player input, so the model is the engine. They produce convincing short interactions and fail at what simulation games need most: exact persistent state, long memory, and inspectable causes. Their realistic near-term role is ideation, previsualization, and non-authoritative views (§9).

**3D, rendering, and assets.** [3D Gaussian Splatting](../wiki/technique/gaussian-splatting.md), [Prompt-to-persistent 3D world generation](../wiki/technique/generated-3d-worlds.md), [Text- and image-to-3D asset generation](../wiki/technique/text-to-3d-assets.md), [Neural rendering in the graphics pipeline](../wiki/technique/neural-rendering-shaders.md), [Real-time generative restyling of game video](../wiki/technique/real-time-video-restyling.md), and [ML reconstruction of the planet from aerial imagery](../wiki/technique/satellite-world-reconstruction.md) cut the authoring cost of what the simulation is drawn with, leaving rules untouched. They are the most mature and the least controversial technically; their risks are provenance and reception.

**Motion.** [Learned kinematic motion synthesis](../wiki/technique/learned-motion-synthesis.md) has shipped in sports and life games; [Learned physics-based character control](../wiki/technique/physics-based-character-control.md) remains research. Both matter to simulation games because canned animation is how most agents' internal states are (poorly) displayed.

**Language agents and dialogue.** [Generative agents (memory stream, reflection, planning)](../wiki/technique/generative-agents.md), [Many-agent LLM societies](../wiki/technique/llm-agent-societies.md), [LLM models of individual human choice](../wiki/technique/human-behavior-simulation-models.md), [On-device small language models for characters](../wiki/technique/on-device-language-models.md), [Grammar-constrained decoding for valid game actions](../wiki/technique/constrained-decoding.md), [Realtime speech-to-speech and expressive TTS for characters](../wiki/technique/realtime-voice-models.md), [LLM game master and narrative director](../wiki/technique/llm-game-master.md), [LLM explanation of simulation state](../wiki/technique/llm-explanation-of-state.md), and [LLM-adjudicated state transitions (LLM as game mechanic)](../wiki/technique/llm-rule-adjudication.md) change who decides what agents do and say, who narrates, and who explains. They relax the authoring and believability ceilings at a cost in determinism and consistency.

**Planning and game theory.** [Monte Carlo tree search for game AI](../wiki/technique/monte-carlo-tree-search.md), [Self-play planning with learned models (AlphaZero, MuZero, Dreamer)](../wiki/technique/model-based-planning-muzero.md), [Regret minimization and search for imperfect-information games](../wiki/technique/imperfect-information-solvers.md), [Language models grounded in strategic planning for negotiation games](../wiki/technique/cicero-strategic-dialogue.md), [Deep reinforcement learning policies for NPC opponents and navigation](../wiki/technique/deep-rl-npc-policies.md), and [Mean field games and mean-field learning](../wiki/technique/mean-field-games.md) produce strong opponents and equilibrium-consistent populations. Their game deployments are few because strength is rarely the design goal; believable and tunable opponents are.

**Design automation.** [Wave Function Collapse and constraint-based tile generation](../wiki/technique/wave-function-collapse.md), [Quality-diversity search (MAP-Elites) for content and balance](../wiki/technique/quality-diversity-search.md), [Learned level and map generation (PCGRL, MarioGPT, LLM generators)](../wiki/technique/learned-level-generation.md), [Automated generation of game rules and mechanics](../wiki/technique/automated-rule-generation.md), [Agent-based automated playtesting and balancing](../wiki/technique/automated-playtesting.md), [Open-ended co-generation of environments and agents](../wiki/technique/open-ended-environment-generation.md), [LLM-written skill libraries (Voyager)](../wiki/technique/voyager-skill-libraries.md), [Generalist instructable game agents (SIMA)](../wiki/technique/generalist-game-agents.md), and [LLM-guided evolutionary program search](../wiki/technique/alphaevolve-algorithm-discovery.md) work on the developer's side: generating content and rules, finding exploits, and estimating difficulty. They preserve determinism because they run offline.

**Simulation science.** [Massively parallel GPU simulation](../wiki/technique/massively-parallel-simulation.md), [Differentiable simulation](../wiki/technique/differentiable-simulation.md), [Graph network simulators and neural operators](../wiki/technique/graph-network-simulators.md), [Subspace neural physics and learned deformers](../wiki/technique/subspace-neural-physics.md), [Machine-learned weather forecasting](../wiki/technique/ml-weather-models.md), [Neural cellular automata](../wiki/technique/neural-cellular-automata.md), [Continuous cellular automata and foundation-model search for artificial life](../wiki/technique/continuous-alife-and-asal.md), and [Simulation-based inference for calibrating simulators](../wiki/technique/simulation-based-inference.md) come from robotics, physics, climate, and artificial life. They relax the compute ceiling and make calibration possible, and they are the least connected to game development today: an operational ML weather model runs at about a thousandth of the energy of the physics model it complements [[17](#ref-src-ecmwf-2025-aifs-operational)], yet none of these techniques is confirmed at runtime in a catalog game.

## 8. Where the techniques land

### 8.1 How techniques change mechanics

Each `affects` edge records one of seven effects. Across 218 edges the most common effect is *deepens* (74 edges): the technique makes an existing mechanic richer, larger, or more varied without changing its role. Explanation is the rarest effect (5 edges), although §6 argued that legibility is often the binding constraint on simulation depth.


| effect | edges |
|---|---|
| deepens | 74 |
| enables-new | 51 |
| replaces-substrate | 33 |
| tunes | 32 |
| cuts-authoring-cost | 13 |
| accelerates | 10 |
| explains | 5 |

*How techniques change mechanics, by effect type.*


The imbalance is a finding about where research effort points. Generating content and replacing substrates (rule-based behavior with language models, numerical physics with learned dynamics) attract most work; explaining a simulation to the person playing it attracts little, even though the techniques it needs (retrieval over structured logs, constrained generation, summarization) are among the most mature.

Exposure concentrates in four families: narrative and generation, control and automation, agents and behavior, and physics and materials: the layers where content is expensive to author or where behavior is expensive to compute. It is low across the economic and logistic core of the genre (resources, logistics, economy, population) and lowest of all in operation and procedure. 99 mechanics are affected by no technique in the set, and they account for 48 percent of all game-to-mechanic uses in the catalog. Of the ten most widely used mechanics, 6 have no technique attached.

In other words, current AI research mostly targets what a simulation game shows and says, not the rule-systems most simulation games are built from. That is partly sensible (production chains and budgets are cheap and legible already) and partly a gap: the economic core is where balance work, legibility problems, and authoring of recipes and scenarios consume design time.

### 8.5 Authoritative state versus presentation

The techniques divide cleanly by whether they touch authoritative simulation state. Those that only change presentation (neural upscaling and frame generation, restyling, asset generation, motion synthesis) preserve determinism and have shipped. Those that would replace rules or physics with learned prediction remain prototypes or research in games. Language characters sit in between: they have shipped, but as companions and conversation partners at the edge of the simulation, and they belong to the 10 techniques that break reproducibility outright when used at runtime. The pattern suggests a design principle that recurs through §9: keep the simulation symbolic, typed, and logged, and let learned models read it, explain it, decorate it, and propose changes to it through validated interfaces.

### 9.2 Five design principles

The opportunities share a small set of principles, each a response to the ceilings in §6 and the evidence in §8.

1. **Keep the simulation symbolic; let models read, explain, decorate, and propose.** Authoritative state stays typed and deterministic. Learned models sit around it as renderers, narrators, explainers, and proposal generators whose outputs pass through validators ([Symbolic simulation, neural rendering](../wiki/opportunity/symbolic-sim-neural-render.md), [Content-elastic event systems](../wiki/opportunity/content-elastic-events.md), [Natural-language legislation](../wiki/opportunity/natural-language-legislation.md)).
2. **Spend inference on salience.** Most ticks need no model. Calls at moments that matter, cached and logged, buy believability at bounded cost ([Salience-gated language agents](../wiki/opportunity/salience-gated-llm-agents.md), [Drama-aware storyteller](../wiki/opportunity/drama-aware-storyteller.md), [Local-first AI simulation games](../wiki/opportunity/local-first-ai-sims.md)).
3. **Explain before you generate.** The binding constraint on depth is comprehension, and explanation is the least-targeted effect in the technique graph. Explanation over logs and sensitivity analysis is mature and underused ([Why-query over the simulation log](../wiki/opportunity/causal-why-query.md), [Bottleneck explainer for production networks](../wiki/opportunity/bottleneck-explainer.md), [Branch preview of policy futures](../wiki/opportunity/branch-preview-forecasts.md), [Illustrated chronicles](../wiki/opportunity/illustrated-chronicles.md)).
4. **Generate offline, verify with agents.** Content, recipes, scenarios, mods, and balance can be generated at design time and checked by automated play before any player sees them ([Parallel autobalancing of economies](../wiki/opportunity/parallel-autobalance.md), [Generated recipe graphs](../wiki/opportunity/generated-recipe-graphs.md), [Quality-diversity scenario libraries](../wiki/opportunity/qd-scenario-libraries.md), [Mechanic modding by description](../wiki/opportunity/language-modding.md)).
5. **Log every model call as an event.** Recording outputs restores replay, multiplayer sync, bug reproduction, and auditability, and the same log powers explanation, forecasting, and chronicles ([Event-sourced simulation runtime](../wiki/opportunity/event-sourced-sim-runtime.md)).

### 9.3 By the ceiling they relax

**Legibility.** [Why-query over the simulation log](../wiki/opportunity/causal-why-query.md) answers why-questions from the event log; [Bottleneck explainer for production networks](../wiki/opportunity/bottleneck-explainer.md) points at the binding constraint in production networks, the most-used and least-AI-exposed part of the genre; [Branch preview of policy futures](../wiki/opportunity/branch-preview-forecasts.md) shows distributions of futures before a decision; [Explained delegation to AI managers](../wiki/opportunity/explained-delegation.md) makes delegated subsystems accountable; [Simulator instructor coaching](../wiki/opportunity/sim-instructor-coach.md) narrates mistakes in operation sims.

**Authoring cost.** [Content-elastic event systems](../wiki/opportunity/content-elastic-events.md) removes the ceiling on event decks; [Generated inspection shifts](../wiki/opportunity/generated-inspection-shifts.md) gives rule-checking games endless fair cases; [Generative decoration catalogs](../wiki/opportunity/generative-decoration-catalogs.md) and [Learned build assist for cities](../wiki/opportunity/learned-build-assist.md) widen creative modes; [Generated recipe graphs](../wiki/opportunity/generated-recipe-graphs.md) and [Quality-diversity scenario libraries](../wiki/opportunity/qd-scenario-libraries.md) cut the cost of progression content; [Mechanic modding by description](../wiki/opportunity/language-modding.md) hands extension to players.

**Agent believability.** [Salience-gated language agents](../wiki/opportunity/salience-gated-llm-agents.md) gives colony and life sims specific minds at bounded cost; [Drama-aware storyteller](../wiki/opportunity/drama-aware-storyteller.md) picks events for characters' arcs; [Negotiating faction AI](../wiki/opportunity/negotiating-faction-ai.md) lets rivals bargain and remember; [Human-calibrated customers](../wiki/opportunity/human-calibrated-customers.md) grounds crowds in models of real choice; [Trainable creatures revival](../wiki/opportunity/trainable-creatures-revival.md) returns to learned creatures with modern learning; [Learned motion for simulated crowds](../wiki/opportunity/neural-npc-motion.md) shows internal state in movement.

**Compute.** [Learned material surrogates at world scale](../wiki/opportunity/learned-material-surrogates.md) extends particle-level materials to whole worlds; [Mean-field crowds and traffic](../wiki/opportunity/mean-field-crowds.md) lets cities hold equilibrium-consistent populations; [Learned regional weather](../wiki/opportunity/learned-weather-layer.md) and [Weather-coupled energy grids](../wiki/opportunity/weather-coupled-grids.md) bring realistic weather at negligible cost.

**Determinism and infrastructure.** [Event-sourced simulation runtime](../wiki/opportunity/event-sourced-sim-runtime.md) and [Local-first AI simulation games](../wiki/opportunity/local-first-ai-sims.md) make AI components operable in long-lived, offline, moddable games; [Symbolic simulation, neural rendering](../wiki/opportunity/symbolic-sim-neural-render.md) separates what must be exact from what may be generated.

**New forms.** [Language-agent society terrarium](../wiki/opportunity/llm-society-terrarium.md) makes watching a language-agent society the game; [Open-ended evolution sandbox](../wiki/opportunity/open-ended-evolution-sandbox.md) builds evolution games on continuous artificial life; [Specification programming games](../wiki/opportunity/specification-programming-games.md) turns programming puzzles into specification and testing; [Intent-level orders](../wiki/opportunity/intent-level-orders.md) and [Teachable sim companion](../wiki/opportunity/teachable-sim-companion.md) move control from clicks to intent and demonstration; [Agent ambassadors between player worlds](../wiki/opportunity/agent-ambassadors-async.md) links single-player worlds through negotiating envoys; [Generated dream and replay views](../wiki/opportunity/dream-replay-layer.md) gives world models a role where drift is a feature; [Factories with a living workforce](../wiki/opportunity/living-workforce-factories.md), [Placement that tells stories](../wiki/opportunity/placement-that-tells-stories.md), and [Research by named scientists](../wiki/opportunity/scientists-not-tech-trees.md) fill white space between common mechanics.

**Beyond entertainment.** [Simulation games as agent benchmarks](../wiki/opportunity/sims-as-agent-benchmarks.md) offers simulation games as long-horizon evaluation environments for AI agents; [Participatory planning sandboxes](../wiki/opportunity/participatory-planning-sandboxes.md) and [Calibrated serious simulations](../wiki/opportunity/calibrated-serious-sims.md) carry calibrated models into planning and education; [Automated mechanic discovery](../wiki/opportunity/mechanic-discovery-search.md) uses this taxonomy as a search space for new mechanics.

### 9.4 Where to start, by kind of builder

- **A small studio** should look first at opportunities with feasibility 4 or 5 and horizon "now": legibility layers over an existing simulation, content-elastic events with validators, salience-gated agents on a local model, and offline balancing. Each can ship as a feature of a conventional design.
- **An engine, middleware, or tools company** has the infrastructure opportunities: event-sourced runtimes with model-call logging, constrained interfaces from language to game actions, headless simulation for agent testing, and calibrated surrogate libraries for weather and materials.
- **A research group** has the open problems: symbolic-to-neural rendering with semantic fidelity guarantees, learned material surrogates that conserve mass and energy, automated discovery of mechanics, and evaluation of explanation quality in games.
- **Organizations outside games** can use simulation games as instruments: agent benchmarks, planning sandboxes, and calibrated serious simulations, where the genre's legibility layer is as valuable as its models.

## 10. Risks and open problems

The opportunities in §9 inherit the risks of their techniques. Each technique records its primary risks from a closed vocabulary:


| Risk | Techniques |
|---|---:|
| Controllability | 34 |
| Compute cost | 29 |
| Evaluation difficulty | 24 |
| Consistency / hallucination | 20 |
| Latency | 13 |
| IP / provenance | 9 |
| Legibility | 9 |
| Player trust / reception | 9 |
| Content safety | 7 |
| Labor displacement | 7 |
| Determinism | 1 |


**Consistency.** Language and world models contradict state, forget, and drift. In a simulation game a contradiction is worse than a gap, because players use the simulation's outputs to build mental models. Constrained decoding, typed write-back, and grounding every generated claim in logged state are necessary; none is sufficient for open-ended generation.

**Determinism.** Runtime generation breaks replays, lockstep multiplayer, and bug reproduction unless outputs are recorded and replayed as events. Games that already depend on determinism (competitive leaderboards, large multiplayer factories) should treat model outputs as inputs from an external system, logged at the boundary.

**Cost.** Per-player-hour inference conflicts with one-time purchases and with how long simulation players play. Local models, salience gating, and caching bound cost; frame-generating world models remain far from affordable at the session lengths simulation games require, as the sixty-second cap on the first consumer world-model product shows [[15](#ref-src-techcrunch-2026-project-genie)].

**Legibility of learned systems.** A learned policy or generated rule can be as opaque as the simulation it replaced. Every learned component that affects state needs an explanation path, or it moves a mechanic down the legibility scale in §5.6.

**Evaluation.** Open-ended outputs are hard to QA. Automated playtesting checks validity and balance, not quality; human evaluation does not scale to generated variety. Simulation games need evaluation methods for generated content analogous to the verification queue in this dataset: sampled, scored against anchors, and logged.

**Player trust and labor.** Reception of generative features has been mixed, and developers' view of generative AI's effect on the industry has turned more negative even as use has grown (§7.2). Disclosure rules on the largest PC store already distinguish pre-generated from live-generated content [[4](#ref-src-valve-2026-steamworks-content-survey)]. Opportunities that make games more legible or let players author more (explanation, modding by description, intent-level orders) are less exposed to this risk than those that replace authored work.

**Safety and provenance.** Live generation in social simulations needs content guardrails, especially where players can steer characters with language. Asset generation carries training-data and likeness questions. These risks are recorded per technique so they can be filtered and tracked.

**Open research problems** recorded on mechanic and technique pages include: grounding generated explanations in simulation logs with measurable faithfulness; conservation guarantees for learned physics; semantic fidelity for neural rendering of symbolic state; inferring needs and preferences from behavior instead of declaring them; and fair, inspectable AI participants in player economies.

### 11.1 Agenda

1. **Instrument a simulation for explanation.** Build the event log with cause links that why-queries, branch previews, and chronicles all need, and measure explanation faithfulness against human audit.
2. **Measure legibility in players, not only in rubrics.** The legibility and emergence scores here are expert judgments; a shared protocol for measuring how quickly players form correct causal models would let designers compare mechanics empirically.
3. **Connect techniques to the economic core.** Production, logistics, and economy mechanics are the most used and the least targeted by current techniques (§8.2). Balance search, recipe generation, and bottleneck explanation are tractable first steps.
4. **Separate authoritative and generated layers.** Develop and benchmark architectures where learned models render, narrate, or propose, and symbolic state decides.
5. **Extend the dataset.** Add mobile and non-English simulation traditions, score mechanics with a second rater, resolve the verification queue, and record design tensions with evidence from postmortems.

### 11.2 How to extend this report

The report is generated. To add a game, mechanic, technique, or opportunity, follow `AGENTS.md`; tables, counts, figures, rankings, and this section's prediction list update on the next build. To change an argument, edit the prose in `report/src/`; every dataset number in it is a token, so the text cannot fall out of date with the data.

## Appendix D. Using and extending this dataset

- **Cite** a specific version by the `dataset_sha256` in `dist/manifest.json` (also printed on this report's title page).
- **Query** with the CSVs in `dist/tables/`, the graph files in `dist/graph/` (JSON Lines, Cytoscape, GraphML), or `make sqlite` for SQL.
- **Browse** the wiki at `dist/wiki/index.md` or the explorer at `site/index.html`.
- **Contribute** by following `AGENTS.md`: open a run, search before creating, fill entities against the schema, run `make check`. The fastest useful contribution is sourcing an entity from `dist/analysis/verification-queue.csv`.
- **Dispute** a fact by setting `status: contested` with a claim that cites the opposing source; disputes are data, not edits.

levels.3: Notable change in cost or variety.

ai_leverage.question: Expert judgment of how much 2024-2026 AI techniques could change this mechanic's design ceiling (cross-checked by `affects` edges in analysis).

levels.5: Content cost is the main limit on the mechanic's depth.

authoring_cost.question: Developer cost of the content this mechanic consumes (animations, writing, assets, tuning data), per unit of player-facing variety.

levels.2: Low; scales linearly with modest constants.
levels.3: Noticeable; a common source of late-game slowdown.
levels.5: Requires specialized hardware or approximation to run at all.

compute_cost.question: Runtime compute at the scale the mechanic is typically used.

levels.1: Outcomes follow authored scripts or a single equation; replays look the same.
levels.2: A few interacting systems; variety comes mainly from parameters or content.
levels.3: Several coupled systems produce situations designers did not script; players tell stories about runs.
levels.4: Many coupled systems; surprising chains are routine and drive community discussion.
levels.5: Emergence is the product; players report histories no one could have authored (Dwarf Fortress tier).

emergence.question: How much of play arises from system interaction rather than authored content?

levels.1: Deterministic and isolated; same input, same visible result.
levels.3: Interacts with other systems to produce unplanned situations.
levels.4: Frequently produces chains of consequences across systems.
levels.5: A primary engine of emergent stories wherever it appears.

emergence_potential.question: How much unscripted variety does this mechanic generate when coupled with others?

levels.4: Feasible with known techniques and normal risk.

feasibility.question: Can a small team (5-15) ship it within 24 months using techniques at their current maturity?

levels.4: Enables a new subgenre or a large new audience.

impact.question: If it works, how much does it change player experience or the market?

levels.2: Influenced a niche or a few titles.
levels.5: Created a lineage or changed the medium (SimCity, The Sims, Dwarf Fortress tier).

influence.question: How strongly did this game shape later simulation design?

levels.1: Opaque; most players misunderstand causes even after many hours.
levels.2: Understood only through wikis or community analysis.
levels.3: Understood after deliberate attention and the game's info tools.

legibility.question: How easily can a typical player form an accurate mental model of the mechanic from play?

levels.1: Incremental polish of an existing pattern.
levels.4: No shipped precedent; adjacent research exists.

novelty.question: How far from shipped practice is this?

levels.4: Lab demo in a game-like environment.
levels.6: Public playable demo or tech preview.
levels.7: Shipped in a commercial game as a minor feature.
levels.8: Shipped as a core feature of a commercial game.
levels.9: Standard practice across multiple shipped titles.

trl.question: Technology Readiness Level for use in simulation games (NASA scale adapted).

levels.4: Sensitive; small changes cause runaway loops or dominant strategies.
levels.5: Chaotic; balance is effectively never settled.

tuning_difficulty.question: How hard is it to balance so the mechanic is neither trivial nor degenerate?
